Q1:
## Introduction

Keyword discipline: the measures are the differentiator here. Q.195 asked only for causes; devote at least half of this answer to what the government has actually done, and assess whether it worked.

Regional disparity in Andhra Pradesh follows a cumulative sequence — natural endowment determined where irrigation was feasible, colonial investment built it in the deltas, the Green Revolution rewarded it, and industry, credit and human capital followed the resulting prosperity. Reversing such a sequence requires deliberate counter-agglomeration, since market forces alone reinforce it.

- The causes — in brief
- **Natural** — Rayalaseema’s 500-700 mm rainfall against high evapotranspiration; Deccan and Eastern Ghats topography preventing gravity irrigation; fertile deltaic alluvium against red and shallow soils
- **Historical** — Cotton’s Dowleswaram anicut (1852) and the Krishna anicut gave the deltas a 170-year head start; the Green Revolution amplified it because the HYV package required assured water
- **Economic** — Industrial and urban concentration around Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Tirupati; connectivity following the coast; credit flowing to where repayment is assured; agglomeration economies making disparity self-reinforcing
- **Social** — AP’s literacy of 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24), the lowest among Indian States, concentrated in the lagging districts; landlessness among SCs; PVTG concentration in the agency areas
- **Institutional** — Unrecorded tenancy excluding cultivators from credit; the unsettled Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II allocation; long gestation of lift irrigation; bifurcation (2014) removing Hyderabad as the State’s services engine

- Measures initiated by the government
- Irrigation — the primary instrument
- **Handri Neeva Sujala Sravanthi** — 40 TMC of Srisailam flood water through a 565-km canal, lifted over 369 metres in 12-13 stages with eight balancing reservoirs; about 6.02 lakh acres and drinking water for nearly 33 lakh people across 81 drought-prone mandals
- **Galeru-Nagari Sujala Sravanthi** — Krishna flood water to Kadapa, Annamayya and Chittoor
- **Poola Subbaiah Veligonda** — 43.50 TMC from Kollam Vagu upstream of Srisailam, by gravity through twin tunnels into Nallamala Sagar
- **Polavaram** — The anchor Godavari project — a national project under Section 90 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014; targeted completion by 2027
- **Polavaram-Banakacherla link (proposed)** — About ₹80,112 crore to divert 200 TMC of Godavari flood water, interlinking Godavari-Krishna-Penna, serving around 80 lakh people; SPV “Jala Harathi Corporation”; contested by Telangana
- **Micro-irrigation** — PMKSY “Per Drop More Crop”; AP among India’s leaders in drip and sprinkler coverage
- **Rayalaseema Drought Mitigation Project and watershed programmes** — Demand-side and rainfed area development

- Industrial dispersal
- Industrial nodes deliberately located inland: Orvakal (Kurnool) with a semiconductor facility and Drone City; Kopparthy (Kadapa); alongside coastal Krishnapatnam.
- 175 MSME parks — one in every assembly constituency under the AP MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29) — the most explicit dispersal instrument the State has adopted.
- AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29): ₹30 lakh crore investment target, US$10 billion FDI, 5 lakh jobs, 175 industrial parks.
- Marquee projects spread across regions: Integrated Steel Plant (Anakapalli), Bulk Drug Park (Nakkapalli), Green Aluminium (Kakinada), Amaravati Quantum Valley, and Google’s US$15 billion AI data centre at Visakhapatnam.
- Infrastructure and connectivity
- Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC) — ADB-supported, part of the East Coast Economic Corridor, India’s first coastal economic corridor.
- New ports at Ramayapatnam (75%), Mulapeta (65%) and Machilipatnam (50%).
- Alluri Sitaramaraju International Airport, Bhogapuram — 97% complete.
- Rural connectivity under PMGSY; AP Logistics Corporation created after the Reimagining Public Finance Summit.
- Targeted area and community programmes
- Special Development Package under the AP Reorganisation Act — ₹50 crore per district per year for five years for seven backward districts (four in Rayalaseema, three in North Coastal Andhra), on the Bundelkhand/KBK model.
- PM JANMAN for PVTGs — 192 new Anganwadi centres sanctioned in PVTG areas.
- Aspirational Districts and Blocks Programmes (NITI Aayog) with real-time indicator dashboards.
- Fifth Schedule protections, PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 in Scheduled Areas.
- Human capital
- School Education ₹32,308 crore in Budget 2026-27, with ₹1,500 crore for infrastructure overhaul; Mega DSC-2025 filled 15,941 teacher posts.
- Thalliki Vandanam — ₹15,000 a year per child, reaching 67.27 lakh students.
- Health ₹19,306 crore; Project Sanjeevani preventive screening; 9,958 Anganwadi Centres upgraded.
- Government ITIs with MoUs with 167 industry partners and 98% placement or apprenticeship.
- Income support and livelihood
- NTR Bharosa pensions — ₹4,000-₹15,000 by DBT, over ₹58,000 crore in 19 months.
- Annadata Sukhibhava — ₹20,000 a year, covering tenant farmers.
- Deepam 2.0 — three free LPG cylinders a year to 1.08 crore women, ₹2,897 crore credited.
- SERP’s SHG network — about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, repayment above 97%.
- APCNF — over 17.7 lakh farmers, with verified income gains of 38-66% and water savings up to 50% — particularly valuable in rain-fed Rayalaseema.
- Administrative and fiscal measures
- Reorganisation into 26 districts (4 April 2022) to improve governance reach in backward areas.
- SC component ₹20,644 crore, ST component ₹9,190 crore, BC ₹51,021 crore in Budget 2026-27.
- 16th Finance Commission grants — RLB basic ₹13,302 crore, ULB basic ₹9,727 crore, disaster management ₹6,125 crore for 2026-31.
- Examining effectiveness — an honest assessment
- **Irrigation** — Partially effective. HNSS and Veligonda have genuinely reduced Rayalaseema’s vulnerability, but distributaries and lining remain incomplete, so created potential exceeds utilised potential; lift energy costs impose a recurring subsidy burden
- **Industrial dispersal** — Promising but unproven. Nodes at Orvakal and Kopparthy and the 175 MSME parks are correctly located, but MoUs must become payrolls — execution on land, power and clearances is the test
- **Service saturation** — Highly effective, but a one-time gain. Housing, electricity, LPG, sanitation and bank accounts lifted the poorest regions fastest — which is why AP’s MPI halved. These gains cannot be repeated
- **Income transfers** — Effective as a floor, limited as a ladder. They prevent destitution; they do not raise productivity
- **Human capital** — The weakest link and the binding constraint. Literacy remains the lowest in India at 72.6%, and no region can move up the value chain faster than its education allows
- **Special packages** — Under-delivered. The Reorganisation Act’s backward-district package was largely released, but the Section 46(2) resource-gap grant delivered only about ₹3,980 crore against an assessed ₹22,113 crore

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh has deployed a comprehensive and correctly targeted set of instruments — lift irrigation for Rayalaseema, industrial nodes and MSME parks inland, targeted tribal programmes, and income floors through DBT. The measures have narrowed the gap in living standards substantially, which is why the State’s multidimensional poverty halved. They have not yet narrowed the gap in productivity and employment, because that depends on the two things hardest to deliver: completed irrigation with functioning distributaries, and an educated workforce. Closing the remaining disparity is therefore less a question of new schemes than of execution and literacy.

## Value addition
- Committee reference: the Srikrishna Committee (2010) remains the standard analytical source on regional development indicators across united Andhra Pradesh.
- Statutory basis of the backward-district package: AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 — special assistance for seven backward districts at ₹50 crore per district per year for five years, on the Bundelkhand and KBK models.
- The dispersal instrument: 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency, under AP MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0.
- Theoretical framing: Myrdal’s cumulative causation and Hirschman’s polarisation effects explain why disparity persists; deliberate counter-agglomeration is the policy answer.
Q2:
## Introduction

Keyword discipline: this question concerns united Andhra Pradesh, so Telangana must be discussed alongside Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra. Answers confined to the residuary State miss a third of the question.

Backwardness means persistent deficiency across socio-economic indicators — per capita income, irrigation coverage, literacy, health, industrialisation and infrastructure — relative to the State average. In united Andhra Pradesh (1956-2014), three regions were identified as backward: Rayalaseema, North Coastal Andhra, and much of Telangana outside Hyderabad. The State’s inability to address this imbalance was the proximate cause of its bifurcation, which makes the question historically consequential.

The three backward regions and their character

- **Rayalaseema** — Semi-arid, groundwater-dependent, chronic drought, lowest canal irrigation; groundnut monoculture; out-migration
- **North Coastal Andhra (Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, and the agency areas)** — Rainfed and shifting cultivation, forest dependence, hilly tribal terrain, lowest literacy and health indicators
- **Telangana (excluding Hyderabad)** — Declining tank irrigation, borewell dependence, feudal agrarian legacy, low industrialisation outside Hyderabad — the region’s grievance was that Hyderabad’s prosperity masked the backwardness of the districts around it

Causes of backwardness

## Natural and agro-climatic
- Rainfall deficiency — Rayalaseema at 500-700 mm; Telangana’s districts largely rain-shadow.
- Topography — the Deccan plateau and Eastern Ghats prevent gravity irrigation; water must be lifted.
- Soil — red, shallow and lateritic soils against fertile deltaic alluvium.
- Declining traditional irrigation — Telangana’s extensive tank systems silted and decayed, replaced by unsustainable borewell extraction.
- Historical and institutional — the causes specific to Telangana
- The Nizam’s land system. Roughly 40% of Hyderabad State’s land was held as jagirs and sarf-e-khas outside normal revenue administration; deshmukhs and doras held vast estates; vetti — hereditary bonded labour — bound cultivators to landlords. This suppressed accumulation, investment and literacy for generations.
- Educational deprivation. Under the Nizam, the medium of instruction was Urdu and school provision was thin, so Telangana entered the union with far lower literacy than the Andhra area — a deficit that compounded across generations.
- The Gentlemen’s Agreement (1956) and its breach. The safeguards agreed at the formation of Andhra Pradesh — the Mulki rules on employment, proportionate budgetary allocation, and a Regional Committee — were widely held to have been diluted, producing the 1969 Telangana agitation, the Six-Point Formula (1973) and Article 371-D (with the AP Administrative Tribunal) as remedies.
- Perceived diversion of resources, particularly of Krishna and Godavari waters and of budgetary surpluses, from Telangana to the Andhra deltas.
- Causes shared across the backward regions
- Colonial irrigation investment favoured the deltas — Cotton’s Dowleswaram anicut (1852) and the Krishna anicut gave Coastal Andhra a head start of more than a century.
- The Green Revolution amplified the gap, because the HYV package required assured irrigation.
- Industrial concentration in Hyderabad and the coastal belt, drawing investment, talent and infrastructure.
- Agglomeration economies made disparity self-reinforcing — investment followed investment.
- Low human capital, limiting occupational mobility.
- Landlessness and unrecorded tenancy excluding cultivators from credit.

The political consequence

The failure to resolve this imbalance produced the 1969 Telangana agitation, the 1972 Jai Andhra movement, the Six-Point Formula (1973), Article 371-D, the Srikrishna Committee (2010), and ultimately the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 and the creation of Telangana on 2 June 2014. Regional backwardness in India is not merely an economic problem — unaddressed, it becomes a constitutional one.

Suggested measures for development

- Water — the first-order intervention Complete lift irrigation for the rain-fed regions — HNSS (40 TMC, 565-km canal, 6.02 lakh acres and drinking water for 33 lakh people), Galeru-Nagari, Veligonda (43.50 TMC) — and

finish Polavaram (targeted 2027). Restore tank systems rather than relying only on new canals. Reduce lift energy costs through solar pumping. Resolve the Krishna allocation before the Tribunal so schemes have assured water rather than contested surplus.

- Demand-side water management APCNF achieves water savings of up to 50% and income gains of 38-66% across 0.92 million hectares — the most cost-effective intervention available for rain-fed regions, since it needs no new infrastructure.
- Deliberate industrial dispersal Locate industry where it would not go unaided — Orvakal and Kopparthy nodes, Drone City at Orvakal, and 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency. Back it with land, assured power, water and single-window clearance, since a park without utilities is only a map.
- Human capital — the binding constraint AP’s literacy of 72.6% is the lowest among Indian States. Scale ULLAS for adult literacy and NIPUN Bharat for foundational learning, with a focus on girls and the lagging districts. Link skilling to industry as the ITI model does — 167 industry MoUs, 98% placement. Enforce the prohibition of child marriage, at 29.3% above the national average.
- Agricultural diversification suited to dryland Millets (Shree Anna), horticulture, oil palm under NMEO, livestock and small ruminants — activities that generate income on low rainfall, unlike paddy.
- Agro-processing at source Food processing grew 7.3% annually (2015-2022); locating primary processing in the backward regions retains value where the produce is grown.
- Connectivity and logistics Roads, rail, cold chain and warehousing in interior districts; the AP Logistics Corporation and UIDF funding.
- Targeted area and community development Continue the Special Development Package (₹50 crore per district per year for seven backward districts), PM JANMAN for PVTGs, and the Aspirational Districts and Blocks dashboards.
- Institutional and governance measures Statutory or administrative regional development boards with earmarked funds and audited outcomes; decentralised planning through the 26-district structure; Article 371-D-type employment safeguards where warranted.
- Fiscal earmarking with accountability Region-wise budget disclosure and outcome audit — since the Telangana grievance was fundamentally about unverifiable allocation, transparency is itself a remedy.

## Conclusion

Backwardness in united Andhra Pradesh arose from agro-climatic disadvantage compounded by a century of unequal irrigation investment, and — in Telangana’s case — by a feudal land system and educational deprivation under the Nizam that no post-1956 policy fully corrected. Its unaddressed persistence, and the perception that constitutional safeguards had been breached, led ultimately to bifurcation. The lesson for the residuary State is direct: regional imbalance must be measured, budgeted for transparently, and corrected through irrigation, education and deliberately located industry — because an imbalance left to market forces does not narrow, and an imbalance left unacknowledged does not remain merely economic.

## Value addition
- Constitutional and institutional milestones: the Gentlemen’s Agreement (1956), Mulki rules, the 1969 Telangana agitation, the 1972 Jai Andhra movement, the Six-Point Formula (1973), Article 371-D with the AP Administrative Tribunal, and the Srikrishna Committee (2010).
- The Nizam-era structure: about 40% of Hyderabad State’s land as jagirs and sarf-e-khas; 6,500 jagirs abolished by the Hyderabad Abolition of Jagirs Regulation, 1949; vetti bonded labour ended in law.
- The peasant movement: the Telangana Armed Struggle (1946-51) spanned some 3,000 villages and redistributed about a million acres before suppression after Operation Polo (September 1948).
- Theoretical framing: Myrdal’s cumulative causation, Hirschman’s polarisation effects, and Williamson’s inverted-U hypothesis on regional convergence.
Q3:
## Introduction

Land reform in Andhra Pradesh has four classic components and a fifth modern one. The fifth — modernisation of land records — has become the most consequential, because the failures of the first four (unrecorded tenancy, assigned land without demarcation, tribal land alienation) all trace back to defective records.

Part A: The scope of land reforms in Andhra Pradesh

- **Abolition of intermediaries** — Zamindari (1948), jagirdari (1949, about 6,500 jagirs), inams (1955-56)
- **Tenancy regulation** — AP (Telangana Area) Act, 1950 — protected tenants and purchase rights; AP (Andhra Area) Act, 1956 — fair rent and tenure without ownership
- **Ceiling on holdings** — AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, with surplus for redistribution
- **Assignment and protection** — Assignment of government land to the landless; AP Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act, 1977; Regulation 1 of 70 for Scheduled Areas
- **Recognition of cultivators** — Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011 and Crop Cultivator Rights Act, 2019
- **Records modernisation** — The subject of Part B

Not attempted: consolidation of holdings — undertaken in Punjab, Haryana and western UP but not in AP, which is a principal reason for the State’s severe fragmentation.

Part B: Assessing computerisation of land records The systems in place

- **CARD (Computer-Aided Registration of Documents), 1998** — AP was a national pioneer — computerised document registration, valuation and encumbrance certificates, cutting registration time from weeks to hours
- **Webland** — The State’s back-end land records database, holding the Record of Rights
- **Meebhoomi (meebhoomi.ap.gov.in)** — The public-facing portal providing Adangal (crop and possession particulars) and 1-B (ownership/title), FMB cadastral maps and digitally signed e-passbooks with QR codes, searchable by survey number, khata number, Aadhaar or pattadar name
- **MeeSeva centres** — Delivery of certified copies and mutation services
- **DILRMP (central)** — Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme — record computerisation, survey and settlement, registration integration
- **ULPIN / Bhu-Aadhaar** — A 14-digit unique land parcel identifier based on longitude and latitude, assigned parcel by parcel
- **Resurvey programme** — A comprehensive land resurvey using drones and GNSS rovers — the first in about a century — refreshing cadastral maps and tagging parcels with ULPIN
- **NGDRS / e-Panjeeyan** — Registration integrated with the revenue record so that a sale triggers auto-mutation

Achievements — the case for success

- Access transformed. A farmer can view Adangal and 1-B records online free of charge, and download a digitally signed e-passbook with a QR code — eliminating dependence on the village revenue officer for basic information. This alone removed a major source of petty rent-seeking.
- Registration modernised. CARD (1998) made Andhra Pradesh one of India’s earliest States to computerise registration, reducing time, discretion and undervaluation.
- Auto-mutation. Integration of registration with the revenue record means a registered sale updates the Record of Rights automatically, closing the historical gap between the deed and the record.
- Spatial accuracy. Drone and GNSS resurvey with ULPIN tagging links each parcel to geo-coordinates rather than to a colonial-era survey number — the first genuine correction of the cadastre in a century.
- A significant procedural reform. The 2025 revenue framework introduced “notional subdivision”: previously a dispute over a small portion locked the entire survey number; now only the disputed portion enters the dispute register, leaving the rest free for transactions. This is a substantial practical gain for farmers whose land was frozen by a neighbour’s litigation.
- Transparency for credit. Digitally signed records are accepted by banks and registrars, easing crop loan and mortgage processing.

Limitations — the case against

- The records remain presumptive, not conclusive. This is the fundamental limitation. Meebhoomi is a revenue record, not a title guarantee. A clean 1-B does not show registered deeds, encumbrances or mortgages, pending litigation, or actual possession on the ground. It is strong supporting evidence, not marketable title.
- The conclusive titling attempt failed politically. The AP Land Titling Act, 2022 — modelled on NITI Aayog’s draft — sought to establish conclusive, State-guaranteed titles with a Title Registration Officer and restricted civil court jurisdiction. It became a major issue in the May 2024 elections and was repealed by the AP Land Titling (Repeal) Act, 2024 (Act 11 of 2024). Conclusive titling therefore remains unachieved, and the episode illustrates that titling reform is politically as difficult as land reform itself.
- Digitisation does not resolve ownership. Computerising a defective record produces an accurate copy of an inaccurate document. Where the underlying entry is wrong — as with land “assigned on paper, physical location not shown,” which the Koneru Ranga Rao Committee identified as the commonest defect — digitisation preserves the error.
- Tenancy remains invisible. Records show the pattadar, not the cultivator. Since AP has among India’s highest tenancy incidence, almost entirely oral, the digitised record systematically excludes the person actually farming.
- Textual and spatial records are not fully reconciled. Resurvey is incomplete, so many parcels still carry survey numbers that do not match ground reality.
- Digital divide. Elderly, illiterate and tribal landholders cannot use the portal, and continue to depend on intermediaries.
- Litigation persists. Land disputes remain a large share of civil litigation, because the record does not settle title.

The verdict

Computerisation in Andhra Pradesh has been highly successful at improving access, speed and transparency, and genuinely innovative in the drone resurvey, ULPIN tagging and notional subdivision. It has not achieved its ultimate purpose, which is to make land ownership certain — because India’s system remains presumptive, and the one attempt to make it conclusive was repealed.

## Conclusion

The scope of land reform in Andhra Pradesh has widened from redistributing land to recording it accurately — a recognition that unclear title now blocks credit, investment and dispute resolution more than concentration of ownership does. Computerisation has delivered impressive access and process gains, but the decisive step — conclusive, State-guaranteed titling — remains unfinished after the 2024 repeal. Completing the resurvey, reconciling textual with spatial records, and building the political consensus for conclusive titling is the land reform agenda for the coming decade.

## Value addition
- Presumptive vs conclusive titling: in India a registered deed records a transaction, not guaranteed ownership

— the State does not warrant title. Conclusive titling (the Torrens system) makes the State the guarantor, with an indemnity fund for wrongful entries.

- The national push: DILRMP (2008, restructured 2016); Union Budget 2024-25 offered incentives to States completing land reforms within three years, including ULPIN/Bhu-Aadhaar assignment to all parcels.
- Comparative note: Telangana replaced its Dharani portal with the Bhu Bharati (Record of Rights) Act, 2024, also introducing Bhu-Aadhaar — the two Telugu States have taken different routes to the same problem.
- AP’s pioneering record: CARD (1998) for registration and e-Seva for citizen services were among India’s earliest e-governance successes, and were cited in the State’s fiscal turnaround of 1997-2005.
Q4:
## Introduction

Agricultural price administration is State intervention to influence the prices farmers receive and consumers pay. It is necessary because agricultural markets exhibit structural failures absent from most other markets — and because the same price is simultaneously a farmer’s income and a consumer’s cost of living.

- The need for administering agricultural commodity prices
- The cobweb phenomenon — the classic case for intervention Farmers decide what to sow months before they sell, using last season’s price as their guide. High prices this year prompt over-sowing next year, causing a crash; the crash prompts under-sowing, causing a spike. Prices therefore oscillate rather than settle. Only an assured floor announced before sowing can break this cycle.
- Inelastic supply and demand Once sown, output cannot be adjusted; and demand for staples barely responds to price. So a small change in output produces a large change in price — the source of agriculture’s extreme volatility.
- Perishability and no holding capacity Most farmers lack storage and must sell immediately after harvest — precisely when supply peaks and prices are lowest. This is the distress sale that price support exists to prevent.
- Asymmetric bargaining power Millions of small, dispersed sellers face a few organised traders. Without a floor price, the buyer sets the terms — especially where the trader is also the lender.
- Investment incentive Farmers will adopt costly input-intensive technology only if returns are predictable. Assured procurement at an assured price was what made the Green Revolution viable.
- Food security — the consumer side The State must also ensure affordable staples. India’s NFSA, 2013 covers about

80.67 crore persons, and PMGKAY has been extended to 31 December 2028 — obligations that require a public stock, which in turn requires procurement.

- Buffer stocks and price stabilisation Stocks must be built in surplus years to release in deficit years, moderating both producer and consumer price swings.
- Terms of trade Left to itself, the relative price of agriculture tends to decline against manufactures. Administered prices correct this drift, protecting the farm sector’s share of national income.
- Steering cropping patterns Price signals can be used deliberately — for instance, to raise pulse and oilseed production, given that India imports 56% of its edible oil.
- The administering machinery At the Centre
- **Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)** — The recommending body — advises MSP for 22 mandated crops plus toria and de-husked coconut, considering cost of production, demand and supply, price trends, terms of trade and the effect on consumers
- **Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA)** — The deciding authority, after consulting State governments. Kharif MSP for 2026-27 was approved on 13 May 2026 — common paddy ₹2,441 per quintal, tur ₹8,450, sunflower seed ₹8,343; estimated payout about ₹2.60 lakh crore for over 824 lakh metric tonnes
- **Food Corporation of India (FCI)** — Procurement, storage, movement and distribution of rice and wheat; buffer stock management
- **NAFED, NCCF, SFAC** — Procurement of pulses and oilseeds under the Price Support Scheme
- **Cotton Corporation of India, Jute Corporation of India** — Price support in fibres
- **PM-AASHA (2018)** — Three components — Price Support Scheme (PSS), Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS) and the Private Procurement and Stockist Scheme (PPSS)
- **Department of Food and Public Distribution** — Issue prices, PDS allocation and buffer norms
- **Essential Commodities Act, 1955** — Stock limits and anti-hoarding controls
- **Directorate of Marketing and Inspection / AGMARKNET** — Market intelligence, grading (Agmark) and price dissemination
- **Price Stabilisation Fund** — Market intervention in onion, potato and pulses
- **Trade instruments** — Export and import duties, quotas and minimum export prices — used to influence domestic prices
- **Tobacco Board, Coffee/Tea/Rubber/Spices Boards** — Commodity-specific price and quality regulation

At the State level (Andhra Pradesh)

- **AP State Civil Supplies Corporation (APSCSCL)** — Procures paddy, mills it and delivers to FCI and the State PDS; AP is a decentralised procurement State
- **Rythu Bharosa Kendras** — Village-level procurement points with e-crop booking establishing eligibility and direct e-payment into farmer accounts — nationally cited best practice
- **Agricultural Market Committees (APMCs)** — Regulated markets where the first sale occurs by open auction, with market fees funding infrastructure
- **AP Marketing Department and Rythu Bazaars** — Direct producer-consumer sale; Digi Rythu Bazaar launched in Visakhapatnam in December 2025
- **Market intervention and bonus** — State bonus over MSP for paddy at times, and price support for crops outside the central ambit — chillies, tobacco, maize, redgram, groundnut
- **Price stabilisation interventions** — In perishables, through market purchase and buffer operations

- The instruments in brief

## Minimum Support Price — the announced floor;

## Procurement price — the price at which the government actually buys;

## Issue price — the subsidised PDS price;
- Deficiency payment — paying the gap between MSP and the actual sale price, without handling the commodity;

## Buffer stocking and open market sale — quantity-side intervention;
- Trade policy — duties and quotas.

## Conclusion

Agricultural prices require administration because farming faces market failures no other sector combines: production decisions taken months before sale, inelastic supply and demand, perishability, no holding capacity, and grossly unequal bargaining power. The machinery is elaborate — CACP recommends, the CCEA decides, FCI and NAFED procure, and States such as Andhra Pradesh deliver through APSCSCL and Rythu Bharosa Kendras. The continuing challenge is that price administration reaches a minority of farmers and crops, and reform therefore lies in deficiency payments, warehouse receipt finance and direct income support — instruments that stabilise income without requiring the State to buy and store the crop.

## Value addition
- The cobweb theorem — the formal explanation of agricultural price oscillation, and the strongest theoretical justification for an announced floor price.
- Cost concepts: A2 (paid-out costs), A2+FL (plus imputed family labour — the basis used), C2 (plus imputed rent and interest on own capital). Government uses A2+FL + 50%; the Swaminathan Commission recommended C2 + 50%.
- Committee reference: the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) recommended decentralised procurement, deficiency payments and cash transfers in cities.
- AP’s delivery innovation: procurement through RBKs with e-crop booking and direct e-payment — resolving both verification and intermediation, the two classic leakages in procurement.
Q5:
## Introduction

Keyword discipline: the second half demands an inventory of statutes. Name the Acts with their years — a list of principles without legislation will not score.

Land reform means the restructuring of rights in agricultural land to achieve equity and productivity together. Land is a State subject (Entry 18, List II), so each State enacted its own laws; Andhra Pradesh’s are further complicated by its dual colonial inheritance — the ryotwari Andhra area of the Madras Presidency and the jagirdari Telangana area of the Nizam’s Hyderabad — which is why the State has never had a single land reform code.

Part A: Why land reforms are implemented

- Social justice and equity Land ownership at independence was extremely concentrated, and landlessness coincided with caste disadvantage. Redistribution was therefore an instrument of social justice, not merely of income transfer.
- Abolition of feudal and intermediary tenures Zamindars, jagirdars and inamdars extracted rent without cultivating. In the Telangana region this extended to vetti — hereditary bonded labour — making reform a question of personal freedom.
- “Land to the tiller” Separating ownership from cultivation destroys the incentive to invest: the owner does not farm, and the tenant-at-will can be evicted before recovering an improvement.
- Productivity — the inverse size-productivity relationship Empirical evidence suggests small owner-cultivated farms achieve higher output per hectare than large ones, because family labour is applied more intensively at no supervision cost. Redistribution therefore promised efficiency as well as equity.
- Employment Owner-cultivated small farms absorb more labour per hectare — significant in a labour-surplus economy.
- Political stability The Telangana Armed Struggle (1946-51), spanning some 3,000 villages and redistributing about a million acres, demonstrated the alternative to reform.
- Constitutional mandate - Article 39(b) — material resources to be distributed to subserve the common good; - Article 39(c) — prevention of concentration of wealth; - Land reform laws were placed in the Ninth Schedule under Article 31B to immunise them from judicial challenge.

Part B: The main land reform laws of Andhra Pradesh Stage 1 — Abolition of intermediaries

- **AP (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948** — Abolished zamindari in the Andhra region and converted estates to ryotwari tenure
- **Hyderabad Abolition of Jagirs Regulation, 1949, with the Jagirs Commutation Regulation** — Abolished about 6,500 jagirs in the Telangana region and brought them under State administration
- **AP (Telangana Area) Abolition of Inams Act, 1955 and the AP (Andhra Area) Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956** — Abolished rent-free and concessional grants

Stage 2 — Tenancy regulation

- **AP (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950** — Conferred protected-tenant status, regulated rent, gave the right to purchase, restricted resumption
- **AP (Andhra Area) Tenancy Act, 1956, amended notably in 1974** — Minimum lease period (extended to six years in 1974), fair rent as a share of produce, eviction only through revenue authorities, compensation for improvements, first option to purchase, bar on sub-letting

Stage 3 — Ceiling on holdings

- **AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973** — Family-based ceilings graded by irrigation and cropping intensity; surplus land to be acquired and redistributed to the landless

Stage 4 — Protection of assigned and tribal land

- **AP Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act, 1977** — Bars sale or transfer of government land assigned to the landless poor, and provides for resumption and re-assignment
- **AP Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation, 1959 — “Regulation 1 of 70”** — Bars transfer of land to non-tribals in Scheduled Areas; reinforced by Samatha v. State of AP (1997), which held that even government land in Scheduled Areas cannot be leased to private mining companies
- **Forest Rights Act, 2006 (central)** — Recognises individual and community forest rights of Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers

Stage 5 — Recognition of the cultivator (the modern phase)

- **AP Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011** — Loan Eligibility Cards valid eleven months, conferring no right, title or interest, enabling tenants to access crop loans, insurance and subsidy. Enacted on the recommendation of the Koneru Ranga Rao Land Committee (2006)
- **AP Crop Cultivator Rights Act, 2019** — Replaced LECs with Crop Cultivator Rights Cards, with owner consent and clearer scheme integration

Stage 6 — Titling and records

- **AP Rights in Land and Pattadar Pass Books Act, 1971** — Governs the Record of Rights and issue of pattadar passbooks
- **AP Land Titling Act, 2022** — Sought to move from presumptive to conclusive titling, on NITI Aayog’s model law — repealed by the AP Land Titling (Repeal) Act, 2024

Also relevant - AP Agricultural Land (Conversion for Non-Agricultural Purposes) Act, 2006; - The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (central).

## Conclusion

Land reforms are implemented to end feudal extraction, match ownership to cultivation, deliver social justice and raise productivity. Andhra Pradesh’s legislative record is comprehensive on paper across all four classic stages — abolition, tenancy, ceilings and protection of assigned and tribal land — and has since added a fifth stage of functional recognition through the 2011 and 2019 Acts. The gap has always been between statute and implementation: abolition succeeded, ceilings barely, and tenancy regulation actively drove leasing underground.

## Value addition
- The four classic stages of Indian land reform: abolition of intermediaries → tenancy reform → ceiling on holdings → consolidation of holdings. The fourth was undertaken in Punjab, Haryana and western UP but not in Andhra Pradesh — a principal reason for the State’s severe fragmentation.
- Committee lineage: J.C. Kumarappa Committee (1949) on agrarian reform; Barucha Committee (1937) under the Nizam; Koneru Ranga Rao Land Committee (2004-06) — 104 recommendations, about 90 accepted.
- Judicial anchors: Samatha v. State of AP (1997); Vemula Bhaskara Rao v. State of AP (2008) on the inadmissibility of unregistered deeds for non-tribals in Scheduled Areas.
- The current reform proposal: the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016 (NITI Aayog) — legalise leasing, protect the owner’s title, give the tenant credit access.

## Introduction

The Green Revolution was the introduction, from the mid-1960s, of a package of technology and supporting policy

— high-yielding variety seeds, assured irrigation, chemical fertiliser, pesticides, mechanisation, institutional credit and price support — that transformed India from a food-deficit importer into a self-sufficient producer. In Andhra Pradesh it took hold most powerfully in the Krishna and Godavari deltas, which had the one prerequisite the technology demanded: assured water.

The components of the package

- **HYV seeds** — Dwarf, fertiliser-responsive wheat (Norman Borlaug) and rice (IR-8, from IRRI); M.S. Swaminathan led the Indian adaptation
- **Assured irrigation** — Canal systems and tube wells — the technology fails without controlled water
- **Chemical fertiliser** — Nitrogen-responsive varieties required heavy NPK application
- **Plant protection** — Pesticides against the pest pressure that monoculture invites
- **Mechanisation** — Tractors, pump sets, threshers
- **Institutional support** — Cooperative and bank credit, Minimum Support Price, FCI procurement, agricultural universities and extension

Impact on Andhra Pradesh — the positive

- Rice productivity and surplus The Krishna-Godavari delta became one of India’s most productive rice tracts. Andhra Pradesh emerged as a major rice surplus State, earning the description “Rice Bowl of India” — and this surplus is what makes the State’s own PDS, covering about 1.46 crore rice cards and 4.3 crore beneficiaries, fiscally possible.
- Food security and price stability Reliable procurement stabilised supply and prices, and underwrote the State’s food subsidy programmes from the ₹2-a-kg rice scheme of 1983 onward.
- Rural incomes and employment Higher yields raised incomes for landowning farmers in the deltas, and double-cropping increased demand for agricultural labour, raising wages.
- Growth of allied industries Rice mills, fertiliser and pesticide distribution, farm machinery, transport and warehousing expanded — the beginnings of AP’s agro-industrial base.
- Institutional development Acharya N.G. Ranga Agricultural University, research stations, extension services and cooperative credit networks were built around the package.
- Foundation for later diversification The irrigation and market infrastructure created for rice later enabled the shift to aquaculture, horticulture and oil palm — the Green Revolution built the platform on which AP’s high-value agriculture now stands.

Impact — the negative

- Regional inequality — the most consequential effect The technology required assured irrigation, which existed in the deltas and not elsewhere. Coastal Andhra prospered; Rayalaseema and the tribal agency areas of North Coastal Andhra were largely bypassed. The Green Revolution therefore widened intra-State disparity, and this remains the principal explanation for AP’s regional imbalance.
- Inequality among farmers The package was input-intensive and capital-intensive. Large and medium farmers with irrigation, credit access and land title captured most of the gain; small, marginal and tenant cultivators — who

could not afford inputs or obtain credit — benefited far less. Land values rose, making entry harder still.

- Ecological costs - Groundwater depletion, particularly in Rayalaseema, aggravated by free or subsidised farm power
- AP budgets about ₹11,000 crore in agricultural power subsidy for 22.5 lakh farmers. - Soil degradation and declining organic carbon from continuous rice monoculture. - Skewed nutrient use — India’s N:P:K ratio far exceeds the recommended 4:2:1 because of the urea subsidy. - Pesticide resistance and residue, severe in cotton and chillies
- the problem that Non-Pesticide Management, pioneered in Andhra Pradesh, was created to address.
- Monoculture and loss of diversity Millets, pulses and traditional varieties were displaced by paddy, narrowing both the cropping system and the diet — an important cause of the nutritional deficits still visible in the State.
- Rising cost of cultivation and indebtedness Dependence on purchased inputs raised costs faster than output prices in many years, contributing to farmer indebtedness — the condition that agriculture’s GNPA of 6.0%, the highest of any sector, still reflects.

The transition since

Andhra Pradesh’s response to these costs has been more radical than most States’: - APCNF (Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming) — the world’s largest agroecology programme, covering over 17.7 lakh farmers across 0.92 million hectares, with verified income gains of 38-66%, water savings up to 50% and emission reductions up to 46% per acre; winner of the Gulbenkian Prize (2024) and the Food Planet Prize (2026).

- Diversification into aquaculture, horticulture and livestock, where national growth rates (fisheries 8.8%, livestock 7.1% a decade) far exceed crops at 3.5%. - Micro-irrigation, Soil Health Cards and millet promotion.

## Conclusion

The Green Revolution made Andhra Pradesh a rice surplus State and underwrote its food security, but it delivered its gains unevenly — to the irrigated deltas and to farmers who could afford the package — and at a real ecological cost in groundwater, soil and biodiversity. The State’s answer has been to move toward the Evergreen Revolution: raising productivity through ecological processes rather than purchased inputs, which is precisely what APCNF has demonstrated at scale.

## Value addition
- Attribution: Norman Borlaug (Nobel Peace Prize, 1970) for dwarf wheat; M.S. Swaminathan as the architect of the Indian programme; C. Subramaniam as the Agriculture Minister who drove it politically; IR-8 rice from the International Rice Research Institute.
- Chronology: the High Yielding Varieties Programme began in 1966-67; the Intensive Agricultural District Programme (1960-61) was its precursor.
- The successor concept: Swaminathan’s Evergreen Revolution — “increasing productivity in perpetuity without ecological harm.”
- AP today: decadal agricultural growth nationally at 4.45% (FY16-FY25), the highest of any decade, driven by allied sectors rather than the cereals the Green Revolution targeted.

- Infant Mortality and Death Rates in Andhra Pradesh in the recent decade

Introduction The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is the number of deaths of infants under one year per 1,000 live births; the Crude Death Rate (CDR) is deaths per 1,000 population. Both are measured through the Sample Registration System (SRS). Andhra Pradesh’s record on child and maternal survival is among the strongest in India — but its crude death rate tells a very different and often misread story.

The trend

- **Indicator** — Andhra Pradesh · India
- **IMR** — Fell from 59 (SRS 2006) to roughly 20-25 currently — below the national figure · 25 (2023), down from 39 (2014)
- **Under-5 Mortality Rate** — 24 — among only twelve States/UTs to have met the SDG target of ≤25 by 2030 · 29 (2023), down from 45 (2014)
- **Maternal Mortality Ratio** — About 30 per lakh live births (SRS 2021-23) — the lowest in India along with Kerala, and below Maldives and Thailand · 88 (2021-23), down from 130 (2014-16)
- **Crude Death Rate** — About 7 per 1,000 · About 6 per 1,000
- **Total Fertility Rate** — About 1.5 (down from 3.0 in 1993) · 1.9 (2023)

Reasons for the improvement in infant and maternal mortality

- High institutional delivery and strengthened antenatal care under NHM and RMNCAH+N.
- Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva providing financial protection, and the earlier Aarogyasri architecture.
- Anganwadi and nutrition delivery — 9,958 centres upgraded, with 192 new centres in PVTG areas.
- High female age at marriage in urban areas, small family norm and near-universal immunisation.
- A relatively dense public and private health infrastructure, especially in the coastal districts.

The crucial analytical point on the death rate

Andhra Pradesh’s crude death rate is slightly higher than India’s — not because health outcomes are worse, but because its population is older. With a TFR of about 1.5 and the 60-plus share at 11% and rising toward 19% by 2047, AP has a larger share of the population in high-mortality age groups. CDR is a composition effect, not a health outcome — which is why age-specific mortality, IMR and MMR are the correct indicators of health performance. Stating this distinction is what separates a strong answer here.

Concerns that remain

- 29.3% of women aged 20-24 were married before 18 (NFHS-5) — above the national average and higher among Scheduled Tribes, keeping neonatal risk elevated.
- 16.1% of children under five are wasted, with 6% severely wasted (NFHS-5).
- Anaemia among women remains widespread, and tribal agency areas lag the coastal districts.

Conclusion Andhra Pradesh has achieved the SDG targets for maternal and under-five mortality well ahead of 2030 — an outstanding record. Its rising crude death rate reflects demographic ageing rather than health failure, and signals the State’s next priority: geriatric care, non-communicable disease management and nutrition, alongside firm enforcement against child marriage.

## Value addition
- Definitions to state precisely: IMR — infant deaths under one year per 1,000 live births; Neonatal Mortality Rate — deaths within 28 days; U5MR — deaths under five per 1,000 live births; MMR — maternal deaths per 1,00,000 live births; CDR — deaths per 1,000 population.

## Introduction

A caution on figures: State plan outlays were revised repeatedly between approval and completion, and the Plan framework was abolished in 2017. Where you cannot recall an exact figure, state the magnitude, the direction of change and the sectoral proportion — the analytical content is what carries the marks, and an invented precise number is worse than an honest approximation.

A State Plan outlay was the total development expenditure approved for a Five-Year Plan, financed from the State’s own resources, central assistance, institutional borrowing and public enterprise contributions. For Andhra Pradesh — an

agrarian State whose growth depended on water — irrigation dominated plan expenditure to an extent unusual even among Indian States.

The scale of the two Plans

- **Tenth Plan** — 2002-07 · A consolidation plan, framed under the fiscal discipline of the AP Fiscal Reforms Programme and the AP FRBM Act, 2005; the State was simultaneously eliminating its revenue deficit, so plan size was constrained
- **Eleventh Plan** — 2007-12 · Several times larger, in line with the national pattern where public sector plan outlay was set about 120% above Tenth Plan realisation at constant prices; driven by Jalayagnam, the welfare expansion and rising central scheme transfers

The dominant head — agriculture including irrigation

For Andhra Pradesh, agriculture together with irrigation consistently commanded the single largest share of plan outlay — considerably above the national average, and in the Eleventh Plan approaching or exceeding a third of the total. The reasons are specific to the State:

- Jalayagnam, launched in 2004, was among the largest irrigation programmes ever undertaken by an Indian State, aiming to complete a large number of major and medium projects simultaneously. It absorbed the bulk of the State’s capital outlay through both Plans.
- Polavaram, the Handri Neeva Sujala Sravanthi lift scheme (40 TMC through a 565-km canal, lifting water over 369 metres), Galeru-Nagari and Veligonda were all in execution.
- Agriculture supported roughly half the workforce, so investment in it was simultaneously a growth strategy and a poverty strategy.
- Drought in Rayalaseema made lift irrigation a political as well as economic imperative.

How the plans were financed

- **State’s own resources** — Balance from current revenues, small savings, provident funds, State PSU contributions
- **Central assistance** — Normal and Additional Central Assistance, Centrally Sponsored Schemes, special plan assistance
- **Borrowings** — Market borrowings (State Development Loans) — which became dominant after the Twelfth Finance Commission (2005) ended Central on-lending; NABARD’s RIDF, LIC and HUDCO
- **External assistance** — World Bank, ADB and JICA-funded projects routed through the Centre

Assessment of the allocation pattern

Strengths - Irrigation investment was correctly prioritised for an agrarian State, and created assets — Polavaram, HNSS, Veligonda — with returns extending over decades. - It supported the State’s strong agricultural performance: AP’s agriculture grew about 6% during the Eleventh Plan against the national target of 4%.

Weaknesses - Allocation exceeded expenditure. As nationally — where 26.48% was allocated to energy in the Tenth Plan but only 16.58% actually spent — AP’s irrigation outlays were repeatedly under-utilised because of land acquisition delays, clearances and weak project preparation. - Concentration on new project starts rather than completion and maintenance, an outcome of the plan/non-plan divide under which maintenance fell under “non-plan” and was starved. - Cost escalation in long-gestation irrigation projects, so that outlay grew without commensurate command area. - Debt financing: with the balance from current revenues weak, plan capital outlay was financed largely by market borrowing, raising the interest burden. - Within agriculture, irrigation crowded out extension, market infrastructure, storage and the rural non-farm sector — the components that convert water into income.

What replaced the framework

The Five-Year Plan system ended with the Twelfth Plan (2012-17), following the replacement of the Planning Commission by NITI Aayog (2015) and the abolition of the plan/non-plan distinction from 2017-18 on the Rangarajan Committee (2011) recommendation. Today the equivalent figures are: - AP capital expenditure of ₹53,915 crore in 2026-27, up from ₹39,498 crore (RE 2025-26); - ₹6,544 crore availed under SASCI in 2025-26 (50-year interest-free central capex loans); - Externally aided finance — World Bank US$800 million and ADB US$788.8 million for Amaravati Phase-I.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s Tenth and Eleventh Plan outlays reflect a State that bet its development strategy on water: agriculture including irrigation took the largest single share, rising sharply in the Eleventh Plan with Jalayagnam. The strategy was sound in direction — irrigation is the binding constraint on AP’s agriculture — but weakened by under-utilisation, cost escalation and neglect of complementary investment in extension, storage and marketing. The same lesson applies to today’s capital budget: an outlay creates a project; only completion and maintenance create an asset.

## Value addition
- Financing shift: the Twelfth Finance Commission (2005) ended Central on-lending to States, pushing them to market borrowings — which is why State Development Loans came to finance most of AP’s plan capital outlay by 2011-12.
- RIDF: operated by NABARD since 1995-96 from shortfalls in banks’ priority sector lending — a major source for AP’s irrigation and rural roads.
- The national benchmark today: the Centre’s effective capital expenditure (₹17.15 lakh crore) now exceeds its fiscal deficit (about ₹16.9 lakh crore) — the standard against which any State’s allocation quality can be judged.
- AP’s current irrigation position: Polavaram targeted for completion by 2027; the proposed Polavaram-Banakacherla link (about ₹80,112 crore, 200 TMC) is contested by Telangana.

## Introduction

The Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) was introduced in June 1997, replacing the universal PDS. Its founding premise was that a universal subsidy was fiscally unsustainable and poorly targeted — much of the benefit reached those who did not need it. TPDS therefore restricted subsidised grain to identified poor households through a differentiated price and quantity structure.

Basic features of TPDS

- **Dual pricing** — Distinct central issue prices for Below Poverty Line (BPL) and Above Poverty Line (APL) households — the core design change from universal PDS
- **Beneficiary categorisation** — BPL and APL, with Antyodaya Anna Yojana (2000) added for the poorest of the poor, receiving 35 kg per household per month at ₹2/kg for wheat and ₹3/kg for rice
- **Quantity entitlement** — Fixed monthly quantity per household (initially 10 kg, later raised to 35 kg for BPL and AAY)
- **Identification** — State governments identify BPL households within central ceilings based on Planning Commission poverty estimates
- **Delivery** — Through fair price shops licensed and supervised by State governments
- **Financing** — Centre bears the food subsidy — the difference between the economic cost to FCI and the central issue price
- **Special schemes** — Annapurna for destitute elderly; later, Mid-Day Meal and ICDS linkages

Performance in the erstwhile (undivided) Andhra Pradesh Strengths

- High coverage: undivided AP maintained one of India’s widest PDS networks, with the State supplementing central entitlements from its own resources.
- The ₹2-a-kg rice scheme (introduced in 1983 and periodically revived) made AP a pioneer of deep food price subsidy in India, and became a political and administrative template widely imitated.
- Strong distribution infrastructure — a dense fair price shop network and an active State Civil Supplies Corporation managing lifting, transport and storage.
- Contribution to food security: the scheme measurably reduced hunger and stabilised food consumption among poor households, particularly in drought years in Rayalaseema.
- Early adoption of reforms: AP was among the earlier States to computerise ration card databases and begin de-duplication.

Weaknesses

- Targeting errors were severe. The BPL/APL classification produced both large exclusion errors (genuinely poor households denied BPL cards) and inclusion errors (non-poor holding BPL cards). Because entitlement depended on a single line drawn by a contested poverty estimate, errors were structural rather than administrative.
- Leakage and diversion to the open market persisted, driven by the wide gap between the issue price and the market price.
- Bogus and duplicate cards inflated apparent coverage and central allotment.
- Quality complaints were widespread.
- Fiscal burden on the State grew as it topped up central entitlements.
- Cereal-centric composition meant the system delivered calories but not nutrition.

The critical assessment of the TPDS design itself

TPDS’s central weakness was conceptual, not operational. It required a precise, current and universally accepted poverty line to identify beneficiaries — something India has never possessed. The Tendulkar (2009) and Rangarajan (2014) committees produced estimates differing by nearly 8 percentage points for the same year, and India has had no officially updated poverty line since 2011-12. Targeting on a contested line inevitably produces contested outcomes.

The transition to NFSA

The National Food Security Act, 2013 effectively abandoned the BPL/APL distinction. It replaced it with: - Priority Households and AAY categories, covering up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population — about 80.67 crore persons; - A legal entitlement of 5 kg per person per month for priority households and 35 kg per household for AAY, at fixed prices; - Food security allowance if grain is not supplied; - The eldest woman aged 18 or above deemed head of household for card issue.

This was a decisive shift from targeting the poor to near-universal coverage with exclusion criteria — an acknowledgement that in India, exclusion errors cost more than inclusion errors.

## Conclusion

TPDS improved fiscal targeting over the universal system and, in undivided Andhra Pradesh, sustained a wide and politically durable food security network. But its reliance on a BPL line that India could never define reliably made large targeting errors inevitable. The NFSA’s move to near-universal coverage, combined with the automation, Aadhaar authentication and portability that followed, has addressed the identification problem far more effectively than any refinement of targeting could have. The remaining challenges — quality, diversification and upstream leakage — are those TPDS never solved either.

## Value addition
- Chronology: universal PDS → Revamped PDS (1992) for tribal, hilly and remote areas → TPDS (June 1997) with BPL/APL → Antyodaya Anna Yojana (2000) → NFSA (2013) → automation, ePoS and ONORC → PMGKAY extended to 31 December 2028.
- Antyodaya Anna Yojana (December 2000): 35 kg per household per month at highly subsidised rates, for the poorest one crore households initially.
- Shanta Kumar Committee (2015): reduce NFSA coverage to 40%, adopt decentralised procurement, introduce cash transfers in large cities, and complete end-to-end computerisation.
- Undivided AP context: the ₹2-a-kg rice scheme of 1983 was among independent India’s earliest large-scale State food subsidy programmes, and shaped the political economy of food policy across southern India.

## Introduction

Measuring poverty requires answering two questions: what threshold defines poverty, and how do we count those below it? India has answered these in two very different ways — through monetary poverty lines based on consumption expenditure, and through multidimensional measures that count deprivations directly.

- Monetary methods — the poverty line approach
- The calorie-norm basis (Alagh Committee, 1979) The poverty line was anchored in a minimum calorie requirement

— 2,400 kcal per capita per day in rural areas and 2,100 kcal in urban areas — converted into the monetary expenditure needed to obtain it. Criticised for ignoring health, education, housing and changing consumption patterns.

- The Lakdawala Committee (1993) Retained the calorie anchor but introduced State-specific poverty lines, updated using CPI-Agricultural Labourers for rural areas and CPI-Industrial Workers for urban areas.
- The Tendulkar Committee (2009) — the last official line - Moved away from calories to a basket including food, education, health, transport and other essentials. - Adopted the Mixed Reference Period (MRP) instead of the Uniform Reference Period. - Used a uniform national urban basket applied across States. - Line for 2011-12: ₹816 per capita per month rural, ₹1,000 urban — giving poverty of 21.9%.
- The Rangarajan Committee (2014) - Reverted to independent rural and urban baskets combining normative food (calorie, protein and fat), essential non-food and behaviourally determined expenditure. - Line for 2011-12: ₹972 rural /

₹1,407 urban — roughly ₹33 and ₹47 a day — giving poverty of 29.5%. - Never officially adopted, so Tendulkar remains the last official estimate.

- World Bank international lines Used for cross-country comparison. In June 2025 the Bank revised the extreme poverty line from $2.15 (2017 PPP) to $3.00 (2021 PPP), and the lower- and upper-middle-income lines to $4.20 and

$8.30. On this basis India’s extreme poverty is about 5.25% (2022-23); but at the $4.20 lower-middle-income line — the more appropriate benchmark for India — about 24% remained poor in 2022.

- Multidimensional methods — counting deprivations directly
- The National Multidimensional Poverty Index (NITI Aayog) Developed with UNDP and OPHI using the Alkire-Foster method:
- **Health** — Nutrition; child and adolescent mortality; maternal health
- **Education** — Years of schooling; school attendance
- **Standard of living** — Cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account

- 12 indicators in total, against the global MPI’s 10.
- Reports headcount ratio (H) — the proportion who are poor — and intensity (A) — the average share of deprivations they suffer. MPI = H × A.
- Current estimate: headcount 11.28% (2022-23), down from 29.17% (2013-14), with about 24.82 crore people escaping multidimensional poverty.
- Inequality-based measures (relative poverty) The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient measure the distribution rather than the level. India’s consumption Gini is about 25.5 (World Bank, 2025) — moderate globally, though wealth inequality is far higher.
- Other approaches - SECC 2011 — the socio-economic and caste census used for beneficiary identification through deprivation criteria rather than an income line. - Head Count Ratio, Poverty Gap Index and Squared Poverty Gap (Foster-Greer-Thorbecke) — measuring incidence, depth and severity respectively. - HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24 — the restored consumption series, now using the Modified Mixed Recall Period.

Comparing the two families

- **What it measures** — Consumption below a threshold · Overlapping deprivations
- **Strength** — Simple, comparable over time, links to income growth · Identifies who is poor and in what way; policy-actionable
- **Weakness** — Line-setting is arbitrary and contested; ignores non-income deprivation · Weighting of indicators involves judgment; not comparable to income data

## Conclusion

India has moved from a single calorie-based line to a plural measurement framework — because poverty itself is plural. The monetary line answers “how many fall below a subsistence threshold”; the MPI answers “who is deprived, and in what dimensions”. The current gap is that India has no officially updated poverty line since 2011-12, so monetary poverty is now described largely through World Bank estimates. Restoring a current national line, alongside the MPI, would give policy both the aggregate benchmark and the diagnostic detail it needs.

## Value addition
- Full lineage: Dadabhai Naoroji’s Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) — the first Indian poverty estimate; National Planning Committee (1938); Dandekar and Rath (1971); Alagh (1979); Lakdawala (1993); Tendulkar (2009); Rangarajan (2014); Saxena and Hashim Committees on BPL identification.
- Methodological note that earns marks: applying the MMRP to 2011-12 data would itself have reduced measured poverty from 22.9% to 16.22% even under the unchanged poverty line — which is why HCES 2022-23 is not strictly comparable with 2011-12.
- Data sources today: HCES for consumption, PLFS for employment and literacy, NFHS for health and nutrition, and the National MPI and SDG India Index for composite tracking.
- Andhra Pradesh: the first Indian State to adopt an MPI (2018) for its own planning.

## Introduction

Self-Help Groups solved a problem formal banking could not: how to lend small sums to people without collateral, credit history or documentation. By substituting joint liability and peer monitoring for collateral, SHGs made the rural poor bankable. Andhra Pradesh built the country’s largest such network — about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, with repayment consistently above 97%.

How the model meets credit requirements

- **Savings first** — Members save regularly before borrowing, building a corpus and a repayment record
- **Internal lending** — The group lends its own savings to members at rates it sets — instant, flexible, no paperwork
- **SHG-Bank Linkage** — Credit-rated groups access bank loans in multiples of their savings, under the NABARD framework established in 1992
- **Joint liability** — Peer pressure and social collateral replace physical collateral, driving repayment above 97%
- **Federated structure** — Village Organisations, Mandal Samakhyas and Zilla Samakhyas aggregate demand, appraise loans and enforce discipline
- **Stree Nidhi** — A dedicated credit cooperative federation providing rapid small-ticket loans, often within days — governed by a committee of 13 directors elected from mandal samakhyas
- **Interest subvention** — Pavala Vaddi and successor schemes reduced the effective cost of borrowing

Examining the role — what SHGs have achieved

- They displaced the moneylender for small credit needs. For consumption smoothing, health emergencies, school fees and small working capital, SHG credit is faster and vastly cheaper than informal borrowing — the single largest welfare gain.
- They proved the poor are bankable. Repayment above 97% without collateral changed banking policy nationally, and demonstrated that the constraint was never borrower reliability but transaction cost.
- They reached those banks would not. Women, landless households, SC and ST families, and tenant cultivators without title — all excluded from conventional agricultural credit, which is tied to land records.
- They provided resilience during the 2010 crisis. When commercial MFI operations collapsed in the State, the SHG network continued lending — the clearest test the model has faced.
- They became a platform beyond credit. The network now delivers pensions, health insurance enrolment, DBT and community-managed agriculture, giving it a value far exceeding its lending function.
- They shaped national policy. The SERP federated model became the design basis for NRLM (2011), now DAY-NRLM.

Scale, in the current national picture

Microfinance in FY25 reached 627 lakh active borrowers with a gross loan portfolio of ₹2.38 lakh crore, of whom 95% are women and 80% rural — Small Finance Banks hold 16% of this market and banks 32%, much of it flowing through SHG linkage.

Limitations — the critical examination

- **Purpose mismatch** — Loans frequently finance consumption, health emergencies, weddings or the repayment of older debt rather than productive assets. Credit that does not raise income cannot be repaid from income
- **Ticket size** — SHG credit suits micro-needs; it cannot finance term investment — irrigation, mechanisation, storage, processing — which is what actually raises productivity
- **Over-indebtedness** — Multiple borrowing from SHGs, banks and MFIs contributed to the 2010 crisis, and to the FY25 stress when MFI loans outstanding fell about 14%
- **Elite capture** — Better-off members within a group can dominate; the poorest and PVTG households remain hardest to include
- **Uneven federation quality** — Governance capacity varies sharply between mandals
- **Sustainability** — Federations depend on project funding, professional management and political continuity
- **Gap in agricultural credit** — SHG credit does not substitute for crop loans and Kisan Credit Cards; tenant cultivators remain excluded from those because credit is tied to land title

The evidence that the limitation is real: across scheduled commercial banks, agriculture’s GNPA stands at 6.0% — the highest of any sector and over a third of all bad loans — showing that rural credit expansion without productivity gains creates stress.

## Conclusion

SHGs have substantially met the small, immediate and collateral-free credit requirements of rural Andhra Pradesh, and did so where the formal system had failed. Their limitation is structural rather than administrative: they are excellent at micro-credit and poor at capital formation. The next stage requires linking SHGs to Farmer Producer Organisations, term credit for assets, and genuine market access, and recognising tenancy for credit purposes — so that the group moves from being a borrowing platform to being an enterprise platform.

## Value addition
- SHG-Bank Linkage Programme: launched by NABARD in 1992 as a pilot with 500 groups — today the world’s largest microfinance programme by outreach.
- AP’s project lineage: APDPIP/Velugu (2000) → APRPRP/Indira Kranthi Patham (2003) → APRIGP (2015-20), covering 150 backward mandals and about 5,000 villages.
- Priority Sector Lending: 40% of ANBC overall; 18% for agriculture, with 10% for small and marginal farmers and 7.5% for micro enterprises.
- Regulatory update: the RBI reduced minimum qualifying assets for NBFC-MFIs from 75% to 60% with effect from 6 June 2025, allowing lenders to diversify after the FY25 stress.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh’s occupational structure is agrarian in employment though diversified in output, and its social

composition — with a substantial Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe population — maps closely onto that structure. Examining the two together shows that occupational disadvantage in the State is not randomly distributed but socially patterned.

Part A: The occupational structure

- **Primary — cultivators, agricultural labourers, aquaculture, livestock, forestry** — Roughly half the workforce · 37%
- **Secondary — manufacturing, construction, mining, utilities** — Modest; construction dominates within it · 23%
- **Tertiary — trade, transport, education, health, IT, tourism** — Rising, urban-concentrated · 40%

Key features

- Agricultural labourers outnumber cultivators — a shift from owner-cultivation to wage labour, reflecting fragmentation of holdings and rising tenancy.
- Tenant cultivators without recorded title are excluded from institutional credit, crop insurance and compensation

— which is why Annadata Sukhibhava (₹20,000 a year) explicitly covers them.

- Distinctive AP occupations: aquaculture and fisheries along the 974-km coastline; horticulture and oil palm; handloom weaving (Mangalagiri, Dharmavaram, Uppada); beedi rolling; barytes and limestone mining in Kadapa and Kurnool.
- Casualisation and informality dominate the non-farm workforce.
- Seasonality and disguised unemployment persist: more workers on the land than the land requires.
- Bifurcation removed Hyderabad, leaving AP only about 29.5% urbanised, so the urban services labour market that would normally absorb surplus farm labour is smaller and dispersed.

Part B: SC and ST population

- **Scheduled Castes** — About 17%
- **Scheduled Tribes** — About 5.5%
- **Together** — Roughly 22-23% — over a fifth of the State

- SC communities are dispersed across the State, concentrated in rural areas and largely dependent on agricultural wage labour.
- ST communities, including Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), are concentrated in the Eastern Ghats agency areas of Alluri Sitharama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam and adjoining districts, and depend on shifting cultivation, forest produce (tamarind, honey, gum karaya, beedi leaf) and wage labour.

Part C: The intersection — where the examination lies

- **Land ownership** — SC households are disproportionately landless, hence over-represented among agricultural labourers rather than cultivators
- **Occupational concentration** — ST households depend on forest produce and shifting cultivation — occupations with low and uncertain returns
- **Wage work** — Both groups are over-represented in casual labour, the most insecure employment category
- **Deprivation** — SC, ST and PVTG households show higher multidimensional deprivation within every district of the State
- **Migration** — Distress migration is concentrated among landless SC and tribal households in Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra

The binding constraint on mobility: Andhra Pradesh’s literacy at 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States, and the deficit is concentrated precisely among rural, SC, ST and older cohorts. Occupational mobility cannot outpace educational attainment.

Policy response

- Budget 2026-27 sub-plans: SC component ₹20,644 crore, ST component ₹9,190 crore, BC component ₹51,021 crore, Minorities ₹6,090 crore.
- Constitutional protection: the Fifth Schedule for Scheduled Areas, PESA (1996), and the Forest Rights Act,

2006; Samatha v. State of AP (1997) barring transfer of Scheduled Area land to private mining companies.

- PM JANMAN for PVTGs — 192 new Anganwadi centres sanctioned in PVTG areas.
- 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency, to disperse non-farm employment.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s occupational structure shows incomplete structural transformation, and its social composition shows that the burden of that incompleteness falls disproportionately on SC, ST and PVTG households — who are concentrated in landless wage labour and forest-dependent livelihoods. Inclusive change therefore requires more than aggregate growth: land and tenancy recognition, education and skilling targeted at the groups furthest behind, and non-farm employment dispersed into the regions where they live. Growth that bypasses the agency areas and the landless will change the State’s occupational statistics without changing who is disadvantaged.

## Value addition
- Definitions: cultivator — one who operates land owned or leased; agricultural labourer — one who works on another’s land for wages in cash or kind; main worker — employed 183 days or more; marginal worker — fewer than 183 days.
- AP demography (Census 2011, residuary State): population 4.94 crore; sex ratio 996; density 308 per sq km; urbanisation about 29.5%.
- Productivity contrast: ASI FY24 net value added per person engaged in factories was ₹10.7 lakh — a multiple of farm earnings, which is the incentive driving occupational change.
- National comparison: roughly 45% of India’s workforce remains in agriculture producing about 15% of GDP; the unincorporated sector employs 12.9 crore.
