## Introduction

Measuring unemployment in India is harder than in an industrial economy because most work is informal, seasonal and self-employed — there is no payroll or unemployment-insurance register to count from. India therefore relies on survey-based estimation using multiple reference periods, supplemented by administrative data.

- What is being measured — types of unemployment
- **Open** — Willing and able to work but no work at all · Urban, educated youth
- **Disguised** — More workers than needed; marginal productivity near zero · Agriculture and family enterprises
- **Seasonal** — Idle between agricultural peaks · Rural India
- **Structural** — Skills do not match available jobs · Educated unemployment
- **Frictional** — Transitional, between jobs · All economies
- **Cyclical** — Demand deficiency in a downturn · Industry and construction
- **Underemployment** — Working fewer hours or below skill level · Pervasive

- The methods of measurement
- Usual Status method (UPS and UPSS) — 365-day reference Classifies a person by the activity pursued for the majority of the preceding year; UPSS additionally counts subsidiary work of 30 days or more. Measures: chronic, long-term unemployment. Limitation: misses seasonality entirely; UPSS gives the lowest unemployment estimate.
- Current Weekly Status (CWS) — 7-day reference A person is employed if she worked at least one hour on any day of the reference week. Measures: short-term and seasonal fluctuation. Limitation: the one-hour rule classifies severely underemployed people as employed.
- Current Daily Status (CDS) — day-by-day over 7 days Records activity in half-day units for each of the seven days, then aggregates into person-days. Measures: the intensity of unemployment — the most rigorous method, capturing underemployment. Limitation: data-intensive and harder to collect.
- The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) — the delivery mechanism Since 2017-18, PLFS applies all these concepts, providing annual rural-plus-urban and quarterly urban estimates; from January 2025 it was revamped to produce monthly bulletins and quarterly rural and urban estimates, with district-level data targeted by 2026.
- Administrative and registry-based methods
- **EPFO / ESIC payroll data** — Net formal-sector job additions · Covers only the formal sector; job changes can be double-counted
- **Employment Exchange registrations** — Job-seekers registered · Registration is voluntary; many register while employed
- **Census (main/marginal workers)** — Decennial structural picture · Last conducted in 2011
- **ASI and ASUSE** — Factory and unincorporated-sector employment · Sector-specific
- **CMIE Consumer Pyramids** — High-frequency private estimates · Methodology differs from official; often diverges

- Why India needs multiple methods

Because the same person can genuinely be described in several ways. A farm labourer with 90 idle days a year is employed under UPSS, possibly employed under CWS, and substantially unemployed under CDS. The gap between the measures is itself the statistic that matters — it quantifies underemployment.

- Persistent measurement challenges
- The informal sector has no records, so estimation depends entirely on household recall.
- Unpaid family work and women’s work are systematically under-reported; the Economic Survey 2022-23 valued unpaid care work at ₹22.7 lakh crore, about 7.5% of GDP — entirely outside labour statistics.
- Disguised unemployment is conceptually real but statistically invisible.
- No Census since 2011, so population denominators rely on projections.
- Divergence between official and private estimates creates public confusion.

## Conclusion

India measures unemployment through a graduated system of reference periods rather than a single count, because its labour market is graduated rather than binary. The reported rate of 3.1% (PLFS 2025) is accurate on its own terms but must be read alongside informality, underemployment and earnings data to describe the real labour market. The shift to monthly PLFS bulletins from 2025 is the single most important recent improvement — moving India from five-yearly snapshots to near-continuous measurement.

## Value addition
- Order to remember: unemployment estimated by CDS > CWS > UPS > UPSS; the spread between CDS and UPSS approximates underemployment.
- Institutional history: quinquennial NSSO Employment-Unemployment Surveys until 2011-12 → NSSO merged into the NSO (2019) → PLFS from 2017-18 → revamped January 2025 with monthly bulletins.
- Current position: LFPR 59.3%, unemployment 3.1% (PLFS 2025); 56.2 crore employed in Q2 FY26 with 8.7 lakh net jobs added over Q1.
- Committee reference: the Task Force on Improving Employment Data (2017, chaired by Arvind Panagariya) recommended shifting to a more frequent PLFS and better use of administrative payroll data — the basis of the current framework.

## Introduction

Plan resource mobilisation refers to how a State finances its developmental outlay as distinct from its routine functioning. Across the Tenth (2002-07) and Eleventh (2007-12) Plans, Andhra Pradesh moved from dependence on central plan assistance towards market-based and institutional finance, within the discipline imposed by the FRBM framework.

## Channels of plan finance
- **State’s own resources (SOR)** — Balance from current revenues, small savings, provident funds, and contributions of State PSUs
- **Central assistance** — Normal Central Assistance, Additional Central Assistance, Centrally Sponsored Schemes, special plan assistance
- **Borrowings and institutional finance** — Market borrowings (SDLs), NABARD’s RIDF, LIC, HUDCO, and negotiated loans
- **Externally aided projects** — World Bank, ADB and JICA-funded programmes routed through the Centre
- **PSU internal resources** — APTRANSCO, APSRTC, APIIC — modest, constrained by low profitability

## The pattern and how it shifted
- Market borrowings became dominant. As the Centre withdrew from on-lending after the Twelfth Finance Commission (2005) disintermediation reform, States borrowed directly from the market. By 2011-12, market borrowings financed the bulk of AP’s fiscal deficit — around ₹15,500 crore.
- Central assistance declined in relative terms, and its composition shifted from untied plan assistance towards tied Centrally Sponsored Schemes, reducing the State’s discretion.
- Institutional finance filled the irrigation gap: NABARD’s RIDF financed major components of Jalayagnam and rural roads — long-gestation assets that market lenders would not fund.
- PSU contribution stayed marginal, reflecting weak balance sheets, particularly in power distribution.
- PPP emerged in ports, roads and power as an off-budget route to capacity creation.
- The FRBM constraint bound the whole system: the AP FRBM Act, 2005 capped the fiscal deficit at 3% of GSDP, forcing the State to prioritise projects and improve revenue effort rather than simply expand the plan size.

## The key limitation

Plan size grew impressively on paper, but utilisation lagged — delayed central releases, high interest obligations pre-empting resources, and weak project preparation meant sanctioned outlays frequently exceeded actual expenditure. The plan/non-plan divide compounded this: new projects were funded as “plan” while their maintenance was starved as “non-plan.”

## What replaced the Plan framework

The Five-Year Plan system ended with the Twelfth Plan (2012-17), following the replacement of the Planning Commission by NITI Aayog (2015) and the abolition of the plan/non-plan classification from 2017-18 on the Rangarajan Committee (2011) recommendation. Today AP mobilises development resources through:

- Budgetary capital expenditure — ₹53,915 crore in 2026-27, up from ₹39,498 crore (RE 2025-26);
- SASCI 50-year interest-free central loans — ₹6,544 crore availed in 2025-26;
- Externally aided projects — World Bank and ADB (about US$1.6 billion for Amaravati), AIIB for AMRUT 2.0;
- Debt cost reduction — the ₹43,298 crore swap of high-cost loans;
- New instruments — the proposed AP Wealth Fund, TReDS bill discounting for State PSEs, and private finance channels opened at the Reimagining Public Finance Summit (November 2025).

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s plan financing shifted decisively from central dependence to market and institutional finance — a gain in autonomy purchased with higher debt exposure. With the Plan framework gone, the same logic now operates through capital budgets and outcome-based allocation. The enduring priority is unchanged: raise resources at the lowest cost, deploy them in assets that generate returns, and maintain what has been built.

## Value addition
- AP FRBM Act, 2005: capped the fiscal deficit at 3% of GSDP, mandated elimination of the revenue deficit, required Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statements, and restricted unproductive borrowing. The 16th FC (2026-31) has now reaffirmed the 3% ceiling for all States and mandated an end to off-budget borrowings.
- Institutional shift: Planning Commission → NITI Aayog (2015); Five-Year Plans → 15-year Vision, 7-year Strategy, 3-year Action Agenda; plan/non-plan → revenue/capital classification (2017-18).
- RIDF: operated by NABARD since 1995-96 from shortfalls in banks’ priority sector lending — a key source for State irrigation and rural road financing.
- Current benchmark: SASCI allocations nationally rose from about ₹12,000 crore (FY21) to around ₹1.5 lakh crore

(FY26), with ₹1,85,000 crore provided in Union Budget 2026-27 — helping States hold capital expenditure at about

## 2.4% of GDP.
- One-line revision point: The question is no longer how large the plan is, but how productive the borrowing behind it is.

## Introduction

Public expenditure is government spending on administration, welfare and development. Since resources are finite and taxation is coercive, classical economists — Adam Smith, Findlay Shirras and Hugh Dalton — laid down principles to ensure that every rupee spent yields more social benefit than the sacrifice involved in raising it.

## The principles, with contemporary application
- **Maximum Social Advantage (Dalton)** — Spend up to the point where marginal social benefit equals marginal social sacrifice — the master principle from which the others follow · Ayushman Bharat: health spending yields productivity gains and prevents catastrophic household expenditure
- **Economy** — Avoid waste; obtain value for money · DBT has generated cumulative savings of over ₹3.5 lakh crore by eliminating duplicate and ghost beneficiaries; over 4 crore duplicate LPG connections deactivated under PAHAL
- **Sanction** — No expenditure without legislative authority · Appropriation Act under Art. 114; no withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund without it
- **Productivity** — Spending should create assets and raise national income · Capex of ₹12.22 lakh crore and effective capex of ₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP) in Budget 2026-27; capex share of Union spending up from 12.5% (FY20) to 22.6% (FY25)
- **Equity** — Reduce inequality and promote social justice · PM-KISAN, MGNREGA, PMAY; Gender Budget outlay of ₹4.49 lakh crore (8.86% of the Budget)
- **Elasticity** — Flexibility to expand or contract with circumstances · Government health expenditure rose from 1.13% of GDP (2014-15) to 1.84% (2021-22) during COVID-19; the FRBM escape clause permitted the FY21 deficit of 9.2%
- **Surplus / solvency** — Avoid chronic deficits; do not borrow for consumption · The debt anchor of 50±1% of GDP by FY31; the 16th FC’s ban on off-budget borrowings
- **Accountability** — Transparent, audited, outcome-linked spending · CAG audits, Public Accounts Committee, Outcome Budgets, Public Financial Management System

## The modern synthesis — “quality of expenditure”

These classical principles now converge in a single measurable idea: the composition of spending matters more than its size. The evidence is visible in India’s recent record — revenue expenditure fell from 13.6% of GDP (FY22) to 10.9% (FY25) while capital outlay rose, and effective capex now exceeds the fiscal deficit, meaning borrowing finances assets rather than consumption. The Quality of Public Expenditure Index reached its highest level since 1991 in 2024-25.

## Where the principles are under strain
- At the State level, unconditional cash transfers — about ₹1.7 lakh crore across States in FY26 — test the equity-versus-productivity balance; the Economic Survey 2025-26 warns they create expenditure rigidity and crowd out capital and human-capital spending.
- Committed expenditure — salaries, pensions, interest and subsidies — absorbed 51.76% of States’ revenue expenditure in FY24, limiting elasticity.
- The 16th FC has accordingly urged States to set clear exclusion criteria for subsidies and to move from unconditional to conditional, time-bound transfers, citing Mexico’s Progresa/Oportunidades model where transfers were linked to school attendance and health check-ups.

## Conclusion

The principles of public expenditure are not archaic maxims but operational tests — does the spending create more welfare than it costs, does it create an asset, does it reach the intended beneficiary, and can it be accounted for? India’s improving expenditure quality shows the principles working; the growing rigidity of State budgets shows where they are being tested. In a welfare state, fiscal discipline and social justice are complements, not opposites — provided spending is productive.

## Value addition
- Quality of Public Expenditure Index — phases: 1991-97 modest improvement; 1997-2003 decline (Fifth Pay Commission, rising interest); 2003-08 improvement under FRBM; 2008-13 stimulus-driven deterioration; 2013-19 State-level improvement aided by the 14th FC; 2019-25 pandemic dip followed by capex-led recovery to the highest level since 1991.
- Wagner’s Law: public expenditure tends to rise faster than national income as economies develop.
- Peacock-Wiseman displacement effect: crises permanently raise the accepted level of public spending — visible in India’s post-COVID expenditure baseline.
- Institutional tools: Public Financial Management System (PFMS), Just-in-Time fund releases, Direct Benefit Transfer, Outcome Budget, and the Treasury Single Account.
- One-line revision point: The test of public expenditure is not what it costs the exchequer, but what it leaves behind.

## Introduction

Exam technique: two short, self-contained notes of roughly 175-200 words each — not two essays. Allocate time equally.

- Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme

Introduction The Kisan Credit Card, introduced in 1998 on a model scheme designed by NABARD, was created to free farmers from the moneylender by giving them a single, flexible, revolving credit line instead of separate seasonal loan applications.

Features

- **Purpose** — Short-term crop loans, post-harvest expenses, consumption needs, farm asset maintenance and working capital for allied activities
- **Coverage** — Extended to allied activities (2004) and to animal husbandry and fisheries (2018-19) — a decisive widening, since allied sectors now grow faster than crops
- **Credit limit** — Raised to ₹5 lakh under the Modified Interest Subvention Scheme (Budget 2025-26)
- **Interest** — 7% nominal, with a 3% prompt repayment incentive, giving an effective rate of 4%
- **Collateral-free limit** — Raised from ₹1.6 lakh to ₹2 lakh (2024)
- **Instrument** — RuPay KCC card enabling ATM and PoS use; validity of five years with annual review
- **Digital backbone** — The Kisan Rin Portal (KRP) integrates MoA&FW, DFS, RBI and NABARD data on disbursement, interest subvention and scheme utilisation

Performance

- Institutional credit to agriculture rose from ₹8.5 lakh crore (2014-15) to ₹25.48 lakh crore (2023-24); short-term credit from ₹6.4 lakh crore to ₹15.07 lakh crore.
- The share of small and marginal farmers accessing agricultural loans rose from 57% (2014-15) to 76% (2023-24) — the most important equity outcome.
- Interest subsidy on KCC loans rose from ₹6,000 crore (2014-15) to ₹14,252 crore (2023-24), totalling about ₹1.44 lakh crore over a decade.
- KCC saturation drives now link every PM-KISAN beneficiary to a card.

Limitations: tenant farmers without recorded title remain largely excluded, since credit is tied to land records; renewal is often mechanical rather than needs-based; and credit sometimes finances consumption rather than production.

- Providing Urban Facilities in Rural Areas (PURA)

Introduction PURA was conceived by Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam and announced in 2003. Its founding idea was to reverse

rural-urban migration not by restricting it but by taking urban amenities to the village — clustering 15-20 villages so that services become viable at scale.

The four connectivities — the conceptual core

- **Physical** — Roads, transport, water supply, sanitation, housing, electricity
- **Electronic** — Telecom, internet, ICT infrastructure
- **Knowledge** — Schools, vocational training, e-learning centres, digital literacy
- **Economic** — Market linkage, skill development, local enterprise, microfinance

Implementation Restructured in 2012 by the Ministry of Rural Development as a public-private partnership, in which a private partner delivered and maintained amenities in a village cluster under a long-term concession, with viability gap funding.

Assessment

Strengths: an intellectually influential concept — rural development as cluster-based infrastructure provision rather than scattered scheme delivery; anticipated later thinking on rural-urban continuum.

Weaknesses: few private partners found rural clusters commercially viable; land acquisition and coordination across departments proved difficult; the scheme achieved limited coverage and was not scaled.

What replaced it: the concept survives in the Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission (SPMRM, 2016), which develops “Rurban clusters” by providing urban amenities while retaining rural character — PURA’s idea with a workable institutional design.

## Value addition
- KCC eligibility: owner-cultivators, tenant farmers, oral lessees and sharecroppers (in principle), SHG and joint liability group members, and those engaged in animal husbandry and fisheries.
- PURA’s intellectual lineage: set out in Dr. Kalam’s India 2020; conceptually related to Gandhi’s gram swaraj but delivered through modern infrastructure rather than self-sufficiency.
- Related current schemes: PM Gram Sadak Yojana, Jal Jeevan Mission, Saubhagya, BharatNet and PMAY-G together deliver much of what PURA envisaged, though sectorally rather than as clusters.
- AP relevance: the 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency, apply the PURA logic of dispersing economic opportunity rather than concentrating it in cities.

## Introduction

A State’s fiscal health depends on two variables it only partly controls — the structure of its borrowings and the flow of resources from the Centre. For Andhra Pradesh, post-bifurcation revenue loss has made both decisive.

## Debt composition of the Andhra Pradesh government

Structure of liabilities (Article 293 governs State borrowing; States may borrow only within India, and require the Centre’s consent while indebted to it)

- **Internal debt** — Open market loans (State Development Loans), special securities issued to NSSF, loans from NABARD, LIC, HUDCO and other institutions · The dominant and rising component
- **Loans from the Central Government** — Block loans, back-to-back external assistance, and SASCI 50-year interest-free capex loans · A small and, until SASCI, shrinking share
- **Public Account liabilities** — Provident funds, small savings, reserve funds, deposits · Recurring, low-cost, but a claim on future resources
- **Contingent liabilities** — Guarantees to State PSUs and corporations · Outside the deficit but a real fiscal risk
- **Off-budget borrowings** — Borrowings by corporations serviced from the budget · ₹1.28 lakh crore = 9.7% of GSDP as of March 2023 (CAG)

Current position: public debt of ₹7,11,094 crore = 36% of GSDP (BE 2026-27), up from ₹6,35,177 crore (RE 2025-26); in 2026-27 the State plans open market loans of ₹76,182 crore and loans from the Government of India of

## ₹19,133 crore.

The composition trend that matters: as the Centre withdrew from on-lending after the Twelfth Finance Commission (2005), States moved to the market. AP’s debt has therefore shifted decisively from cheap, long-tenure central loans to market-priced SDLs, raising its average cost of borrowing — which is precisely why the State’s swap of ₹43,298 crore of high-cost loans (from 12.3% down to 9% or below), saving ₹327 crore a year, matters.

- Resource inflows from the Central government
- **Share in central taxes** — Art. 270; Finance Commission formula — AP’s share now 4.22% under the 16th FC · ₹64,362 crore
- **Grants-in-aid** — Art. 275 — Finance Commission grants, centrally sponsored schemes, externally aided project pass-throughs · ₹32,458 crore
- **Finance Commission local body grants** — Art. 280(3)(bb) and (c) · RLB basic ₹13,302 crore and ULB basic ₹9,727 crore for 2026-31; ₹3,797 crore released to local bodies in 2025-26
- **Disaster management grants** — SDRF/NDRF · ₹6,125 crore for 2026-31
- **Capex loans** — SASCI — 50-year interest-free · ₹6,544 crore availed in 2025-26
- **Special assistance** — AP Reorganisation Act provisions · Partially delivered

Together, central transfers fund about 41% of AP’s revenue receipts — a dependence that is both a cushion and a vulnerability.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s debt profile shows rising reliance on market borrowings at higher cost, while its resource inflows show heavy dependence on central transfers whose composition is now shifting from grants to untied devolution. Fiscal stability therefore requires action on both fronts: actively managing the cost and transparency of debt — as the debt swap and the 16th FC’s off-budget disclosure mandate require — and broadening own-tax revenue so that transfers supplement rather than substitute for the State’s own effort.

## Value addition
- Grants-in-aid (Art. 275): Finance Commission-recommended transfers from the Consolidated Fund of India to correct vertical and horizontal imbalance, enabling States with weak revenue capacity to maintain essential services — a core instrument of cooperative fiscal federalism.
- 16th FC transparency mandate: all off-budget borrowings to be discontinued and brought within the definition of debt, with uniform definitions of debt and fiscal deficit across States — directly relevant to AP’s ₹1.28 lakh crore.
- National context: total Union transfers to States in Budget 2026-27 are ₹26.2 lakh crore, of which tax devolution is

₹15.26 lakh crore and grants and loans ₹10.94 lakh crore, including ₹1.85 lakh crore of capex loans.

## Introduction

Before 1991, Indian banking was characterised by administered interest rates, high pre-emption (CRR 15%, SLR 38.5%), directed credit and opaque accounting. The Narasimham Committee I (1991) and II (1998) launched a transformation that has been extended by the IBC (2016), consolidation, digitalisation and the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025.

## Wave 1 — Prudential and competitive reforms (1991 onwards)
- Freed resources: CRR reduced from 15% to 3.00% and SLR from 38.5% to 18%, releasing lendable funds.
- Prudential norms: income recognition and asset classification, Basel capital adequacy, and provisioning brought Indian accounting to global standards.
- Competition: entry of new private banks (1993-94 and 2003-04) forced efficiency; deregulated interest rates ended cross-subsidy pricing.
- Autonomy: the Board for Financial Supervision (1994) and gradual dilution of government equity improved governance.

## Wave 2 — Asset quality and resolution (2015 onwards)
- Asset Quality Review (2015) forced honest recognition, revealing the twin-balance-sheet problem.
- Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 created a time-bound, creditor-in-control resolution regime, shifting the credit culture from “borrower’s default” to “borrower’s risk.”
- Recapitalisation and consolidation: over ₹3.5 lakh crore of PSB capital infusion; 27 PSBs merged into 12 (2020); NARCL created for legacy stress; PCA framework to discipline weak banks.

## Wave 3 — Digital and governance reforms
- JAM trinity, UPI, Account Aggregator, e-KYC and digital lending directions; PSBs’ common Credit Assessment Model for MSME lending.
- Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025 — governance, audit quality and depositor protection.

## Measurable impact
- **Indicator** — Then · Now
- **GNPA of SCBs** — 11.2% (March 2018) · 2.2% (September 2025)
- **Net NPA** — ~6% · 0.5% — record low
- **CRAR** — ~13% · 17.2%
- **Profitability** — Losses in PSBs (2016-18) · RoA 1.3%, RoE 12.5%
- **Financial inclusion** — ~35% account ownership (2011) · ~89% (Global Findex 2025)

The improvement is not cosmetic: transmission works better (lending rates fell 59-69 bps against the 125 bps repo cut), and India received three sovereign rating upgrades in FY26, with agencies citing financial-sector resilience.

## Costs and unfinished agenda
- Financial exclusion in the transition: branch rationalisation and commercial pricing initially reduced rural credit depth; the RRB and SFB route was needed to correct it.
- Concentration risk: mergers created fewer, larger banks — efficient, but with cultural integration and “too big to fail” concerns.
- Agriculture stress persists: GNPA at 6.0%, over a third of all bad loans.
- Privatisation stalled, and PSB governance still depends on government appointment processes.
- New risks: cyber fraud, third-party/fintech dependencies, and climate-related exposures.

## Conclusion

Economic reforms converted Indian banking from a directed, loss-prone arm of the state into a well-capitalised, competitive and technologically advanced system that withstood the pandemic and a global rate shock without a systemic crisis. The next phase must address governance depth in PSBs, agricultural asset quality, and the safe integration of fintech — so that resilience translates into sustained, inclusive credit growth.

## Value addition
- Narasimham Committee I (1991): reduce CRR/SLR, prudential norms, four-tier banking structure, greater RBI supervisory role, recapitalisation of weak banks, autonomy in appointments.
- Narasimham Committee II (1998): mergers of strong banks, capital adequacy to 9%, narrow banking for weak banks, Asset Reconstruction Companies.
- Landmark laws: SARFAESI Act, 2002; DRT Act, 1993; IBC, 2016; Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 (cooperative banks under RBI); Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025.
- PSB consolidation timeline: SBI associates merged (2017) → Bank of Baroda–Vijaya–Dena (2019) → four-way merger reducing 27 PSBs to 12 (1 April 2020).

## Introduction

The economy of united Andhra Pradesh was popularly classified into three regions — Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema and Telangana — a division rooted in geography, irrigation and colonial administrative history (Madras Presidency versus the Nizam’s dominions). The classification was not merely descriptive: the wide gap in regional GSDP shares became the economic basis of the statehood movement.

## The three regions and their economic character
- **Coastal Andhra (9 districts)** — Krishna–Godavari deltas; canal irrigation; 974 km coastline · Paddy, sugarcane, aquaculture; ports at Visakhapatnam and Kakinada; heavy industry (steel, petrochemicals, pharma)
- **Rayalaseema (4 districts)** — Semi-arid Deccan fringe; groundwater-dependent · Groundnut, millets, horticulture; cement, silk, mining (barytes); chronic drought and out-migration
- **Telangana (10 districts)** — Deccan plateau; declining tank irrigation, borewell dependence · Hyderabad as the IT, pharma, real estate and services hub; coal (Singareni)

## Relative shares in GSDP (united AP, based on A.P. Statistical Abstract and Planning Department data)
- Coastal Andhra: 43–45% — agriculture, ports and industry
- Telangana: 40–42% — driven almost entirely by Hyderabad’s services economy
- Rayalaseema: 15–17% — the persistent laggard

## Implications of the disparity
- Coastal Andhra generated rural affluence; Telangana generated concentrated urban prosperity in one city; Rayalaseema generated out-migration and dependence on drought relief.
- The mismatch between Telangana’s contribution and its perceived share of benefits fuelled the statehood demand; Rayalaseema’s backwardness produced repeated demands for special packages, from the Srikrishna Committee (2010) onwards.
- Regional imbalance was thus not just an economic fact but the central political fault line of the State.

## The position after 2014
- Residuary Andhra Pradesh comprises only two of the three regions — Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema — having lost Hyderabad and roughly a third of the undivided State’s revenue.
- Coastal Andhra now accounts for the overwhelming share of State output, with Rayalaseema contributing

roughly a quarter of population and a smaller share of GSDP — meaning the internal disparity has, if anything, sharpened.

- Administrative reorganisation into 26 districts (4 April 2022) was partly aimed at improving governance reach in backward areas.
- Policy has responded with deliberate spatial balancing: industrial nodes at Orvakal and Kopparthy in Rayalaseema alongside Krishnapatnam on the coast; Drone City at Orvakal (Kurnool); the Rayalaseema Drought Mitigation Project; and the three-capital debate itself, which was framed as decentralised development.

## Conclusion

The tri-regional classification captured genuine differences in resource endowment, irrigation and urbanisation, and the GSDP shares showed Coastal Andhra and Telangana as growth engines with Rayalaseema left behind. Bifurcation resolved one imbalance but inherited another. Balanced regional development in residuary Andhra Pradesh — through irrigation in Rayalaseema, port-led growth on the coast, and dispersed industrial nodes — remains the State’s central developmental test.

## Value addition
- GSDP is the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a State’s boundaries in a year, without duplication — the primary indicator of State-level economic growth, compiled sector-wise per NSO methodology.
- Base-year revision: the national accounts series moved from 2004-05 → 2011-12 (2015) → 2022-23, released 27 February 2026 — regional and sectoral comparisons must now use the new base.

## Introduction

Monetary policy is the central bank’s regulation of the money supply, interest rates and credit availability to achieve macroeconomic objectives. In India it is conducted by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934, with the Monetary Policy Committee constituted under Section 45ZB pursuing an inflation target notified by the Government under Section 45ZA.

## Types of monetary policy
- Expansionary (accommodative): lower rates and ample liquidity to revive demand, investment and employment — as in 2020-21 and again through the 2025-26 easing cycle.
- Contractionary (tight): higher rates and liquidity absorption to cool an overheating economy — as in the 250 bps tightening of 2022-23.
- Neutral: the current stance, preserving the option to move either way as data evolve.

## Objectives — a working hierarchy
- **Price stability (primary)** — Maintain CPI at 4% ±2%, “while keeping in mind the objective of growth” — the statutory phrasing · Inflation fell from 8.6% (2013-14) to 1.7% (FY26, April-December)
- **Growth (co-equal in framing)** — Ensure adequate, affordable credit for productive activity · 125 bps of easing since February 2025 supported an 8% H1 FY26 expansion
- **Financial stability** — Sound banks, orderly markets, functioning payment systems · SCB GNPA at 2.2%, CRAR 17.2%
- **Exchange rate stability** — Contain excessive volatility without targeting a level · Reserves of about US$676 billion deployed to smooth 2026 rupee volatility
- **Financial inclusion** — Priority sector lending, refinance, digital payments infrastructure · UPI at ~85% of retail digital payments

## How the objectives interact

The objectives are complements over the medium term and trade-offs in the short run. Low, predictable inflation is pro-growth — it lowers risk premia, protects real wages and enables long-term investment. But in a supply shock the trade-off bites: in June 2026 the MPC held rates despite cutting its growth forecast to 6.6%, because the inflation projection had risen to 5.1%. That choice — accepting slower growth to protect the price anchor — reveals the true hierarchy.

## Conclusion

The RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016 settled a long debate by making price stability the primary objective while retaining growth in view — a design reaffirmed when the Government renotified the 4% ±2% target for 2026-31 on 25 March 2026. Monetary policy is thus not a growth engine but a stability foundation: by anchoring expectations and safeguarding the financial system, it creates the conditions in which fiscal and structural policy can deliver inclusive growth.

## Value addition
- Monetary Policy Committee: six members — RBI Governor (Chair), Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer, and three Government-appointed external members (four-year terms, non-renewable); decisions by majority, Governor holds the casting vote; minutes published on the 14th day.
- Statutory sections to cite: 45ZA (target), 45ZB (MPC), 45ZI (meetings), 45ZL (minutes), 45ZN (failure report).
- Framework lineage: Chakravarty Committee (1985) → multiple-indicator approach (1998) → Urjit Patel Committee (2014) → RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016 → FIT renewals in 2021 and 2026.
- One-line revision point: Price stability is not one objective among many — it is the precondition for the rest.

## Introduction

The Tenth Plan (2002-07) was framed as India entered its second decade of liberalisation, with growth established but its benefits visibly uneven. Its distinguishing innovation was to pair the growth target with monitorable socio-economic targets — the first time an Indian Plan committed to measurable human development outcomes.

## The important objectives

## High and sustained growth
- Achieve 8% GDP growth per annum — the most ambitious target set until then — to sustain the momentum of the 1990s reforms. (Actual: 7.7%.)

## Doubling per capita income
- Double per capita income in ten years, implying about 7% annual growth. (Per capita income rose from ₹24,143 in 2002 to ₹38,005 in 2007 at current prices.)

## Poverty reduction
- Reduce the poverty ratio by 5 percentage points by 2007 and by 15 percentage points by 2012. (Fell from 26.1% to 21.8% by 2004-05.)

## Employment generation
- Create 50 million work opportunities during the Plan, recognising that growth alone was not generating jobs.

(About 47 million created, but predominantly informal.)

## Human development
- Universal access to primary education by 2007; raise literacy to 75%; reduce the gender gap in literacy and wage rates by at least 50%; reduce IMR to 45 per 1,000 and MMR to 2 per 1,000; reduce decadal population growth to 16.2%.

## Environmental sustainability
- Increase forest and tree cover to 25% by 2007; provide potable drinking water to all villages; and clean all major polluted rivers.

## Regional and social equity
- Reduce inter-State disparities through State-wise growth targets — a genuine innovation — with special focus on SC/ST welfare, gender equality and backward regions.

## The conceptual advance

The Tenth Plan was the first to accept that a single national growth number tells you nothing about development. By disaggregating targets by State and by social indicator, it created the framework of accountability that the Eleventh Plan extended and that survives today in NITI Aayog’s SDG India Index and sectoral rankings.

## Conclusion

The Tenth Plan’s objectives combined ambitious growth with an unprecedented commitment to measurable human development. Growth and partial poverty reduction were achieved; agriculture, employment quality and social indicators fell short. Those gaps were not failures of intent but of implementation capacity and sectoral neglect — and their diagnosis directly produced the Eleventh Plan’s turn to “Faster and More Inclusive Growth.”

## Value addition
- Plan themes for quick revision: Tenth (2002-07) — 8% growth with monitorable targets; Eleventh (2007-12) — “Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth”; Twelfth (2012-17) — “Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth.”
- Key launches during the Tenth Plan: Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan scaled up, National Rural Health Mission (2005), MGNREGA (2005), Right to Information Act (2005), NHDP/Golden Quadrilateral, Bharat Nirman (2005), and the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) inserting Article 21A — the right to free and compulsory education.
- Andhra Pradesh in this period: VAT (2005), the AP FRBM Act, 2005, revenue deficit eliminated by 2005-06, and the launch of Jalayagnam (2004).

## Introduction

National income data drives budget-making, monetary policy, devolution of taxes and international comparison. Yet in an economy where nine of ten workers are informal, the Census is overdue, and a large share of output never passes through a market, measurement is inherently difficult. The IMF’s “C” grade (2025) for India’s national accounts underlines the challenge.

## Structural problems
- Informal sector dominance: ~90% of workers are informally employed (ILO); street vendors, home-based workers and micro-units leave no accounting trail. Growth was long extrapolated from decade-old benchmarks.
- Non-monetised transactions: subsistence farming, self-consumption of produce, barter and unpaid family labour lack market prices.
- Unpaid care work: women’s domestic and care work — captured by the Time Use Survey — is economically valuable but excluded from GDP.

## Statistical and data problems
- Outdated sampling frame: delay in the Census forces PLFS / NSS to extrapolate from 2011 population projections.
- Production–expenditure discrepancy: sizeable gaps between GVA-based and expenditure-based GDP estimates.
- Fast-changing sectors: gig work, quick commerce and digital platforms outpace survey design.
- Double-counting risk where intermediate consumption is imperfectly netted out.

## Valuation problems
- Public goods (defence, administration, free health and education) are valued at input cost, understating their true worth.
- Single deflation: deflating only output, and using WPI (a goods index) to deflate services, distorts real growth — the IMF’s central critique.
- Illegal / unreported activity: smuggling, black money and informal lending stay outside GDP.
- Negative externalities: pollution and resource depletion add to GDP instead of being netted out.

## Reforms addressing these gaps
- **Problem** — Reform
- **Outdated base year** — New GDP series, base 2022–23 (Feb 2026)
- **Single deflation** — Double deflation in manufacturing and agriculture
- **Informal sector coverage** — ASUSE + PLFS integration
- **Production–expenditure discrepancy** — Supply and Use Tables (SUT) framework
- **Coverage and timeliness** — GST, e-Vahan, PFMS, MCA21 administrative data
- **Absence of income data** — First Household Income Survey, 2026

## Conclusion

## Introduction

National income is the total value of final goods and services produced in an economy in a year. Because every rupee of output is simultaneously somebody’s income and somebody’s expenditure, the circular flow can be measured at three points — output, income or spending — yielding three approaches that should, in principle, give an identical figure.

BodyCircular Flow: Production (Value Added) → Factor Incomes (W, R, I, P) → Expenditure (C + I + G + X − M) → back to Production

## The three approaches
- **Approach** — Formula · Indian Illustration · Limitation
- **Production / Value Added** — Σ (Value of Output − Intermediate Consumption) · Services ≈ 51.1% of GDP, industry 24.3%, agriculture 15.2% (FY26 FAE) · Informal and own-account output under-recorded
- **Income** — NI = Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Mixed Income · Mixed income is large, as ~55% of workers are self-employed · Self-employed income hard to separate from return to capital
- **Expenditure** — GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) · PFCE 61.5% of GDP (highest since FY12); GFCF 30.0% (FY26 FAE) · Weak rural consumption and investment data

## Reconciliation in India
- MoSPI / NSO publishes GDP from both the production side (GVA) and the expenditure side, aligned with the UN SNA 2008.
- Key bridge: GVA at basic prices + Product Taxes − Product Subsidies = GDP at Market Prices.
- Supply and Use Tables (SUT) are used to close the statistical discrepancy between the two sides.

## The new series (base year 2022–23, released 27 February 2026)
- Double deflation in manufacturing and agriculture, replacing single deflation.
- Administrative data integrated: GST returns, e-Vahan portal, PFMS, MCA21.
- ASUSE + PLFS used to capture the household and informal sector dynamically.
- Coverage of gig, platform and hired domestic workers; segregation of multi-activity enterprises; GST data for regional allocation of private corporate output.

## Conclusion

## Introduction

Procurement price policy is the framework under which the government buys agricultural produce at an assured price to support farmers, build buffer stocks and supply the public distribution system. Three concepts must be distinguished:

- **Minimum Support Price (MSP)** — The floor price at which government agencies will buy; a guarantee against distress sale
- **Procurement Price** — The price at which the government actually buys for the buffer stock and PDS — historically set at or above MSP
- **Issue Price** — The subsidised price at which grain is released through the PDS

- The Government of India’s policy and machinery
- **Recommending body** — The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP), which recommends MSP for 22 mandated crops plus toria and de-husked coconut, considering cost of production, demand and supply, price trends, terms of trade and the likely effect on consumers
- **Deciding authority** — The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), after consulting State governments
- **The formula since 2018-19** — MSP fixed at at least 1.5 times the A2+FL cost of production
- **Cost concepts** — A2 — all paid-out costs; A2+FL — A2 plus imputed unpaid family labour (the basis used); C2 — A2+FL plus imputed rent on owned land and interest on owned capital. The Swaminathan Commission recommended C2+50%
- **Procuring agencies** — FCI for rice and wheat; NAFED, NCCF and SFAC for pulses and oilseeds under PSS; the Cotton Corporation of India and Jute Corporation for fibres
- **PM-AASHA (2018)** — Three components — Price Support Scheme (PSS), Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS) and the Private Procurement and Stockist Scheme (PPSS)
- **Latest decision** — MSP for Kharif Marketing Season 2026-27, approved by the CCEA on 13 May 2026: common paddy ₹2,441 per quintal (up ₹72 from ₹2,369), Grade A paddy ₹2,461; tur ₹8,450; moong ₹8,780; sunflower seed ₹8,343 (the largest absolute increase, +₹622); cotton medium staple ₹8,267. Estimated margins over cost: moong 61%, bajra and maize 56%, tur 54%. Estimated payout about ₹2.60 lakh crore, with over 824 lakh metric tonnes to be procured

- Andhra Pradesh’s role and policy
- **Nature of the State’s role** — Procurement is operationally a State function — the Centre sets the price, the State buys. AP is a decentralised procurement State for rice
- **Agency** — The AP State Civil Supplies Corporation (APSCSCL) procures paddy, mills it into rice and delivers to FCI and the State PDS
- **Village-level procurement** — Rythu Bharosa Kendras function as procurement points, with e-crop booking establishing the farmer’s eligibility and direct e-payment into the farmer’s bank account — eliminating the intermediary
- **Bonus and additional support** — The State has at times paid a bonus over MSP for paddy, and operates price support for crops outside the central ambit — chillies, tobacco, maize, redgram, groundnut
- **Market intervention** — Price stabilisation fund operations in perishables; Rythu Bazaars for direct sale; Digi Rythu Bazaar launched in Visakhapatnam in December 2025
- **The PDS link** — AP’s 1.46 crore rice cards covering about 4.3 crore beneficiaries, with rice at ₹1 per kg, are supplied from this procurement — so procurement policy and food policy are a single system in the State

- Critical examination — what the policy achieves
- It prevents distress sale. A floor price removes the trader’s ability to exploit a farmer who must sell immediately after harvest.
- It underwrites food security. Procurement built the buffer stock that made the NFSA, 2013 — covering about 80.67 crore persons — and PMGKAY (extended to 31 December 2028) possible.
- It stabilises prices for both producer and consumer, dampening the boom-and-bust cycle.
- It made the Green Revolution viable — assured procurement at an assured price was what persuaded farmers to adopt input-intensive HYV technology.
- It transfers income measurably. The FY27 kharif payout of about ₹2.60 lakh crore is a substantial income transfer to farmers.
- Critical examination — the weaknesses
- **Announcement is not procurement** — MSP is effective only where the government actually buys. Procurement is overwhelmingly concentrated in paddy and wheat and in a few States, so for most crops and most farmers the MSP is a notice board rather than a price. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) noted that only a small fraction of farmers actually sell at MSP
- **The contested cost basis** — Using A2+FL rather than C2 excludes the imputed rent on owned land — the farmer’s largest implicit cost. The same MSP therefore shows a 50% margin on one basis and little or none on the other, which is why farmers and government can both quote figures honestly and disagree entirely
- **Cropping pattern distortion** — Assured procurement of paddy and wheat entrenched a water-intensive cycle in water-scarce regions, while pulses and oilseeds remained under-produced — India still imports 56% of its edible oil
- **Regional bias** — Procurement infrastructure is dense in Punjab, Haryana, Telangana and coastal Andhra Pradesh, and thin in the eastern and rain-fed States — so the policy transfers most to those already best served by irrigation
- **Fiscal and storage cost** — Buffer stocks frequently exceed norms; carrying cost, storage loss and the food subsidy bill are large. The World Bank has estimated that grain lost to inadequate storage could feed a third of India’s poor
- **Tenant exclusion** — Procurement is keyed to the land record, so the unrecorded tenant — who bore the entire cost and risk of cultivation — often cannot sell in her own name. AP’s Crop Cultivator Rights Cards and e-crop booking are attempts to correct this
- **Middlemen and quality deductions** — Arbitrary moisture and quality deductions at procurement centres erode the effective price received
- **Delayed payment** — A guaranteed price paid late is a diluted guarantee; direct e-payment through RBKs is AP’s answer to this
- **Consumer-side tension** — High MSP raises the food subsidy bill and, potentially, retail prices — the classic producer-consumer trade-off
- **The legal MSP question** — Farm unions demand a statutory guarantee at C2+50%; the fiscal implication is very large, and the 2020 farm laws — which sought to expand trade outside APMC yards — were repealed in 2021 after sustained protest, leaving the reform question unresolved

- Reform directions
- Price deficiency payment (PDPS) in place of physical procurement for crops the government cannot store — cheaper, avoids storage loss, and can cover more crops.
- Decentralised procurement, as recommended by the Shanta Kumar Committee, reducing transit and carrying cost.
- Widening the crop basket toward pulses, oilseeds and millets — backed by the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (₹11,440 crore, self-sufficiency by December 2027) and the National Mission on Edible Oils.
- Warehouse receipt finance (e-NWR), so the farmer can store and sell when prices recover instead of at harvest.
- e-NAM expansion — now 1,656 mandis with cumulative trade of ₹4.84 lakh crore.
- Direct income support — PM-KISAN and Annadata Sukhibhava — which supports income without distorting crop choice.
- Recognising tenancy so procurement benefits reach the actual cultivator.

## Conclusion

Procurement price policy has been indispensable and unevenly effective. It underwrote India’s food security, made the Green Revolution viable and transfers a very large sum to farmers annually — the FY27 kharif payout alone is about ₹2.60 lakh crore. But it protects a minority of farmers growing a minority of crops in a minority of States, distorts cropping toward water-intensive cereals, and excludes the unrecorded tenant. Andhra Pradesh’s contribution has been on the delivery side — RBK-based procurement with e-crop booking and direct e-payment, which is genuinely best practice. The reform agenda is to broaden the crop and geographic coverage, shift partly to deficiency payments and income support, and make procurement follow the cultivator rather than the land title.

## Value addition
- Institutional detail: MSP is recommended by the CACP for 22 mandated crops plus toria and de-husked coconut, and decided by the CCEA; Rabi MSP for 2026-27 was approved on 1 October 2025 and Kharif on 13 May 2026.
- The cost formula dispute: government uses A2+FL + 50%; the Swaminathan Commission (National Commission on Farmers, 2004-06) recommended C2 + 50% — the difference is the entire political controversy.
- Committee reference: the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) on FCI restructuring recommended decentralised procurement, cash transfers in cities, and reducing NFSA coverage from 67% to 40%.
- AP’s delivery innovation: procurement through Rythu Bharosa Kendras with e-crop booking and direct e-payment — a model that resolves both verification and intermediation, and is cited nationally as best practice.

## Introduction

Keyword discipline: this question asks about both inter-regional and inter-district disparity. Address the district dimension explicitly — that is what distinguishes this answer from Q.196.

Inter-regional disparity in Andhra Pradesh refers to gaps between Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra; inter-district disparity refers to gaps between districts within those regions — West Godavari against Vizianagaram, or Chittoor against Anantapur. The two are related but distinct, and the causes operate at both scales simultaneously.

- Natural and geographical causes
- Rainfall and agro-climate. Rayalaseema receives 500-700 mm against far higher potential evapotranspiration, while the deltas enjoy both monsoon rainfall and canal water. Anantapur is among India’s most drought-prone districts.
- Topography. Flat alluvial deltas permit gravity irrigation; the Deccan fringe of Rayalaseema and the hilly Eastern Ghats of the agency areas do not.
- Soil. Fertile deltaic alluvium against red and shallow soils in Rayalaseema and lateritic soils in the north-east.
- Coastline. The 974-km coastline gives coastal districts ports, fisheries and aquaculture — advantages entirely absent inland.
- Mineral endowment. Barytes and limestone in Kadapa and Kurnool; bauxite in the Eastern Ghats — but extraction has not generated proportionate local prosperity.
- Historical causes
- Colonial irrigation investment. Cotton’s Dowleswaram anicut (1852) and the Krishna anicut created a 170-year head start for the deltas — the single deepest cause.
- Differential land tenure. The Andhra area was ryotwari; the Telangana area (in the united State) was jagirdari with vetti bonded labour — producing different agrarian structures and different levels of accumulation.
- The Green Revolution. Because the HYV package required assured irrigation, it amplified rather than reduced the pre-existing gap.
- Economic causes
- Irrigation access — the proximate determinant of agricultural productivity and hence of rural income.
- Industrial concentration. Investment clusters around Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada-Guntur and Tirupati, drawn by ports, power, connectivity and urban labour markets.
- Urbanisation. The State is only about 29.5% urbanised, and urban centres are coastal — so non-farm employment is spatially concentrated.
- Connectivity. National highways, ports and airports follow the coast; interior districts have thinner road, rail and logistics networks.
- Credit flow follows prosperity. Banks lend where repayment is assured, which is where irrigation already exists — so the delta absorbs a disproportionate share of institutional credit.
- Agglomeration economies. Once a district acquires industry, further investment follows — disparity is self-reinforcing unless deliberately countered.
- Social and human capital causes

1. Literacy. AP’s overall literacy of 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States, and the deficit is concentrated in the lagging districts. Census 2011 showed West Godavari 74.63% and Krishna 73.74% against Vizianagaram 58.89% and Kurnool 59.97%.

- Social composition. SC households are disproportionately landless; ST and PVTG populations are concentrated in the Eastern Ghats agency areas of Alluri Sitharama Raju and Parvathipuram Manyam, where deprivation is highest.
- Health and nutrition. Child marriage at 29.3% (NFHS-5) is above the national average and higher among Scheduled Tribes; wasting affects 16.1% of children under five.
- Out-migration drains the working-age population from Rayalaseema and the agency areas.
- Institutional and policy causes
- Unrecorded tenancy. With among India’s highest tenancy incidence, almost entirely oral, cultivators in high-tenancy districts are excluded from credit, insurance and compensation.
- Inter-State water disputes. Krishna allocation unsettled before the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II, creating uncertainty for Rayalaseema schemes.
- Project delays. Lift irrigation schemes have long gestation, high cost and heavy energy requirements — so they were repeatedly deferred while delta systems already functioned.
- Bifurcation (2014). The loss of Hyderabad removed the State’s largest urban labour market and its principal services engine, reducing the escape route from rural poverty everywhere, but especially for interior districts.
- Administrative reach. The reorganisation into 26 districts (4 April 2022) was partly intended to improve governance penetration in backward areas.
- The inter-district dimension specifically

Disparity is not merely between the three regions but sharp within each: - Within Coastal Andhra: West Godavari, East Godavari, Krishna and Guntur prosper on delta irrigation, while Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Parvathipuram Manyam — also coastal — lag badly, because they lie outside the delta command. - Within Rayalaseema: Chittoor and Tirupati benefit from proximity to Bengaluru and Chennai, temple tourism and industry, while Anantapur and Sri Sathya Sai face severe drought. - Within any district: tribal agency mandals lag the plains mandals of the same district.

The lesson: using regional averages conceals district and mandal-level deprivation. This is precisely why NITI Aayog moved from State-level to district (112 Aspirational Districts) and block-level (500 Aspirational Blocks) targeting.

## Conclusion

Disparities in Andhra Pradesh arise from a compounding sequence: natural endowment determined where irrigation was feasible, colonial investment built it there, the Green Revolution rewarded it, industry and urbanisation followed the resulting prosperity, and credit and human capital followed industry. Each stage reinforced the last. Reversing it therefore requires deliberate counter-agglomeration — irrigation for the rain-fed regions, industry located in Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra, and above all education, since no district can move up the value chain faster than its literacy allows.

- Committee reference: the Srikrishna Committee (2010) on Telangana examined regional development indicators across united Andhra Pradesh in detail and remains the standard analytical source on the State’s regional imbalance.
- Theoretical framing: Myrdal’s cumulative causation and Hirschman’s polarisation effects explain why disparity is self-reinforcing; Williamson’s inverted-U hypothesis suggests it eventually narrows with development.
- Administrative response: reorganisation into 26 districts (April 2022); 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency, as an explicit dispersal mechanism.
- The measurement point: AP was the first Indian State to adopt its own MPI (2018), precisely to identify sub-State pockets of deprivation that averages conceal.

## Introduction

Microfinance is the provision of small-value financial services — credit, savings, insurance and remittances — to low-income households without collateral or credit history. It solved a problem formal banking could not: how to lend small sums to people the banking system regarded as unbankable. Andhra Pradesh is central to this story — it built India’s largest microfinance network and also produced the 2010 crisis that reshaped the sector’s regulation nationally.

The gap microfinance fills

Institutional credit in Andhra Pradesh follows the land record. Since the State has among India’s highest tenancy incidence, almost entirely oral and unrecorded, and since a large share of rural households are landless, the formal system systematically excluded: - Tenant cultivators and landless agricultural labourers; - Women, who rarely hold land in their own names; - SC, ST and PVTG households, disproportionately landless; - Anyone needing credit for consumption — illness, education, weddings — which no bank finances.

Significance of microfinance institutions

- Substituting collateral with social capital — the core innovation By using joint liability and peer monitoring in place of physical collateral, microfinance made the poor bankable. Andhra Pradesh’s SERP network of about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women achieves repayment consistently above 97% — proof that the constraint was never borrower reliability but transaction cost.
- Displacing the moneylender For small, immediate needs, microfinance is faster and vastly cheaper than informal borrowing. Nationally, among unincorporated manufacturing units, formal credit use rose from 48% (2021-22) to 51% (2023-24), with reliance on moneylenders and suppliers falling.
- Women’s economic agency The FY25 microfinance profile shows 627 lakh active borrowers, a gross loan portfolio of ₹2.38 lakh crore, and 95% women borrowers with 80% rural — the largest financial-inclusion channel for women in India. In Andhra Pradesh, Stree Nidhi goes further: it is a credit cooperative federation whose Managing Committee has 13 of 20 directors elected from mandal samakhyas — women as directors of a financial institution, not merely its clients.
- Speed and flexibility Internal group lending disburses within days without documentation — critical because agriculture is calendar-bound and credit arriving after the sowing window is worth a fraction of its value.
- Consumption smoothing Microfinance lends for health emergencies, school fees and lean-season consumption, protecting households from distress sale of assets. This is the single largest welfare contribution, and precisely what banks will not do.
- A platform beyond credit The SHG network became the delivery channel for pensions, health insurance enrolment, DBT and Community-Managed Sustainable Agriculture — its institutional value now exceeds its lending value.
- National influence The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, launched by NABARD in 1992, grew into the world’s largest microfinance programme by outreach; AP’s federated SERP model became the design basis for NRLM (2011), now DAY-NRLM.

The 2010 crisis — the necessary qualification

Andhra Pradesh was the epicentre of India’s microfinance crisis: - Over-lending and multiple lending by commercial MFIs to the same households; - Coercive recovery, publicly linked to borrower suicides; - A regulatory vacuum — MFIs operated as NBFCs without conduct regulation; - Institutional conflict, as commercial MFIs targeted the very SHG members the State network served.

The AP Microfinance Institutions (Regulation of Money Lending) Ordinance, 2010 effectively halted commercial MFI operations in the State. Nationally, it produced the Malegam Committee (2011), the creation of the NBFC-MFI category, caps on interest and indebtedness, and a prohibition on coercive recovery. India’s microfinance regulation was born from Andhra Pradesh’s crisis.

Crucially, the SHG network survived and kept lending when commercial MFIs collapsed — the strongest evidence for the community-owned model over the commercial one.

Continuing risks

- Purpose mismatch: loans often finance consumption or debt-swapping rather than enterprise. Credit that does not raise income cannot be repaid from income.
- Over-indebtedness recurred in FY25, when MFI loans outstanding fell about 14%; the RBI responded by reducing NBFC-MFI qualifying assets from 75% to 60% (June 2025), letting lenders diversify.
- Elite capture within some federations, with the poorest and PVTG households hardest to include.
- Ticket size suits micro-needs but cannot finance term investment — irrigation, mechanisation, storage.

## Conclusion

Microfinance institutions have been decisive in meeting the credit needs of precisely those Andhra Pradesh’s formal system excluded — women, the landless, tenants and those needing consumption credit. The State’s community-owned SHG model, with repayment above 97%, has proved more durable than the commercial MFI model that collapsed in 2010. The next stage is to move from credit-led to enterprise-led microfinance: linking SHGs to Farmer Producer Organisations, term credit and market access, so that group membership generates income rather than only access to loans.

## Value addition
- The two models contrasted: the SHG-Bank Linkage model (NABARD, 1992) is savings-led and community-governed; the MFI model is credit-led and externally governed — the 2010 crisis was fundamentally a clash between them.
- Malegam Committee (2011) recommendations: create the NBFC-MFI category; cap margin and interest; bar lending to a borrower already indebted to two other MFIs; cap total indebtedness; prohibit coercive recovery and collection at the borrower’s residence.
- RBI’s 2022 framework replaced rigid caps with a household income-based repayment capacity test, limiting repayment obligations to 50% of monthly household income.
- The interest gap that explains the demand: the KCC’s effective rate is 4% after subvention, against informal rates several times higher — microfinance sits between the two.

My considered view is that land reforms in Andhra Pradesh have provided tenants ample protection on paper and almost none in practice — and, more troublingly, that the protection itself became the cause of the exclusion. This is the paradox that defines tenancy policy in the State.

What the law provided — the case that protection was sufficient

- The Telangana area — AP (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 - Conferred protected-tenant status; - Regulated rent; - Gave protected tenants the right to purchase the land they cultivated; - Restricted the landlord’s right of resumption.
- The Andhra area — AP (Andhra Area) Tenancy Act, 1956 - Minimum lease period, extended to six years by the 1974 amendment; - Fair rent fixed as a share of gross produce, differentiated between wet and dry land; - Eviction only through revenue authorities on specified grounds; - Right of restoration if wrongfully evicted; - Compensation for improvements made by the tenant; - First option to purchase if the landlord sold; - Bar on sub-letting, preventing a second layer of intermediaries.
- Constitutional protection Land reform laws were placed in the Ninth Schedule under Article 31B, immunising them from judicial challenge.

On the statute book, therefore, the protection was substantial and, by the standards of the 1950s, progressive.

Why it proved insufficient — the case against

- The protection created the concealment Because a recorded tenant acquired security and possible purchase rights, landowners responded rationally: they stopped recording tenancies altogether. Andhra Pradesh consequently has among India’s highest tenancy incidence and among its lowest recorded tenancy — the gap between the two is the measure of the reform’s failure.
- The unrecorded tenant lost more than tenure He lost access to institutional credit, crop insurance, input subsidy, calamity compensation and procurement benefits — all of which follow the land record. The Koneru Ranga Rao Land Committee (2006) established that this exclusion also made tenants ineligible for loan waivers and relief operations, so they were doubly penalised: excluded when things went well, and excluded again when the State intervened after failure.
- The consequence was debt, not merely insecurity Denied bank credit, tenants borrowed informally at punitive rates. The Committee identified this chain explicitly as driving tenants into the debt trap and, in the agrarian distress of that period, to suicide.
- Practices that defeated the law - Annual rotation of tenants, so no continuous possession could mature into a claim. - Oral, seasonal arrangements with no documentary trace. - Rents above the statutory ceiling, unenforceable because the tenancy itself was denied. - Eviction by simple refusal to renew, requiring no legal process at all.
- Enforcement machinery was weak Remedies lay with revenue authorities who were under-staffed, and a tenant seeking a remedy had first to prove a tenancy the landlord denied — an evidentiary burden almost impossible to discharge without documents.
- The Andhra area Act was deliberately “soft” Unlike the Telangana Act of 1950, it regulated the relationship without conferring ownership — so even fully implemented, it offered less than its Telangana counterpart.

The corrective phase — a change of approach

Recognising that conferring rights had produced exclusion, the State shifted to functional recognition:

- **AP Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011** — Loan Eligibility Cards, valid eleven months, expressly conferring no right, title or interest — enabling credit, insurance and subsidy without creating tenancy
- **AP Crop Cultivator Rights Act, 2019** — Crop Cultivator Rights Cards, with owner consent and clearer scheme integration
- **Annadata Sukhibhava** — ₹20,000 a year paid directly, explicitly covering tenant farmers — bypassing the lender entirely

But uptake has remained limited, because owners — conditioned by fifty years of tenancy legislation — still fear that any documentation may eventually ripen into a claim. The corrective is sound in design and constrained by the distrust the original protection created.

## Conclusion

I do not consider that land reforms in Andhra Pradesh have provided sufficient protection to tenants. They provided sufficient rights and insufficient reach: by making recorded tenancy dangerous for the landowner, the law drove the relationship underground and thereby stripped the tenant of the credit, insurance and relief that matter more, in practice, than tenure security. The route forward is the one the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016 proposes

— legalise and record leasing while guaranteeing the owner’s title against adverse possession, so that recognition costs the owner nothing and gains the tenant everything. Protection that cannot be claimed is not protection.

## Value addition
- The two Acts contrasted: AP (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 — protected-tenant status and purchase rights; AP (Andhra Area) Tenancy Act, 1956 — regulation without ownership, with a “soft” 1974 amendment extending the minimum lease to six years.
- The diagnostic authority: the Koneru Ranga Rao Land Committee (2006) — 104 recommendations, about 90 accepted — whose tenancy chapter produced the 2011 Act.
- The credit consequence quantified: agriculture’s GNPA across scheduled commercial banks stands at 6.0%, the highest of any sector; the excluded tenant borrows informally at several times the KCC’s effective 4%.
- The national reform proposal: the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016 legalises leasing, protects the owner against adverse possession, and extends credit, insurance and disaster relief to the recorded tenant.

The apparent contradiction dissolves once the two measures are separated:

Agriculture produces 37% of the State’s value added but supports about 50% of its workers.

This is the productivity gap. Services have overtaken agriculture in output but not in employment, because services growth in AP is concentrated in skill-intensive urban activity that the rural workforce cannot enter — a constraint sharpened by the State’s literacy rate of 72.6%, the lowest among Indian States.

Two features separate Andhra Pradesh from the national pattern:

## Introduction

Indian employment is seasonal, intermittent and largely informal, so a single question — “are you employed?” — cannot capture it. The NSSO therefore developed a family of concepts using different reference periods and activity statuses, so that the same worker can be classified differently depending on the lens applied. Since 2017-18 these concepts are applied through the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), conducted by the National Statistical Office (NSO), which replaced the quinquennial Employment-Unemployment Survey.

- Activity status — the building block

Every person is classified into one of three categories:

- **Working (employed)** — Engaged in any economic activity
- **Seeking or available for work (unemployed)** — Not working but willing and available
- **Neither** — Students, homemakers, elderly, disabled — outside the labour force

The first two together constitute the labour force.

- Reference periods — the four measures
- **Usual Principal Status (UPS)** — 365 days · The activity on which a person spent the majority of time in the preceding year · Long-term, “chronic” employment status
- **Usual Principal and Subsidiary Status (UPSS)** — 365 days · UPS plus anyone who worked in a subsidiary capacity for 30 days or more · The broadest measure — yields the highest employment and lowest unemployment
- **Current Weekly Status (CWS)** — 7 days · A person is employed if she worked at least one hour on any one day in the reference week · Captures short-term and seasonal fluctuation
- **Current Daily Status (CDS)** — Each day of 7 days · Activity recorded in half-day units for each of the seven days · The most rigorous — captures underemployment and intermittent work; yields the highest unemployment

The relationship to remember: Unemployment measured by CDS > CWS > UPS > UPSS. The gap between them is itself the measure of underemployment and seasonality — which is why the four measures are read together rather than in isolation.

- The key rates
- **Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR)** — Persons working or seeking work ÷ total population · 59.3% (male 79.1%, female 40.0%; rural 62.8%, urban 52.2%)
- **Worker Population Ratio (WPR)** — Persons employed ÷ total population · Employment of about 56.2 crore persons (Q2 FY26)
- **Unemployment Rate (UR)** — Unemployed ÷ labour force · 3.1%

- Other essential classifications
- Employment status: self-employed (own-account workers, employers, unpaid family helpers); regular wage/salaried; casual labour.
- Census counterparts: main workers (employed 183 days or more in a year) and marginal workers (fewer than 183 days) — the latter being a proxy for underemployment.
- Informal employment: workers without written contracts, paid leave or social security — the dominant category in India.
- Why the low unemployment rate is misleading

India’s UR of 3.1% looks enviable by global standards, but it reflects the reality that the poor cannot afford to be unemployed — they take whatever work is available, however unproductive. The real problem appears not in the unemployment rate but in underemployment, informality and low earnings: the unincorporated sector employs 12.9 crore persons, and 42% of formal manufacturing workers are contractual. This is why the CDS measure and the quality-of-employment indicators matter more than the headline rate.

- The institutional evolution — worth stating
- NSSO conducted quinquennial Employment-Unemployment Surveys until 2011-12.
- NSSO merged into the NSO in 2019.
- PLFS (from 2017-18) replaced the EUS, providing annual rural-plus-urban estimates and quarterly urban estimates.
- PLFS was revamped from January 2025 — monthly bulletins from April 2025, quarterly rural and urban estimates, with district-level estimates targeted by 2026.

## Conclusion

The NSSO framework’s real insight is that employment in India is a matter of degree, not a binary. By varying the reference period from a year to a single day, it converts a simple question into a spectrum that reveals seasonality, subsidiary work and underemployment. With PLFS now producing monthly data, India has moved from a five-yearly snapshot to near-real-time labour statistics — a decisive improvement for policy that must respond to shocks within months, not years.

## Introduction

India’s anti-poverty architecture has evolved through three distinct generations — from area and asset-based programmes in the 1970s and 1980s, to rights-based entitlements in the 2000s, to saturation and direct-transfer delivery since 2014. Together they have contributed to a fall in the National MPI headcount from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23).

Generation 1: Asset and area-based (1970s-1990s)

- IRDP (1978) — subsidised credit for income-generating assets to identified BPL families.
- NREP and RLEGP — rural wage employment through public works.
- JRY (1989), later SGSY (1999) for self-employment through SHGs, and SJSRY (1997) for the urban poor.
- PMRY for educated unemployed youth. Limitation: dependent on official BPL lists, prone to leakage and elite capture.

Generation 2: Rights-based entitlements (2005 onwards)

- MGNREGA (2005) — a legal guarantee of 100 days of wage employment per rural household; demand-driven and self-selecting, with one-third of work reserved for women; recently restructured under the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika Mission (Rural) Act, 2025, a change several States have contested.
- National Food Security Act, 2013 — legal entitlement to subsidised foodgrain, covering about 80.67 crore persons.
- Right to Education (Art. 21A, 2009) and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 — poverty reduction through rights rather than schemes.

Generation 3: Saturation and direct transfer (2014 onwards)

- **Livelihoods — rural** — DAY-NRLM · SHG federations with credit linkage; built on the Andhra Pradesh SERP model
- **Livelihoods — urban** — DAY-NULM, PM SVANidhi · Skills, self-employment, shelters; collateral-free micro-loans to street vendors with interest subvention
- **Housing** — PMAY (Gramin and Urban) · Grant and credit-linked subsidy; assets typically in women’s names
- **Health** — Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY · ₹5 lakh per family per year; extended in 2024 to all citizens aged 70 and above
- **Income support** — PM-KISAN · ₹6,000 a year in three instalments by DBT; linked to the Kisan Credit Card
- **Nutrition** — POSHAN 2.0, PM POSHAN · Supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, school meals
- **Basic services** — Jal Jeevan Mission, Swachh Bharat, Saubhagya, Ujjwala · The saturation approach that drove most of the MPI decline
- **Social security** — NSAP, PMJJBY, PMSBY, Atal Pension Yojana · Pensions and micro-insurance for the unorganised sector
- **Skills and jobs** — Skill India, PMKVY, ELI Scheme (₹99,446 crore) · ELI targets over 3.5 crore jobs including 1.92 crore first-timers
- **Credit** — PMMY (MUDRA), Stand-Up India, PM Vishwakarma · Collateral-free credit to first-time and small borrowers

The delivery revolution

The JAM trinity, PFMS, Just-in-Time releases and the Aadhaar-enabled Payment System underpin all of the above. Cumulative DBT savings exceed ₹3.5 lakh crore, and One Nation One Ration Card made food entitlements portable across States for migrant workers.

Achievements: about 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty in nine years; rural poverty fell from 32.59% to 19.28% between 2015-16 and 2019-21; improvement in nutrition, years of schooling, sanitation and cooking fuel drove most of the decline.

India’s anti-poverty programmes have moved from assets to rights to saturation, and each generation corrected a weakness of the last. The architecture now delivers reliably at scale — the delivery problem has largely been solved. The unfinished task is the design one: consolidating fragmented schemes, updating beneficiary databases, building an urban livelihoods mission, and shifting from unconditional transfers to conditional, time-bound support that builds capability rather than only providing relief.
