## Introduction

India’s Constitution creates a deliberate asymmetry: the Union commands the more elastic and buoyant taxes, while the States bear the heavier expenditure responsibilities — health, education, police, agriculture, irrigation. The Finance Commission, under Article 280, exists to correct this designed imbalance. Dr. Ambedkar described the arrangement as one of “federalism with a strong centre”; the Finance Commission is the mechanism that keeps that centralisation fiscally fair.

## Constitutional mandate

Constituted by the President every fifth year or earlier, comprising a Chairperson and four members. Its recommendations are advisory, but must be laid before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum on action taken (Art. 281) — a transparency requirement that has made near-total acceptance the constitutional convention.

## Core functions
- **Vertical devolution** — Determines the States’ share of the divisible pool — currently 41% under the 16th FC
- **Horizontal devolution** — Distributes that share among States using a formula balancing need, capacity and performance
- **Grants-in-aid (Art. 275)** — Recommends revenue-deficit, sectoral, state-specific and disaster grants
- **Strengthening the third tier** — Recommends measures to augment State Consolidated Funds to supplement panchayat and municipal resources, based on State Finance Commission reports
- **Disaster financing** — Frames the architecture of the National and State Disaster Response Funds
- **Fiscal consolidation** — Advises on deficit and debt paths for both levels of government
- **Other referred matters** — Any question of sound finance referred by the President — the source of much of its modern innovation

## Role in Indian federalism
- Corrects vertical imbalance: the Union collects the bulk of revenue; the States spend the bulk of it. Devolution closes that structural gap.
- Corrects horizontal imbalance: the income-distance criterion transfers proportionately more to poorer States — a fiscal expression of the Preamble’s commitment to equality.
- Depoliticises transfers: a formula-based, quinquennial award insulates resource-sharing from year-to-year political bargaining.
- Provides predictability: a five-year entitlement enables States to plan capital investment beyond the annual budget cycle.
- Deepens decentralisation: direct grants to panchayats and municipalities have made the Finance Commission the single most important funder of India’s third tier.
- Incentivises reform: through criteria such as demographic performance, forest cover, tax effort and now

contribution to GDP, it shapes State behaviour without commanding it.

## Limitations
- Advisory status: the Union may deviate, and has done so on specific recommendations.
- Cess and surcharge outside the divisible pool (Art. 271) shrink the effective share below the notional figure — the sharpest and most persistent State grievance.
- Terms of Reference are set by the Union, which can shape outcomes before deliberation begins.
- Contested criteria: population weight versus demographic performance divides north and south; equity versus contribution divides poorer and richer States.
- Parallel channels: centrally sponsored schemes and, earlier, Planning Commission transfers created routes outside the Commission’s purview.

## Conclusion

The Finance Commission is the constitutional linchpin of Indian fiscal federalism — an expert, periodic, formula-driven arbiter between competing legitimate claims. Its advisory status has proved a strength rather than a weakness: precisely because it cannot compel, it has had to persuade, and the consistent acceptance of its awards across seventy-five years and every political configuration is the measure of its authority. Its central unfinished task is to bring cess and surcharge within the divisible pool, so that the share it recommends is the share States actually receive.

## Value addition
- The 16th Finance Commission (Chairperson: Dr. Arvind Panagariya) — constituted 31 December 2023, report submitted 17 November 2025, tabled in Parliament 1 February 2026; award period 2026-27 to 2030-31, effective 1 April 2026. Vertical share 41%; new criterion Contribution to GDP (10%); grants of ₹9.47 lakh crore, of which

₹7.91 lakh crore for local bodies and ₹1.56 lakh crore for disaster management.

- Devolution history: 10th FC 29.5% → 13th FC 32% → 14th FC 42% → 15th FC 41% → 16th FC 41%.
- State Finance Commissions: Art. 243-I and Art. 243-Y — the Governor must constitute an SFC every five years; the Union Finance Commission has repeatedly flagged delays in their constitution as the weakest link in Indian fiscal federalism.
- Andhra Pradesh’s trajectory: 4.31% (14th) → 4.05% (15th) → 4.22% (16th), worth ₹64,362 crore in 2026-27.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh has been among the World Bank’s most engaged Indian States since the 1980s. The relationship has passed through three phases — project lending (irrigation, power, roads), policy-based structural adjustment in the late 1990s, and a current phase of results-based urban and capital-city financing. Its record is genuinely mixed, which is what makes it an instructive case in external assistance.

## Nature and scope

Long-term concessional loans (IBRD/IDA) plus technical assistance, routed through the Union Government under Article 293(1), since States cannot borrow abroad directly. Major engagements included the AP Economic Restructuring Project (APERP), the Irrigation Sector Restructuring Project, the Road Sector Project and Urban Reforms Projects.

## Developmental gains
- **Power** — The AP Power Sector Restructuring Project (1999-2004) supported unbundling of the APSEB into generation, transmission and distribution companies, cutting T&D losses and improving commercial discipline
- **Roads** — The Roads and Buildings Project (2003-09) upgraded over 2,000 km of state highways, improving market access and logistics
- **Rural livelihoods** — Support to SERP / Indira Kranthi Patham built a network of about 11 lakh SHGs covering over 1 crore women — arguably the most successful community institution-building in India, and the platform that later helped AP recover from the 2010 microfinance crisis
- **Governance** — Treasury computerisation, e-governance and public financial management reform under the Public Management and Fiscal Services Project

## Criticisms — the other side
- Conditionality and the reform agenda: APERP-linked conditions on downsizing public employment, privatising utilities and cutting subsidies were widely seen as socially regressive and politically imposed; the electoral reaction of 2004 is often read partly as a verdict on them.
- Fiscal burden: external assistance is debt, not aid. Debt servicing rose to nearly 20% of revenue receipts by 2010-11, and exchange-rate movements add a currency risk the State does not control.
- Displacement and environment: irrigation projects, including the Srisailam Left Bank Canal, raised resettlement and ecological concerns.
- Ownership question: externally designed programmes can substitute donor priorities for State priorities, and technical assistance can crowd out domestic institutional capacity.

## The current phase — a different model

Multilateral engagement with AP has revived on a much larger scale and on a results-based rather than conditionality-heavy design:

- World Bank: US$800 million — Amaravati Integrated Urban Development Program (approved December 2024; 29-year maturity with a 6-year grace period).
- ADB: US$788.8 million — Amaravati Inclusive and Sustainable Capital City Development Program (¥121.97 billion), approved December 2024.
- Together about US$1.6 billion (₹13,500 crore) for Phase-I of a ₹15,000 crore programme, with the Centre funding the balance and servicing the loans; by early 2026 the World Bank had released US$340 million.
- Additionally, AIIB-assisted AMRUT 2.0 projects and an extra ₹4,000 crore under UIDF.

## Conclusion

World Bank assistance materially modernised Andhra Pradesh’s power sector, highways, rural institutions and treasury systems — gains that outlived the projects themselves. But the experience also shows that external finance carries a policy price and a debt cost. The lesson for the current Amaravati programme is that external capital works best when it funds assets that generate returns, is embedded in State-owned priorities, and is matched by domestic institutional capacity to execute — not when it substitutes for either.

## Value addition
- World Bank Group: founded 1944 (Bretton Woods); comprises IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. IBRD lends to middle-income countries on near-market terms; IDA provides concessional credit. India graduated from IDA in 2014 and now borrows chiefly from IBRD.
- Routing rule: States cannot borrow externally on their own — Article 293(1) confines State borrowing to within India; external loans are contracted by the Union and passed on as back-to-back loans or grants.
- Amaravati programme scale: master plan of 217 sq km for 3.5 million people by 2050, built on a land-pooling scheme of about 33,000 acres — one of the world’s largest participatory land assemblies.
- Related institutions in AP: ADB-supported Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC), part of the East Coast Economic Corridor — India’s first coastal economic corridor.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh has recorded one of India’s steadier declines in poverty. Measured by the official Tendulkar methodology, the incidence in the undivided State fell from about 44.6% in 1993-94 to 29.9% in 2004-05 and to roughly 9.2% by 2011-12 — placing it well below the national average of 21.9%. On the multidimensional measure, the State now belongs to the group of 14 States with low multidimensional poverty.

The long-run trend (Tendulkar methodology, undivided Andhra Pradesh)

- **Year** — Poverty incidence · National average
- **1993-94** — ~44.6% · 45.3%
- **2004-05** — ~29.9% · 37.2%
- **2011-12** — ~9.2% (rural ~11.0%, urban ~5.8%) · 21.9%

A necessary caveat: these are the last official consumption-based estimates. India has had no updated official poverty line since 2011-12, so post-2011 trends must be read from the National MPI and consumption surveys rather than from a poverty line.

The multidimensional trend

- AP’s MPI headcount more than halved between 2015-16 and 2019-21.
- The group of States with low multidimensional poverty doubled from 7 to 14 in that period, with Andhra Pradesh among the new entrants alongside Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Haryana, Manipur and Uttarakhand.
- Nationally, rural poverty fell from 32.59% to 19.28% over the same period — the saturation effect that drove AP’s decline too.

Key trends to highlight

- Rural poverty fell fastest. MGNREGA wages, SHG credit, pensions, housing, electrification, LPG and sanitation saturation lifted rural standard-of-living indicators sharply — which is where the largest deficits had been.
- The rural-urban gap narrowed, but urban poverty improved more slowly, being concentrated in slums and among informal migrant workers where deprivation is about housing, tenure and services rather than about employment days.
- Regional  disparity  persists.  The  Krishna-Godavari  delta  districts  outperform  Rayalaseema  —  semi-arid, groundwater-dependent, drought-prone — and North Coastal Andhra, with its tribal agency areas.
- Social disparity persists. SC, ST and PVTG households show higher deprivation within every district.
- Bifurcation reset the baseline. The loss of Hyderabad in 2014 removed the State’s largest urban labour market, so the residuary State is only about 29.5% urbanised — a structural constraint on further poverty reduction through urban employment.

Drivers of the decline

- Growth and diversification: per capita GSDP reached ₹2,70,295 (2023-24) against India’s ₹2,15,935; aquaculture, horticulture and food processing raised rural incomes.
- Irrigation expansion through Jalayagnam, HNSS, Polavaram and allied projects.
- Community institutions: the SERP network of about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women.
- Welfare delivery through DBT: NTR Bharosa pensions (over ₹58,000 crore in 19 months), Annadata Sukhibhava, Deepam 2.0 reaching 1.08 crore women, Talliki Vandanam covering 67.27 lakh students.
- Basic-service saturation in housing, electricity, sanitation and cooking fuel.

What remains

AP’s literacy at 72.6% is the lowest among Indian States, its fertility has fallen to about 1.5 with the 60-plus share rising toward 19% by 2047, and agriculture still holds a disproportionate share of the workforce. Further poverty reduction must therefore come from productivity and human capital, not from further service saturation.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s poverty incidence has fallen substantially and consistently, moving the State into India’s low-poverty group. But the decline so far has been driven largely by income support and basic-service saturation — gains that cannot be repeated. Sustaining progress requires the harder work of raising farm and non-farm productivity, closing the literacy gap, and creating formal jobs — which is precisely the agenda of Zero Poverty through the P4 model under Swarna Andhra @2047.

## Value addition
- Measurement caution to state in the answer: Tendulkar-based estimates end at 2011-12; the Rangarajan Committee (2014) proposed a higher line (₹972 rural / ₹1,407 urban) implying substantially higher poverty, but was never officially adopted.
- AP’s pioneering role: the first Indian State to adopt a Multidimensional Poverty Index (2018), ahead of the National MPI baseline of 2021.
- National MPI method: 12 indicators across health, education and standard of living, equally weighted dimensions, Alkire-Foster method; MPI = headcount (H) × intensity (A).
- Institutional backbone: SERP and Stree Nidhi in rural areas, MEPMA for the urban poor.

Demography studies population size, composition and distribution through indicators such as fertility, mortality, sex ratio, density and urbanisation. Andhra Pradesh’s demographic profile is distinctive among Indian States: it has completed its demographic transition early, with fertility now far below replacement level and an ageing population — making its challenges the opposite of the northern States’.

Core demographic features (Census 2011, residuary Andhra Pradesh)

- **Indicator** — Value
- **Population** — 4.94 crore (about 4.1% of India)
- **Decadal growth (2001-11)** — 10.98% against India’s 17.64%
- **Sex ratio** — 996 females per 1,000 males — above the national 943
- **Child sex ratio (0-6)** — 939
- **Density** — 308 persons per sq km
- **Urbanisation** — About 29.5% — a predominantly rural State
- **Literacy** — 67.35% (male 74.77%, female 59.96%)

Changes over time — five clear trends

- Population growth has decelerated sharply Decadal growth fell from 14.59% (1991-2001) to 10.98% (2001-11), well below the national rate. AP was among the earliest States to stabilise its population.
- Fertility has collapsed below replacement The total fertility rate fell from 3.0 in 1993 to 1.7 (NFHS-5, 2019-21) and to about 1.5 currently — against the replacement level of 2.1 and the national 1.91. Urban TFR is 1.47, rural 1.78. Over 77% of currently married women and 74% of men aged 15-49 report not wanting more children.
- The population is ageing rapidly Those aged 60 and above form about 11% of the population and are projected to reach 19% by 2047 — an ageing trajectory closer to that of an upper-middle-income country than of most Indian States.
- Sex ratio has improved, child sex ratio has not The overall sex ratio (996) is among the healthiest in India, but the child sex ratio fell to 939, indicating persistent son preference despite the PCPNDT Act.

and Nellore. With about two-thirds of the population still rural, AP lags the roughly 50% urbanisation typical at its income level — a constraint on productivity, since urban agglomeration drives services growth.

Other significant features

- Literacy is the weakest indicator: PLFS 2023-24 records AP at 72.6%, against India’s 80.9% — the lowest among Indian States.
- Social composition: SCs about 17% and STs about 5.5%, with PVTG populations concentrated in the Eastern Ghats agency areas.
- Migration: significant out-migration of skilled youth to Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai, alongside in-migration of labour to aquaculture and construction.

Recognising the demographic risk, Andhra Pradesh repealed the two-child norm for local body elections through the AP Municipal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2024 and corresponding Panchayat Raj amendments — reversing a 1994 rule. In March 2026 the State announced India’s first Population Management Policy, to be implemented from 1 April 2026. Telangana followed with its Panchayat Raj (Amendment) Bill, 2026.

Andhra Pradesh’s demography reflects a State that has succeeded at population stabilisation and must now manage its consequences. Falling fertility, rising longevity and out-migration mean the working-age share will peak within roughly a decade. The policy priority therefore shifts from controlling numbers to raising the productivity of a shrinking cohort — through literacy, skilling, female workforce participation and health — while simultaneously building pension and geriatric care systems for a population that will be substantially older by 2047.

- Definitions: Total Fertility Rate — average number of children a woman would bear over her reproductive life; replacement level is 2.1. Sex ratio — females per 1,000 males. Demographic transition — the shift from high birth and death rates to low ones.

## Introduction

Allocation reveals intent; expenditure reveals capacity. Comparing Andhra Pradesh’s Tenth (2002-07) and Eleventh (2007-12) Plans shows a clear evolution of intent — from growth-first to inclusion-first — but a persistent failure to convert allocation into outcomes.

## Tenth Plan (2002-07): growth-focused with social overtones
- Energy dominated, absorbing about 26.48% of total plan outlay nationally — necessary to power projected industrial and agricultural growth.
- Social sector received about 22.77% — significant, but the operating assumption remained that growth would trickle down.
- Agriculture was treated as the core instrument of poverty reduction, with targeted sectoral interventions.

## Eleventh Plan (2007-12): the inclusion thrust
- Total public sector outlay rose about 120% over Tenth Plan realisation at constant prices — a decisive commitment to public spending.
- Social sector allocation more than doubled as a proportion of budgetary support, with health and education the largest gainers, reflecting an explicit acknowledgement that Tenth Plan growth had not been inclusive.
- Infrastructure investment was targeted to double, with irrigation, power and rural connectivity central to AP’s own strategy.
- Agriculture’s growth target was raised to 4% against the 2.13% realised in the Tenth Plan.

## Critical examination

## The allocation-expenditure gap — the central criticism

Allocations were routinely not spent. In the Tenth Plan, 26.48% was allocated to energy but only 16.58% actually spent — a shortfall of nearly ten percentage points. The causes were structural: weak project preparation, delayed central releases, land acquisition and clearance delays, and mid-year expenditure cuts to meet FRBM ceilings. Announcing a larger plan is not the same as delivering one.

## Financing quality

Both Plans leaned heavily on market borrowings; nationally, about 73.9% of Tenth Plan public sector resources came from borrowings, with the balance from current revenues negative at 9.6% of plan resources. AP borrowed to invest while running revenue pressures — sustainable only if the assets created generated returns, which irrigation projects did only with long lags.

## Composition bias

Capital outlay was skewed towards new project starts (politically visible) over completion and maintenance of existing assets — an outcome directly produced by the plan/non-plan distinction, since maintenance fell under “non-plan.”

## Sectoral concentration

Within AP, irrigation absorbed a disproportionate share, crowding out allocations for agricultural extension, market infrastructure and rural non-farm enterprise — the components that convert irrigation into income.

## Conclusion

The two Plans show a genuine and welcome maturation of allocation philosophy — from growth-first to a balanced emphasis on social equity. But allocation patterns were the easier half of the problem. The recurring gap between planned and actual expenditure, and the reliance on borrowing against a negative revenue balance, meant that the binding constraint was never the size of the plan but the capacity to execute and finance it. That constraint is what the shift to outcome budgeting, PFMS and Just-in-Time fund releases now seeks to address.

## Value addition
- Why the plan/non-plan divide was abolished: the Rangarajan Committee (2011) held it dysfunctional — it biased spending toward new schemes and starved maintenance; discontinued from 2017-18, replaced by revenue-capital classification and outcome budgets.
- RIDF: operated by NABARD since 1995-96 from shortfalls in banks’ priority sector lending — a major source of AP’s irrigation and rural road financing during both Plans.
- AP Budget 2026-27 (the modern equivalent of “plan allocation”): capital expenditure ₹53,915 crore; ₹6,544 crore availed under SASCI in 2025-26 against ₹4,090 crore in 2023-24; ₹4,000 crore additional under UIDF over two years; World Bank (US$800 mn) and ADB (US$788.8 mn) for Amaravati Phase-I.
- National benchmark: the Centre’s effective capital expenditure (₹17.15 lakh crore) now exceeds its fiscal deficit (~₹16.9 lakh crore) — the standard against which any State’s allocation quality can be judged.

## Introduction

The Eleventh Plan (2007-12) demanded a large expansion of public investment, with the national public sector outlay set about 120% above Tenth Plan realisation at constant prices. Andhra Pradesh followed the same trajectory. The question is not whether support increased — it clearly did — but whether it was adequate to make the public sector viable.

## Where financial support was substantial
- **Irrigation** — Jalayagnam absorbed the largest single share of plan capital outlay · Generous in quantum — but directed at new project expansion, not efficiency or maintenance
- **Power** — Large subsidies to APTRANSCO and DISCOMs to sustain free/low agricultural tariffs; APDRP for distribution modernisation · Kept tariffs low and lights on, but institutionalised loss-making
- **Transport** — APSRTC received recurring support · Insufficient for fleet modernisation or debt reduction
- **Social sector** — Aarogyasri, fee reimbursement, Indiramma housing, plus central flagships · Improved service delivery measurably

## Where support was inadequate
- Industrial PSUs: enterprises such as Nizam Sugars, APSCo and the spinning mills received support oriented towards restructuring and disinvestment rather than capacity revival. Investment in new public enterprises during the Plan was minimal.
- Maintenance starvation: the plan/non-plan divide meant new assets were funded generously as “plan” while their upkeep was starved as “non-plan” — the structural flaw the Rangarajan Committee (2011) later cited in recommending the classification’s abolition.
- Financing quality was poor: nationally, about 73.9% of public sector plan resources in the Tenth Plan came from borrowings, and the balance from current revenues was negative to the tune of 9.6% of plan resources — a pattern that persisted into the Eleventh Plan. AP financed most of its plan capital outlay through market borrowings and RIDF, not from its own surplus.
- External pressures squeezed the plan: the Sixth Pay Commission award and rising fertiliser and petroleum subsidies compressed the fiscal space available for capital support.
- PPP as a substitute, not a supplement: the explicit turn to public-private partnership in urban water supply, health insurance and ports signalled that the State did not expect the public sector to carry the investment burden alone.

## The verdict

Financial support to the public sector increased in quantum but was inadequate in quality and purpose. It sustained services — irrigation water, subsidised power, bus transport, health insurance — without restoring the institutions that deliver them to commercial viability. Support financed operations, not transformation; and because it was debt-financed against a negative balance from current revenues, it built future liabilities rather than future capacity.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s public sector received rising but structurally misdirected support during the Eleventh Plan. Adequate support would have meant tariff and subsidy reform, PSU restructuring with capital infusion, and protected maintenance budgets — not merely larger transfers. That lesson is now being acted upon: the State’s current approach combines debt cost reduction (₹43,298 crore of high-cost loans swapped), clearance of ₹24,811 crore of legacy liabilities, and a proposed AP Wealth Fund, alongside the 16th Finance Commission’s call to review and close 308 inactive State PSEs nationally.

- **Land revenue** — Agricultural landholding · Traditional; now a minor yield
- **Professional tax** — Persons in professions, trades, callings and employment, under the AP Tax on Professions, Trades, Callings and Employments Act, 1987 · Constitutionally capped at ₹2,500 per person per year under Article 276(2)
- **Property tax** — Annual rental/capital value of buildings — levied by municipalities and panchayats · A key own-source of local bodies; the 16th FC ties grants to notified floor rates
- **Taxes on agricultural income** — Entry 46, List II · Not levied by AP in practice

## Indirect taxes levied by Andhra Pradesh
- **State GST (SGST)** — Intra-State supply of goods and services under Art. 246A — the largest single own-tax head; subsumed sales tax, entry tax, luxury tax, entertainment tax and octroi
- **Sales tax / VAT (residual)** — Retained on petroleum products and alcoholic liquor for human consumption, which remain outside GST
- **State excise duty** — Manufacture and sale of alcoholic beverages — a high-yield, politically sensitive head
- **Stamp duty and registration fees** — Property transactions and legal instruments; buoyant with real-estate activity
- **Motor vehicle tax** — Vehicles registered in the State under the AP Motor Vehicles Taxation Act
- **Electricity duty** — Consumption of electricity, collected through DISCOM bills

## How State budgets actually classify these

State accounts do not use the direct/indirect labels; they group own tax revenue into two heads, and quoting these earns credit:

- Taxes on Property and Capital Transactions — land revenue, stamps and registration, urban immovable property tax;
- Taxes on Commodities and Services — SGST, sales tax on petroleum and liquor, state excise, motor vehicle tax, electricity duty, entertainment tax.

## Assessment of the structure
- Heavily indirect: the overwhelming share of AP’s own tax revenue comes from commodities and services, chiefly liquor, petroleum and SGST. This makes collection efficient but the incidence regressive, since indirect taxes take a larger share of poorer households’ income.
- Direct taxes are structurally weak — the professional tax ceiling of ₹2,500 has not been revised since 1988, and land revenue is nominal.
- Consumption dependence means receipts are vulnerable to price and demand shocks, and to any future inclusion of petroleum in GST.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s tax system rests on a broad indirect base and a very thin direct one — efficient to collect but narrow and regressive. Strengthening fiscal capacity requires modernising property valuation and stamp duty administration, revising the professional tax ceiling nationally, and broadening the base to capture the industrial and services investment now flowing into the State — so that revenue grows with the economy rather than only with consumption.

## Value addition
- AP own tax revenue trajectory: about 5.9% of GSDP (2022-23 Actuals) → 6.7% (2024-25) → ₹1,25,846 crore in BE 2026-27.
- Constitutional limits on State taxation: Art. 276(2) caps professional tax at ₹2,500 per person per year; Art. 286

bars taxation of inter-State supplies; Art. 265 — no tax except by authority of law; Art. 246A and 279A govern GST.

- Post-GST reality: taxes subsumed include state VAT, central sales tax, purchase tax, luxury tax, entry tax, entertainment tax (except that levied by local bodies), and taxes on advertisements, lotteries and betting.
- National benchmark: States’ own tax revenue rose from 46% of revenue receipts (FY22) to about 50% (FY25) — AP’s 54% compares favourably, though its composition is narrower than that of Tamil Nadu or Karnataka.

## Introduction

The Tenth Plan (2002-07) was the first plan to set monitorable socio-economic targets alongside a growth number, marking a conceptual advance. Its performance record is genuinely mixed: it delivered India’s fastest growth to that date, yet failed on precisely the inclusion indicators it had pioneered measuring.

## Targets versus outcomes
- **Target** — Outcome · Verdict
- **GDP growth of 8%** — 7.7% achieved — the highest of any Plan until then, with 9%-plus in 2005-07 · Near-miss; strong
- **Reduce poverty by 5 percentage points** — Fell from 26.1% (1999-2000) to 21.8% (2004-05) · Achieved on paper; uneven across States
- **50 million work opportunities** — About 47 million created · Quantitatively close; qualitatively weak
- **Universal primary education by 2007** — Literacy at 64.8% (2001 Census); enrolment rose but universality unmet · Missed
- **Agricultural growth of 4%** — About 2.13% realised for the Plan as a whole · Clear failure

## Achievements
- Growth momentum consolidated: the reform dividend of the 1990s finally translated into sustained high growth; per capita income rose from ₹24,143 (2002) to ₹38,005 (2007) at current prices.
- Agricultural recovery within the Plan: after a devastating drought caused negative 7.2% growth in 2002-03, agriculture rebounded to average nearly 5% in the later years — showing resilience even as the Plan average disappointed.
- Infrastructure investment: NHDP and the Golden Quadrilateral, the telecom revolution, and Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana for rural electrification.
- Institutional legacy: MGNREGA (2005), SSA, NRHM and the Right to Information Act (2005) were all launched or scaled during this Plan — arguably its greatest contribution.

## Critical shortcomings
- Agriculture lagged badly, raising food security concerns and deepening rural distress — the sector employing half the workforce grew at half its target.
- Jobless growth emerged: employment growth fell to 0.28% per annum (2004-05 to 2009-10) even as GDP accelerated; 47 million “work opportunities” were overwhelmingly informal and casual.
- Regional imbalance widened: Bihar, Odisha, UP and Madhya Pradesh fell further behind the western and southern

States.

- Social indicators underperformed: malnutrition, maternal mortality and gender gaps improved far more slowly than income.
- Inequality rose: the urban-rural and formal-informal divides widened — the trickle-down assumption underlying the Plan was empirically refuted.

## The critical verdict

The Tenth Plan succeeded on growth and failed on inclusion — and this failure was consequential rather than incidental. It directly produced the Eleventh Plan’s theme of “Faster and More Inclusive Growth” and the rights-based turn in Indian policy (employment, information, education, food). In that sense, the Plan’s most important outcome was the diagnosis it forced.

## Conclusion

The Tenth Plan proved that India could grow at 8%; it also proved that growth alone would not deliver poverty reduction, decent work or human development. Its shortfalls redefined Indian planning around inclusion, rights and outcomes — a reorientation that continues today through the SDG framework and the goals of Viksit Bharat @2047.

## Value addition
- Ninth Plan (1997-2002): built on four dimensions — quality of life, generation of productive employment, regional balance and self-reliance; special emphasis on agriculture and rural development, with the financial sector integrated into planning for the first time.
- Tenth Plan innovation: the first Plan with State-wise growth targets and monitorable socio-economic indicators, moving planning beyond a single national GDP number.
- Andhra Pradesh in the Tenth Plan: VAT introduction (2005), the AP FRBM Act, 2005, and elimination of the revenue deficit by 2005-06 — the State outperformed the national fiscal record even as it shared the national inclusion deficit.

Credit control means regulating the cost, volume and direction of credit. The RBI does this under the RBI Act, 1934 and the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, balancing price stability, financial stability and inclusive growth.

## Instruments of credit control
- **Quantitative (general)** — Repo, SDF, MSF, CRR, SLR, OMOs, VRR/VRRR · Repo 5.25%, CRR 3.00%, SLR 18%
- **Qualitative (selective)** — Risk weights, margin requirements, moral suasion, PSL directions · Risk weights on unsecured retail and NBFC exposures calibrated 2023-25
- **Macro-prudential** — Countercyclical buffers, LCR/NSFR, large-exposure framework, PCA for weak banks · LCR norms revised 2025
- **Developmental/directed** — 40% PSL mandate; refinance via NABARD/SIDBI; ECLGS-type support · Agriculture sub-target 18% of ANBC

## Evidence that credit control has worked
- Asset quality is at a generational best. SCB GNPA down to 2.2% and NNPA to 0.5%, with CRAR at 17.2% (September 2025); PSBs recorded GNPA of 1.93% and CRAR of 16.6% (31 March 2026) — a reversal of the 2015-18 twin-balance-sheet crisis.
- Counter-cyclical capacity was demonstrated during COVID-19 through liquidity of about ₹17.2 lakh crore, TLTROs, moratoria and the ECLGS.
- Direction of credit shifted deliberately: the 2023 risk-weight increase cooled unsecured personal lending; its 2025 rollback revived credit as stress subsided — a textbook use of a qualitative tool.
- Transmission improved markedly in FY26, as shown by the 59–69 bps decline in lending rates against a 125 bps repo cut.

## Critical limitations
- Incomplete and asymmetric transmission: lending rates fall faster than deposit rates, squeezing bank margins and limiting how far cuts can go.
- Administered rate floor: small savings returns held above formula-implied levels prevent deposit repricing.
- Shrinking reach of the bank channel: in April–November 2025, resource flows to the commercial sector from non-bank sources rose 29.3%, as large corporates turned to bonds, external borrowing and internal accruals — the repo rate simply does not price much of that credit.
- Sectoral blind spots persist: agriculture’s GNPA remains 6.0% against 1.9% for industry, and accounts for over a third of total GNPAs — showing that directed lending without appraisal capacity creates stress.
- Crowding-out risk from large government borrowing, and heterogeneity between banks, NBFCs and fintechs, dilute uniform effectiveness.

## Conclusion

The RBI’s credit control has succeeded in its core objectives — inflation is anchored, banks are strongly capitalised, and asset quality is at multi-decadal bests. But as finance disintermediates towards markets and NBFCs, the interest rate channel alone is a blunter tool than it once was. Effective credit direction now requires fiscal instruments — credit guarantees such as CGTMSE, interest subvention and refinance — working alongside the RBI’s monetary and macro-prudential levers.

## Value addition
- PSL targets for agriculture: 18% of ANBC or CEOBSE (whichever is higher) for domestic commercial banks, RRBs and SFBs; within it, 14% for non-corporate farmers and 10% for small and marginal farmers; a 7.5% sub-target for micro enterprises. (ANBC = Adjusted Net Bank Credit; CEOBSE = Credit Equivalent of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure.)
- Banking health indicators (September 2025): RoA 1.3%, RoE 12.5%, half-yearly slippage ratio stable at 0.7%.
- Structural context: India’s corporate bond market is only 15–16% of GDP (₹53.6 trillion) against Korea’s 79% — deepening it is essential for a market-based transmission channel.
- Institutional: PSBs’ common Credit Assessment Model (CAM) for MSME lending; RBI’s Framework for Formulation of Regulations (May 2025).

## Introduction

Indian banking is a multi-layered architecture with the Reserve Bank of India as apex regulator under the RBI Act, 1934, and operations governed by the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Its tiers are deliberately differentiated so that scale, risk appetite and social mandate are matched to institution type.

## The apex — Reserve Bank of India

Monetary authority, issuer of currency, banker to government (Sections 20, 21, 21A), regulator and supervisor of banks and NBFCs, manager of foreign exchange, and lender of last resort.

## Commercial banking system
- **Public Sector Banks** — 12 (after the 2020 mega-merger of 27 into 12) · Largest share of deposits and branch network
- **Private Sector Banks** — 21 · Technology-led, higher efficiency and margins
- **Foreign Banks** — 44 · Branch/subsidiary model, trade and corporate focus
- **Small Finance Banks** — Niche · 75% priority sector lending; small borrowers, MSMEs
- **Payments Banks** — Niche · Deposits and remittances; cannot lend

Scheduled banks are those in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, eligible for refinance and clearing access.

## Rural and cooperative tier
- Regional Rural Banks: 28, with about 22,158 branches across roughly 730 districts; ownership 50:35:15

(Centre : Sponsor Bank : State); regulated by RBI, supervised by NABARD.

- Cooperative banks: Urban Cooperative Banks and a three-tier rural structure (State, District Central and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies) — brought fully under RBI supervision by the 2020 amendment.

## Development finance and non-banks
- DFIs: NABARD (rural), SIDBI (MSME), EXIM Bank (trade), NHB (housing), and NaBFID (2021) for infrastructure.
- NBFCs: regulated through the Scale-Based Regulation framework in four layers — Base, Middle, Upper and Top.
- New-age intermediaries: Account Aggregators, fintech lenders and digital platforms operating on India Stack.

## Legal and policy framework

Banking Regulation Act, 1949; RBI Act, 1934; DICGC Act, 1961 (deposit insurance now ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank); IBC, 2016 for resolution; and the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025, which amended five statutes at once to modernise governance.

## Health of the structure (2025-26)

SCBs’ GNPA at 2.2% and NNPA at 0.5% — multi-decadal lows — with CRAR at 17.2% (September 2025); PSBs at GNPA 1.93%, CRAR 16.6% (March 2026). RRBs recorded an all-time-high CRAR of 14.4%.

## Conclusion

India’s banking structure is diversified by design — universal banks for scale, niche banks for depth, cooperatives and RRBs for rural reach, DFIs for long-gestation finance, and NBFCs for underserved segments. The current strength of balance sheets shows the architecture is sound; the next frontier is consolidating weak cooperatives, deepening the corporate bond market and integrating fintech safely.

## Value addition
- Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025 (Act 16 of 2025, assent 15 April 2025): amends the RBI Act 1934, BR Act 1949, SBI Act 1955 and the two Bank Nationalisation Acts (1970, 1980). Key changes — up to four nominees per account/locker (from 1 November 2025); “substantial interest” threshold raised from ₹5 lakh (fixed in 1968) to ₹2 crore; cooperative bank directors’ maximum tenure raised from 8 to 10 years, aligning with the 97th Constitutional Amendment; PSBs empowered to fix auditors’ remuneration; unclaimed shares and dividends transferable to the IEPF.
- Deposit protection: unclaimed deposits beyond ten years move to the RBI’s Depositor Education and Awareness (DEA) Fund.
- Open structural questions (RBI discussion paper themes): small versus large banks, universal versus niche licensing, on-tap authorisation, UCB conversion, foreign bank presence, and optimal government ownership in PSBs.

## Introduction

Since 1991 India’s tax policy has moved from a high-rate, narrow-base, exemption-heavy regime to a moderate-rate, broad-base, technology-enabled system. Guided by the Chelliah Committee (1991) and the Kelkar Task Force (2002), reforms sought simplicity, neutrality and buoyancy.

## Direct tax rationalisation
- Personal income tax compressed into three slabs by 1997-98; peak corporate rate cut from 50% (1990-91) to 30%, then to 22% (domestic) and 15% (new manufacturing) in 2019.
- Base broadening through MAT, fewer exemptions, transfer pricing (2001) and GAAR (2017).
- Budget 2025-26: nil tax on income up to ₹12 lakh (₹12.75 lakh for salaried), with revised slabs and TDS/TCS thresholds.
- Income-tax Act, 2025 — enacted 21 August 2025, effective from tax year 2026-27; replaces the 1961 Act through textual and structural simplification without changing rates or policy, ensuring continuity and certainty.

## Indirect tax transformation
- Service tax (1994) — began on three services at 5%, later a major revenue head.
- State VAT (2003-05) — ended cascading, steered by the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers.
- GST (1 July 2017) via the 101st Constitutional Amendment, 2016 — destination-based with input tax credit; the

GST Council (Art. 279A) institutionalised cooperative federalism.

- GST 2.0 (September 2025): simplification to a two-slab structure (5% and 18%) plus a 40% demerit rate; essentials, life-saving drugs and farm equipment moved to nil/5%.

## Anti-evasion and black money measures
- Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) Act, 2015; Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016; strengthened transfer pricing and automatic information exchange.

## Administrative and digital reforms
- PAN/TAN, TIN (2003), e-filing, e-invoicing, Faceless Assessment and Appeals (2019 onwards), PAN 2.0 / TIN 2.0, pre-filled returns, Vivad se Vishwas dispute settlement.
- NUDGE (behavioural, data-driven compliance): over 8,500 deductors revised TDS returns, bringing about ₹4,825 crore into the system — a shift from post-facto enforcement to prevention.
- Budget 2026-27 easing: TCS on LRS education/medical remittances cut from 5% to 2%, return-revision window extended to 31 March, decriminalisation of specified defaults.

## Outcomes
- Direct-tax-to-GDP at 6.64%, a 24-year high; direct taxes ≈ 59% of gross tax revenue.
- Gross GST at a record ₹22.27 lakh crore in FY26; Centre’s revenue receipts up from 8.5% of GDP (FY16-20) to 9.1% (FY22-25).

Unfinished agenda: petroleum, electricity and alcohol outside GST; inverted duty structures; a rising cess-surcharge share outside the divisible pool straining federal trust; and an estimated ₹48,000 crore revenue foregone from GST 2.0.

## Conclusion

From Chelliah to GST 2.0 and the Income-tax Act, 2025, India’s tax system has become simpler, broader and more trust-based, delivering record collections without punitive rates. Sustaining buoyancy requires bringing residual sectors into GST, curbing litigation, and preserving federal balance in revenue sharing.

## Value addition
- Committees: Chelliah (Tax Reforms Committee, 1991), Kelkar Task Force (2002), Vijay Kelkar on GST (2009).
- Constitutional basis: Art. 246A, 269A, 279A (GST Council); Art. 265 — no tax except by authority of law.
- GST 2.0: two slabs (5%, 18%) + 40% on tobacco, pan masala, aerated drinks and luxury goods; farm machinery and irrigation equipment cut 12% → 5%; two-wheelers, small cars, TVs, ACs, cement 28% → 18%.
- Income-tax Act, 2025 — three guiding principles: structural simplification, no policy change, no rate change.

## Introduction

National Income measures what an economy produces; the Human Development Index, introduced by UNDP in 1990 under Mahbub ul Haq and drawing on Amartya Sen’s capability approach, measures how well its people live. The question is whether the latter can replace the former.

## Why National Income alone is insufficient
- Growth ≠ welfare: India is the world’s 4th largest economy but ranks 130 / 193 on HDI (HDR 2025) — a striking growth–welfare gap.
- Distribution-blind: GDP records the average, not the median; consumption Gini 0.237 rural / 0.284 urban (HCES 2023–24).
- Omissions: unpaid care work, environmental depletion, health and education outcomes are excluded.
- Deprivation persists: MPI 11.28% (2022–23); extreme poverty 5.3% at the revised World Bank line of $3/day.

## HDI as a superior welfare measure
- **Dimension** — Indicator
- **Health** — Life expectancy at birth
- **Education** — Mean years + Expected years of schooling
- **Income** — GNI per capita (PPP)

- Multidimensional: combines the means (income) with the ends (health, knowledge).
- Policy-shaping: redirects budgets toward human capital — the logic behind NEP 2020, Ayushman Bharat and POSHAN 2.0.
- Comparable over time: India’s HDI rose from 0.676 (2022) to 0.685 (2023) — Medium HD, nearing the 0.700 High HD threshold; ahead of Pakistan (168th) and Nepal (145th).
- Reveals what GDP hides: Kerala’s HDI far exceeds that of richer states, proving welfare is a policy choice, not an automatic by-product of income.

## But HDI is not a full substitute
- It contains GNI per capita — so it presupposes national income accounting.
- Ignores inequality, gender gaps, sustainability, freedom and security; equal weighting of three dimensions is arbitrary.
- Cannot perform National Income’s operational functions: taxation, fiscal deficit, tax devolution, monetary policy and growth forecasting all require GDP.
- Hence the family of supplements: IHDI, GDI, GII, Planetary Pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI), MPI, SDG India Index.

## Conclusion

## Introduction

The Evergreen Revolution, a concept of Prof. M.S. Swaminathan, means “increasing productivity in perpetuity without ecological or social harm.” It is the deliberate successor to the Green Revolution, which raised yields but degraded soil, depleted groundwater and raised input costs. The question is therefore not whether Andhra Pradesh uses modern inputs and knowledge — it does — but whether it uses them in a way that can be sustained indefinitely.

How present input use and technical knowledge FACILITATE the Evergreen Revolution

- Natural farming at scale — the strongest facilitator Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming (APCNF), implemented by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha, is described internationally as the world’s largest agroecology programme: - Grown 25-fold from 40,000 farmers in 2016 to over 17.7 lakh farmers across 8,168 gram panchayats and more than 0.92 million hectares. - Verified outcomes: incomes up 38-66%, water savings up to 50%, greenhouse gas emissions down up to 46% per acre. - Nine principles including 365-day green cover, diverse crops, minimal tillage and on-farm bio-stimulants, with no synthetic fertilisers, pesticides or herbicides. - Won the Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity (2024) and the Food Planet Prize (2026) — USD 1.5 million. - Targets all 6 million farmers across 8 million hectares by 2031.

This is precisely what Swaminathan meant: productivity raised while the resource base is restored.

- Water-efficient technology Micro-irrigation (drip and sprinkler) under PMKSY’s “Per Drop More Crop”, and the System of Rice Intensification, cut water use substantially in a State where groundwater stress is acute.
- Knowledge institutions and extension - Acharya N.G. Ranga Agricultural University and ICAR research stations.

- Rythu Bharosa Kendras as village-level advisory, input-testing and procurement points — bringing extension to the farmer rather than expecting the reverse. - APCNF’s farmer-to-farmer extension model, in which practising farmers serve as extension agents — far more credible than departmental instruction.

- Soil and nutrient management Soil Health Cards guiding balanced application; Integrated Nutrient Management; biofertilisers.
- Diversification into low-input, high-value activity AP’s shift toward aquaculture, horticulture, oil palm and livestock raises value per hectare — nationally, livestock grew 7.1% and fisheries 8.8% a decade against crops at 3.5%.
- Digital and precision tools Agristack, satellite advisories, drone spraying (Namo Drone Didi), AI-enabled quality assessment on e-NAM, and weather-based advisories.
- Millets and climate-resilient crops Renewed promotion of Shree Anna — drought-tolerant, nutritious and low-input

— in the semi-arid Rayalaseema tract.

How present input use OBSTRUCTS the Evergreen Revolution

- Chemical input imbalance India’s N:P:K consumption ratio far exceeds the recommended 4:2:1, driven by the urea subsidy. Excess nitrogen degrades soil organic carbon and pollutes groundwater. AP shares this pattern outside the natural-farming districts.
- Groundwater depletion Free or heavily subsidised agricultural power — AP budgets about ₹11,000 crore in farm power subsidy for 22.5 lakh farmers — makes extraction effectively costless at the margin, encouraging over-pumping. Rayalaseema’s water table decline is the direct consequence.
- Salinisation from aquaculture Conversion of delta paddy land to shrimp and fish ponds has salinised adjoining land and groundwater in West Godavari, Krishna and Nellore — a textbook case of productivity gained at a neighbour’s ecological expense.
- Pesticide dependence Chillies, cotton and paddy in AP have historically seen heavy pesticide use, with resistance, residue and health consequences — the problem that Non-Pesticide Management, pioneered in the State, was designed to address.
- Extension reach remains thin The farmer-to-extension-worker ratio is poor outside APCNF districts; many farmers still rely on input dealers for technical advice — a conflict of interest, since the adviser profits from the sale.
- Fragmentation limits technology adoption With average holdings below a hectare, mechanisation and precision technology are uneconomic on individual plots, and custom hiring centres are unevenly available.
- Tenancy blocks long-term investment An unrecorded tenant with an eleven-month arrangement has no incentive to invest in soil health — the returns accrue to the owner. Since AP has among India’s highest tenancy incidence, this is a structural barrier to any practice with a multi-year payback.
- Uneven diffusion Technology reaches the irrigated delta far faster than Rayalaseema and the tribal agency areas. The verdict — how far?
- **Direction** — Correct — natural farming, micro-irrigation, diversification and digital advisory all point toward the Evergreen model
- **Scale** — Substantial but partial — 17.7 lakh of about 60 lakh farmers are in APCNF, so roughly a quarter
- **Ecological outcome** — Mixed — genuine gains where natural farming has spread; continuing groundwater depletion and salinisation elsewhere
- **Institutional support** — Strong — RySS, RBKs, ANGRAU and SHG networks give AP an extension architecture few States match
- **Binding constraint** — Subsidised power and water, and unrecorded tenancy — both of which reward short-term extraction over long-term stewardship

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh has advanced further toward an Evergreen Revolution than most Indian States, chiefly because APCNF has demonstrated that productivity and ecological restoration can rise together — and that doing so raises income by cutting costs. But present input use still obstructs the goal wherever water and power are priced at zero, aquaculture externalities are unregulated, and the cultivator has no secure interest in the land. Achieving the Evergreen Revolution therefore depends less on new technology than on correcting these three incentives — which is a matter of pricing, regulation and tenancy recognition rather than of agronomy.

## Value addition
- Definition to quote: M.S. Swaminathan defined the Evergreen Revolution as “increasing productivity in perpetuity without associated ecological harm” — the phrase itself earns credit.
- Contrast: Green Revolution — yield through external inputs; Evergreen Revolution — yield through ecological processes, integrated pest and nutrient management, and conservation farming.

Keyword discipline: this question is about poverty levels by region — not about disparity in general. Keep the focus on deprivation indicators and their spatial pattern.

Andhra Pradesh has achieved a substantial reduction in poverty and now belongs to the group of 14 States with low multidimensional poverty — up from just seven such States in 2015-16, with the State’s headcount ratio more than halving between 2015-16 and 2019-21. But this aggregate conceals a persistent spatial hierarchy: poverty in Andhra Pradesh is not randomly distributed but concentrated in identifiable regions.

The regional hierarchy of poverty

- **Coastal Andhra — Krishna-Godavari delta (West and East Godavari, Krishna, Guntur, Nellore)** — Lowest poverty in the State · Assured canal irrigation, double cropping, aquaculture and horticulture; strong non-farm economy; better literacy and health indicators
- **North Coastal Andhra (Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram Manyam, Alluri Sitharama Raju)** — Highest poverty, particularly in the tribal agency areas · Rain-fed and shifting cultivation, forest dependence, poor connectivity, highest deprivation among PVTG households
- **Rayalaseema (Kurnool, Nandyal, Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, Kadapa, Annamayya, Chittoor, Tirupati)** — High poverty, with severe volatility · Semi-arid, groundwater-dependent; drought-driven distress; out-migration; historically the region of highest farmer distress

The district-level evidence from Census 2011 illustrates the same pattern through literacy — West Godavari (74.63%) and Krishna (73.74%) at the top against Vizianagaram (58.89%) and Kurnool (59.97%) at the bottom.

The dimensions of the difference

- Income poverty The last official consumption-based estimates (Tendulkar methodology, 2011-12) placed undivided AP at about 9.2% overall — rural about 11.0% and urban about 5.8% — but the State average concealed a delta-to-Rayalaseema spread of several multiples.
- Multidimensional poverty The National MPI measures deprivation directly across 12 indicators in health, education and standard of living. On this measure: - Nutrition and child mortality deprivation is highest in the tribal agency areas. - Years of schooling and school attendance deprivation is concentrated in Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra — consistent with AP’s overall literacy of 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24), the lowest among Indian States. - Standard-of-living indicators (cooking fuel, sanitation, housing, assets) improved fastest everywhere through saturation delivery, which is why the rural-urban gap narrowed.
- Occupational poverty The delta supports irrigated cultivation and aquaculture; the lagging regions depend on casual agricultural labour, forest produce and out-migration — the most insecure income categories.
- Social poverty SC, ST and PVTG households show higher deprivation within every district, but they are concentrated in North Coastal Andhra’s agency areas — so social and spatial disadvantage compound.
- Rural-urban difference The State is only about 29.5% urbanised, and urban poverty is concentrated in slums and among informal migrant workers in Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Guntur — different in character from rural poverty, being about housing, tenure and services rather than about land or water.

Why the differences exist

- **Irrigation** — Colonial-era canal investment — Cotton’s Dowleswaram anicut (1852) and the Krishna anicut — gave the deltas assured water; Rayalaseema requires costly lift irrigation
- **The Green Revolution reinforced it** — The HYV package required assured water, so it delivered gains to the deltas and bypassed rain-fed regions
- **Agro-climatic endowment** — Rayalaseema receives 500-700 mm against far higher evapotranspiration; the agency areas are hilly and forested
- **Industrial and urban concentration** — Investment clusters around Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Tirupati
- **Landlessness and tenancy** — Concentrated among SC and tribal households; unrecorded tenancy excludes cultivators from credit and insurance
- **Human capital** — Literacy and school completion lag precisely where poverty is highest, capping occupational mobility
- **Bifurcation** — The loss of Hyderabad in 2014 removed the State’s largest urban labour market, reducing the escape route from rural poverty

What has narrowed the gap

Basic-service saturation — housing under PMAY, electrification, LPG under Deepam 2.0 (1.08 crore women), sanitation and bank accounts — lifted standard-of-living indicators fastest in the poorest regions, which is why the State’s MPI halved. NTR Bharosa pensions (₹4,000-₹15,000 by DBT, over ₹58,000 crore in 19 months), Annadata Sukhibhava (₹20,000 a year covering tenants) and MGNREGA provided income floors. APCNF raised incomes 38-66% by cutting input costs — particularly valuable in rain-fed tracts.

But this is a one-time gain. Service saturation cannot be repeated; further poverty reduction in the lagging regions must come from productivity and employment.

## Conclusion

Poverty in Andhra Pradesh follows a clear geography: lowest in the irrigated delta, highest in the tribal agency areas of North Coastal Andhra, and severe though volatile in Rayalaseema. The differences trace primarily to irrigation access, agro-climatic endowment and human capital — the first two historical, the third remediable. Since the easy gains from service saturation are largely exhausted, closing the remaining gap requires completing Rayalaseema’s lift irrigation, closing the literacy deficit, and locating non-farm employment in the lagging regions — the logic behind the industrial nodes at Orvakal and Kopparthy and the 175 MSME parks.

## Introduction

Keyword discipline: “Elucidate” asks you to explain the operational problems clearly. Q.172 traces the historical decline; this answer examines how cooperatives function today and where delivery breaks down.

In Andhra Pradesh, the cooperative credit structure — PACS at the village, District Central Cooperative Banks at the district, and the AP State Cooperative Bank (APCOB) at the apex, with long-term credit through cooperative agriculture and rural development banks — remains the formal lender physically closest to the farmer. Its problem is not proximity but capacity: it is present where credit is needed and least able to supply it.

Problems in providing adequate credit

- Inadequate resource base - PACS depend on borrowings from DCCBs and NABARD refinance rather than on local deposit mobilisation, so their lending capacity is externally determined. - Thin capital and small membership contributions limit the loan volume that can be sanctioned. - The result is rationing: the scale of finance sanctioned falls short of actual cultivation cost, forcing the farmer to top up from a moneylender — so cooperative credit becomes a partial solution that leaves the borrower in the informal market anyway.
- Accumulated overdues and NPAs - High overdues freeze the revolving fund: a PACS that cannot recover cannot re-lend, so default by some members denies credit to all. - Successive loan waivers, while providing relief, weakened the repayment culture on which the mutual-liability model depends.
- Governance and political interference - Boards are elected, and elections have frequently been delayed, with administrators appointed in place of elected bodies. - Credit decisions are influenced by local political affiliation; enforcement against influential defaulters is weak, while small borrowers are pursued. - Elite capture: larger and better-connected farmers obtain a disproportionate share of the loanable funds.
- Exclusion of the actual cultivator - Membership and lending are tied to land ownership, so the tenant cultivator

— and Andhra Pradesh has among India’s highest tenancy incidence, almost all of it oral — is excluded. - Agricultural labourers, artisans and women without land likewise fall outside the membership base. - SC, ST and PVTG households, being disproportionately landless, are structurally under-represented.

- Delay and procedural burden - Loan sanction requires no-dues certificates, land records and multiple approvals, so credit often arrives after the sowing window — when it is worth a fraction of its value. - Renewal is frequently mechanical rather than needs-based.
- Narrow product range - Overwhelmingly short-term crop loans; very limited term credit for irrigation, mechanisation, storage or processing. - Allied activities — dairy, poultry, fisheries — are under-financed even though they now grow far faster than crops (livestock 7.1%, fisheries 8.8% a decade, against crops at 3.5%). - No consumption credit, which is precisely the need that keeps the moneylender in business.
- Technology lag - Slow adoption of core banking, digital payment and KCC issuance meant better-off farmers migrated to commercial banks and RRBs, leaving cooperatives with the least profitable business and a weaker deposit base.
- Regional imbalance within the State - Cooperatives are stronger in the irrigated delta districts and weaker in Rayalaseema and the tribal agency areas — so their coverage is thinnest where distress is deepest.
- Dual control - Subject simultaneously to the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies (management, audit, elections) and the RBI (banking regulation), with neither able to act decisively. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 has since brought cooperative banks more fully under RBI supervision.
- Weak professional management - Limited technical staff for credit appraisal, risk assessment and recovery; secretaries are often under-trained and under-paid relative to the responsibility carried.

Consequence

Because cooperative credit is inadequate in amount, late in timing and narrow in purpose, the farmer supplements it informally. That is the mechanism by which institutional presence coexists with informal dependence — and it explains why Andhra Pradesh, despite a dense cooperative network, saw the 2010 microfinance crisis originate within its borders.

Reforms under way

- Computerisation of PACS and conversion into multi-service centres handling credit, input supply, procurement, storage, fair price shops and common service centres.
- The Ministry of Cooperation (2021) and the World’s Largest Grain Storage Plan in the Cooperative Sector, building godowns at PACS level through AIF and AMI convergence.
- Vaidyanathan Committee recapitalisation linked to governance reform.
- KCC issuance through PACS and linkage with the Kisan Rin Portal.
- At State level, Rythu Bharosa Kendras now perform part of the village-level input, advisory and procurement function that PACS were meant to provide.

## Conclusion

Cooperatives in Andhra Pradesh suffer from a compounding set of problems — a weak resource base producing inadequate loans, overdues freezing the revolving fund, governance capture distorting allocation, land-linked membership excluding the actual cultivator, and delay defeating timeliness. Their revival matters because no other formal institution is physically present in most villages. The path is clear enough: deposit mobilisation and recapitalisation, professional management insulated from local politics, membership de-linked from land title, term and allied-sector lending, and full digitisation — so that the institution closest to the farmer becomes the one most able to serve her.

## Value addition
- AP structure: APCOB at the apex, DCCBs at district level, PACS at village level; long-term credit through cooperative agriculture and rural development banks.
- Complementary institutions in the State: SERP and Stree Nidhi SHG credit (about 11 lakh SHGs, over one crore women, repayment above 97%) have substantially filled the space cooperatives vacated for small borrowers.
- The regulatory correction: the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 resolved the banking side of dual control; 97th Constitutional Amendment (2011) added Art. 43B and made forming cooperatives a right under Art. 19(1)(c).
- Asset-quality context: agriculture’s GNPA across scheduled commercial banks stands at 6.0% — the highest of any sector — which is why lenders of every type ration credit to this segment.

## Introduction

The PDS is already a shared responsibility: the Centre procures, allocates and subsidises; States identify beneficiaries, transport, store and distribute. The question is whether the balance should shift decisively toward the States. It is a genuine question of fiscal federalism, not merely of administration.

The present division of responsibility

- **Procurement through FCI at Minimum Support Price** — Identification of beneficiaries within NFSA ceilings
- **Determination of NFSA coverage (75% rural, 50% urban) and central issue prices** — Issue of ration cards and their revalidation
- **Allocation of foodgrain to States** — Transportation, storage and delivery to fair price shops
- **Bearing the food subsidy** — Licensing and supervision of fair price shops
- **Buffer stock management** — Additional State schemes over NFSA entitlements

The case FOR making it a State responsibility

- Local knowledge in identification. States and local bodies know their populations; Gram Sabhas can identify the genuinely poor far better than a formula applied from Delhi. Exclusion errors are largely an identification problem.
- Regional dietary diversity. A uniform rice-and-wheat basket ignores local staples. States could distribute millets in the Deccan, coarse grains in tribal belts, and pulses and edible oil according to local nutritional deficits — a genuine advantage in a country of dietary diversity.
- Demonstrated State capacity to innovate. States that have taken ownership have outperformed: Chhattisgarh’s PDS reform (de-privatised shops, computerisation, doorstep delivery) is the standard reference; Tamil Nadu’s universal PDS; Odisha’s e-KYC drive that detected over 40 lakh ghost beneficiaries; Andhra Pradesh’s rice at ₹1 per kg with 29,796 outlets.
- Accountability is clearer. When one government both funds and delivers, citizens know whom to hold responsible. Shared responsibility allows each level to blame the other for failure.
- Decentralised procurement reduces cost. Buying paddy locally rather than transporting it across the country cuts transit losses and carrying costs — a Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) recommendation.
- Constitutional logic. Public health, sanitation and relief of the disabled are State subjects; food distribution sits

naturally alongside them, and the 73rd and 74th Amendments give local bodies a delivery role.

The case AGAINST

- Fiscal capacity is the decisive objection. Food subsidy is among the largest items of central expenditure. Most States cannot bear it — combined State fiscal deficit stood at 3.2% of GDP (FY25 PA), committed expenditure absorbed 51.76% of States’ revenue expenditure (FY24), and unconditional cash transfers already reached about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26. Adding food subsidy would break several State budgets.
- Food security is a national obligation. The NFSA, 2013 creates a legal entitlement, and the Supreme Court in PUCL v. Union of India (2001) treated food as an aspect of the right to life under Article 21. A right cannot vary by the fiscal fortune of one’s State.
- Surplus and deficit States differ fundamentally. Punjab, Haryana and Andhra Pradesh are surplus producers; Bihar, Jharkhand and the North-East are deficit States. Only a national agency can move grain between them — leaving it to States would leave deficit States exposed.
- Buffer stock and price stabilisation are national functions. Managing strategic reserves against drought, war and price shocks requires national scale and cannot be fragmented.
- MSP and procurement are linked to PDS. Dismantling central procurement would undermine the price support on which farmers in surplus States depend.
- Interstate portability requires a national system. One Nation One Ration Card, operational in all 36 States and UTs, works precisely because entitlements are nationally standardised. State-run systems would fragment portability for migrant workers — the group most in need of it.
- Race to the bottom risk. Fiscally stressed States might reduce coverage or quality, and the poorest States — with the greatest need — have the weakest capacity.

A reasoned verdict

The sound principle is “national entitlement, State delivery, shared finance” — broadly the present arrangement, but with a clearer allocation of functions:

- **Legal entitlement and minimum norms** — Centre — a right must be uniform
- **Food subsidy financing** — Centre, since only it has the fiscal capacity
- **Buffer stock, price stabilisation, inter-State movement** — Centre
- **Beneficiary identification and revalidation** — States and local bodies
- **Basket composition (millets, pulses, oil)** — States, within a nutritional floor
- **Procurement** — Decentralised to States, with central reimbursement
- **Distribution, storage, FPS supervision, quality assurance** — States

## Conclusion

Making the PDS wholly a State responsibility would improve targeting and dietary relevance but jeopardise fiscal viability, inter-State equity and the enforceability of a national right. The better reform is not to transfer responsibility but to sharpen it — the Centre guaranteeing the entitlement and the money, the States owning identification, procurement and delivery, and both accountable through transparent, portable, digitised systems. Food security is a national promise that must be kept locally, not a local promise that varies nationally.

## Value addition
- NFSA, 2013: covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population — about 80.67 crore persons; 5 kg per person per month for priority households, 35 kg per household for Antyodaya Anna Yojana families; food security allowance if grain is not supplied; women aged 18 and above deemed head of household for card issue.
- PMGKAY: free foodgrain under NFSA extended for five years from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2028.
- Shanta Kumar Committee (2015): reduce NFSA coverage to 40%; decentralised procurement; cash transfers in large cities; FCI to outsource storage and movement; end-to-end computerisation.
- Constitutional and judicial: food and civil supplies fall under the Concurrent List; PUCL v. Union of India (2001) established the right to food as part of Article 21.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh presents a puzzle: it has India’s densest network of women’s institutions, the country’s lowest maternal mortality (about 30 per lakh live births), and a long history of women-centred programming — yet female workforce participation, literacy and political representation lag. The question is therefore not whether empowerment is happening, but why it is happening more slowly than the investment would predict.

Social issues constraining the pace

- Early marriage — the State’s most serious gender indicator 29.3% of women aged 20-24 were married before the legal age of 18 (NFHS-5) — higher than the national average, and higher still among Scheduled Tribes. Early marriage terminates education, brings early childbearing, and permanently forecloses workforce entry. No other single factor slows the pace as much.
- The education deficit is concentrated among women Female literacy was 59.96% against male 74.77% (Census 2011), and the State’s overall literacy of 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States. Since occupational mobility cannot outpace educational attainment, this caps how fast anything else can move.
- Son preference persists The child sex ratio (0-6) stood at 939 in Census 2011 even as the overall sex ratio, at 996, was among India’s healthiest — showing that discrimination operates before birth and in early childhood rather than in survival thereafter.
- The unpaid care burden Nationally, women’s unpaid care work was valued at ₹22.7 lakh crore, about 7.5% of GDP (Economic Survey 2022-23). It is invisible in statistics and absorbs the time that paid work would require — the proximate reason for low participation.
- Mobility, safety and social norms Restricted mobility, safety concerns and family resistance limit market access, travel for work and enterprise beyond the home. Stree Shakti free bus travel and the Shakti App address this, but norms change more slowly than schemes.
- Intersecting disadvantage SC, ST and PVTG women face compounded constraints — landlessness, forest-dependent livelihoods and geographic isolation in the Eastern Ghats agency areas.

Economic issues constraining the pace

- Participation has not followed credit AP’s female LFPR of about 35.8% trails the national 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24)

— despite about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women. Access to credit has not translated into paid employment, which is the central economic finding.

- Enterprises remain sub-scale Women’s establishments are overwhelmingly own-account; nationally 83.19% have no hired worker. Credit finances consumption and debt-swapping more than enterprise, so incomes do not compound.
- Occupational concentration Women are concentrated in agriculture, aquaculture processing, construction, beedi rolling and handloom — low-wage, seasonal and informal work. Skilling too has tended to channel women into traditionally feminised, low-margin trades.
- Asset ownership Land and property are typically registered in male names, so women lack collateral. PMAY houses registered in women’s names are a genuine corrective, but agricultural land ownership remains male-dominated.
- Over-indebtedness risk The 2010 microfinance crisis originated in the State, and the FY25 stress — when MFI loans outstanding fell about 14% — shows the vulnerability persists. Debt without income growth sets empowerment backwards.
- The urbanisation constraint Bifurcation removed Hyderabad, leaving AP only about 29.5% urbanised. Urban labour markets are where women’s non-farm employment usually grows; AP’s is smaller and more dispersed than in comparable States.

The critical insight

The pace is slow because programmes have addressed access — accounts, loans, transfers, schemes — while the binding constraints are time, mobility, education and norms. A woman with a loan but no childcare, no safe transport, incomplete schooling and a marriage at seventeen cannot convert credit into livelihood. Empowerment is being supplied faster than it can be absorbed.

Where the pace has been fast

It is worth noting the counter-evidence: AP achieved the SDG maternal mortality target well ahead of schedule (MMR about 30, the lowest in India with Kerala) and an under-5 mortality rate of 24. Where the intervention was medical and institutional — antenatal care, institutional delivery, health insurance — progress was rapid. Where it depends on household behaviour and social norms, it has been slow. That contrast is the answer to the question.

## Conclusion

The pace of women’s empowerment in Andhra Pradesh is constrained less by resources or programme design than by social norms and time poverty. Accelerating it requires attacking the specific bottlenecks: enforcing the prohibition of child marriage, closing the female literacy gap through ULLAS and NIPUN Bharat, providing childcare and safe transport so that participation becomes feasible, linking skilling to industry rather than to tradition, and recognising unpaid work in policy. The State has proved it can move outcome indicators quickly when the intervention is institutional; the task now is to apply the same rigour where the constraint is social.

## Value addition
- Key AP gender indicators: child marriage 29.3% (NFHS-5, above the national average); child sex ratio 939; overall sex ratio 996; female literacy 59.96% (Census 2011); female LFPR about 35.8%; MMR about 30; U5MR 24.
- National comparison: India ranks 131 of 148 (WEF 2025) with parity of 64.1%; educational attainment 97.1% but political empowerment weakest — women in Parliament down from 14.7% to 13.8%.
- Constitutional and legal instruments: Art. 15(3), 39(a) and (d), 42; Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006; POSH Act, 2013; Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 (26 weeks); 106th Amendment, 2023.

The demographic dividend is the growth potential that arises when the working-age population (15-59) exceeds the dependent population. For Andhra Pradesh, the crucial fact is that this window is closing earlier than for India as a whole: the State’s total fertility rate has fallen from 3.0 in 1993 to about 1.5 today — far below the replacement level of 2.1 — and the share of people above 60 is 11%, projected to reach 19% by 2047.

Andhra Pradesh’s distinctive demographic position

- **Total fertility rate** — 1.7 (NFHS-5); ~1.5 currently — urban 1.47, rural 1.78 · 1.91 (NFHS-5)
- **Population aged 60+** — 11%, rising to 19% by 2047 · Lower
- **Implication** — Window closing by the late 2030s · Window open to roughly mid-century

The State has therefore moved from a population control to a population management posture: it repealed the two-child norm for local body elections through the AP Municipal Laws (Amendment) Act, 2024 and corresponding Panchayat Raj amendments, and the Chief Minister announced in March 2026 that AP would introduce India’s first Population Management Policy, to be implemented from 1 April 2026.

Suggested steps

- Fix the literacy and foundational learning base first AP records 72.6% literacy (PLFS 2023-24) — the lowest among Indian States. No skilling strategy can succeed on that base. Scale ULLAS for adult literacy and NIPUN Bharat for foundational literacy and numeracy, with a focus on girls and the backward districts.
- Skill for the industries actually coming to the State Align training with the investment pipeline — semiconductors (Orvakal), green hydrogen and aluminium (Kakinada), bulk drugs (Nakkapalli), data centres (Visakhapatnam), drones (Orvakal) and quantum computing (Amaravati). Strengthen ITIs and polytechnics, expand apprenticeships under PM-NAPS, and use the Employment Linked Incentive Scheme (₹99,446 crore) to subsidise first-time formal hiring.
- Convert investment commitments into jobs The Global Partnership Summit 2025 yielded commitments above

₹13.25 lakh crore with 16.13 lakh jobs potential, and Google’s US$15 billion AI data centre at Visakhapatnam is India’s largest single FDI commitment. Priority now is execution — land, power, clearances and last-mile infrastructure — so that MoUs become payrolls.

- Raise female labour force participation This is the largest untapped reserve. Nationally FLFPR (UPSS) rose to 41.7% (2023-24), but AP’s remains around 35.8%. Expand childcare through upgraded Anganwadis (9,958 already upgraded), safe transport (Stree Shakti), women’s hostels near industrial parks, and the One Family–One Entrepreneur programme targeting one lakh women entrepreneurs a year.
- Absorb labour into rural non-farm activity With agriculture still holding an unusually high share of AP’s workforce, expand food processing, aquaculture value addition, horticulture and logistics — the 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency, are the delivery vehicle.
