- Prepare simultaneously for ageing Because the window is closing, AP must build pension coverage (Atal Pension

Yojana), geriatric care and elder-friendly infrastructure now — alongside the NTR Bharosa pension architecture — rather than after the dividend expires.

- Retain and attract talent Out-migration to Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai drains the very cohort the dividend depends on. Quality-of-life investment in Visakhapatnam, Amaravati and Tirupati, plus the Ratan Tata Innovation Hub, are the retention strategy.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s demographic dividend is real but time-bound, and shorter than India’s. A dividend is only a dividend if the young are educated, skilled, healthy and employed; otherwise it becomes a liability. With literacy the lowest in the country and fertility already well below replacement, the State’s window demands urgency rather than gradualism — education and skilling at scale in this decade, matched to the industrial investment now arriving, is the single most important determinant of whether Swarna Andhra @2047 is achieved.

Cotton, tobacco (AP is India’s principal Virginia tobacco producer), groundnut, sugarcane, chillies and turmeric occupy substantial area, linking farming to processing and export markets.

- Cereals — declining share, not declining importance

Rice remains the staple and the basis of the State’s procurement and PDS system, but its share of agricultural value has fallen as higher-value activities expand. Coarse cereals — Shree Anna — are receiving renewed policy attention.

Drivers of the change

- Small holdings force high-value choices: with average holdings below a hectare, only high-value output can generate a viable income.
- Irrigation expansion through Jalayagnam, HNSS and Polavaram enabled diversification.
- Price and demand pull: rising urban demand for protein, fruit and vegetables; export markets for shrimp.
- Policy support: National Mission on Edible Oils, MIDH, PM Matsya Sampada Yojana, and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund for cold chains.
- Technology: hatcheries, feed technology, micro-irrigation and improved planting material.

Analysis of the consequences — a balanced assessment

Positive: - Higher income per hectare and better use of scarce land. - Export earnings — nationally, agricultural exports reached about ₹4.4 lakh crore in FY25, with AP’s shrimp a major component. - Employment in processing and logistics — food processing grew 7.3% annually (2015-2022). - Reduced dependence on monsoon-sensitive cereals.

Risks — which a good answer must state: - Water and soil stress: aquaculture has caused salinisation of adjoining paddy land and groundwater in delta districts — the classic externality of pond conversion. - Market and price volatility: shrimp and chilli prices depend on export demand and tariffs; a single bad year can devastate a farmer who has abandoned foodgrain. - Capital intensity and debt: aquaculture requires heavy upfront investment, so failure produces indebtedness rather than merely a poor season. - Input dependence: high fertiliser, feed and chemical use, against which the APCNF natural farming programme is the counter-movement. - Food security within the State: conversion of paddy land raises questions about local grain availability, though AP remains a surplus rice producer.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s agricultural output has moved decisively from volume to value — from cereals to aquaculture, horticulture and livestock — and this is the correct direction for a State of small holdings. The change explains why agriculture retains an unusually high 37% share of the State’s GSVA. The task now is to make the new structure sustainable and less risky: regulating aquaculture to prevent salinisation, expanding processing and cold chains so value is captured locally, diversifying export markets, and scaling community-managed natural farming to reduce input dependence.

## Value addition
- National comparison: decadal agricultural growth of 4.45% (FY16-FY25) — the highest of any decade — driven by

livestock (7.1%) and fisheries (8.8%) against crops at 3.5%.

- AP’s distinction: India’s leading aquaculture State; leading producer of chillies and among the leaders in oil palm, cocoa and papaya; 974-km coastline, second only to Gujarat.
- Supporting missions: PM Matsya Sampada Yojana for fisheries; National Mission on Edible Oils (oil palm); Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (₹11,440 crore, self-sufficiency by December 2027); MIDH for horticulture.
- Sustainability counterweight: APCNF covers over 17.7 lakh farmers across 0.92 million hectares in the State, with verified income gains of 38-66% and water savings up to 50%.

## Introduction

“Intensity of unemployment” refers not to how many are unemployed but to how deeply and for how long — the number of idle days, the severity of income loss, and the depth of the lean season. MGNREGS was designed precisely for this: it does not create permanent jobs, it fills the gap between agricultural seasons when rural labour has nothing to do.

Channels of impact

- Direct — filling the lean season The scheme provides wage employment exactly when farm work is unavailable, converting complete idleness into paid days. Because it is demand-driven, take-up rises automatically where and when distress is greatest — the intensity of unemployment is therefore attacked at its peak rather than on average.
- Indirect — the rural wage floor By offering a statutory minimum wage to anyone willing to do manual work, MGNREGS raises the reservation wage across the rural labour market. Employers must match or exceed it, so wages rise even for workers who never enrol. This is arguably its largest effect, and it is invisible in enrolment statistics.
- Migration and bargaining power Assured local work reduces distress migration, keeping families together and easing pressure on urban slums. Workers who are not forced to migrate can also negotiate better local terms.
- Women’s participation With at least one-third of beneficiaries mandated to be women and equal wages guaranteed, MGNREGS became one of the largest formal entry points for rural women into paid work — contributing to the rise in female LFPR (UPSS) from 23.3% (2017-18) to 41.7% (2023-24).
- Counter-cyclical absorption — the clearest evidence During COVID-19, MGNREGS expanded rapidly to absorb returning migrants — demand-driven, open-ended funding allowed it to scale within weeks. No fixed-budget scheme could have responded this way, and this episode is the strongest single piece of evidence for its design.
- Asset creation with second-round employment effects Water conservation structures, farm ponds, watershed works, rural connectivity and plantations raise agricultural productivity, which generates further farm employment in subsequent seasons — converting a wage programme into an investment programme where asset quality is good.
- Consumption and local demand Wages paid directly into bank accounts sustain rural consumption in the lean season, supporting local trade and preventing distress sale of assets.

Limitations that qualify the assessment

- **Rationing of work** — In many districts, employment provided falls short of employment demanded, so the 100-day entitlement is not fully realised
- **Wage payment delays** — A delayed wage does not smooth the lean season — it merely postpones distress
- **Only 100 days** — Even fully realised, this covers about a third of the year; it reduces but cannot eliminate unemployment intensity
- **Household, not individual, entitlement** — 100 days per household spread across multiple adults is thin
- **Asset quality varies** — Where assets are poor, the second-round productivity effect does not materialise
- **No skill formation** — It provides unskilled manual work, so it does not raise a worker’s long-term earning capacity
- **Urban gap** — There is no urban equivalent, so urban informal workers have no comparable cushion

The balanced verdict

MGNREGS has significantly reduced the intensity of rural unemployment — cutting idle days, raising wage floors, reducing distress migration and absorbing shocks. It has not reduced the structural unemployment that arises from too many workers on too little land with too few skills. It is a stabiliser, not a transformer — and it was never designed to be the latter.

## Conclusion

Assessed against its own objective — livelihood security through 100 days of guaranteed work — MGNREGS has succeeded, particularly in smoothing seasonal distress and in its counter-cyclical role during the pandemic. Sustaining and extending that success requires timely wage payment, durable and productive assets, convergence with agriculture and watershed programmes, and an urban counterpart. But the permanent reduction of rural unemployment will come from elsewhere: agro-processing, MSMEs, skilling and formal job creation through the Labour Codes and the ELI Scheme. MGNREGS keeps the floor from giving way; something else must build the staircase.

## Value addition
- Statutory entitlements: 100 days per rural household per year; work within 15 days of demand or an unemployment allowance; work within 5 km or a 10% wage premium; one-third women; equal wages; Gram Sabha social audit; worksite crèche, drinking water, shade and first aid.
- Permissible works: water conservation and harvesting, drought proofing, irrigation canals, land development, flood control, rural connectivity, and works on land of SC/ST, BPL and small and marginal farmers.
- Recent development: MGNREGA has been restructured under the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika Mission (Rural) Act, 2025, a change contested by several States seeking to preserve the original guarantee.
- Current context: unemployment 3.1% (PLFS 2025); 56.2 crore persons employed in Q2 FY26; employment elasticity improved to 1.11% job growth per 1% value added (2017-23).

## Introduction

Poverty estimation in India determines who receives subsidised food, housing and health cover — so the choice of line and method is never merely statistical. The controversies of the last decade have converged on one uncomfortable fact: India

has had no officially updated poverty line since 2011-12, and now relies substantially on World Bank estimates to describe its own poverty.

Controversy 1: Which line — Tendulkar or Rangarajan?

- **Committee** — Line (2011-12, per capita per month) · Poverty estimate for 2011-12
- **Tendulkar (2009)** — ₹816 rural / ₹1,000 urban · 21.9%
- **Rangarajan (2014)** — ₹972 rural / ₹1,407 urban (about ₹33 and ₹47 a day) · 29.5%

The Rangarajan Committee was constituted precisely because the Tendulkar line was criticised as too low to represent a decent minimum. Its higher line implied about 9 crore more poor people — but the government never officially adopted it, so the Tendulkar estimate remains the last official figure. Two official committees producing two very different numbers for the same year is the root of the credibility problem.

Controversy 2: The missing survey (2017-18)

The NSSO’s Consumer Expenditure Survey for 2017-18 was not released, on the stated ground of “data quality”; leaked findings suggested a fall in real rural consumption. The result was a twelve-year gap in comparable consumption data — precisely the period covering demonetisation, GST and the pandemic.

Controversy 3: The HCES methodology change — the central technical dispute

The Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (2022-23 and 2023-24) finally restored the data series, but with three significant changes:

- The Modified Mixed Recall Period (MMRP) replaced the Uniform Reference Period (URP) — shorter recall for frequently purchased items, longer for infrequent ones.
- Three separate questionnaires were used instead of one.
- The imputed value of free items received under government schemes (foodgrain, cycles, uniforms) was accounted for.

Each change is defensible on its own; together they make the new series not strictly comparable with 2011-12. The scale of the effect is measurable: applying MMRP to the 2011-12 data would itself have reduced measured poverty from 22.9% to 16.22% even under the old poverty line. Critics therefore argue that a substantial part of the reported decline is a methodological artefact; defenders argue MMRP measures actual consumption more accurately.

Controversy 4: The rural-urban line divergence

Rural and urban poverty lines differ, and the ratio between them determines the rural-urban split of the poor. Critics argue that urban lines understate the true cost of urban living — rent, transport and services — so urban poverty is systematically underestimated. This matters practically: it is one reason India has no urban equivalent of MGNREGA.

Controversy 5: Reliance on external estimates

With no national line, India’s poverty is now widely described using World Bank figures. In June 2025 the Bank revised the international poverty line from $2.15 (2017 PPP) to $3.00 (2021 PPP), raising global extreme poverty by about 125 million people. On the new line, India’s extreme poverty is estimated at 5.25% in 2022-23, against 27.12% in 2011-12.

But the choice of line changes the picture entirely: at the lower-middle-income line of $4.20 a day — the more appropriate benchmark for India’s income level — about 24% of Indians, nearly one in four, were poor in 2022. Quoting only the 5.25% figure without this qualification is the commonest error in answers on this topic.

Controversy 6: The consequences for targeting

- Beneficiary identification still rests substantially on the 2011 Census and SECC 2011 — now fifteen years old.
- NFSA coverage of about 80.67 crore persons is based on 2011 population ratios, so both inclusion and exclusion errors persist.
- Without a current line, there is no agreed basis for deciding who should enter or exit welfare eligibility.

## Conclusion

The controversies are not primarily about arithmetic but about method, transparency and consequence — the poverty number decides entitlements for hundreds of millions. India’s response has been to shift toward the National MPI, which measures deprivation directly across 12 indicators and avoids the line-setting problem altogether. That is a genuine advance, but it does not remove the need for a current, officially adopted consumption poverty line and an updated beneficiary database — without which welfare targeting is being run on fifteen-year-old assumptions.

## Value addition
- World Bank June 2025 revision: IPL $2.15 → $3.00; lower-middle-income line $3.65 → $4.20; upper-middle-income line $6.85 → $8.30, based on 2021 PPPs from the International Comparison Program and 1,747 national poverty lines across 163 countries. Most of the increase came from revised national poverty lines, not price changes.
- Estimation lineage: Dandekar and Rath (1971); Alagh (1979) calorie norms — 2,400 kcal rural and 2,100 kcal urban; Lakdawala (1993); Tendulkar (2009); Rangarajan (2014); the Saxena and Hashim Committees on BPL identification.
- What replaced the line: NITI Aayog’s National MPI (12 indicators, Alkire-Foster method) and the SDG India Index; the National MPI reports headcount 11.28% in 2022-23.
- AP relevance: Andhra Pradesh was the first Indian State to adopt its own MPI (2018) for poverty-reduction planning, ahead of the national baseline of 2021.

## Introduction

Institutional credit — from commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks, cooperatives and SHG federations — is the alternative to the moneylender. Its inadequacy in rural Andhra Pradesh is not primarily a shortage of volume, since the State has one of India’s densest SHG networks, but a mismatch in who receives credit, for what purpose, and on what terms.

Dimensions of inadequacy

- The tenant farmer gap — the sharpest failure A large share of AP’s cultivators are tenants without recorded title, and institutional credit is tied to land records. Tenants therefore cannot access crop loans, insurance or compensation, and fall back on informal lenders at punitive rates. The State’s Crop Cultivator Rights Cards and the explicit inclusion of tenant farmers in Annadata Sukhibhava (₹20,000 a year) are responses to precisely this gap.
- Purpose mismatch — credit for consumption, not investment SHG and microfinance lending has often financed consumption, health emergencies, weddings and the repayment of older debt rather than productive assets. Credit that does not raise income cannot be repaid from income — the mechanism behind recurring distress.
- Coverage gaps within rural society Small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans, SC/ST and PVTG households, and women outside SHG membership remain underserved. Allied activities — dairy, fisheries, poultry — receive far less than crop loans despite higher and steadier returns.
- The short-term bias Institutional lending is skewed towards short-term crop loans, partly because of interest subvention design, while term credit for irrigation, farm mechanisation, storage and processing — the investment that actually raises productivity — remains scarce.
- Regional concentration Credit flows follow prosperity. The Krishna-Godavari delta districts absorb a disproportionate share, while Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra — the drought-prone and tribal regions with the greatest need — receive less.
- Institutional weaknesses - Cooperatives — PACS and District Central Cooperative Banks — suffer from weak capital, poor governance and political interference. - Bank branch density is thinner in interior and agency areas; Business Correspondents partly bridge this but with limited product range. - Documentation, delays and collateral requirements deter the very borrowers the system is meant to serve.
- The legacy of the 2010 microfinance crisis The crisis originated in Andhra Pradesh, and the AP Microfinance Institutions (Regulation of Money Lending) Ordinance, 2010 effectively halted commercial MFI operations in the State. It produced the Malegam Committee (2011) and the NBFC-MFI category — India’s microfinance regulation was born from AP’s experience — but it also left a period of credit contraction in rural areas.
- Asset quality as a constraint on future lending Across scheduled commercial banks, agriculture’s GNPA stands at 6.0% — the highest of any sector, and over a third of all bad loans, against 1.9% for industry and 1.1% for personal loans. High delinquency makes banks cautious, which further restricts supply to the segment that needs it most.

What has improved

- RRB consolidation: 28 RRBs with about 22,158 branches; consolidated CRAR at an all-time high of 14.4% (FY25); the credit-deposit ratio rose to 73.8% (March 2025) — the highest in 35 years, meaning rural deposits are being lent locally rather than parked.
- SERP and Stree Nidhi: about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, repayment above 97%, with Stree Nidhi providing rapid small-ticket credit.
- Formalisation is rising: among unincorporated manufacturing units nationally, formal credit use rose from 48% (2021-22) to 51% (2023-24), with commercial bank borrowing up 6 percentage points and reliance on moneylenders and suppliers falling.
- Priority Sector Lending discipline: 18% of ANBC to agriculture, with 10% for small and marginal farmers and 7.5% for micro enterprises.

## Conclusion

Rural credit in Andhra Pradesh is inadequate less in quantity than in composition and reach — too short-term, too crop-focused, too concentrated in the delta, and structurally closed to tenant cultivators. Correcting it requires recognising tenancy for credit purposes, expanding term lending for irrigation and processing, strengthening cooperatives, and financing allied activities. Credit becomes a poverty-reduction instrument only when it funds an asset that generates the income to repay it.

## Value addition
- Priority Sector Lending targets: 40% of ANBC overall; 18% for agriculture, within which 14% for non-corporate farmers and 10% for small and marginal farmers; 7.5% for micro enterprises. RRBs and SFBs face higher overall PSL obligations (75% for SFBs).
- Institutional architecture: NABARD as apex refinancer, operating the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) since 1995-96 from shortfalls in banks’ PSL; the Kisan Credit Card, now linked with PM-KISAN for faster credit.
- Microfinance today (FY25): 627 lakh active borrowers; gross loan portfolio ₹2.38 lakh crore; 95% women, 80% rural; the RBI reduced NBFC-MFI qualifying assets from 75% to 60% (June 2025) to let lenders diversify after FY25 stress.
- AP context: agriculture contributes about 37% of GSVA while employing a much larger share of the workforce — the productivity gap that adequate term credit is meant to close.

## Introduction

The structure of landholdings — how land is distributed by size class — determines the viability of farming, access to credit and the capacity to mechanise. Across the past two decades Andhra Pradesh has followed the national trajectory but in an accentuated form: holdings have become smaller, more numerous and more fragmented, while cultivation has increasingly passed to tenants who do not own the land they till.

Classification of operational holdings (Agriculture Census)

- **Marginal** — Below 1 hectare
- **Small** — 1 – 2 hectares
- **Semi-medium** — 2 – 4 hectares
- **Medium** — 4 – 10 hectares
- **Large** — Above 10 hectares

The national benchmark (Agriculture Census 2015-16)

- Average operational holding fell from 2.28 hectares (1970-71) to 1.08 hectares (2015-16).
- Small and marginal holdings constitute about 86.2% of all holdings but operate only about 47.3% of the area
- the defining asymmetry of Indian agriculture.

The changing structure in Andhra Pradesh

- Marginalisation — the dominant trend The share of marginal holdings (below 1 hectare) has risen steadily, and together with small holdings now accounts for the overwhelming majority of the State’s operational holdings. The average size has fallen below the national average, to under a hectare.
- Rising number, falling size Total holdings increased even as total operated area remained broadly constant — the arithmetic of subdivision. Inheritance under personal law divides holdings each generation, and there is no

counteracting mechanism of consolidation.

- Decline of large holdings Medium and large holdings have shrunk in both number and share, partly through ceiling legislation (the AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973) but far more through partition among heirs.
- Fragmentation within holdings Even a single “holding” is often several non-contiguous plots, raising cultivation costs, wasting land on boundaries and making irrigation and mechanisation uneconomic.
- The rise of tenancy — the distinctive AP feature Andhra Pradesh has among the highest incidence of tenancy in India, particularly in the Krishna-Godavari delta. Crucially, most of it is oral and unrecorded, because owners fear that a recorded tenant may acquire rights under tenancy law. The consequence is severe: the actual cultivator has no access to institutional credit, crop insurance, input subsidy or calamity compensation, all of which follow the land record rather than the plough.
- Diverging land use Alongside fragmentation, land has shifted from cereals toward aquaculture ponds, horticulture and oil palm, especially in the coastal districts — changing not just the size but the use of holdings.

Causes of the change

- Inheritance and partition — the principal driver.
- Ceiling legislation, which limited legal accumulation.
- Absence of consolidation programmes, unlike Punjab and Haryana.
- Distress sales by small farmers during drought and debt cycles.
- Land diversion to non-agricultural use around Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada-Amaravati and Tirupati.
- Occupational shift without land transfer — households move to non-farm work but retain the land, so ownership fragments faster than cultivation.

Economic consequences

- **Uneconomic mechanisation** — Tractors and modern equipment cannot be justified on a fragmented plot
- **Low marketable surplus** — Production barely above subsistence weakens the farm-market link
- **Poor credit access** — Small holdings offer little collateral; agriculture’s GNPA stands at 6.0%, the highest of any sector
- **Weak bargaining power** — In both input and output markets — which is why Farmer Producer Organisations were created to restore scale artificially
- **Tenant exclusion** — The actual cultivator remains outside every formal support system

## Conclusion

Over two decades Andhra Pradesh’s landholding structure has moved decisively toward smaller, more numerous, more fragmented holdings cultivated increasingly by unrecorded tenants. Since consolidation is neither politically nor legally feasible, the practical response is to restore scale without altering ownership — through FPOs (about 56.32 lakh farmers nationally), custom hiring centres, and contract and group farming — and to recognise tenancy for credit purposes, which the State has begun through Crop Cultivator Rights Cards and by extending Annadata Sukhibhava (₹20,000 a year) to tenant farmers.

## Value addition
- Data source: the Agriculture Census, conducted quinquennially by the Department of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare; 2015-16 was the last fully released round, with the 2021-22 round in progress. An “operational holding” is land used wholly or partly for agriculture and operated as one technical unit, regardless of title.
- The consolidation contrast: Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh undertook systematic consolidation of holdings (chakbandi); the southern States, including Andhra Pradesh, largely did not.
- The policy answer: the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016 (NITI Aayog) would legalise and record tenancy so tenants can access credit and insurance while owners retain title.
- Digital infrastructure: the Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme (DILRMP) and Agristack aim to make records accurate enough for credit to follow the cultivator.

## Introduction

The Eleventh Plan (2007-12) set Andhra Pradesh a GSDP growth target of 9.5%, aligned to the national theme of Faster and More Inclusive Growth. The State’s strategy combined irrigation-led agricultural revival, industrial diversification and a services boom centred on Hyderabad, layered with an unusually large welfare architecture.

## Primary sector — revival with fragility
- Agriculture and allied activities grew at an average of about 6%, well above the national 4% target — a genuine achievement.
- The driver was Jalayagnam, the State’s massive irrigation programme, supported by improved rural credit, Rythu Mitra Groups for extension, and input subsidies.
- Diversification into horticulture, fisheries and aquaculture raised rural incomes and reduced dependence on paddy.
- But: erratic monsoons, groundwater depletion and cost escalation in irrigation projects made gains fragile, and productivity remained uneven — Rayalaseema and Telangana lagged the coastal deltas.

## Secondary sector — growth without depth
- Industry grew at about 9.8%, led by pharmaceuticals, cement, automobiles and IT hardware.
- The Hyderabad-Vijayawada corridor and APIIC’s industrial parks improved the investment climate; the State ranked among India’s leaders in ease of doing business.
- But: growth was concentrated in a few capital-intensive sectors. Traditional manufacturing, handlooms and small industry stagnated under power shortages, credit constraints and competition — meaning industrial growth generated fewer jobs than its rate suggested.

## Tertiary sector — the engine, and the imbalance
- Services emerged as the dominant driver, contributing over 56% of GSDP.
- IT exports from Hyderabad grew exponentially, alongside real estate, banking, transport and trade.
- But: the gains were overwhelmingly urban and Hyderabad-centric. Employment creation in high-end services partly offset agrarian distress in aggregate statistics while doing little for the rural workforce — a spatial imbalance that carried direct political consequences.

## Social and human development

The State pursued an ambitious welfare agenda — Aarogyasri health insurance, fee reimbursement for higher

education, Indiramma housing, and pensions — alongside central flagships (NRHM, SSA, MGNREGA). These improved health and education access measurably, but were largely revenue expenditure, contributing to the rising revenue deficit that constrained later capital spending.

## Overall evaluation
- Growth target broadly met, with all three sectors performing at or above national averages.
- Inclusiveness only partly achieved: growth was concentrated in one metropolitan region and a few sectors; regional disparity between Coastal Andhra, Telangana and Rayalaseema widened rather than narrowed.
- Fiscal sustainability weakened, as welfare commitments and irrigation borrowings expanded faster than own revenue.
- The unaddressed regional imbalance became a central factor in the political momentum toward bifurcation.

## Conclusion

The Eleventh Plan delivered Andhra Pradesh strong sectoral growth — 6% in agriculture, 9.8% in industry and a services boom — but exposed the limits of aggregate performance as a measure of development. Growth that concentrates spatially and sectorally does not automatically become inclusive. That lesson directly shapes the residuary State’s current strategy: dispersed industrial nodes at Orvakal, Kopparthy and Krishnapatnam, port-led growth along the coast, and MSME parks in all 175 assembly constituencies.

## Value addition
- Rythu Mitra Groups: farmer collectives created by AP’s Department of Agriculture in 2003 to strengthen extension services and improve small and marginal farmers’ access to inputs, credit and knowledge.
- Jalayagnam: AP’s flagship irrigation programme launched in 2004 to complete a large number of major and medium projects, financed substantially through NABARD’s RIDF and market borrowings.
- Contrast with today: AP’s current sectoral shares (2023-24, current prices) are roughly agriculture 37%, manufacturing 23%, services 40% — an unusually high farm share reflecting the loss of Hyderabad and the rise of aquaculture and horticulture.
- AP’s present growth architecture: Global Partnership Summit 2025 commitments of ₹13.25 lakh crore across 610 MoUs; Google’s US$15 billion AI data centre at Visakhapatnam; capital expenditure raised to ₹53,915 crore in 2026-27.
- One-line revision point: The Eleventh Plan proved Andhra Pradesh could grow fast; it also proved that fast growth in one city is not development for one State.

## Introduction

Expenditure on health and education is the clearest measure of a State’s commitment to human capital. For Andhra Pradesh, the last decade spans the post-bifurcation fiscal shock, the pandemic, a welfare expansion, and the current consolidation — so the trend is best read in three phases rather than as a single line.

Current position (AP Budget 2026-27)

- **School Education** — ₹32,308 crore (including ₹1,500 crore for school infrastructure overhaul)
- **Health, Medical & Family Welfare** — ₹19,306 crore
- **Higher Education** — ₹2,567 crore
- **Skill Development and Training** — ₹1,232 crore
- **Women, Children, Differently Abled and Senior Citizens** — ₹4,582 crore

Together, education and health account for a substantial share of the State’s total expenditure of ₹3,32,205 crore against a GSDP of about ₹19.8 lakh crore.

Evaluating the trend — three phases

Phase 1 (2014-19): recovery under constraint After bifurcation, the residuary State lost roughly a third of its revenue base while retaining most of its population. Social-sector allocations grew in absolute terms but were squeezed as a share of a stressed budget; the revenue deficit of ₹24,194 crore in 2014-15 left limited room for expansion.

Phase 2 (2019-24): welfare expansion, weak capital formation Spending rose sharply, but was overwhelmingly revenue expenditure — DBT transfers rather than institutional capacity. The record shows the cost of that composition: the Nadu-Nedu school infrastructure programme left works worth about ₹7,876 crore incomplete, and the health sector accumulated ₹6,486 crore in unpaid liabilities, delaying reimbursements to empanelled hospitals.

Phase 3 (since 2024-25): consolidation with outcome focus Legacy liabilities have been largely cleared; capital expenditure has risen to ₹53,915 crore (from ₹39,498 crore in RE 2025-26); and the composition has shifted toward outcome-linked programmes — Project Sanjeevani in health, and Learning Excellence in Andhra Pradesh in education. The State’s fiscal position has improved in parallel: revenue deficit down from 3.79% of GSDP (FY25) to 1.11% (BE 2026-27).

Evaluation — three findings

- Growth in spending has been real but composition-weak. Allocations grew steadily, yet capital outlay remains about 16% of total expenditure, so much of the increase funded salaries, transfers and subsidies rather than durable

capacity.

- Outcomes have lagged inputs. Despite sustained education spending, AP records 72.6% literacy (PLFS 2023-24)

— the lowest among Indian States — showing that expenditure alone does not produce learning. Health spending has expanded coverage under Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva to about 1.43 crore households with cover up to ₹25 lakh, but preventive and primary care were under-funded until recently.

- Arrears are a hidden form of under-spending. Budget allocations mean little if reimbursements are delayed — the

₹6,486 crore of health liabilities and the April 2026 suspension of services by private hospitals show that timeliness of payment is part of expenditure quality.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s health and education expenditure has grown consistently in absolute terms over the decade, and the recent shift toward clearing arrears, restoring capital works and outcome-based programmes is the right correction. The decisive test now is not how much is allocated but what it buys: foundational literacy and numeracy, functioning primary health centres, and teachers and doctors actually in position. Given AP’s literacy standing and its rapidly ageing population, human-capital spending is not a welfare choice for the State — it is the binding constraint on Swarna Andhra @2047.

## Value addition
- National benchmarks: government health expenditure 1.13% of GDP (2014-15) → 1.84% (2021-22), against the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5%; the Twelfth Plan set the same target and missed it.
- Education benchmark: the Kothari Commission (1966) and NEP 2020 both recommend 6% of GDP on education — a target never achieved nationally.
- Quality of expenditure: nationally, revenue expenditure fell from 13.6% of GDP (FY22) to 10.9% (FY25) while capital outlay rose — the Quality of Public Expenditure Index reached its highest level since 1991 in 2024-25. AP’s capital share, at about 16% of spending, still trails that shift.
- Caution from Economic Survey 2025-26: unconditional cash transfers across States of about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26 create expenditure rigidity that crowds out human-capital investment.

Note: the Scale-Based Regulatory framework was issued on 22 October 2021 and came into effect on 1 October 2022.

NBFCs are the second engine of India’s credit system, reaching borrowers banks find costly to serve — MSMEs, vehicle buyers, microfinance clients and infrastructure projects. But the IL&FS (2018) and DHFL (2019) failures exposed asset-liability mismatches and contagion risk, prompting the RBI to move from light-touch to proportionate, risk-calibrated regulation.

## Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) — the architecture
- **Base (NBFC-BL)** — Smallest, non-deposit-taking · Light-touch
- **Middle (NBFC-ML)** — Deposit-taking, HFCs, larger NBFCs · Enhanced governance and exposure norms
- **Upper (NBFC-UL)** — Top systemically important NBFCs identified annually · Bank-like norms — CET-1 of 9%, differential provisioning, mandatory listing
- **Top (NBFC-TL)** — Empty by design; populated only on extreme risk · Highest supervision

## Capital, governance and risk management
- Common Equity Tier-1 requirement for the Upper Layer; a Chief Risk Officer mandated for NBFCs with assets above

₹5,000 crore; independent internal audit and compliance functions; Board-approved risk appetite frameworks.

## Curbing regulatory arbitrage and interconnectedness
- Prudential exposure limits on bank lending to NBFCs, restricting the financing of speculative or unsecured group activities; risk weights on such exposures were raised in 2023 and calibrated back in 2025 as stress moderated.
- Non-Fund Based Credit Facilities Directions, 2025 — uniform treatment of guarantees and letters of credit across banks and NBFCs.

## Conduct regulation — protecting the borrower
- Digital Lending Directions: disbursal and repayment only through borrower bank accounts (no pass-through pools), consent-based data use, mandatory Key Facts Statement disclosing the all-inclusive Annual Percentage Rate, cooling-off periods, and a public directory of digital lending apps. The RBI has explicitly cautioned against perpetual credit lines and evergreening.
- Fair Practices Code on recovery conduct and grievance redressal, with an ombudsman route.

## Sector-specific calibration
- Project finance: the revised framework effective 1 October 2025 eased provisioning for under-construction infrastructure while retaining early risk assessment and post-completion monitoring.
- Microfinance: responding to FY25 stress — when MFI loans outstanding fell 14% on over-lending — the RBI’s circular of 6 June 2025 reduced the minimum qualifying assets for NBFC-MFIs from 75% to 60%, letting them diversify risk; self-regulatory organisations simultaneously capped borrower indebtedness. Stress began easing from Q2 FY26.

## Supervision

Unified, risk-based supervision with off-site surveillance, early warning systems, and the RBI’s Framework for Formulation of Regulations (7 May 2025) mandating consultation, impact analysis and periodic review.

## Conclusion

The RBI’s approach has evolved from uniform prescription to proportionality — regulation scaled to size, activity and systemic importance. The result is a sector that has absorbed the microfinance cycle without contagion, while conduct regulation has curbed the excesses of digital lending. The continuing task is to keep pace with fintech innovation without either stifling credit access or importing bank-like risk into a lightly capitalised sector.

## Value addition
- Banks vs. NBFCs: NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits; are outside the payment and settlement system and cannot issue cheques on themselves; and DICGC deposit insurance is not available to their depositors.
- Microfinance profile (FY25): active borrowers up from 330 lakh (FY14) to 627 lakh; gross loan portfolio up nearly seven-fold to ₹2.38 lakh crore; 95% women borrowers, 80% rural; operations across 685 districts. Market share — NBFC-MFIs 39%, banks 32%, SFBs 16%, other NBFCs 12%.
- Andhra Pradesh link: the 2010 AP microfinance crisis and the AP Microfinance Institutions (Regulation of Money Lending) Ordinance, 2010 were the direct trigger for the Malegam Committee (2011) and the creation of the NBFC-MFI category — India’s microfinance regulation was born in Andhra Pradesh.

## Introduction

Agriculture’s share in national income has fallen from over 50% in 1950–51 to 15.2% of nominal GDP in FY26 (First Advance Estimates), even as India recorded 7.4% real GDP growth in FY26 — the fastest-growing major economy for the fourth consecutive year (Economic Survey 2025–26). This inverse movement is not coincidence but the signature of structural transformation: as high-productivity sectors expand, the aggregate growth rate rises while agriculture’s relative share necessarily contracts.

## Theoretical foundation
- Fisher–Clark hypothesis & Kuznets: development entails a systematic shift primary → secondary → tertiary.
- Lewis dual-sector model: transfer of surplus labour from low-productivity agriculture to the modern sector raises aggregate output without reducing farm output.
- Engel’s Law: as incomes rise, the income elasticity of demand for food falls; demand shifts to manufactures and services, which then grow faster.

## Structural transformation of India’s GDP
- **Sector (share of GDP)** — 1950–51 · 1990–91 · FY26 (FAE) · FY26 real growth
- **Agriculture & allied** — ~52% · ~29% · 15.2% · 3.1%
- **Industry** — ~15% · ~26% · 24.3% · 6.2% (Mfg 7.0%)
- **Services** — ~33% · ~45% · 51.1% · 9.1%

- *Source: MoSPI / Economic Survey 2025–26*

## How the decline enabled faster growth
- Resource reallocation to high-productivity uses: labour and capital moved to sectors growing at 7–9% against agriculture’s 3%; this compositional shift mechanically lifts aggregate growth.
- Weighted-average effect: with services at 51% of GDP growing 9.1%, aggregate growth is now far less hostage to monsoon volatility than in the 1960s–70s.
- Higher savings & investment: GFCF reached 30.0% of GDP in FY26, financing industrial and infrastructure capex — impossible in a subsistence-agriculture economy.
- Growth acceleration record: ~3.5% (1950–80) → ~5.8% (1980–2000) → 7%+ post-2000. ES 2025–26 growth accounting now places potential growth at ~7%, up from 6.5%.
- Linkages & multipliers: the Green Revolution supplied raw material to agro-industries; rising rural incomes fuelled demand for manufactures. Rural FMCG volumes grew 7.7–8.4% in FY26, outpacing urban.
- Allied sectors as stabilisers: livestock and fisheries grew a steady 5–6%; livestock GVA rose about 195% (FY15–FY24), diversifying farm incomes.

## Balanced caveat (essential for high marks)
- Employment has not shifted proportionately: agriculture still absorbs about 42% of the workforce (PLFS, Q2 FY26, CWS) while producing 15% of GDP — a productivity gap of roughly 1 : 4, meaning disguised unemployment persists.
- Services-led, not manufacturing-led: unlike East Asia, India’s transition bypassed mass low-skill industrial employment — the “premature deindustrialisation” concern.
- Important nuance: ES 2025–26 clarifies that manufacturing’s falling nominal share reflects relative price (terms-of-trade) effects, not declining activity — in real terms it has been stable at 17–18%.
- AP illustration: agriculture & allied still contribute about 37% of GSVA and support nearly 60% of the population, yet AP grew at 9.24% real (2024–25) against the national 6.4% — because growth came from high-value diversification (aquaculture: 30% of India’s fish production; largest fruit producer at 15.6% of national output; 1st in egg production).

ConclusionThe falling income share of agriculture is a symptom of maturity, not malaise — it reflects faster expansion elsewhere, not agrarian collapse. The unfinished task is to convert this relative decline into absolute strengthening: raising farm productivity, deepening allied and agro-processing value chains, and building job-rich manufacturing so that labour follows income out of agriculture. Only then will structural transformation become genuinely inclusive, in line with Viksit Bharat @2047.

## Introduction

India is richly endowed — minerals, a 7,500-km coastline, high solar insolation, fertile plains and a young workforce — yet endowment becomes income only when combined with capital, technology and infrastructure. Public debt bridges the gap between long-gestation investment needs and limited current revenue, making it a legitimate instrument of development rather than a mere fiscal expedient.

## Why borrowing is justified
- Breaking the low-savings trap: as Nurkse argued, developing economies face a vicious circle — low income, low savings, low investment. Public borrowing mobilises scattered domestic savings into large, indivisible projects that no private investor would finance alone.
- The Golden Rule of public finance: borrow only to invest. In BE 2026-27, effective capital expenditure (₹17.15 lakh crore) exceeds the fiscal deficit (≈₹16.9 lakh crore) — evidence that current borrowing is asset-creating.
- Intergenerational fairness (benefit principle): a port or irrigation project serves 40 years; financing it from one year’s taxes would burden a single generation. Debt aligns who pays with who benefits.
- Turning resources into value chains: critical minerals, green hydrogen and blue-economy assets need upfront outlays — the National Green Hydrogen Mission (Phase 2, ₹25,000 crore in Budget 2026-27) and the National Critical Mineral Mission illustrate resource-linked, debt-supported investment.
- Counter-cyclical stabiliser: during shocks (2008, 2020), borrowing sustained demand and protected capacity — a luxury that debt-constrained economies lack.
- Crowding-in: public capex reduces logistics and power bottlenecks, raising private returns. The Centre’s capex share rose from 12.5% (FY20) to 22.6% of expenditure (FY25 PA), alongside recovering private investment.

## Andhra Pradesh — the argument in miniature

Borrowed and grant-financed capital is converting the State’s coastal endowment into productive assets: Polavaram irrigation; new ports at Ramayapatnam (75%), Mulapeta (65%), Machilipatnam (50%); Alluri Sitaramaraju (Bhogapuram) International Airport, 97% complete; and capital expenditure raised to ₹53,915 crore in 2026-27, aided by ₹6,544 crore of SASCI interest-free loans.

## Conditions that keep debt developmental
- g > r: nominal growth (~10%) must exceed the cost of borrowing.
- Absorptive capacity: projects must be appraised, executed on time and maintained.
- Transparency: off-budget borrowing defeats the purpose — hence the 16th FC’s mandate to bring all such liabilities on-budget.
- Avoid revenue-deficit borrowing: debt for salaries and untargeted transfers builds no repayment capacity.

## Conclusion

Public debt is not the opposite of prudence; imprudent debt is. For a resource-rich but capital-scarce economy, borrowing to build irrigation, ports, power and skills is precisely how latent endowment is converted into national income. The test is simple and can be applied to every rupee borrowed: does it create an asset that will help repay it?

## Value addition
- Concepts to quote: Golden Rule of public finance; Domar condition (debt ratio falls when g > r); Nurkse’s vicious circle of poverty; benefit principle of intergenerational equity.
- Productive-debt evidence: effective capex 4.4% of GDP and over 32% of total Union expenditure (BE 2026-27); SASCI 50-year interest-free capex loans to States raised to ₹1.85 lakh crore.
- Returns justify confidence: average return on inward FDI in India ≈ 7.3% (2014-23), higher than Thailand, Brazil, Mexico and South Africa.
- Caution from the Economic Survey 2025-26: unconditional cash transfers financed by borrowing raise expenditure rigidity and crowd out capital and human-capital spending.
- AP practice: debt swap of ₹43,298 crore of high-cost loans (12.3% → ≤9%), saving ₹327 crore a year.

## Introduction

Under Flexible Inflation Targeting, the RBI is mandated to keep CPI inflation at 4% ±2% — a target renotified under Section 45ZA for 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031. Over the last two years the RBI has run a full policy arc: a prolonged pause to consolidate disinflation, an aggressive easing cycle as inflation collapsed, and a return to caution as supply shocks re-emerged in 2026.

## Interest rate strategy — patience, then decisive easing
- **2022-23 tightening** — Repo raised 250 bps (4.00% → 6.50%) · Anchor expectations after the post-Ukraine price surge
- **Feb 2023 – Feb 2025 pause** — Held at 6.50% for eleven meetings; stance “withdrawal of accommodation” · Let disinflation consolidate without choking growth
- **Feb 2025 – Feb 2026 easing** — Cumulative 125 bps cut to 5.25%; stance shifted to neutral · Inflation collapsed; space opened for growth support
- **June 2026 pause** — Held at 5.25%, unanimous 6-0 · West Asia conflict, fuel price increases, monsoon risk

## Liquidity management — the durable-liquidity push
- CRR cut in phases, releasing about ₹2.5 lakh crore.
- Open market purchases of ₹6.95 lakh crore (February 2025 to January 2026) and a forex swap of about US$25 billion to inject durable liquidity.
- VRRR and SDF used to absorb transient surpluses — system liquidity averaged a surplus of ₹1.89 lakh crore in FY26, yet the WACR stayed only 8 bps below the repo rate.

## Exchange rate management — the imported-inflation defence

Forex reserves peaked at a record US$728.49 billion (27 February 2026) before the RBI sold dollars to curb volatility as West Asian tensions pushed the rupee from about ₹83 to ₹95–96 per dollar; reserves have since rebuilt to about US$676 billion (17 July 2026). The RBI’s stated position is that it intervenes for orderly conditions, not for a target rate.

## Coordination with fiscal supply-side measures

Buffer-stock releases, export restrictions on rice, duty cuts on crude edible oils (20% → 10%, June 2025) and the GST 2.0 rate rationalisation attacked prices directly — the supply-side work monetary policy cannot do.

## Assessment of outcomes
- Headline CPI fell to 1.7% (April–December 2025) — the lowest average in the current series, with 0.3% in October 2025; core inflation excluding gold and silver was down to about 2.3%.
- Disinflation without a growth sacrifice: GDP grew 8% in H1 FY26; India’s inflation (2.8%) was below the world average (4.2%).
- Transmission was effective: WALR on fresh rupee loans fell 59 bps and on outstanding loans 69 bps (February–November 2025).
- The limits are now visible: in June 2026 the MPC raised the FY27 inflation projection to 5.1% and cut growth to 6.6%, conceding that energy and geopolitical shocks lie outside monetary control.

## Conclusion

The RBI’s strategy was sequenced, data-driven and instrument-diverse — rates for demand, liquidity for transmission,

forex for imported inflation, and coordination for supply shocks. Its success in achieving record-low inflation alongside strong growth validated the FIT framework and contributed to three sovereign rating upgrades. The 2026 pause is not a failure but a reminder that credibility is preserved by knowing when not to act.

## Value addition
- Current policy setting: repo 5.25%, SDF 5.00%, MSF/Bank Rate 5.50%, CRR 3.00%, SLR 18.00%, neutral stance.
- June 2026 MPC: FY27 GDP forecast cut to 6.6%; CPI forecast raised to 5.1%, with Q3 FY27 projected at 5.9%, near the 6% upper tolerance limit.
- Sovereign validation: S&P upgraded India from BBB- to BBB; CareEdge Global initiated coverage at BBB+; the 10-year yield spread over US Treasuries more than halved.
- Failure clause: if CPI stays outside 2–6% for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the Government under Section 45ZN — invoked once, in 2022.

## Introduction

The Twelfth Plan (2012-17), themed “Faster, Sustainable and More Inclusive Growth,” was for Andhra Pradesh the most disrupted plan in its history — it began for a united State of 23 districts and ended for a residuary State without Hyderabad. Its features must therefore be read as intentions partly executed and partly overtaken by events.

## Important features

## Objectives and strategic focus
- A GSDP growth target of about 10%, above the national 8%, with emphasis on economic diversification and human development.
- A shift from output targets to outcome indicators in health, education and rural livelihoods.

## Inclusive and balanced regional development
- Explicit priority to narrowing gaps between Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema and Telangana.
- Special area development programmes for backward districts such as Anantapur and Vizianagaram.
- Strengthening Panchayati Raj Institutions for decentralised planning.

## Agriculture and rural sector
- A Primary Sector Mission targeting 6% agricultural growth through crop diversification, irrigation efficiency and livestock development.
- Implementation of RKVY and the National Food Security Mission; micro-irrigation and watershed management prioritised for drought-prone tracts.

## Industry and infrastructure
- Industrial Investment Promotion Policy (2010-15), APIIC land banks and PPP projects.

## Flagship concepts: Pharma City, the Information Technology Investment Region (ITIR) and port-led development at Krishnapatnam, Kakinada and Gangavaram.
- Power sector reform and renewable energy (wind and solar parks) for energy security.

## Social sector and human resources
- Expansion of RMSA in secondary education and Aarogyasri in health.
- Skill Development Missions to address youth unemployment.

## Fiscal and governance reform
- Results-based monitoring, adherence to AP FRBM targets, and e-governance through Mee-Seva citizen service centres.

The Twelfth Plan’s real significance for Andhra Pradesh lies less in what it achieved than in the priorities it bequeathed. Port-led development, industrial corridors, skill missions and outcome-based governance all survived the Plan’s collapse and became the organising principles of post-2014 development. The State’s current Swarna Andhra @2047 vision — a US$2.4 trillion economy guided by the ten “Padhi Sutralu” — is the direct institutional descendant of the Twelfth Plan’s

approach, minus the Plan.

## Introduction

Public expenditure was classified into Plan (Five-Year/Annual Plan outlays) and Non-Plan (committed liabilities) until 2017. During the reform period, Andhra Pradesh’s spending tilted increasingly towards non-plan commitments, shaping both its fiscal stress and its welfare model.

- **Feature** — Plan expenditure · Non-plan expenditure
- **Purpose** — New schemes, asset creation · Salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies, maintenance
- **AP examples** — Jalayagnam, Rajiv Vidya Mission, industrial corridors · Pay revisions, debt servicing, power and rice subsidy
- **Nature** — Discretionary; borrowed/CSS-funded · Committed, inflexible, recurring

## Relative importance during the reform period
- Non-plan dominance: committed items (salaries + pensions + interest) absorbed the larger share of revenue expenditure, compressing developmental space.
- Plan spending survived through mega-projects: Jalayagnam irrigation, Vision 2020 infrastructure and the World Bank-assisted AP Economic Restructuring Project kept plan outlays high — but largely debt-financed.
- Welfare turn (post-2004): Aarogyasri, fee reimbursement, Indiramma housing and subsidised rice were essentially

revenue/non-plan — high in equity value, low in asset creation.

- Correction attempts: the AP FRBM Act, 2005 and the AP Fiscal Reforms Programme eliminated the revenue deficit by 2005-06, proving that composition, not size, was the binding constraint.
- Structural flaw exposed: projects were funded as “plan” while their upkeep was starved as “non-plan” — the central critique that ended the classification.

## Why the distinction was abandoned
- Rangarajan Committee on Efficient Management of Public Expenditure (2011) held the divide dysfunctional; discontinued from 2017-18 with the end of Five-Year Plans and the replacement of the Planning Commission by NITI Aayog. Budgets now use revenue vs. capital and outcome-based classification.

- Revenue expenditure ₹2,56,143 crore vs. capital expenditure ₹53,915 crore (~16% of total), up from ₹39,498 crore in 2025-26 (RE).

During the reform period non-plan expenditure gained prominence through committed and welfare obligations, while plan spending retained developmental relevance through irrigation and infrastructure. ## Introduction

Exam technique: “Write a brief note” signals a short, self-contained answer of roughly 175-200 words of substance, not a full essay. Give the pattern, the causes in one line each, and the corrective — then stop.

Irrigation in Andhra Pradesh is distributed as unevenly as its rainfall, and the pattern of access — not soil quality or farmer enterprise — is the principal determinant of which region prospers.

The pattern of disparity

- **Coastal Andhra (Krishna-Godavari delta)** — Assured canal irrigation from the Godavari and Krishna anicuts; gravity flow over flat alluvium · Highest — supports double and triple cropping, aquaculture and horticulture
- **Rayalaseema** — Predominantly groundwater (borewells); limited canal command; requires costly lift irrigation · Lowest — rainfall of 500-700 mm against far higher evapotranspiration; water tables declining
- **North Coastal Andhra** — Tanks, minor irrigation and rainfed cultivation; hilly, tribal agency terrain · Low — limited canal potential

Causes in brief

- Colonial investment followed the deltas — Sir Arthur Cotton’s Dowleswaram anicut on the Godavari (1852) and the Krishna anicut at Vijayawada created assured irrigation more than 170 years ago.
- Geography — the deltas are flat and command-able by gravity; Rayalaseema is an elevated Deccan fringe where water must be lifted. HNSS raises water over 369 metres through 12-13 stages.
- The Green Revolution reinforced the gap, since the HYV package required assured water.
- Inter-State disputes — Krishna allocation remains unsettled before the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II, creating uncertainty for Rayalaseema schemes dependent on Srisailam flood water.
- Project delays and energy cost in lift schemes.

Consequences

Divergent cropping patterns, income and productivity gaps, concentration of poverty and farmer distress in the rain-fed regions, and out-migration from Rayalaseema and the agency areas.

Corrective measures

Handri Neeva Sujala Sravanthi (40 TMC, 565-km canal, about 6.02 lakh acres and drinking water for nearly 33 lakh people across 81 drought-prone mandals); Galeru-Nagari; Poola Subbaiah Veligonda (43.50 TMC by gravity through twin tunnels); Polavaram as the anchor Godavari project; the proposed Polavaram-Banakacherla link (about ₹80,112 crore, 200 TMC); micro-irrigation under PMKSY; and demand-side management through APCNF, which achieves water savings of up to 50%.

## Conclusion

Irrigation disparity in Andhra Pradesh is historically created and geographically reinforced — the deltas inherited assured canal water while Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra must lift or harvest it. Lift schemes have narrowed the gap without closing it; doing so requires completing the pending projects, resolving the Krishna allocation, reducing lift energy costs through solar pumping, and managing demand as much as expanding supply.

## Value addition
- Historical anchor: the Dowleswaram (Sir Arthur Cotton) anicut, 1852 — the single most consequential

investment in the State’s agricultural history.

- Institutional framework: Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014; Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II (Brijesh Kumar Tribunal).
- The energy cost: lifting water 369 metres makes HNSS power-intensive; AP budgets about ₹11,000 crore in agricultural power subsidy for 22.5 lakh farmers.
- AP allocations: capital expenditure of ₹53,915 crore in 2026-27, with irrigation the largest single head historically.

Tax devolution is the transfer to States of their share in the net proceeds of central taxes under Article 270, distributed as per Finance Commission awards under Article 280. Consolidating this requires deepening skill development through APSSDC, extending digital and financial services into Rayalaseema and tribal belts, and integrating services with manufacturing — the pathway envisioned under Swarna Andhra Vision 2047, which targets a $2.4 trillion GSDP, per capita income above $42,000, and zero poverty through the P4 (Public–People–Philanthropic Partnership) model.

## Introduction

The Human Development Index (HDI), conceived by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen (UNDP, 1990), measures achievement in health, education and standard of living. In the HDR 2025 ("A Matter of Choice: People and Possibilities in the Age of AI"), India ranked 130 out of 193 with an HDI value of 0.685 — improved, but still in the medium human development category. This growth–development gap reflects deficits in the quality rather than the quantity of growth.

## India's HDI profile (HDR 2025)
- **Dimension** — Indicator · India (2023)
- **Health** — Life expectancy at birth · 72.0 years (58.6 in 1990)
- **Education** — Mean years of schooling · 6.9 years
- **Education** — Expected years of schooling · 13 years
- **Living standard** — GNI per capita (PPP) · $9,046
- **Overall** — HDI value / rank · 0.685 / 130

## Factors responsible for the relatively low level
- Health-sector under-investment: Public health expenditure has hovered around ~2% of GDP — far below the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5%. Malnutrition, anaemia and stunting persist despite MMR falling 86% and U5MR 78% since 1990.
- Learning poverty, not schooling poverty: Enrolment is near-universal, but ASER finds roughly half of Grade 5 students cannot read a Grade 2 text. Mean years of schooling (6.9) remains below the global average — the single weakest HDI component for India.
- Inequality as the biggest drag: Inequality erodes 30.7% of India's HDI value (IHDI) — one of the highest losses in the region. The top 1% hold 22.6% of national income (WIR 2026).
- Informality and low earnings: Over 80% of workers are informal; PLFS analysis suggests nearly 64% of workers earn below minimum wages, capping the income dimension.
- Gender deficit: Female LFPR is 40.0% (PLFS 2025) against male 79.1%; 53% of women stay out of the workforce due to care burdens (ILO); India ranks 131/148 on the Global Gender Gap Index. Women are 43% of STEM graduates but only ~27% of the STEM workforce.
- Regional divergence: Kerala, Goa and Himachal approach high-HDI norms, while Bihar, UP and Jharkhand lag — national averages mask a two-speed India.

## Conclusion

India's HDI shortfall stems not from economic stagnation but from inequitable and under-financed human capital formation. With HDI at 0.685, India stands just short of the 0.700 "high human development" threshold. Sustained investment in health and education financing, closing the gender gap, and leveraging AI-driven skilling — aligned with SDGs 3, 4, 5 and 10 and Viksit Bharat @2047 — can convert India's demographic dividend into a genuine human development dividend.

## Introduction

Rural credit in India is classified as institutional — from banks, cooperatives and regulated non-banks — or non-institutional — from moneylenders, traders, landlords and relatives. The great achievement of the last seven decades has been the reversal of their shares: the All-India Rural Credit Survey (1954) found that moneylenders supplied over 90% of rural credit; today institutional sources dominate. But the reversal is incomplete, and the reasons why are the substance of this answer.

- Composition of institutional credit
- **Commercial banks** — The largest single supplier, obliged under Priority Sector Lending to direct 18% of ANBC to agriculture, with 14% for non-corporate farmers and 10% for small and marginal farmers
- **Regional Rural Banks** — 28 RRBs nationally with about 22,158 branches, obliged to lend 75% of ANBC to the priority sector; consolidated CRAR at an all-time high of 14.4% (FY25) and a credit-deposit ratio of 73.8% (March 2025) — the highest in 35 years, meaning rural deposits are being lent locally
- **Cooperatives** — Three-tier — PACS at village level, DCCBs at district level, APCOB at the apex — for short and medium-term credit, with cooperative agriculture and rural development banks for long-term. Historically the nearest lender to the small farmer, now the weakest tier, through poor capital, governance capture and political interference
- **SHG-Bank Linkage** — Launched by NABARD in 1992; in Andhra Pradesh, SERP’s network of about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, with repayment consistently above 97% — the State’s distinctive strength
- **Stree Nidhi** — A credit cooperative federation for rapid small-ticket lending, governed by a Managing Committee of 20 directors of whom 13 are elected from mandal samakhyas
- **NBFC-MFIs and Small Finance Banks** — Micro-credit; nationally, NBFC-MFIs hold 39% of the microfinance market, banks 32%, SFBs 16%
- **NABARD** — Apex refinancing institution, operating the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) from banks’ PSL shortfalls

By purpose: institutional credit is heavily skewed toward short-term crop loans (largely through the Kisan Credit Card — limit ₹5 lakh, collateral-free to ₹2 lakh, effective interest 4%), with term credit for irrigation, mechanisation and storage relatively scarce.

- Composition of non-institutional credit
- **Professional moneylenders** — Highest interest, minimal documentation, immediate disbursement
- **Agricultural moneylenders / landlords** — Often also the landowner from whom the borrower leases land — so debt reinforces tenurial dependence
- **Input dealers and commission agents (arhtiyas)** — The most consequential category. The lender is simultaneously the seller of inputs and the buyer of the crop, so the farmer loses on the loan, on inputs and on the sale price — an interlocked transaction from which exit is difficult
- **Relatives and friends** — Interest-free or low-interest, but limited in amount and availability
- **Chit funds and informal groups** — Rotating savings and credit, widely used in coastal Andhra

- The long-run shift, and why it stalled

The shift achieved: institutional credit to agriculture rose nationally from ₹8.5 lakh crore (2014-15) to ₹25.48 lakh crore (2023-24); short-term credit from ₹6.4 to ₹15.07 lakh crore; and the share of small and marginal farmers accessing agricultural loans rose from 57% to 76%. Among unincorporated manufacturing units, formal credit use rose from 48% (2021-22) to 51% (2023-24), with reliance on moneylenders and suppliers falling.

Why non-institutional credit survives:

- The tenant cannot borrow formally. Andhra Pradesh has among India’s highest tenancy incidence, almost entirely oral and unrecorded. Since institutional credit follows the land record, the actual cultivator is invisible to the banking system and must borrow informally. This is the single largest explanation.
- No formal consumption credit. Illness, weddings, education and festivals must be financed, and no bank lends for them. The moneylender does.
- Speed and simplicity. Loan sanction requires documents, no-dues certificates and branch visits; agriculture is calendar-bound, and credit that arrives after sowing is worth a fraction of its value.
- Inadequate scale of finance. Sanctioned limits often fall short of actual cultivation cost, so the farmer tops up informally — institutional and non-institutional credit are complements, not substitutes, for many households.
- Existing default. A farmer already in default is ineligible for fresh institutional credit and has nowhere else to go.
- Bank caution. With agriculture’s GNPA at 6.0% — the highest of any sector and over a third of all bad loans — lenders ration credit precisely to those most in need.
- Weak cooperatives. The institution physically closest to the village is the least able to lend.
- The consequences of the composition
- High effective cost — informal rates run at several times the KCC’s 4%.
- The debt trap — compounding, rollover, distress sale and eventually asset loss, with debt inherited by the next generation.
- Loss on both sides of the transaction where the lender is also the buyer.
- Exclusion from relief — during the farm loan redemption scheme, only institutional loans were waived, so the most indebted cultivators, holding informal debt, received nothing.
- Measures narrowing the gap
- Crop Cultivator Rights Cards under the AP Crop Cultivator Rights Act, 2019, and the earlier Loan Eligibility Cards under the Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011.
- KCC extension to allied activities (2004) and to animal husbandry and fisheries (2018-19); saturation drives linking every PM-KISAN beneficiary to a card.
- The Kisan Rin Portal integrating MoA&FW, DFS, RBI and NABARD data on disbursement and interest subvention.
- DILRMP land records digitisation and Agristack Farmer IDs, to let credit follow the cultivator rather than the title.
- RRB consolidation into 28 banks under “One State, One RRB” from 1 May 2025.
- PACS computerisation and conversion into multi-service centres.
- Regulated microfinance — the RBI reduced NBFC-MFI qualifying assets from 75% to 60% (June 2025) to let lenders diversify after the FY25 stress, when MFI loans outstanding fell about 14%.
- Income support — Annadata Sukhibhava (₹20,000 a year, covering tenants) and PM-KISAN — reducing the need to borrow at all.

## Conclusion

The composition of rural credit in Andhra Pradesh has shifted decisively from non-institutional to institutional sources over seven decades — and the State’s SHG network, with repayment above 97%, is among India’s strongest institutional achievements. But the shift remains incomplete for a specific and identifiable reason: institutional credit follows the land record, while a large share of cultivation is done by unrecorded tenants. Completing the transition therefore

requires less new lending than a change in what lending is keyed to — recognising the cultivator, financing consumption formally, expanding term credit, and reviving the cooperative tier that stands closest to the village.

## Value addition
- The historical benchmark: the All-India Rural Credit Survey (1954) found moneylenders supplied over 90% of rural credit and recommended cooperative expansion — the origin of India’s institutional credit architecture.
- Committees to cite: R.V. Gupta Committee (1998) which designed the KCC; Vaidyanathan Committee (2004) on cooperative credit revival; Radhakrishna Committee (2007) on agricultural indebtedness.
- Microfinance profile (FY25): 627 lakh active borrowers; gross loan portfolio ₹2.38 lakh crore; 95% women and 80% rural — and Andhra Pradesh, where the 2010 crisis originated, is where India’s microfinance regulation was born.
- The interest gap that explains everything: KCC effective rate 4% against informal rates several times higher — the measure of what exclusion costs a farmer.

## Introduction

Land reform in India was never merely an agricultural policy. In an agrarian society, land determines income, credit, social status, political power and personal dignity simultaneously. Redistributing it was therefore intended to change the structure of rural society, not just the pattern of cultivation.

The socio-economic basis for land reform

## Social basis
- Abolition of feudal relations. The zamindari, jagirdari and inam systems created a class that extracted rent without cultivating. In the Telangana region under the Nizam, this extended to vetti — hereditary bonded labour — making reform a question of personal freedom, not only of property.
- Caste and land overlapped. Landlessness was concentrated among Scheduled Castes; landownership among dominant castes. Redistributing land was therefore an instrument of social justice, not just economic equity.
- Dignity and citizenship. A tenant-at-will could not vote, testify or organise freely against the person who controlled his livelihood. Security of tenure was a precondition of political equality.
- Political stability. The Telangana Armed Struggle (1946-51), which redistributed around a million acres across some 3,000 villages before being suppressed, demonstrated the alternative to reform.
- Economic basis
- “Land to the tiller.” Absentee landlordism separated ownership from cultivation, so neither party had a full incentive to invest — the owner did not farm, and the tenant-at-will could be evicted before recovering an investment.
- The inverse size-productivity relationship. Empirical studies found small farms often achieve higher output per hectare, because family labour is applied more intensively and supervised at no cost. If so, redistribution raises output as well as equity.
- Employment. Owner-cultivated small farms absorb more labour per hectare than large mechanised farms —

important in a labour-surplus economy.

- Investment incentive. A secure cultivator invests in bunding, wells, manure and improved seed; a tenant-at-will does not.
- Rent extraction. Rack-renting transferred the agricultural surplus to landlords who invested it in trade, moneylending or urban property rather than in land improvement.
- Constitutional basis - Article 39(b) — material resources to be distributed to subserve the common good; Article 39(c) — prevention of concentration of wealth. - Land reform laws were placed in the Ninth Schedule under Article 31B to protect them from judicial challenge. - Land is a State subject (Entry 18, List II), so reform proceeded through State legislation with central guidelines.

Appraising implementation in Andhra Pradesh

Stage 1: Abolition of intermediaries — largely successful

- Hyderabad Abolition of Jagirs Regulation, 1949 abolished about 6,500 jagirs; the AP (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 abolished zamindari in the Andhra region.
- Vetti was legally ended, and the social power of the dora and deshmukh class was broken.
- Verdict: the most complete success. Abolishing a legal category is administratively achievable — and it was achieved.

Stage 2: Tenancy reform — failed in effect, and counter-productive

- AP (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 conferred protected-tenant status and purchase rights; the AP (Andhra Area) Tenancy Act, 1956 regulated rent and tenure without conferring ownership, with a “soft” 1974 amendment extending the minimum lease to six years.
- The result was the opposite of the intent. Because a recorded tenant acquired protection, landlords stopped recording tenancies. Andhra Pradesh today has among India’s highest tenancy incidence and lowest recorded tenancy.
- The unrecorded tenant lost not only tenure security but access to institutional credit, crop insurance, input subsidy and calamity compensation — all of which follow the land record.
- Verdict: a failure whose consequences persist, and the reason the State later shifted from conferring rights to

functional recognition through Loan Eligibility Cards and Crop Cultivator Rights Cards.

Stage 3: Ceiling on holdings — marginal in outcome

- The AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 imposed family-based ceilings with surplus for redistribution.
- Benami and fictitious partitions before enactment defeated the law; exemptions for plantations, orchards and trusts allowed large holdings to survive legally; ceiling cases ran for decades in litigation.
- Land actually declared surplus and redistributed was a small fraction of holdings above ceiling.
- Verdict: largely unsuccessful.

Stage 4: Assignment of government land — partial, and poorly executed

- Pattas were distributed to landless SC and ST families from government and ceiling-surplus land.
- But the Koneru Ranga Rao Land Committee (2006) documented that assignment was frequently a paper transaction: in the Telangana region, 14.3 lakh acres were distributed to 10.1 lakh beneficiaries (about 1.4 acres each), yet nearly 10 lakh acres had not been properly handed over. Its most damning finding was that land was “assigned on paper, physical location not shown,” so the same land was assigned repeatedly.
- Assigned land was often unirrigated, rocky or inaccessible, so a patta conferred title without livelihood; informal alienation reversed redistribution despite the AP Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act, 1977.
- Verdict: significant in scale, weak in substance.

Stage 5: Tribal land protection — statutorily strong, practically weak

- AP Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation, 1959 (Regulation 1 of 70) bars transfer of land to non-tribals in Scheduled Areas; Samatha v. State of AP (1997) extended this to government land leased for private mining.
- Yet the Koneru Ranga Rao Committee found that about 48% of tribal lands had passed to non-tribals in violation of the Regulation.
- Verdict: strong law, weak enforcement.

Stage 6: Bhoodan — symbolically important, materially limited

Vinoba Bhave began the Bhoodan movement at Pochampally, Nalgonda, on 18 April 1951 — India’s first Bhoodan village, prompted directly by the Telangana struggle. Much donated land, however, was infertile or disputed, and a significant share was never actually transferred.

The overall appraisal

Andhra Pradesh’s land reforms succeeded where the target was an institution — jagirdari, zamindari, vetti — and

failed where the target was an asset. Abolishing a legal category could be done by statute; taking land from those who held power in the village could not. The result was a transformation of agrarian social relations without a corresponding transformation of land distribution.

## Conclusion

The socio-economic basis of land reform — ending feudal extraction, matching ownership to cultivation, and delivering social justice — remains valid. Andhra Pradesh’s implementation record is differentiated: intermediary abolition succeeded completely, ceiling redistribution barely, and tenancy reform actively harmed those it meant to help. The contemporary agenda follows from that appraisal: recognising tenancy so credit reaches the cultivator, completing conclusive land titling under DILRMP, enforcing Scheduled Area protections, and improving the productivity of already-assigned land — since for most of the rural poor, further redistribution is no longer the realistic route out of poverty.

## Value addition
- Committee lineage: the J.C. Kumarappa Committee (1949) on agrarian reform; the Barucha Committee (1937) under the Nizam; the Koneru Ranga Rao Land Committee (2004-06) — 104 recommendations, about 90 accepted.
- The four stages of Indian land reform: abolition of intermediaries → tenancy reform → ceiling on holdings → consolidation of holdings (the fourth, largely undertaken only in Punjab, Haryana and western UP, and not in Andhra Pradesh).
- Judicial anchor: Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) on Fifth Schedule protection; Vemula Bhaskara Rao v. State of AP (2008) on the inadmissibility of unregistered deeds for non-tribals.
- The modern instrument: the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016 (NITI Aayog) — legalise leasing, protect the owner’s title, give the tenant credit access.
