## Introduction

Before 2005, rural employment programmes were schemes — discretionary, budget-limited and supply-driven. The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 converted employment from a scheme into a legally enforceable right. That single change in legal character is the source of most of its superiority.

The earlier programmes

- **NREP** — 1980 · Wage employment through public works
- **RLEGP** — 1983 · Landless employment guarantee (limited)
- **Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY)** — 1989 · Merged NREP and RLEGP; village-level works
- **Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS)** — 1993 · Assured 100 days in lean season in select blocks — but administratively, not legally
- **Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY)** — 2001 · Merged JRY and EAS; food-for-work component
- **NFFWP** — 2004 · Food for work in 150 backward districts

Comparative assessment

- **Legal status** — Executive schemes; no enforceable claim · Statutory right — the world’s largest rights-based employment guarantee
- **Nature of provision** — Supply-driven — work offered where and when funds allowed · Demand-driven — work must be provided within 15 days of application
- **Entitlement** — Discretionary and variable · 100 days per household per year, guaranteed
- **Failure remedy** — None · Unemployment allowance payable by the State if work is not provided
- **Targeting** — Official BPL lists, prone to inclusion and exclusion errors · Self-selecting — the statutory minimum wage screens beneficiaries automatically; no list required
- **Coverage** — Selected blocks or districts · Universal across rural India
- **Women’s participation** — Incidental · At least one-third of beneficiaries mandated; equal wages for men and women
- **Planning** — Centrally or district-designed works · Gram Sabha identifies and prioritises works — genuine decentralised planning under the 73rd Amendment
- **Transparency** — Weak · Social audit by the Gram Sabha is statutory; muster rolls, job cards and MIS in the public domain
- **Payment** — Cash, with high leakage · Bank/post office accounts and DBT, sharply reducing intermediation
- **Worksite conditions** — Unspecified · Statutory facilities — drinking water, shade, first aid, crèche
- **Funding** — Fixed allocation; work stopped when funds ran out · Open-ended demand-based funding, making it a genuine automatic stabiliser

Why these differences matter in practice

- Rights create accountability. A scheme’s failure is an administrative shortfall; a right’s failure is a legal breach that triggers an unemployment allowance and can be litigated.
- Demand-driven design makes it counter-cyclical. MGNREGA expanded automatically during COVID-19 to absorb returning migrants — no earlier scheme could have done so, because their budgets were fixed in advance.
- Self-selection solves the targeting problem that defeated IRDP and JRY. Only those genuinely needing manual work at the statutory wage will apply.
- It sets a rural wage floor, raising bargaining power even for workers who never enrol — an effect earlier schemes never achieved at scale.
- Social audit institutionalised transparency, making MGNREGA the first Indian programme with statutory community verification.

Where the superiority is qualified

- Wage delays undermine the guarantee — a right paid late is a right diluted.
- Rationing in practice: in many districts, work provided falls short of work demanded, so the 100-day entitlement is not always realised.
- Asset quality varies widely with local administrative capacity.
- It provides work, not employment — wage labour rather than skilled or productive jobs.
- Recent restructuring under the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika Mission (Rural) Act, 2025 has itself been contested, with several States passing resolutions to preserve the original guarantee — a reminder that the legal character is precisely what beneficiaries value.

## Conclusion

MGNREGA’s superiority lies not in its size but in its legal architecture — a justiciable right, demand-driven delivery, self-selection, statutory social audit and decentralised planning. Earlier programmes depended on administrative goodwill and available funds; MGNREGA depends on a citizen’s application. That shift from beneficiary to rights-holder is its lasting contribution to Indian public policy, and it is why any dilution of its statutory character attracts such resistance.

## Value addition
- Statutory features to quote precisely: work within 15 days of demand, failing which an unemployment allowance is payable; work within 5 km of the residence, or a 10% wage premium; one-third participation by women; Gram Sabha social audit; worksite facilities including crèche.
- Constitutional basis: Art. 41 (right to work), Art. 43 (living wage), and the 73rd Amendment for Gram Sabha planning.
- Institutional innovation: MGNREGA was among the first programmes with a public MIS, geo-tagged assets and Aadhaar-based payment — the template later applied across DBT.
- AP relevance: MGNREGA works converged with SERP’s SHG network, and the State used the programme extensively for watershed, farm-pond and horticulture works that raised agricultural productivity.

## Introduction

Two reforms transformed the fair price shop from a local monopoly into a competitive service point. Automation — the electronic Point of Sale device with Aadhaar authentication — made every transaction verifiable. Portability — the right to collect from any shop — removed the shop’s captive customer base. Together they changed the incentive structure of the PDS more than any subsidy reform.

- Fair Price Shop Automation — advantages
- **Elimination of ghost and duplicate cards** — Aadhaar-seeded biometric authentication ensures the person collecting exists and is entitled
- **Real-time transaction recording** — Each sale is time-stamped on a central server; the dealer cannot later fabricate distribution against undelivered stock
- **Automatic stock reconciliation** — Opening balance, sales and closing balance are computed by the system, exposing shortfalls immediately
- **Prevention of short-weighing and over-charging** — The device prints a receipt showing entitlement, quantity and price
- **Beneficiary confirmation** — SMS alerts and public dashboards let the household verify what was recorded in its name
- **Faster dealer settlement** — Commission and subsidy claims are computed automatically from verified transactions
- **Data for policy** — Real-time offtake data reveals demand patterns, seasonal variation and shops with anomalous activity

- Portability within a district — advantages
- **Breaks the dealer’s monopoly** — A cardholder dissatisfied with quality, weighment or behaviour can simply go elsewhere — the strongest disciplinary mechanism available
- **Introduces competition** — Dealers compete on service and quality to retain customers, since commission follows the transaction
- **Serves mobile populations** — Agricultural labourers, construction workers and seasonal migrants within the district can draw rations where they are working
- **Reduces access hardship** — Beneficiaries in remote hamlets can use the nearest convenient shop rather than the officially assigned one
- **Reduces denial** — “Stock not available” as an excuse loses force when the beneficiary has alternatives
- **Improves quality indirectly** — Since customers can leave, poor grain quality now has a commercial cost to the dealer

- The combined effect — why the two work together

Automation without portability gives verification without choice: the dealer’s conduct is recorded, but the beneficiary is still captive. Portability without automation gives choice without verification: entitlements could be claimed twice at different shops. Together they create verified choice — the beneficiary can move, and the system knows exactly what she drew and where.

- How the reform has since been extended
- Intra-State portability: Andhra Pradesh’s revamped system allows collection from any ration shop in the State, not merely within a district.
- Inter-State portability: One Nation One Ration Card, operational across all 36 States and UTs, allows an AP beneficiary to draw entitlements anywhere in India using Aadhaar alone — decisive for the country’s large circular-migrant workforce.
- Smart Ration Cards with QR codes issued across AP from August 2026.
- Limitations to acknowledge
- Authentication failures exclude the elderly, manual workers with worn fingerprints, and areas with poor connectivity.
- Stock management becomes harder when demand shifts unpredictably between shops — requiring buffer stocking and flexible allotment.
- Dealer viability worsens where customers migrate away, since low commissions already make many outlets marginal.
- Quality is still not verified by the system; only identity and quantity are.
- Upstream diversion — in procurement, transport and storage — is untouched by shop-level automation, as the May 2025 PDS rice scam in the State showed.

## Conclusion

Automation and portability together represent the single most effective structural reform in the history of the PDS, because they changed incentives rather than merely tightening rules. The beneficiary gained choice, and therefore power; the dealer lost a captive market and gained an audit trail. The reform’s logical completion is nationwide

portability through ONORC, which is now operational — but its benefits will remain partial until grain quality, dealer margins and upstream supply-chain integrity receive the same attention that the shop counter has.

## Value addition
- Enabling technology: ePoS devices, Aadhaar-based biometric and iris authentication, the IM-PDS portal for national de-duplication, the Annavitran portal for portability tracking, and the Mera Ration app.
- ONORC: launched in 2019 and operational in all 36 States and UTs; particularly significant for the estimated tens of millions of circular migrants who previously lost entitlements on moving.
- AP status: 29,796 fair price shops; 1.46 crore rice cards covering about 4.3 crore persons; Smart Ration Cards with QR codes from August 2026.
- Committee support: the Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) recommended end-to-end computerisation of the PDS as a precondition for any further reform.

## Introduction

Rural unemployment in India is rarely open unemployment. It takes the forms of disguised unemployment — more workers on the land than the land needs — and seasonal unemployment between sowing and harvest. Its consequences are therefore felt less as idleness than as low and insecure incomes, which is what makes it socially corrosive.

Forms of rural unemployment

- **Disguised** — Marginal productivity of additional workers approaches zero; removing them would not reduce output
- **Seasonal** — Work concentrated in agricultural peaks, idleness between them
- **Underemployment** — Working fewer days or hours than desired — the marginal worker category of the Census
- **Educated unemployment** — Rural youth with degrees unable to find commensurate work

Consequences on society

- Economic - Persistent poverty and indebtedness: irregular income forces borrowing for consumption at high informal rates, creating debt cycles. - Depressed rural demand, which slows the wider economy. - Distress sale of assets — land, livestock, jewellery — during lean seasons, permanently reducing household capacity.
- Demographic and spatial - Distress migration to cities, producing slum growth, overcrowded services and insecure urban informal work; migrants fall between State jurisdictions for entitlements. - Family separation and the burden of “left-behind” households run by women and the elderly. - Depopulation of the working-age cohort in backward districts — visible in Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra.
- Social - Agrarian distress and farmer suicides, particularly where debt and crop failure coincide. - Child labour and school dropout, as households need every earning hand — one reason Andhra Pradesh’s literacy remains the lowest among Indian States at 72.6%. - Early marriage of girls and worsened nutritional outcomes. - Crime, alcoholism and social tension, with idle youth vulnerable to exploitation. - Erosion of dignity and mental health, which the capability approach identifies as deprivation in itself.
- Political - Populist competition in cash transfers rather than structural reform — State-level unconditional transfers reached about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26, creating expenditure rigidity.

Two effective remedial measures

Measure 1: Strengthen the demand-driven employment guarantee, and extend the logic to towns

MGNREGA works because it is self-selecting — the wage rate screens beneficiaries automatically, so no official targeting list is required. To make it more effective: - Timely wage payment, since delays convert a guarantee into uncertainty; - Higher-quality durable assets — farm ponds, watershed works, rural roads, plantations — that raise future agricultural productivity rather than merely providing wages; - Convergence with agriculture, horticulture and watershed programmes so that the asset created has a purpose; - Crucially, an urban counterpart, since India still has no urban equivalent of MGNREGA’s legal guarantee even though urban informal work is more precarious and living costs higher.

Measure 2: Build the rural non-farm economy through skilling and enterprise

The permanent solution is to move labour off the land into higher-productivity work without requiring migration: - Agro-processing and value addition at source — food processing, aquaculture processing, horticulture cold chains — which retain value in the countryside; - MSME clusters near rural populations, such as Andhra Pradesh’s 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency; - Credit for enterprise, not consumption — PMEGP, MUDRA, PM Vishwakarma, and term credit for equipment rather than only crop loans; - Demand-linked skilling — AP’s government ITIs have signed MoUs with 167 industry partners, with 98% of trainees securing placement or apprenticeship, showing what industry linkage achieves; - Formalisation support through the Labour Codes and the ELI Scheme (₹99,446 crore), which subsidises first-time formal hiring.

## Conclusion

Rural unemployment in India is a problem of productivity and security rather than of idleness — and its consequences run from indebtedness and migration to child labour and distress. An employment guarantee provides the floor; a rural non-farm economy provides the exit. Neither alone suffices: the guarantee prevents destitution, but only enterprise and skills convert a farm labourer into a productive worker.

## Value addition
- Employment position: unemployment 3.1% (PLFS 2025) — low precisely because disguised and underemployment are not captured as unemployment; rural LFPR 62.8% against urban 52.2%.
- Structural context: roughly 45% of India’s workers remain in agriculture, producing about 15% of GDP; the unincorporated sector employs 12.9 crore.
- Programmes: MGNREGA (restructured under the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika Mission (Rural) Act, 2025), DAY-NRLM, PMEGP, PM Vishwakarma, PMKVY, PM-NAPS.
- Constitutional anchor: Art. 41 (right to work and public assistance); Art. 43 (living wage and decent conditions).

## Introduction

Poverty removal requires action on three fronts simultaneously: growth that generates employment, capabilities that let people take those jobs, and protection against shocks that would otherwise undo both. India’s record shows what happens when these work together — the National MPI headcount fell from 29.17% (2013-14) to 11.28% (2022-23), with about 24.82 crore people escaping multidimensional poverty.

Effective strategies — a five-part framework

- Employment-intensive growth (the primary engine) No country has ever eliminated poverty through transfers alone. Growth must be in labour-absorbing sectors — manufacturing, construction, agro-processing, logistics, tourism. India’s employment elasticity improved to 1.11% job growth per 1% value added (2017-23) from near zero in the 2000s, and ASI FY24 recorded over 10 lakh new factory jobs.
- Human capital formation (the enabler) Health, nutrition, schooling and skills determine whether a person can take a job at all. This is where Andhra Pradesh’s constraint is sharpest — its literacy at 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States.
- Asset creation and productive credit (the ladder) Land, housing, livestock, tools and working capital convert labour into income. SHG credit, MUDRA, PM SVANidhi and the Kisan Credit Card serve this function; among unincorporated manufacturing units, formal credit use rose from 48% (2021-22) to 51% (2023-24).
- Social security and risk protection (the floor) Health insurance, pensions, food security and employment guarantees prevent one shock from causing permanent impoverishment. The four Labour Codes (effective 21 November 2025) extend social security to gig and platform workers for the first time.
- Empowerment and institutions of the poor (the multiplier) Organising the poor changes bargaining power. Andhra Pradesh’s SERP network — about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, with repayment above 97% — is the clearest Indian demonstration.

The experience of anti-poverty programmes — six lessons

- **Self-selection works better than official targeting** — MGNREGA’s wage rate screens beneficiaries automatically; schemes relying on beneficiary lists still built on the 2011 Census suffer inclusion and exclusion errors
- **Institutions outlast schemes** — SERP’s SHG federation survived the 2010 microfinance crisis, three project cycles and successive governments, and became the delivery platform for pensions, health insurance and DBT
- **Delivery technology transformed leakage, not design** — Cumulative DBT savings exceed ₹3.5 lakh crore; over 4 crore duplicate LPG connections deactivated under PAHAL
- **Saturation works — but only once** — Housing, electricity, cooking fuel, sanitation and bank accounts drove most of the MPI decline; those gains cannot be repeated, so the next phase must come from jobs and learning
- **Cash cannot buy what does not exist** — Transfers fail where the school or clinic is absent — the strongest argument for public provision alongside cash
- **Timeliness is part of the entitlement** — MGNREGA wage delays and health reimbursement arrears convert a guarantee into uncertainty

## What has not worked
- Credit without markets: SHG loans often financed consumption or debt-swapping rather than enterprise.
- Urban neglect: there is still no urban equivalent of MGNREGA’s legal guarantee.
- Fragmentation: dozens of schemes with separate guidelines raise compliance costs; the Chief Ministers’ Sub-Group on Rationalisation of CSS (2015) only partly resolved this.
- Unconditional transfers at State level reached about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26, creating expenditure rigidity that crowds out capital spending.

## Conclusion

The strategies that work are complementary, not alternative: growth creates the jobs, human capital makes people employable, assets and credit give them a ladder, and social security stops them falling off it. India’s experience shows that programmes are highly effective at reducing destitution and absorbing shocks, and only partly effective at creating durable livelihoods. The next phase must therefore shift from protection to productivity — conditional and time-bound transfers, an urban livelihoods mission, and formal job creation through the Labour Codes and the Employment Linked Incentive Scheme (₹99,446 crore).

## Value addition
- Programme lineage: IRDP (1978), NREP, RLEGP, JRY, SGSY, SJSRY, PMRY → consolidated into MGNREGA (2005), NRLM (2011, now DAY-NRLM), DAY-NULM, PMAY, PM SVANidhi.
- World Bank (2025): India’s extreme poverty at 5.25% in 2022-23 under the new $3.00 (2021 PPP) line; but at the lower-middle-income line of $4.20, about 24% of Indians — nearly one in four — remained poor in 2022.
- Employment position: 56.2 crore persons employed in Q2 FY26; unemployment 3.1%; FLFPR (UPSS) up from 23.3% (2017-18) to 41.7% (2023-24).
- AP innovation: the P4 (Public-Private-People Partnership) model for Zero Poverty — the first of the ten “Padhi Sutralu” under Swarna Andhra @2047.

The Andhra Pradesh Rural Inclusive Growth Project (APRIGP) was a World Bank-assisted project (P152210) implemented by the Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty (SERP) from 1 February 2015 to 1 February 2020. Its development objective was “to enable selected poor households to enhance agricultural incomes and secure increased access to human development services and social entitlements” — a deliberate shift from credit-led self-help to income, human development and entitlement together.

The four pillars (substantive components)

- **1. Value chain development** — Raise the income of 250,000 small and marginal farmers by at least 50% through higher productivity and better market access · Farmer Producer Organisations, collective procurement and marketing, custom hiring centres, the Rural Retail Chain with mandal-level nodal stores
- **2. Human development** — Increase poor households’ access to health, nutrition, sanitation and pre-school education, and change behaviour at individual, household and community levels · Community-based monitoring; strengthening ICDS, health and sanitation delivery; making service providers accountable to community organisations
- **3. Social protection and access to entitlements** — Ensure the poor actually receive what they are legally entitled to · One Stop Shops (OSS) at mandal level for information, enrolment and grievance redressal on MGNREGA wages, pensions and insurance
- **4. ICT and partnerships** — Build the digital backbone for delivery and monitoring · ICT systems at SERP — FPO management information systems, human-development and OSS dashboards, real-time tracking

Plus a fifth, enabling component: Project implementation support (about US$20 million) — human resources, safeguards, financial management, procurement, and staff recruitment and training across all components.

Coverage and beneficiaries

- 150 most backward mandals of Andhra Pradesh, covering about 5,000 villages.
- Priority beneficiaries: small and marginal farmers, and SC/ST households that were geographically and socially excluded and had low income levels.
- Delivery through the existing SHG federation architecture — village organisations, mandal samakhyas and zilla samakhyas.

Key result indicators

- **Enhanced income of producers in project mandals** — 250,000 producers
- **Share of beneficiaries from the poorest and SC/ST households** — 70%
- **Households adopting appropriate health, nutrition and sanitation behaviours** — 250,000 poor households
- **Households with enhanced access to systems delivering improved information, enrolment and payment for social protection** — 500,000 poor households

What APRIGP contributed

- It converged livelihood, human development and entitlement in a single project, rather than treating them as separate silos — the central design innovation.
- It used community institutions as the demand side of accountability, asking SHG federations to hold line departments to account rather than merely receiving services.
- It built SERP’s digital capability, which later carried DBT, pensions and welfare delivery at scale.

Limitations

- Coverage was confined to 150 mandals, so State-wide replication depended on convergence with other programmes.
- The goal of making the State poverty free by 2017 was aspirational rather than achievable.
- Sustaining FPOs beyond project support — the classic weakness of producer-organisation models — required market linkages that outlast the funding cycle.

## Conclusion

APRIGP was the third generation of Andhra Pradesh’s World Bank-assisted rural poverty programmes, after APDPIP (2000) and APRPRP (2003), and the first to make income, human development and entitlements a single integrated objective. Its enduring legacy is institutional — a digitally enabled SERP and a federated SHG network that remains the State’s principal instrument for delivering welfare, credit and now the P4 (Public-Private-People Partnership) model under Swarna Andhra @2047.

- Lineage of AP’s rural poverty projects: APDPIP (2000) — US$111 million IDA credit, six poorest districts; APRPRP (2003) — US$150 million credit with additional financing of US$65 million (2007) and US$100 million (2009); APRIGP (2015-20).

## Introduction

The Andhra Pradesh Budget 2016-17 was among the first full budgets of the residuary State — a reconstruction budget, framed to build a capital, an administration and an economy simultaneously, on a revenue base shorn of Hyderabad.

## Distinct aspects of the 2016-17 budget
- **Expansionary despite stress** — Total expenditure of ₹1,35,689 crore, a 20.9% increase over RE 2015-16
- **Capital and infrastructure priority** — Polavaram, road connectivity, power sector strengthening, and Amaravati capital construction
- **Social sector emphasis** — Higher allocations for school education, rural development and health
- **Apparent fiscal compliance** — Fiscal deficit ₹20,497 crore = 3% of GSDP — within the FRBM ceiling; revenue deficit ₹4,868 crore = 0.7% of GSDP; primary deficit ₹8,239 crore (1.2%)

The distinctive feature worth noting: on paper this was a compliant budget — 3% fiscal deficit, sub-1% revenue deficit. In practice, actual outturns reported by CAG were materially worse, because the budget rested on optimistic revenue assumptions and on central assistance that did not fully materialise.

## Reasons for the revenue deficit in residuary AP
- Loss of the revenue base: Hyderabad contributed the dominant share of the undivided State’s own tax and non-tax revenue; the residuary State retained most of the population and welfare obligations without it.
- Rising committed expenditure: an entire new administrative apparatus — secretariat, directorates, high court, capital city — plus salaries, pensions and interest.
- Dependence on central transfers: with roughly 40% of revenue receipts coming from the Centre, delays and shortfalls in devolution and special assistance translated directly into deficit.
- Weak own-tax effort: limited industrial activity, a narrow base concentrated in liquor and petroleum, and collection systems still being rebuilt.
- Welfare continuity: schemes inherited from the united State continued as recurring revenue commitments.

## Reasons for the fiscal deficit
- Large capital outlay: Polavaram, Amaravati, ports and irrigation absorbed heavy investment — legitimate, asset-creating borrowing.
- Borrowing-driven financing: with limited own revenue, market borrowings financed most capital spending;

## outstanding liabilities rose to about 27.9% of GSDP.
- Delayed central assistance: slow reimbursement for Polavaram, incomplete revenue-deficit grants, and unresolved apportionment under Schedules IX and X of the Reorganisation Act.
- Regional balancing obligations: simultaneous investment needed in Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra alongside the capital region.

## The analytical distinction to make

AP’s revenue deficit is structural and worrying — it reflects borrowing for consumption. Its fiscal deficit is partly developmental — much of it financed irrigation, ports and a capital city, which are self-liquidating over time. Conflating

the two misreads the State’s fiscal position.

## Conclusion

The 2016-17 budget captured the transitional predicament of a State rebuilding itself: expansionary in intent, constrained in resources, and compliant on paper more than in outturn. Its deficits arose from structural revenue loss, not fiscal indiscipline. The correction has come only gradually — the revenue deficit has fallen from 3.79% of GSDP (FY25) to 1.11% (BE 2026-27) and the fiscal deficit from 5.11% to 3.84%, as own revenue strengthened and debt costs were actively reduced.

## Introduction

Central bank autonomy means operational independence — freedom in choosing instruments to achieve a mandate — rather than freedom to choose the mandate itself. In India the mandate (the 4% ±2% inflation target) is set by the Government under Section 45ZA, while the instrument choice rests with the MPC under Section 45ZB — the textbook design of “goal dependence with instrument independence.”

## Why autonomy matters
- The time-inconsistency problem (Kydland–Prescott): governments face a standing temptation to deliver short-term stimulus before elections, at the cost of higher inflation later. Delegating to an insulated authority removes that temptation from the decision loop.
- Anchoring expectations: credible commitment means wage- and price-setters expect low inflation, so disinflation costs less output. India’s FY26 experience illustrates this — CPI fell to 1.7% (April-December 2025) alongside 8% GDP growth in H1 FY26: disinflation without a growth sacrifice.
- Avoiding fiscal dominance: an autonomous central bank refuses monetisation of deficits. The RBI has confined itself to secondary-market operations rather than direct deficit financing.
- Empirical support: cross-country evidence consistently links greater central bank independence to lower inflation with no systematic growth penalty; studies of RBI independence from 1982-83 to 2021-22 find the same association in India.

## How autonomy is exercised in India
- Statutory: MPC with three external members appointed by the Government; decisions by majority with the Governor’s casting vote.
- Operational: the RBI alone decides on liquidity, OMOs, CRR and forex intervention — as seen in FY26’s ₹2.39 lakh crore of OMO purchases and a US$5 billion swap.
- Rule-bound relations with the Centre: the Economic Capital Framework converted the once-contentious surplus transfer into a formula, yielding ₹2,86,588 crore in FY26 while raising the risk buffer to 6.5%.

## Autonomy must coexist with accountability
- Publication of MPC resolutions and minutes with voting patterns; the bi-annual Monetary Policy Report.
- A statutory failure clause — a report to Parliament through the Government if CPI stays outside 2–6% for three consecutive quarters (Sec. 45ZN), invoked in 2022.
- The mandate itself is periodically re-legitimised: the target was renotified on 25 March 2026 for 2026-31, a democratic reaffirmation rather than a technocratic assumption.
- Section 7 of the RBI Act preserves the Government’s ultimate power to direct in the public interest — a reminder that autonomy in India is statutory, not constitutional.

## Risks of politicisation — global cautionary tales

Turkey’s repeated dismissal of governors produced currency collapse and runaway inflation; Argentina’s monetary financing of deficits ended in chronic instability. Pressure on central banks in advanced economies in recent years has renewed the global debate. India has had its own episodes of strain, notably around 2018-19, resolved without institutional rupture.

## Conclusion

Autonomy is not an end in itself — it is a commitment technology that makes low inflation credible and therefore cheap to achieve. India’s design gets the balance broadly right: the elected government sets the goal, the central bank chooses the instruments, and transparency binds both. Preserving this equilibrium — insulated in operation, answerable in outcome — remains essential to macroeconomic stability as India pursues Viksit Bharat @2047.

## Value addition
- RBI as banker to government: Section 20 obliges the RBI to undertake the Union’s receipts, payments and public debt management; Section 21 gives it the right to transact Union government business; Section 21A covers State governments by agreement — such agreements exist with all States except Sikkim.
- Design principle: goal dependence + instrument independence — the Government sets the target (Sec. 45ZA); the MPC sets the rate (Sec. 45ZB).
- Validation: three sovereign rating upgrades in FY26 (Morningstar DBRS, S&P Global, R&I), with agencies citing the credibility of inflation targeting; the sovereign 10-year yield spread over US Treasuries more than halved.
- Current setting: repo 5.25%, neutral stance, unanimous 6-0 vote (June 2026) — a hold taken against growth-supportive pressure, which is itself evidence of autonomy in practice.
- One-line revision point: An independent central bank is not one that answers to no one — it is one that answers for outcomes rather than to instructions.

## Introduction

Literacy is both an outcome of development and an input into it. Andhra Pradesh’s literacy has risen steadily in absolute terms, but the State has consistently lagged the national average — and on the most recent official data it records the lowest literacy rate among all Indian States. Stating that plainly, with the number, is what distinguishes a strong answer here.

The long-run trend (Census data, undivided Andhra Pradesh)

- **Census year** — Literacy rate
- **1981** — ~29.9%
- **1991** — ~44.1%
- **2001** — 60.47%
- **2011** — 67.02% (male 74.88%, female 59.15%)

For residuary Andhra Pradesh, Census 2011 records 67.35% (male 74.77%, female 59.96%) against a national average of 74.04% — placing the State around 32nd among States and Union Territories.

The current position (PLFS 2023-24, persons aged 7 and above)

- **Indicator** — Andhra Pradesh · India
- **Literacy rate** — 72.6% · 80.9%
- **Rank** — Lowest among States · —
- **Gap from the leader (Mizoram 98.2%)** — 25.6 percentage points · —

India’s own progress provides the contrast: literacy rose from 18.3% (1951) to 80.9% (2023-24), with rural at 77.5% and urban at 88.9%, and male at 87.2% against female at 74.6%.

Key disparities within Andhra Pradesh

- Gender gap: male 74.88% against female 59.15% in Census 2011 — a gap of nearly 16 percentage points, wider than the national gap.
- Rural–urban gap: urban literacy was 80.09% (male 85.79%, female 73.31%) against a much lower rural figure — the State is 66.6% rural, which drags the average down.
- District disparity (Census 2011): West Godavari (74.63%) and Krishna (73.74%) at the top; Vizianagaram (58.89%) and Kurnool (59.97%) at the bottom — the coastal delta outperforms both Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra.
- Social disparity: SC, ST and PVTG communities in the agency areas lag substantially.

Why Andhra Pradesh lags

- A historically agrarian, rural-majority population with high early workforce participation and child labour in agriculture and aquaculture.
- Weak adult literacy outcomes — the State’s deficit is concentrated in older cohorts rather than in current school enrolment, which is near-universal.
- Dropout at the secondary stage, particularly for girls in backward districts.
- Bifurcation effect: the loss of Hyderabad, which had the highest district literacy in the undivided State (83.25%), mechanically lowered the residuary State’s average.
- Quality versus access: near-universal enrolment coexists with weak foundational literacy and numeracy, so enrolment gains have not translated fully into functional literacy.

Policy response

- ULLAS / New India Literacy Programme (2022-27) — adult and foundational literacy, under which Mizoram and Tripura were declared fully literate in 2025.
- NIPUN Bharat under NEP 2020 for foundational literacy and numeracy.
- Samagra Shiksha, and at State level Talliki Vandanam (₹15,000 a year per child from Class 1 to Intermediate) to keep children in school, alongside School Education allocation of ₹32,308 crore in Budget 2026-27.
- Swarna Andhra @2047 targets literacy above 75%.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s literacy has risen strongly in absolute terms — from under 30% in 1981 to 72.6% today — but the State’s relative position remains its weakest human-development indicator. Closing the gap requires a twin strategy: adult literacy at scale through ULLAS for the older cohorts where the deficit is concentrated, and foundational literacy and numeracy under NIPUN Bharat for the young, with a deliberate focus on girls and the backward districts of Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra. Literacy is the precondition for the State’s skilling and deep-tech ambitions, not a separate social objective.

## Value addition
- Definition: the Census defines a literate as a person aged 7 years and above who can both read and write with understanding in any language; the crude literacy rate uses total population as the denominator, the effective literacy rate uses population aged 7+.
- Statistical note: no Census has been held since 2011, so PLFS is the current official source for literacy — an important point to state, since quoting only Census 2011 dates an answer.
- National comparison: Mizoram 98.2%, Nagaland 95.7%, Tripura 95.6% at the top; Andhra Pradesh 72.6% at the bottom.
- AP allocations (Budget 2026-27): School Education ₹32,308 crore; Higher Education ₹2,567 crore; Skill Development ₹1,232 crore.
Q93:
## Introduction

The Eleventh Plan confronted an uncomfortable fact: India grew at 8-9% between 2004 and 2008, yet employment growth collapsed. NSSO data showed overall employment growth falling from 2.93% per annum (1999-2000 to 2004-05) to just 0.28% (2004-05 to 2009-10). The Planning Commission named this the central weakness of the reform period.

## Weaknesses identified

## Jobless or low-quality growth
- Employment elasticity — jobs created per unit of growth — fell from about 0.44 in the 1990s to near 0.01 in the 2000s.
- Manufacturing, expected to absorb surplus farm labour, stagnated in job creation.
- Services growth was concentrated in IT, finance and telecom — high value added, low employment intensity.

## Informalisation and precarious work
- Over 92% of the workforce remained informal (NSSO, 2009-10); even within the organised sector, nearly a third were contract or casual workers.
- Growth was not translating into decent work — security, social protection, or written contracts.

## Skill mismatch and human capital deficit
- Educated unemployment rose to 17.8% among graduates and above (2009-10), while industry simultaneously reported skill shortages.
- Only a tiny fraction of the workforce had received formal vocational training.

## Gender and social inequalities
- Female labour force participation fell from 29.0% (2004-05) to 23.3% (2009-10) — women withdrew from the workforce even as household incomes rose.
- SC, ST and Muslim workers were disproportionately in casual and low-paid work.

## Regional imbalance and agrarian distress
- Employment growth concentrated in a few States and urban agglomerations; agriculture continued to hold about half the workforce while producing a shrinking share of output — the classic productivity gap.

## The Plan’s response

The National Skill Development Mission targeting 500 million skilled persons by 2022; MGNREGA as an employment guarantee and wage floor; NRLM for rural livelihoods; and a push for labour-intensive manufacturing.

## What has changed since — and what has not
- **Female LFPR (UPSS)** — 23.3% (2009-10) · 41.7% (2023-24) — a genuine structural improvement
- **Unemployment rate** — ~6% (2017-18) · 3.1% (2025); 56.2 crore persons employed in Q2 FY26, with 8.7 lakh net jobs added over Q1
- **Employment elasticity** — ~0.01 (2000s) · 1.11% job growth per 1% value added (2017-23)
- **Formal manufacturing jobs** — Stagnant · ASI FY24: +6% employment, over 10 lakh jobs; 57 lakh added over FY15-FY24
- **Informality** — 92%+ · Still dominant — the unincorporated sector alone employs 12.9 crore persons
- **Contractualisation** — ~1/3 in organised sector · 42% of manufacturing workers are contractual (ASI 2023-24) — the weakness has deepened

## Conclusion

The Eleventh Plan’s diagnosis was accurate and remarkably durable: India’s problem was never the quantity of open unemployment but the quality, formality and productivity of work. Two of its five weaknesses — female participation and headline unemployment — have improved substantially. The others — informality, contractualisation and the agriculture-employment overhang — persist. The current policy answer lies in the four Labour Codes (effective 21 November 2025), the Employment Linked Incentive Scheme, and manufacturing-led job creation under PLI.

## Value addition
- Four Labour Codes, effective 21 November 2025: Code on Wages (2019), Industrial Relations Code (2020), Code on Social Security (2020), and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (2020) — consolidating 29 central laws; universal minimum wage, statutory appointment letters, annual health check-ups, and social security

extended to gig and platform workers. Draft Central Rules gazetted on 30 December 2025.

- Employment Linked Incentive (ELI) Scheme: outlay ₹99,446 crore; jobs created between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2027; target of over 3.5 crore jobs including 1.92 crore first-timers. Part A — one month’s EPF wage up to

₹15,000 in two instalments for first-time EPFO registrants earning up to ₹1 lakh a month; Part B — up to ₹3,000 per month per additional employee for two years, extended to years 3-4 for manufacturing.

- PLFS revamped from January 2025 — monthly bulletins from April 2025 and quarterly rural plus urban estimates, with district-level estimates targeted by 2026.
- PLFS 2025: LFPR 59.3% (male 79.1%, female 40.0%); rural 62.8% vs urban 52.2%; unemployment 3.1%.

## Introduction

Regional Rural Banks were conceived on the recommendation of the Narasimham Working Group (1975) to combine the local feel of cooperatives with the business discipline of commercial banks. The first five were set up on 2 October 1975 by ordinance, later replaced by the RRB Act, 1976.

## Need for their emergence
- A credit vacuum: commercial banks were urban-oriented even after the 1969 nationalisation; cooperatives were financially weak and politically captured; the rural poor depended on moneylenders.
- Targeted mandate: RRBs were required to lend 75% of adjusted net bank credit to the priority sector — the highest of any bank class — focused on small and marginal farmers, artisans, agricultural labourers and rural entrepreneurs.
- Low-cost model: lower establishment costs and locally recruited staff made small-ticket rural lending viable.
- Delivery arm of the state: RRBs became the conduit for MGNREGA wages, pensions, PM-KISAN and DBT in rural areas.

## Problems faced
- **Weak viability** — High operating costs, low-yield mandated lending, elevated NPAs; many RRBs ran accumulated losses
- **Restricted operations** — Narrow district-level jurisdiction prevented portfolio diversification and risk-pooling
- **Technology lag** — Late adoption of Core Banking Solutions left them uncompetitive as banking digitised
- **Human resources** — Difficulty attracting and retaining skilled staff in rural postings
- **Governance conflict** — Tripartite ownership — Centre 50%, Sponsor Bank 35%, State 15% — produced divided accountability and political interference
- **Fragmentation** — 196 small, undercapitalised entities lacked economies of scale

## Revisions and reforms
- Amalgamation: a phased consolidation from 2005 cut the number of RRBs from 196 to 28, completed under the

“One State, One RRB” policy with effect from 1 May 2025.

- RRB (Amendment) Act, 2015: raised authorised capital to ₹2,000 crore, permitted capital-raising from sources beyond the three sponsors (subject to a 51% government floor), and allowed a wider business scope.
- Recapitalisation: successive infusions, notably in FY22 and FY23, restored capital adequacy.
- Technology and product upgrades: Core Banking Solutions, internet and mobile banking, UPI participation, and Business Correspondent networks.
- Supervisory clarity: regulated by the RBI, supervised by NABARD, with refinance support.

## Current performance — the reforms have delivered
- 28 RRBs operate about 22,158 branches across roughly 730 districts.
- Consolidated CRAR reached an all-time high of 14.4% at the end of FY25; GNPA improved to 5.4%; net profit rose to about ₹6,800 crore.
- The credit-deposit ratio rose from 71.4% (March 2024) to 73.8% (March 2025) — the highest in 35 years, showing deposits are being deployed locally rather than parked.
- RRBs have consistently exceeded the 75% priority sector lending target, fulfilling their founding purpose.

## Conclusion

RRBs were created to fill a credit vacuum and, after decades of weak viability, have been restructured into fewer, larger, better-capitalised and digitally enabled institutions. With record capital adequacy, improving asset quality and the highest credit-deposit ratio in 35 years, they are today a credible pillar of rural finance. The remaining agenda is professional governance, agriculture-sector asset quality, and diversification into allied and non-farm rural enterprise.

## Value addition
- Ownership ratio: 50:35:15 (Government of India : Sponsor Bank : State Government); regulated by RBI, supervised by NABARD.
- Institutional lineage: Narasimham Working Group (1975) → RRB Act, 1976 → Kelkar Committee (1986) → Bhandari Committee (1994) → Vyas Committee (2004, amalgamation) → RRB (Amendment) Act, 2015 → “One State, One RRB” (2025).
- Andhra Pradesh: the State’s RRBs were merged into a single entity under the One State–One RRB policy, sponsored by Union Bank of India, deepening rural credit delivery alongside SERP’s SHG network and Kisan Credit Card saturation.
- Caution point: agriculture’s GNPA across scheduled commercial banks stands at 6.0% — the highest of any sector — a reminder that rural credit expansion must be matched by appraisal capacity, crop insurance and risk mitigation.
- One-line revision point: RRBs were born to bridge a gap, nearly died of fragmentation, and have been rescued by consolidation, capital and technology.
Q95:
## Introduction

The ratio of revenue receipts to GSDP measures a State’s fiscal capacity — how much of the income generated within its borders it can convert into public resources. Andhra Pradesh’s ratio rose through 2002-07 and fell through 2008-14, tracking almost exactly the twin cycles of reform-led buoyancy and crisis-plus-welfare strain.

## Phase I: The rise, 2002-2007 — reform plus growth
- **High growth** — India, and AP, grew above 8% a year; the tax base expanded faster than GSDP itself in trade and services
- **VAT (2005)** — Replaced cascading sales tax, curbed evasion, widened the base — the single biggest structural gain
- **FRBM discipline** — The AP FRBM Act, 2005 and the AP Fiscal Reforms Programme forced revenue effort alongside expenditure control; AP eliminated its revenue deficit by 2005-06
- **Administrative modernisation** — Computerisation of commercial taxes, CARD for registration, e-Seva — reduced leakage and raised stamp and registration yields
- **Buoyant central transfers** — Twelfth Finance Commission award and rising central tax collections raised the transfer component
- **Non-tax revenue** — Improved returns from restructured PSUs and higher royalties

## Phase II: The decline, 2008-2014 — crisis, welfare and dilution
- **Global financial crisis (2008)** — Slowdown in trade, manufacturing and property transactions cut sales tax, stamp duty and registration receipts
- **Fiscal stimulus and tax concessions** — Excise and customs cuts at the Centre, plus State-level exemptions, reduced buoyancy just as spending rose
- **Welfare expansion** — MGNREGA, food and fertiliser subsidies, fee reimbursement, Aarogyasri and Rs.2-a-kg rice — expenditure grew faster than GSDP while receipts lagged
- **Weak non-tax revenue** — Falling PSU dividends and stagnant user charges
- **Inflation and real erosion** — High inflation raised committed expenditure (dearness allowance, subsidies) faster than real revenue growth
- **Political and administrative disruption** — The Telangana agitation from 2009 and the run-up to the 2014 bifurcation created investment uncertainty and revenue leakage in the final years

## Analytical point for the examiner

The two phases illustrate that the receipts-to-GSDP ratio depends on three multiplicands — the tax base, the effective rate, and collection efficiency. In 2002-07 all three improved simultaneously. In 2008-14 the base slowed, exemptions cut the effective rate, and administrative attention was diverted — a triple squeeze. The lesson is that fiscal capacity is built in good years and defended in bad ones.

## Where the State stands now

Andhra Pradesh’s own tax revenue is budgeted at ₹1,25,846 crore in 2026-27 — around 6.5-7% of GSDP — with revenue receipts of ₹2,34,140 crore. Deficits have narrowed sharply (revenue deficit 1.11%, fiscal deficit 3.84% of GSDP), but the composition remains narrow, resting heavily on excise, liquor and petroleum sales tax.

## Conclusion

The 2002-07 rise reflected the payoff of VAT, FRBM discipline and administrative modernisation during a growth upswing; the 2008-14 decline reflected external shock, welfare expansion and eroded tax effort. Sustaining a high receipts-to-GSDP ratio therefore demands a broader base, digitised administration, realistic user charges, and counter-cyclical prudence — saving in good years so that welfare in bad years need not be financed by borrowing.

## Value addition
- AP fiscal trajectory: revenue deficit 3.79% of GSDP (FY25 Accounts) → 2.33% (FY26 RE) → 1.11% (BE 2026-27); fiscal deficit 5.11% → 4.57% → 3.84%.
- Reform milestones: AP Fiscal Reforms Programme (with multilateral support) → VAT (2005) → AP FRBM Act, 2005 → revenue surplus achieved 2005-06 → post-2014 structural deficit.
- Nationally comparable context: States’ own tax revenue registered a post-pandemic CAGR of 12.6%, raising own tax as a share of revenue receipts from 46% (FY22) to about 50% (FY25); but total State revenue receipts fell from 13.3% to 12.2% of GDP, showing the same capacity constraint across States.
- NITI Aayog Fiscal Health Index (2026) — five pillars: quality of expenditure, revenue mobilisation, fiscal prudence, debt index and debt sustainability.
- One-line revision point: Fiscal capacity is not a function of tax rates alone — it is base × rate × compliance, and all three move with the business cycle.

## Introduction

By the late 1990s Andhra Pradesh faced a fiscal crisis — a revenue deficit approaching 3% of GSDP, a ballooning power subsidy and an interest burden crowding out development. Between 1997 and 2005 the State eliminated its revenue deficit entirely, achieving a revenue surplus by 2005-06. This was among India’s most-studied episodes of sub-national fiscal consolidation.

## A framework for discipline
- The Andhra Pradesh Fiscal Reforms Programme (APFRP), supported by the World Bank and DFID with the AP Economic Restructuring Project, tied external assistance to measurable fiscal milestones — subsidy rationalisation, expenditure control and improved expenditure quality.
- The AP Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2005 then institutionalised the gains, mandating elimination of the revenue deficit, a 3% fiscal deficit ceiling, and Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statements — converting a reform programme into a legal obligation.

## Revenue mobilisation
- Introduction of VAT (2005), replacing the cascading sales tax — the single largest structural gain, widening the base and curbing evasion.
- Modernisation of the Commercial Taxes Department with computerised assessment and cross-verification.
- Buoyant state excise and stamps and registration receipts, the latter helped by rising property transactions and better valuation.
- Rationalisation of user charges in irrigation, water supply and transport.

## Expenditure rationalisation
- Control of the wage bill through a recruitment freeze and restrictions on new posts.
- Targeted subsidy reform, particularly in power and food.
- Shift of spending towards maintenance of existing assets and away from unproductive commitments.

## Sectoral and public enterprise restructuring
- Unbundling of the APSEB (1999-2000) into generation, transmission and distribution companies under the AP Electricity Reform Act, 1998 — reducing transmission and distribution losses and improving commercial discipline.
- Chronically loss-making State PSUs were restructured, merged or divested, easing the drain on the exchequer.

## Administrative and governance reform
- CARD (Computer-Aided Registration of Documents) transformed stamp duty and registration collection.
- e-Seva improved citizen service delivery and reduced leakage.
- Better cash and debt management, and treasury computerisation.

## The favourable macro context

Reform coincided with the national growth acceleration after 2003, which raised the tax base independently of policy — a reminder that consolidation is far easier in an upswing.

## Why the achievement did not last
- The post-2004 welfare expansion — Aarogyasri, fee reimbursement, Indiramma housing, subsidised rice — was predominantly revenue expenditure, and the revenue deficit returned.
- Jalayagnam was financed through borrowings, raising the interest burden.
- Structurally, the State’s own-tax base remained narrow, so gains depended on buoyancy rather than breadth.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh eliminated its revenue deficit through a coherent combination of legal discipline (FRBM), tax reform (VAT), expenditure control, utility restructuring and digital administration — reinforced by a growth upswing. The episode’s enduring lesson is that fiscal consolidation is achievable but not self-sustaining: without a permanently broadened tax base, a single cycle of welfare expansion can reverse it. That is precisely the discipline the State is rebuilding today, with the revenue deficit compressed to 1.11% of GSDP in 2026-27.

## Value addition
- AP FRBM Act, 2005: eliminate the revenue deficit, cap the fiscal deficit at 3% of GSDP, mandate MTFP statements, and restrict unproductive borrowing. The 16th FC (2026-31) has reaffirmed the 3% GSDP ceiling for all States.
- Twelfth Finance Commission (2005) incentivised State-level FRBM legislation through debt consolidation and relief, and ended Central on-lending — pushing States to the market.
- AP’s current consolidation: revenue deficit 3.79% (FY25) → 2.33% (FY26 RE) → 1.11% (BE 2026-27); fiscal deficit 5.11% → 4.57% → 3.84%; own tax revenue budgeted at ₹1,25,846 crore.
- Warning from the Economic Survey 2025-26: unconditional cash transfers across States, about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26, create precisely the expenditure rigidity that reversed AP’s earlier surplus.

## Introduction

GST was designed to replace a fragmented indirect tax system in which goods crossed state borders through check-posts and taxes were levied on taxes. Its objectives were simultaneously economic (efficiency), administrative (compliance) and constitutional (cooperative federalism).

## Objectives of GST
- One nation, one tax, one market — replace excise, service tax, VAT, octroi, entry tax, purchase tax and CST with a single levy.
- Eliminate cascading — the seamless input tax credit chain ensures tax is paid only on value added at each stage.
- Widen the base and improve compliance — the ITC chain makes evasion self-defeating, since a buyer’s credit depends on the seller’s compliance.
- Improve logistics efficiency — abolish inter-state check-posts and enable warehousing decisions driven by economics rather than tax arbitrage.
- Formalise the unorganised sector — bring textiles, construction and trade into the tax net.
- Promote cooperative federalism — the GST Council (Art. 279A) as India’s first genuinely federal fiscal institution, with pooled sovereignty.

## Impact on economic growth
- **Efficiency and trade** — Removal of cascading and internal barriers lowers the effective tax rate and expands internal trade · Studies estimate potential GDP gains of several percentage points from higher internal and external trade
- **Logistics** — Truck turnaround times fell with check-post abolition; national warehousing replaced state-wise depots · LPI rank improved from 44th (2018) to 38th (2023); logistics cost estimated at 7.97% of GDP (NCAER, 2023-24)
- **Formalisation and revenue** — Digital trail widened the base · Registrations grew to over 1.5 crore; gross collections ₹22.27 lakh crore in FY26, with April 2026 at a record ₹2.43 lakh crore
- **Consumption stimulus** — GST 2.0 rate cuts on 375 items raised real purchasing power · Contributed to CPI inflation falling to 1.7% in FY26 (April-December); high-frequency indicators — e-way bills, auto sales, UPI — strengthened after September 2025
- **Investment climate** — Predictable, uniform taxation improves ease of doing business · Supported record FDI of US$94.52 billion in FY26
- **Fiscal capacity** — Buoyant indirect tax revenue funds capital expenditure · Enabled effective capex of ₹17.15 lakh crore in FY27

## A balanced verdict — what GST has not delivered
- Incomplete coverage: petroleum, electricity, alcohol and real estate remain outside, so cascading persists in the most input-intensive sectors.
- Revenue-neutrality was not achieved initially, requiring compensation cess until 2022 and leaving several States fiscally anxious.
- Compliance burden on small firms remains real, despite the composition and QRMP schemes.
- Federal friction: the end of the compensation regime and the rising share of cess and surcharge outside the divisible pool have strained Centre-State trust.
- Pass-through of rate cuts to consumers is not institutionally guaranteed in the absence of a standing anti-profiteering authority.

## Conclusion

GST has substantially achieved its administrative and market-unification objectives, and GST 2.0 has finally delivered the rate simplification promised in 2017. Its growth contribution operates less through a dramatic one-time jump than through steady gains in efficiency, formalisation and fiscal capacity. Completing the reform — bringing petroleum and electricity into the net, and rebuilding federal trust on revenue sharing — would convert a good tax into a great one.

## Value addition
- Constitutional anchors: Art. 246A (simultaneous power to legislate), Art. 269A (IGST levy and apportionment), Art. 279A (GST Council), Art. 366(12A) (definition of GST).
- Committee lineage: Kelkar Task Force (2003) recommended a national GST; the Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers steered VAT and then GST design; the Thirteenth Finance Commission Task Force modelled the revenue-neutral rate.
- GST 2.0 (22 September 2025): four slabs merged into 5% and 18% plus a 40% demerit rate; rate cuts on about 375 items; estimated revenue foregone about ₹48,000 crore.
- Andhra Pradesh link: SGST is the State’s single largest own-tax head; but AP retains sales tax on petroleum and liquor — outside GST — which is simultaneously its fiscal cushion and the source of its narrow tax base.

## Introduction

Bifurcation left Andhra Pradesh without a capital city, with Hyderabad serving as joint capital for a maximum of ten years under the Reorganisation Act. The AP Capital Region Development Authority Act, 2014 created the statutory vehicle to plan, finance and build a greenfield capital at Amaravati on the Krishna river.

## Need for the CRDA Act
- No administrative capital: the State urgently required a seat of government — Secretariat, Assembly, High Court, Raj Bhavan and directorates.
- Planned urbanisation: to avoid the unplanned sprawl that had characterised Indian city growth, the project drew on models such as Singapore and Putrajaya, with a master-planned, sustainable design.
- A growth pole: the capital was conceived as an economic engine for the Krishna-Guntur belt and, through it, for balanced State development.
- A legal framework for land assembly: building a city on 217 sq km of fertile, privately owned delta land required a statutory mechanism for land pooling, compensation and dispute resolution that ordinary acquisition law could not provide without prolonged conflict.

## Salient features
- **The Authority** — CRDA constituted under the Act, headquartered at Amaravati, to plan, coordinate, execute and supervise development, chaired by the Chief Minister
- **Jurisdiction** — A Capital Region of about 8,603 sq km, within which a Capital City Area of 217.23 sq km was designated
- **Land Pooling Scheme** — The Act’s signature innovation — farmers voluntarily surrendered land in exchange for developed returnable plots plus an annuity, avoiding compulsory acquisition. About 33,000 acres were pooled from over 24,000 farmers — one of the world’s largest participatory land assemblies
- **Planning powers** — Authority to prepare Perspective, Master and Infrastructure Plans, integrating land use, transport, housing, water and environment, with development control regulations
- **Participation and transparency** — Mandated citizen consultation and GIS-based monitoring of planning and implementation

- **Amaravati Development Corporation** — An executing arm for project implementation

## Why the land pooling model mattered

It shifted the compensation logic from a one-time cash payment to participation in the appreciation of the asset — farmers became stakeholders in the city’s value rather than displaced sellers. The masterplan envisages a city of about

## Introduction

The controversy is often mis-stated as a fight over the repo rate. Since the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (2015) and the RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016, the policy rate is the statutory remit of the MPC, while the inflation target is notified by the Union Government. The real friction lies in administered interest rates on small savings schemes, set quarterly by the Ministry of Finance.

## Where the friction arises
- Small savings schemes — PPF, NSC, Sukanya Samriddhi, Senior Citizens’ Savings Scheme — are set by the MoF, which since 2016 has followed a formula linking them to comparable secondary-market G-sec yields with a spread, revised quarterly.
- In practice, discretion intervenes. The RBI has flagged that post-2016, small savings rates were often 65–100 bps above formula-implied levels. When market yields soften but administered rates stay put, banks cannot cut deposit rates without losing deposits — putting a floor under lending rates.
- The 2021 episode is illustrative: a steep MoF cut announced on 31 March 2021 was rolled back within hours, revealing the political sensitivity of the instrument.

## The two legitimate positions
- **Market-consistent, formula-based resets so the repo transmits cleanly** — Protect small savers, pensioners and risk-averse households from abrupt income cuts
- **Deposit-rate rigidity blunts monetary policy and squeezes bank margins** — Small savings finance the NSSF and part of the fiscal deficit — cuts affect funding costs
- **Predictability strengthens the framework’s credibility** — Households have limited alternatives; social protection is a legitimate fiscal objective

## The wider institutional dimension

The interest-rate issue is one facet of a recurring Centre–RBI negotiation that has also covered:

- Surplus transfers — resolved through the Bimal Jalan Committee (2018) Economic Capital Framework, which set a rule-based Contingent Risk Buffer band. Under it, the RBI transferred a record ₹2,86,588 crore for FY26, while raising the CRB to 6.5% — a demonstration that rules, not bargaining, now govern the transfer.
- Prompt Corrective Action norms and regulatory perimeter, which strained relations in 2018-19.

## Evidence that transmission, not authority, is the real issue

FY26 shows what happens when frictions ease: with surplus liquidity of about ₹1.89 lakh crore, the WALR on fresh rupee loans fell 64 bps to 8.71% against a 100 bps repo cut. Where administered rates and deposit stickiness persist, pass-through is slower and asymmetric — faster on loans than on deposits, compressing bank margins.

## Way forward
- Rules first: publicly commit to the 2016 formula, with any saver-protection spread disclosed and justified.
- Smoother resets: use moving-average G-sec benchmarks and caps on quarter-to-quarter changes to protect savers

without breaking market linkage.

- Broaden the saver’s toolkit: expand floating-rate savings bonds, inflation-indexed instruments and annuity products so social protection does not depend on rigid administered rates.

## Conclusion

There is no constitutional or statutory dispute over who sets the policy rate — the MPC does. The controversy is narrower but genuine: administered small savings rates, when held above market-implied levels, dilute the very transmission the framework was built to deliver. A steadier, rules-first regime would reconcile the saver’s interest, the exchequer’s needs and the RBI’s operational independence.

## Value addition
- RBI surplus transfers to the Centre: FY23 ₹87,416 cr → FY24 ₹2,10,874 cr → FY25 ₹2,68,590 cr → FY26 ₹2,86,588 crore (record), approved at the 623rd Central Board meeting (22 May 2026); CRB retained at 6.5%; RBI balance sheet ₹91.97 lakh crore (+20.61%).
- Legal basis: Section 47, RBI Act, 1934 — net profits, after provisions, are transferred to the Centre; framework based on the Bimal Jalan Committee (2018), first examined by the Y.H. Malegam Committee.
- Section 7, RBI Act: empowers the Centre to issue directions in the public interest after consultation with the Governor — never formally invoked, but its shadow shaped the 2018 debate.
- Context (FY26): the rupee moved from about ₹83/US$ to ₹96/US$ by May 2026, boosting RBI income from foreign exchange operations and explaining the record surplus.
Q101:
## Introduction

The FRBM Act, 2003 (effective July 2004) was India’s first attempt to place a statutory limit on fiscal discretion, responding to a decade in which the combined deficit approached 10% of GDP and interest payments consumed a third of revenue. Its purpose was to make fiscal prudence a legal obligation rather than a political choice.

## Highlights of the Act
- **Fiscal targets** — Reduce fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP and eliminate the revenue deficit by March 2009
- **Monetisation ban** — RBI prohibited from subscribing to primary issues of government securities from 1 April 2006 — ending automatic deficit financing
- **Transparency** — Three statements to be laid with the Budget: Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement, Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement, Macroeconomic Framework Statement
- **Escape clause** — Deviation permitted on grounds of national security, national calamity or other exceptional circumstances, with reasons stated to Parliament
- **Rolling targets** — Three-year rolling projections for key fiscal indicators
- **Federal extension** — The Twelfth Finance Commission (2005) incentivised States to enact their own FRBM laws — Andhra Pradesh did so in 2005

## Evolution of the framework
- FRBM (Amendment) Act, 2012: introduced Effective Revenue Deficit (revenue deficit minus grants for capital asset creation) and added the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework.
- N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee (2017): recommended shifting the anchor from deficit to debt — 40% of GDP for the Centre and 60% for the general government — with an independent Fiscal Council and a narrowly defined escape clause.
- Budget 2025-26 onwards: the Centre formally adopted a debt-to-GDP anchor of 50±1% by 31 March 2031 in place of annual deficit targets — a concrete commitment with a specific date that preserves policy flexibility.
- 16th Finance Commission (2026-31): recommends the Centre reach a fiscal deficit of 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31, caps States at 3% of GSDP, and requires all off-budget borrowings to be brought on-budget and included in the definition of debt.

## Evaluating the record
- Successes: the fiscal deficit fell to 2.5% of GDP in 2007-08; the monetisation ban permanently ended the inflationary financing of deficits; transparency in fiscal reporting improved substantially.
- Failures: the 3% target has been achieved only once since 2003; escape clauses were invoked liberally after the 2008 crisis and again for COVID-19, when the deficit reached 9.2% of GDP (FY21); off-budget borrowings and guarantees undermined the letter of the law.
- Recovery: the deficit has since been reduced to 4.8% (FY25), 4.4% (FY26) and 4.3% (BE 2026-27), with outstanding liabilities at 55.6% of GDP, earning three sovereign rating upgrades in FY26.

## Conclusion

The FRBM Act’s numerical targets were repeatedly missed, but its institutional legacy is decisive — it ended monetisation, embedded medium-term fiscal statements, and created a shared vocabulary of fiscal discipline for the Centre and the States. Its logical culmination is the current framework, which anchors policy to a debt path rather than an annual number — a design better suited to a volatile world, provided the commitment is honoured.

## Value addition
- Key definitions: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total non-debt receipts; Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts; Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments; Effective Revenue Deficit = revenue deficit − grants for capital asset creation (recommended by the Rangarajan Committee, 2010).
- Union Budget 2026-27 deficits (% of GDP): fiscal 4.3, revenue 1.5, primary 0.7, effective revenue 0.3.
- Accountability: the CAG was entrusted with periodic review of FRBM compliance by the 2012 amendment; Section 7A provides for ex-post evaluation.
- Unimplemented recommendation: an independent Fiscal Council for ex-ante scrutiny of budget projections —

urged by the 13th and 14th Finance Commissions and the N.K. Singh Committee.

- AP parallel: the AP FRBM Act, 2005 helped the State eliminate its revenue deficit by 2005-06; AP’s fiscal deficit is now budgeted at 3.84% of GSDP (2026-27).

## Introduction

NITI Aayog was established by a Cabinet Resolution of 1 January 2015, which explicitly set out the philosophy behind the new institution. Its guiding principles marked a departure from the Planning Commission’s premise — that development is designed at the centre — towards the premise that development is delivered by States and communities, with the Centre as enabler.

## The guiding principles of the founding Resolution
- **Antyodaya** — Prioritise service and upliftment of the poorest and most vulnerable first · Aspirational Districts (112) and Aspirational Blocks (500) Programmes
- **Inclusion** — Give voice to those at risk of exclusion — SCs, STs, OBCs, women, and the disadvantaged · Multidimensional Poverty Index; targeted gender and tribal interventions
- **Village** — Integrate villages into the development process by drawing on their strengths · Bottom-up planning; Gram Panchayat Development Plans
- **Demographic dividend** — Treat India’s youth as its greatest asset through education, skilling and opportunity · Skill India, Atal Innovation Mission, Atal Tinkering Labs
- **People’s participation** — Development must be a movement, not a scheme · Consultation with civil society, industry, academia; crowd-sourced platforms
- **Governance** — Transparent, accountable, outcome-oriented and technology-driven administration · SDG India Index, Fiscal Health Index, real-time dashboards
- **Sustainability** — Ancient Indian tradition of ecological balance made central to policy · Composite Water Management Index; energy and climate strategies

## The “pillars of effective governance” articulated in the same Resolution

Pro-people, Pro-activity, Participation, Empowerment, Inclusion of all, Equality of opportunity, and Transparency — the values NITI Aayog was intended to embody as an institution.

## Additional structural principles
- Cooperative and competitive federalism: States as equal partners through the Governing Council of all Chief Ministers and Lt. Governors and through Regional Councils; competition induced through published rankings rather than fund control.
- Knowledge and innovation hub: evidence-based policy through a Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office, resource centres and research partnerships.
- Flexibility over rigidity: the 15-year Vision, 7-year Strategy and 3-year Action Agenda replaced fixed Five-Year Plans.

## Assessment — principle versus practice
- Where it has worked: the Aspirational Districts Programme has demonstrably improved health and education indicators through real-time monitoring; the SDG India Index score rose to 71 in 2023-24 from 57 in 2018, with 32 States and UTs now front-runners; NITI’s indices have become genuine drivers of State-level reform.
- Where it falls short: without financial powers, NITI Aayog can persuade but not compel; Governing Council meetings have been infrequent; and poorer States often lack the technical capacity to act on its advice — so competitive federalism can widen gaps rather than close them.

## Conclusion

NITI Aayog’s guiding principles — Antyodaya, inclusion, participation, sustainability and cooperative federalism — represent a genuine philosophical advance: development conceived as a shared national movement rather than a centrally directed allocation. Their realisation depends on two things the Resolution could not legislate: regular, meaningful consultation with States, and investment in State capacity so that every State can act on the evidence NITI Aayog generates.

## Value addition
- Aspirational Districts Programme indicators and weights: Health & Nutrition 30%, Education 30%, Agriculture & Water Resources 20%, Financial Inclusion & Skill Development 10%, Basic Infrastructure 10%.
- NITI indices: SDG India Index, Fiscal Health Index (2nd edition, 2026), Composite Water Management Index, India Innovation Index, Export Preparedness Index, School Education Quality Index, National MPI.
- Evidence of impact: about 24.8 crore people exited multidimensional poverty over nine years (NITI Aayog MPI); SDG India Index — Kerala and Uttarakhand top at 79, Bihar lowest at 57.
Q103:
## Introduction

Revenue deficit (RD) is the excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts — the amount a government must borrow simply to run itself. Effective revenue deficit (ERD), introduced in Budget 2011-12 and given statutory form by the FRBM (Amendment) Act, 2012, refines this by removing grants that, though classified as revenue expenditure in Union accounts, actually create capital assets in the States.

## The concepts
- RD = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts. A high RD means borrowing for consumption — fiscally the least defensible form of deficit, since it creates a liability without a corresponding asset.
- ERD = RD − Grants-in-Aid for Creation of Capital Assets (GiACA). Why ERD was introduced — the accounting problem it solves

When the Centre gives a State ₹1,000 crore to build a highway or a school, the Union classifies it as a grant, hence revenue expenditure — because the Centre acquires no asset. But an asset is created, in the State’s books. Counting it as consumption therefore:

## Overstates the Centre’s consumptive spending and understates national capital formation;
- Creates a perverse incentive to cut transfers to States during consolidation, since grants inflate the reported RD;
- Obscures expenditure quality, the very thing fiscal rules are meant to reveal.

## The justification, in four points
- Recognises asset-building expenditure and separates it from true consumption.
- Protects federal transfers during fiscal consolidation — an important safeguard for States like Andhra Pradesh, which depend on central grants for roughly 14% of their revenue receipts.
- Improves transparency for Parliament, auditors and rating agencies.
- Encourages capital formation and inter-generational equity — the Rangarajan Committee’s core argument.

## The current figures
- **Indicator** — Union Budget 2026-27 (BE)
- **Revenue deficit** — 1.5% of GDP
- **Effective revenue deficit** — 0.3% of GDP
- **Fiscal deficit** — 4.3% of GDP
- **Primary deficit** — 0.7% of GDP

The gap between RD (1.5%) and ERD (0.3%) — about 1.2 percentage points of GDP — is precisely the measure of grants that build assets in the States.

## Critical assessment
- Strength: ERD is the sharpest available measure of pure consumption borrowing, and the narrowing gap between RD and ERD over the years signals genuine improvement in expenditure quality.
- Weakness: critics — including the N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee (2017) — argued that ERD created scope for creative reclassification, since labelling a grant as “capital-creating” is partly discretionary. Accordingly, ERD was dropped as a statutory target in the post-2018 framework, though it continues to be disclosed in Budget documents.
- The FRBM’s original target of eliminating ERD by 2014-15 was never met.

## Conclusion

The effective revenue deficit was a genuine conceptual advance: it corrected an accounting distortion that penalised federal transfers and misrepresented capital formation. Even though it is no longer a statutory target, it remains a valuable diagnostic — and its steady decline to 0.3% of GDP is among the clearest evidence that India’s fiscal consolidation has improved the quality, not merely the quantity, of public spending.

## Value addition
- Rangarajan Committee on Public Expenditure (2010) proposed the ERD concept; Budget 2011-12 introduced it; the FRBM (Amendment) Act, 2012 made it a statutory target with a roadmap to zero by 2014-15 — later abandoned.
- Where GiACA goes: centrally sponsored schemes such as PMAY, Jal Jeevan Mission, PMGSY and Samagra Shiksha — all revenue grants from the Centre that build physical assets in States.
- The broader trend: revenue expenditure fell from 13.6% of GDP (FY22) to 10.9% (FY25), while effective capital expenditure reached 4% of GDP in FY25 and 4.4% in FY27 (BE).
- One-line revision point: Revenue deficit tells you the government borrowed to eat; effective revenue deficit tells you how much of that meal was actually a building.
