## Introduction

The Twelfth Five-Year Plan (2012-17) — India’s last — carried the theme “Faster, Sustainable and More Inclusive Growth.” Its distinguishing contribution was to treat inclusion not as redistribution after growth, but as a set of measurable capabilities that determine whether people can participate in growth at all.

Salient features of the inclusive growth strategy

- Poverty and livelihood security - Reduce the head-count poverty ratio by 10 percentage points over the Plan period. - Generate 50 million new work opportunities and provide skill certification to an equal number. - MGNREGA as a wage floor; NRLM for rural livelihoods; targeted support to small and marginal farmers.
- Health as capability - Raise public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP. - Reduce IMR to 25, MMR to 1 per 1,000 and TFR to 2.1. - Halve under-nutrition among children aged 0-3 relative to NFHS-3 levels. - Expand the National Health Mission and move toward universal health coverage.
- Education and skills - Raise mean years of schooling to above 7. - Eliminate gender and social gaps in enrolment at all levels. - RMSA for secondary education; the National Skill Development Mission to build employability.
- Regional balance - Backward Regions Grant Fund and special area programmes; focus on the eastern States, hill areas and tribal districts. - Rural connectivity through PMGSY and electrification through RGGVY.
- Empowerment of women and disadvantaged groups - Gender budgeting institutionalised; SHG-based livelihood promotion. - Scheduled Caste and Tribal Sub-Plans; targeted scholarships and hostel support. - Recognition that social exclusion, not only income poverty, blocks participation.
- Environmental sustainability as a condition of inclusion - Green cover to rise by 1 million hectares annually; 30,000 MW of renewable capacity added; energy efficiency improved by 20-25%. - The insight that the poor depend most directly on natural resources, so environmental degradation is itself a form of exclusion.
- Service delivery and accountability - Aadhaar-linked delivery and DBT to cut leakage; banking access for 90% of households; 90% rural electrification. - Outcome and performance-based budgeting, decentralisation and e-governance.

Assessment

- Growth fell short — about 6.5-7% against the 8% target, hit by the 2013 taper tantrum and stalled investment.
- Public health expenditure never reached 2.5% of GDP — it was about 1.13% in 2014-15, rising to 1.84% only by 2021-22.
- Poverty and deprivation did fall substantially over the decade.
- Institutional discontinuity: the Planning Commission was abolished midway (2015), leaving the Plan without its architect.

## Conclusion

The Twelfth Plan’s inclusive growth strategy was conceptually ahead of its delivery. Its three-way integration of growth, inclusion and sustainability, and its insistence on measurable human-development targets, mapped almost directly onto the Sustainable Development Goals adopted in 2015. Those priorities outlived the Plan itself — they now run through the SDG India Index (composite score 71 in 2023-24), the National Multidimensional Poverty Index, and the Viksit Bharat @2047 framework.

## Value addition
- Evolution of the theme: Tenth Plan (2002-07) — 8% growth with monitorable targets; Eleventh (2007-12) — “Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth”; Twelfth (2012-17) — “Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth.”
- What replaced the Plans: NITI Aayog’s 15-year Vision, 7-year Strategy and 3-year Action Agenda (2015); “Strategy

for New India @75” (2018); and the SDG framework.

- Outcome evidence since: about 24.8 crore people exited multidimensional poverty in nine years; female LFPR rose to 41.7% (2023-24) from 23.3% (2017-18); unemployment at 3.1% (2025).
- National Policy on Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (2015) operationalised the Plan’s skilling pillar through PMKVY, PM-NAPS and the National Skills Qualification Framework.

## Introduction

National income accounting estimates the value of goods and services produced in an economy. Since weights become obsolete as economies change, periodic rebasing is essential. India has undertaken two major revisions: the 2015 shift to base 2011–12, and the New GDP Series with base 2022–23, released on 27 February 2026 by MoSPI — the most comprehensive overhaul in a decade.

## Rationale for revision
- Consumption patterns, urbanisation, digital trade and the gig economy have transformed since 2011–12.
- Outdated weights distort deflators, sectoral shares and policy ratios (fiscal deficit, debt-to-GDP).
- The IMF assigned India's national accounts a "C" grade, citing irregular rebasing, single deflation and weak informal-sector coverage.

## Changes in the 2015 revision (base 2011–12)
- Headline shifted from GDP at factor cost → GDP at market prices, with GVA at basic prices, aligning with the UN System of National Accounts (SNA 2008).
- MCA21 database used for the corporate sector; NBFCs, mutual funds and stock exchanges brought in.
- Result: FY14 growth revised upward from 4.7% to 6.9%.

## Changes in the New Series (base 2022–23, February 2026)
- **Double deflation** — Both input and output prices deflated in manufacturing & agriculture — replacing single deflation (the IMF's core critique)
- **Administrative data** — GSTN, e-Vahan portal, PFMS integrated for high-frequency, granular estimation
- **Informal sector** — ASUSE (now quarterly) + PLFS (now monthly) replace decade-old benchmarks
- **SUT integration** — Supply & Use Tables reconcile production-side and expenditure-side discrepancies
- **New economy coverage** — Hired domestic workers, digital, platform and gig activities captured
- **Enterprise refinement** — Segregation of multi-activity enterprises; GST data for regional allocation
- **PFCE estimation** — Direct estimation + commodity-flow approach

Parallel rebasing: CPI to base 2024 (released 12 Feb 2026, using HCES 2023–24 with state-specific baskets) and IIP to 2022–23 (28 May 2026, with chain-based indices and seasonal adjustment).

## Impact
- FY26 real growth revised up to 7.6%, while nominal GDP fell 3.3–3.8%.
- Consequently the FY26 fiscal deficit estimate rose from 4.36% to 4.51% of GDP, and central debt to 57.5% — showing how rebasing reshapes fiscal ratios.
- Enhanced global credibility; but back-series comparability and perception gaps (high growth vs modest job creation) persist.

## Conclusion

The 2022–23 rebasing marks a decisive move from periodic data collection to a continuous, technology-enabled, AI-ready statistical system. Sustaining this requires a statutory National Statistical Commission (27th Report, Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance), a chain-weighted system, the delayed Census, and the first-ever Household Income Survey (2026) — for evidence-based governance is only as strong as its statistics.

## Introduction

National income measures the aggregate value of goods and services produced in an economy over a period. Economists use a family of interrelated concepts to capture output, income and expenditure. However GDP — though the most cited indicator — measures the size of the pie, not its distribution, durability or dignity.

GDP (market value of final goods & services produced within the country)Depreciation → NDP+ Net Factor Income from Abroad → GNPDepreciation → NNPNet Indirect Taxes → National Income (NNP at factor cost)÷ Population → Per Capita Income → Personal Income → Disposable IncomeGDP (market value of final goods & services produced within the country)Depreciation → NDP+ Net Factor Income from Abroad → GNPDepreciation → NNPNet Indirect Taxes → National Income (NNP at factor cost)÷ Population → Per Capita Income → Personal Income → Disposable IncomeConcepts of National Income — the derivation chain

- GDP: India is the 4th largest economy (~$4.2–4.3 trillion, IMF 2025); real growth 7.4% (FAE) / 7.6% (new series) in FY26.
- GNP: Reflects India's global earnings — record remittances of $129.1 billion (2024), a 14.3% global share.
- NDP / NNP: Net of depreciation, showing sustainable production capacity.
- Per Capita Income: ~$2,880 (nominal, IMF 2025) — a reminder that India is a large economy but a lower-middle-income country.

## Limitations of GDP as a welfare measure
- Blind to inequality: India's top 1% hold 22.6% of national income (World Inequality Report 2026); inequality erodes 30.7% of India's HDI value (IHDI, HDR 2025) — among the steepest losses globally.
- Excludes non-market work: Unpaid domestic and care work is invisible; 53% of Indian women remain outside the labour force due to care responsibilities (ILO).
- Ignores environmental cost: GDP counts pollution-generating output but not natural capital depletion. India's energy-related CO2 emissions rose 5.3% in 2024.
- Silent on human development: Despite fast growth, India ranks 130/193 on HDI (HDR 2025) and shares its HDI value with Bangladesh — a country with far lower per capita GDP.
- Averages conceal deprivation: MPI headcount stood at 11.28% (2022–23) even as GDP grew 6–7% annually.
- Says nothing about composition or durability: Defence spending, disaster reconstruction and hospital bills all raise GDP.

## Conclusion

The national income family remains indispensable for macroeconomic management, but GDP is a thermometer, not a diagnosis. True progress must be read alongside HDI, IHDI, MPI, SDG India Index and Green GDP. As the Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Commission (2009) cautioned, "what we measure affects what we do" — India's shift toward multidimensional metrics is therefore a shift toward better policy.

## Introduction

Structural transformation is the long-term reallocation of labour and capital from low-productivity activities (agriculture) to higher-productivity ones (industry, modern services). Theorised by Arthur Lewis (surplus labour), Kuznets and Chenery, it is the core mechanism through which per capita incomes rise. India's transformation is real — but partial and asymmetric.

## Shift in output structure (near-complete)

Agriculture: ~55% (1950–51) → 15.2% (FY26, FAE).

- Industry: rose to ~27% (1980s) → 24.3%; manufacturing only 12.8%.
- Services: 30% → 51.1% of GDP, 53.6% in H1 FY26 — the highest ever.

## Shift in employment structure (incomplete)
- Agriculture still holds 42.4% of workers (PLFS Q2 FY26, CWS).
- Overall LFPR 59.3% and unemployment 3.1% in 2025 (PLFS), with female LFPR at 40.0% — the binding constraint.

## Services-led, manufacturing-light path
- Unlike East Asia's manufacturing-driven catch-up, India's path is services-first.
- Union Budget 2026–27's two-track manufacturing strategy — deepening technology-intensive sectors (semiconductors, biologics) while scaling labour-intensive ones (textiles, sports goods) — is a deliberate correction, aiming to move India up the "smiling curve" from assembly to design and R&D.

## Persistent informality and job quality
- Over 80% of workers are informal; e-Shram records over 150 million informal non-farm workers.
- Gig workforce rose from 77 lakh (FY21) to 120 lakh (FY25); ~40% earn below ₹15,000/month.
- Contractual workers now form 42% of manufacturing employment (ASI 2023–24).
- Yet job quality is better in services: 51.5% of service workers hold regular wage jobs vs 25.5% in industry and 1% in agriculture.

High agrarian employment → weak manufacturing absorption → construction & low-end services as residual absorbers → informality →productivity gap persistsHigh agrarian employment → weak manufacturing absorption → construction & low-end services as residual absorbers → informality →productivity gap persistsNature — a summary flow

## Conclusion

India's structural transformation is real in output but incomplete in employment. Completing it requires competitive manufacturing, formalisation through the four Labour Codes, targeted skilling, and raising female LFPR towards ~55% by 2050 — identified by the Economic Survey 2025–26 as critical to sustaining high growth toward Viksit Bharat @2047.
Q108:
## Introduction

Independent India chose planned development to overcome colonial stagnation, adopting the Planning Commission (1950) and Five-Year Plans within a mixed-economy framework. The 1950–91 era sought to build, through the state, the capital base that a war-drained private sector could not.

## Objectives of Planning — the four pillars
- **Growth** — Raise national income and per-capita income
- **Modernisation** — Technology, heavy industry, scientific temper
- **Self-reliance** — Reduce dependence on food and capital-goods imports
- **Equity & Social Justice** — Land reforms, poverty reduction, regional balance

Strategy shifts: Harrod–Domar (1st Plan) → Mahalanobis heavy-industry model (2nd Plan) → Gadgil Formula (4th Plan) → ‘Garibi Hatao’ (5th Plan) Plan Holiday 1966–69 | Rolling Plan 1978–80

## Major achievements
- Agriculture: foodgrain output rose from 50.8 MT (1950–51) to 176 MT (1990–91); the Green Revolution ended ‘ship-to-mouth’ dependence on PL-480 imports.
- Industry: a diversified base built via PSUs — SAIL, BHEL, ONGC, HAL; industrial growth averaged 6–7% in the 1980s.
- Infrastructure & institutions: Bhakra-Nangal, IITs, ISRO, DAE, IDBI and NABARD; the savings rate rose from ~8.9% (1950–51) to ~24% (1990–91) — a genuine break from colonial stagnation.
- Human development: literacy rose from 18.3% (1951) to 52% (1991); life expectancy from 32 to 59 years.
- Andhra Pradesh: Nagarjuna Sagar (1955–67) and Srisailam projects, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant (sanctioned 1971), Hindustan Shipyard, BHEL Ramachandrapuram and SHAR, Sriharikota (1971) — planning’s visible footprint in the state.

## Critical appraisal — the shortfalls
- Growth underperformance: ~3.5% average GDP growth — the “Hindu rate of growth” (Raj Krishna) — with per-capita growth barely 1.2%.
- License–Permit–Quota Raj: the Bhagwati–Desai critique showed that controls bred rent-seeking and delay; a rising ICOR signalled falling capital productivity.
- Equity failure: poverty still ~45% (1983); land-ceiling laws largely evaded; illiteracy ~48% in 1991.
- Employment failure: capital-intensive heavy industry could not absorb surplus labour, entrenching agrarian underemployment.
- PSU inefficiency and mounting subsidies fed fiscal stress, culminating in the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis.

## Introduction

Measuring development is harder than measuring growth, because development is normative and multidimensional. As Amartya Sen argued, development is the expansion of capabilities and freedoms, not merely the rise of income. India’s challenge is to capture that broader reality in numbers.

## Difficulties in measuring the developmental level
- No single yardstick: GDP captures output but not distribution, health, dignity or sustainability — India is the 4th largest economy yet ranks 130/193 on HDI.
- Aggregation and weighting problem: composite indices assign arbitrary weights; a high score can mask acute deprivation in one dimension.
- Informality and non-market activity: ~90% informal workers and unpaid care work escape both output and welfare accounting.
- Inter- and intra-state disparity: national averages conceal that Kerala and Bihar are effectively at different development stages; district-level data remains thin.
- Data timeliness: delayed Census, decadal NFHS / HCES rounds and outdated sampling frames weaken comparability.
- Sustainability blind spot: GDP treats resource depletion and pollution as income rather than cost.

## Does India’s current method overcome them? — A balanced assessment
- **Strength (Yes, partly)** — Persisting Gap (Not fully)
- **GDP at market prices; new base 2022–23, double deflation, SUT** — GDP still the headline metric of “development”
- **National MPI (NITI Aayog with UNDP & OPHI, via MPICC) — 11.28% in 2022–23** — MPI depends on decadal NFHS rounds; lags reality
- **SDG India Index — India’s composite score 71 (2023–24), 16 goals, 113 indicators** — Eight of 17 SDGs off-track for 2030
- **HCES 2023–24 yields fresh Gini (0.237 rural, 0.284 urban)** — No official income survey until 2026
- **Monthly PLFS, eSankhyiki (770+ indicators), Fiscal Health Index** — Unpaid care work and Green GDP still outside the accounts
- **Aspirational Districts & Blocks Programme — sub-district measurement** — Census delay weakens every survey frame

Justification: India has moved from a single-metric (GDP) approach to a dashboard model of development measurement — GDP + MPI + SDG India Index + NFHS

+ PLFS + EnviStats. This substantially but not completely overcomes the difficulties, since sustainability and unpaid work remain unmeasured and the statistical calendar remains disrupted.

## Introduction

The Government of Andhra Pradesh constituted a Land Committee under the chairmanship of Sri Koneru Ranga Rao, then Minister for Municipal Administration and Urban Development, through G.O.Ms.No.977 dated 1 December 2004 and G.O.Ms.No.1091 dated 23 December 2004 of the Revenue (ASN.I) Department. It submitted its Land Committee Report in 2006. The Committee was constituted because, five decades after independence, land reform had produced records rather than results — land assigned on paper was frequently not in the hands of the assignee.

The Committee’s terms of reference

- Assess the overall implementation of the government’s land distribution programmes.
- Suggest measures for their more effective implementation.
- Recommend changes and amendments to Acts and Rules for improved enforcement of land-related legislation.
- Identify obstacles to implementation and propose an action plan with timelines.
- Monitor implementation of its own recommendations.

Reasons for constituting the Committee

- The gap between assignment on record and possession on the ground The most immediate reason. Government land had been assigned to the landless poor over decades, but the Committee found that assignment was often a paper transaction. Its finding that in Telangana 14.3 lakh acres had been distributed to 10.1 lakh beneficiaries (about 1.4 acres each), yet nearly 10 lakh acres had not been properly handed over to lawful owners, quantified the problem for the first time.
- “Assigned on paper, physical location not shown” The Committee identified this as the most common defect in assigned lands: because no survey number or boundary was demarcated, the same land was assigned and reassigned several times, producing multiple ownership claims and endless litigation. Its documented example — about 1,500 acres in Chandanavelli village, Shabad mandal, Ranga Reddy district — became the standard illustration.
- Alienation of assigned land Land assigned to the poor was being sold or transferred in violation of the AP Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act, 1977, so redistribution was quietly reversing.
- Tribal land alienation on a large scale The Committee documented that about 48% of tribal lands in Andhra Pradesh had passed to non-tribals in violation of the Land Transfer Regulation (1/70) — despite decades of statutory protection. It recommended that unregistered deeds (sada bainamas) predating the LTR be inadmissible as evidence of a non-tribal’s right in Scheduled Areas. The government issued a memo to that effect in 2008, and the position was upheld in Vemula Bhaskara Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2008).
- The plight of unrecorded tenants — the most consequential reason The Committee found that neither the Telangana Act of 1950 nor the Andhra area Act of 1956 (with its “soft” 1974 provisions) had induced tenants to record their tenancies. Without recorded rights, tenants could not access institutional credit, and were therefore also ineligible for loan waivers and relief operations. This forced them into high-interest informal borrowing, the debt trap and — in the acute agrarian distress of the period — farmer suicides. This finding led directly to the AP Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011.
- Defective and outdated land records Records of Rights were unreliable, surveys were decades old, and textual and spatial records did not reconcile — producing a large share of the State’s civil litigation.
- Absence of a consolidated inventory of government land No reliable inventory existed of assignable government land, so land that could have been distributed remained unidentified while encroachments went unchecked.
- Other unresolved land categories Endowment lands, unsettled inams, homestead sites and Bhoodan lands

each carried unresolved title questions, addressed in separate chapters of the report.

- Political and agrarian context The Committee was constituted in 2004, at a time of acute agrarian distress in the State, with farmer suicides prominent in public debate. Land access for the poor was a central commitment of the incoming government.

## The Committee’s structure and output

The report ran to twelve chapters — Management of Government Lands, Record of Rights, Tenancy, Land Reforms, Homesteads, Land Records, Endowment Lands, Unsettled Inams, Tribal Land Issues, Land Litigations, Training the Revenue Machinery in a pro-poor perspective, and Opportunities for enhancing the poor’s access to land. It made 104 recommendations, of which about 90 were accepted by the government.

## Principal recommendations
- Mandatory Gram Sabha approval for land assignments, with participation of the poor and weaker sections — the Committee’s signature recommendation.
- Physical demarcation of assigned land with survey numbers, and issue of pattadar passbooks to assignees.
- Regular land surveys and updating of records.
- Preparation of inventories of government land available for assignment.
- Limiting assignments to viable smallholding sizes.
- Action against unauthorised alienation of assigned land.
- Inadmissibility of sada bainamas for non-tribals in Scheduled Areas.
- Recognition of tenant cultivators for credit purposes — leading to the 2011 Act.

## Conclusion

The Koneru Ranga Rao Land Committee was constituted because Andhra Pradesh’s land reforms had generated entitlements without delivering possession — land assigned but not demarcated, tribal land protected but alienated, tenants legislated for but unrecorded. Its enduring contribution was diagnostic and institutional: it quantified the gap, insisted that Gram Sabha approval and physical demarcation replace paper assignment, and produced the recognition that a tenant needs access to credit more urgently than a claim to title — a recognition embodied in the AP Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011 and today’s Crop Cultivator Rights Cards.

## Value addition

- Related inquiry: the government simultaneously commissioned J.M. Girglani, IAS (Retd.) to study Telangana tribal land rights.
- Legislative outcome: AP Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011 — Loan Eligibility Cards valid for 11 months, conferring no right, title or interest in the land; succeeded by the AP Crop Cultivator Rights Act, 2019.
- Judicial reinforcement: Vemula Bhaskara Rao v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2008) — unregistered sale papers cannot establish a non-tribal’s right under the Land Transfer Regulation.

Q111:
## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh’s tenancy legislation is regionally divided by its colonial inheritance. The Andhra area was part of the Madras Presidency under the ryotwari system, where the cultivator held directly from the State; the Telangana area was under the Nizam, with jagirdari and zamindari intermediaries and the vetti bonded-labour system. Two different histories therefore produced two different tenancy laws, and the State has never had a single tenancy statute.

Evolution of tenancy reform

- **Colonial — Andhra area** — Ryotwari settlement under the Madras Presidency; direct State-cultivator relationship, but widespread informal sub-letting
- **Colonial — Telangana area** — Jagirdari, zamindari and the vetti system under the Nizam; the Barucha Committee (1937) recommended occupancy rights for those cultivating uninterruptedly for 12 or more years
- **Post-independence — Telangana** — Hyderabad Abolition of Jagirs Regulation, 1949; Hyderabad (later AP Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 — protected tenants, regulated rent, gave the right to purchase
- **Post-independence — Andhra** — Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Tenancy Act, 1956 — the subject of this question
- **Ceiling stage** — AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973
- **Tribal protection** — AP Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation, 1959 (Regulation 1 of 70)
- **Recognition stage** — Koneru Ranga Rao Land Committee (2004-06) → AP Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011 (Loan Eligibility Cards) → AP Crop Cultivator Rights Act, 2019 (Crop Cultivator Rights Cards)

Main features of the AP (Andhra Area) Tenancy Act, 1956

- **Security of tenure** — A minimum lease period was prescribed, and the landlord could terminate the tenancy only on specified grounds — chiefly default in rent payment, damage to the land, or bona fide personal cultivation
- **Regulation of rent (fair rent)** — Maximum rent fixed as a share of gross produce, differentiated by land type — a lower share for dry land and a higher share for wet, irrigated land — replacing rack-renting
- **Written lease and record** — Provision for a written lease deed and registration of the tenancy, so that the relationship became legally visible
- **Protection against eviction** — Eviction only through the prescribed authority (Tahsildar or Revenue Divisional Officer), not by the landlord’s unilateral act
- **Right of restoration** — A tenant wrongfully evicted could apply for restoration of possession
- **Compensation for improvements** — A tenant who improved the land was entitled to compensation on surrendering it
- **Right of first refusal** — The tenant was given the first option to purchase if the landlord sold the land
- **Dispute resolution** — Vested in revenue authorities rather than civil courts, to make remedies quicker and cheaper
- **Bar on sub-letting** — The tenant could not sub-let, preventing a second layer of intermediaries

The amendments

- The 1974 amendment is the most significant. It extended the minimum lease period to six years, restricted the landlord’s right of resumption for personal cultivation, and tightened eviction grounds — a decisive strengthening of tenant security on paper.
- Subsequent amendments adjusted rent ceilings and procedural provisions.
- Critically, however, the Andhra-area Act’s provisions were described even in official assessments as “soft” — they regulated the tenancy relationship without conferring ownership, unlike the more radical Telangana Act of 1950.

Assessment — why tenancy reform produced the opposite of its intent

This is the analytical heart of the answer.

- Landlords stopped recording tenancies. Because a recorded tenant acquired protected status and possible purchase rights, owners simply refused to create written leases. Tenancy became oral, seasonal and deniable.
- Andhra Pradesh consequently has among India’s highest tenancy incidence with among its lowest recorded tenancy — the gap between reality and record is the reform’s true legacy.
- The unrecorded tenant lost everything the law was meant to give: no security of tenure, and additionally no access to institutional credit, crop insurance, input subsidy or calamity compensation, all of which follow the land record.
- The credit consequence proved fatal. Unable to obtain bank loans, tenants borrowed informally at punitive rates — the mechanism the Koneru Ranga Rao Committee (2006) identified as driving tenants into the debt trap and, in the worst cases, to suicide.
- Frequent rotation of tenants became standard practice to prevent any claim maturing.

The corrective — a change of approach

Recognising that protection had produced exclusion, the State changed strategy: instead of conferring rights on tenants, it created instruments that recognise cultivation without creating tenancy rights.

- AP Land Licensed Cultivators Act, 2011 — introduced Loan Eligibility Cards (LECs), valid for 11 months, enabling the cultivator to access crop loans, insurance and input subsidy without acquiring any right, title or interest in the land. This was enacted directly on the Koneru Ranga Rao Committee’s recommendation.
- AP Crop Cultivator Rights Act, 2019 — replaced LECs with Crop Cultivator Rights Cards (CCRC), requiring the landowner’s consent and again expressly conferring no tenancy rights.
- Annadata Sukhibhava — ₹20,000 a year, explicitly covering tenant farmers alongside small and marginal farmers.

Uptake has nonetheless remained partial, because landowners still fear that any documentation may eventually ripen into a claim.

## Conclusion

Tenancy reform in Andhra Pradesh evolved from regionally divided colonial inheritances, through the protective legislation of 1950 and 1956, to a modern approach that abandons rights-conferral in favour of functional recognition. The 1956 Act’s features — security of tenure, fair rent, written leases, compensation for improvements — were sound in design but self-defeating in effect, because they gave landlords every reason to keep tenancy invisible. The lesson, now embodied in the LEC and CCRC and in the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016, is that legalising and recording tenancy while protecting the owner’s title serves the tenant better than protection that drives the relationship underground.

## Value addition
- The regional divide: AP (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 (conferred protected-tenant status and purchase rights) versus AP (Andhra Area) Tenancy Act, 1956 (regulated the relationship without conferring ownership) — a distinction worth stating explicitly.
- Historical precursor: the Barucha Committee (1937) under the Nizam recommended occupancy rights for peasants cultivating uninterruptedly for 12 or more years.
- The national reform proposal: the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016 (NITI Aayog) legalises leasing, protects the owner’s title against adverse possession, and gives the tenant access to credit and insurance — the framework AP’s CCRC anticipates.
- Constitutional protection: land reform laws were placed in the Ninth Schedule under Art. 31B; land is a State subject under Entry 18, List II.
Q112:
## Introduction

Output is total production; productivity is output per hectare. The distinction matters because in Andhra Pradesh since 2000-01, output rose substantially while crop productivity growth was modest — the State’s agricultural gains came far more from shifting to higher-value activities than from raising cereal yields.

- Food crops — trends since 2000-01
- **Rice** — Remains the dominant food crop and the basis of the State’s procurement and PDS system. Output rose with irrigation expansion; yields are among India’s highest in the delta but have approached a plateau, with diminishing returns to fertiliser
- **Coarse cereals (jowar, bajra, ragi, maize)** — Area declined as farmers shifted to paddy where water became available and to commercial crops elsewhere; maize expanded on poultry-feed demand. Millets have received renewed attention as Shree Anna since the International Year of Millets, 2023
- **Pulses (redgram, blackgram, greengram)** — Area and output rose modestly; productivity remains low, as pulses are largely grown rainfed on residual moisture. The Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (₹11,440 crore, 2025-26 to 2030-31) targets self-sufficiency by December 2027

- Non-food crops — trends
- **Oilseeds (groundnut, sunflower)** — Groundnut area in Rayalaseema declined with recurring drought and poor returns; productivity remains volatile and rainfall-dependent. Oil palm expanded strongly in the delta under the National Mission on Edible Oils — significant, since India imports 56% of its edible oil
- **Cotton** — Area expanded with Bt cotton adoption; yields rose then plateaued, with resistance and input-cost pressures
- **Chillies** — Andhra Pradesh became India’s leading producer; high value, high input, export-linked and price-volatile
- **Tobacco** — AP remains India’s principal Virginia tobacco producer, with area regulated by the Tobacco Board
- **Sugarcane** — Area contracted with mill closures and payment arrears
- **Horticulture** — The strongest growth area — mango, banana, papaya, lime, cocoa, tomato. Nationally, horticulture output (362.08 MT in 2024-25) now exceeds foodgrain output, contributing about 33% of agricultural GVA

- The decisive shift — allied activities, not crops

The most important trend is not within crops at all: - Nationally, decadal agricultural growth reached 4.45% (FY16-FY25) — the highest of any decade — driven by livestock at 7.1% and fisheries and aquaculture at 8.8%, against crops at only 3.5%. - Livestock GVA rose about 195% between FY15 and FY24; fish production rose over 140% between 2014 and 2025. - In Andhra Pradesh specifically, large areas of delta paddy land were converted to aquaculture ponds, because returns per hectare are several times those from rice. The State became India’s leading producer of inland fish and shrimp.

Evaluation: output and value rose strongly; crop productivity growth was modest. AP’s agricultural success since 2000-01 is a story of diversification and land-use change, not of yield breakthroughs.

- Reasons for regional variations in productivity
- Irrigation — the primary determinant | Region | Position | |—|—| | Coastal Andhra delta | Assured canal irrigation, gravity-fed; highest productivity in the State | | Rayalaseema | Groundwater-dependent, 500-700 mm rainfall against high evapotranspiration; lowest productivity | | North Coastal Andhra | Tanks, minor irrigation, rainfed; hilly agency terrain; low productivity |
- Soil quality Fertile deltaic alluvium against red, shallow and lateritic soils in Rayalaseema and the north-east.
- Cropping pattern follows water Where water is assured, farmers grow high-yielding paddy and horticulture; where it is not, they grow low-yielding drought-tolerant crops. The productivity gap is therefore partly a crop-choice gap, not only an efficiency gap — an important analytical distinction.
- Input access and credit Fertiliser, quality seed and plant protection are input-intensive. Delta farmers with assured water and institutional credit can afford the package; rain-fed farmers, and especially unrecorded tenants excluded from crop loans, cannot. Agriculture’s GNPA at 6.0% — the highest of any sector — reflects the risk lenders see in rain-fed cultivation.
- Extension reach Advisory services are denser in the delta; elsewhere many farmers rely on input dealers for technical advice — a conflict of interest, since the adviser profits from the sale.
- Fragmentation and tenancy Average holdings are below a hectare. An unrecorded tenant on an eleven-month arrangement has no incentive to invest in soil health, since the returns accrue to the owner — a structural barrier to any practice with a multi-year payback.
- Human capital AP’s literacy of 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States, and the deficit is concentrated in the lagging regions — capping the adoption of improved practice.
- Ecological degradation now cuts both ways The delta’s advantage is being eroded by salinisation from aquaculture and waterlogging, while Rayalaseema faces groundwater collapse. Productivity gaps may narrow for the wrong reason.

## Conclusion

Since 2000-01 Andhra Pradesh has raised agricultural output and value substantially while achieving only modest gains in crop productivity — the growth came from diversification into aquaculture, horticulture and livestock rather than from higher cereal yields. Regional productivity variation traces primarily to irrigation access, soil, crop choice, input affordability and human capital, in that order. Narrowing it requires completing lift irrigation and tank rehabilitation, recognising tenancy so cultivators can invest, strengthening extension, and scaling low-input natural farming — since APCNF’s income gains of 38-66% came from cutting costs, the one route available to a

rain-fed smallholder.

## Value addition
- National benchmarks: foodgrain production reached a record 3,577.3 lakh metric tonnes in 2024-25, up 254.3 LMT over the previous year; horticulture 362.08 MT; agricultural exports about ₹4.4 lakh crore in FY25.
- Sub-sector growth (FY16-FY25): livestock 7.1%, fisheries 8.8%, crops 3.5%; overall 4.45% — the highest of any decade.
- AP’s leading crops: chillies (India’s largest producer), oil palm, cocoa, papaya, lime, tobacco (Virginia), mango and banana.
- The sustainability counterweight: APCNF covers over 17.7 lakh farmers across 0.92 million hectares, with verified income gains of 38-66%, water savings up to 50% and emission reductions up to 46% per acre.

## Introduction

Keyword discipline: this question asks you to evaluate — to judge outcomes against indicators. Q.142 asks you to elaborate on the measures themselves. Do not write the same answer for both.

Andhra Pradesh has one of India’s longest-running and most institutionally developed women-empowerment architectures,

built on SHG federations rather than departmental delivery. Evaluating it requires asking not how much has been spent but what has changed in women’s incomes, health, safety and decision-making.

Evaluation framework: measure programmes against four tests — reach, income effect, agency, and outcome indicators.

Domain 1: Economic empowerment — strong on reach, weak on scale

- **SERP / SHG federations** — The State’s outstanding success. About 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, repayment above 97%; survived the 2010 microfinance crisis; became the national template for NRLM (2011)
- **Stree Nidhi** — Genuine institutional transfer — the Managing Committee has 13 directors elected from mandal samakhyas; women govern a financial institution
- **Adabidda Nidhi** — ₹1,500 a month by DBT to women aged 19-59 — reliable income transfer, but a transfer rather than an income source
- **One Family–One Entrepreneur** — Targets one lakh women entrepreneurs a year — the right objective, but outcomes depend on market linkage rather than credit alone

Verdict: AP has solved credit access and institutional participation, but not enterprise scale. Most women’s units remain own-account; the Sixth Economic Census found 83.19% of women-owned establishments nationally had no hired worker, and AP accounted for 10.56% of all women-owned establishments.

The decisive indicator: AP’s female labour force participation is about 35.8%, still below the national 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24) — despite the densest SHG network in India. Credit has not converted into workforce participation, which is the sharpest evaluative finding available.

Domain 2: Health and nutrition — the strongest performance

- Maternal Mortality Ratio at about 30 per lakh live births (SRS 2021-23) — the lowest in India along with Kerala, and below Maldives and Thailand. AP was among the eight States achieving the SDG target of ≤70 well ahead of 2030.
- Under-5 Mortality Rate at 24 — among twelve States/UTs meeting the SDG target of ≤25.
- Project Sanjeevani marks a genuine design shift from curative reimbursement to preventive screening; the Kuppam pilot screened 63,867 individuals across 41 tests, identifying over 6,300 high-risk cases.
- Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva covers about 1.43 crore households with cover up to ₹25 lakh.

Verdict: outcome indicators, not just outlays, have moved — the clearest evidence of programme effectiveness anywhere in the State’s record.

But: 29.3% of women aged 20-24 were married before 18 (NFHS-5) — higher than the national average, and higher still among Scheduled Tribes. Child marriage remains the State’s most serious unresolved gender indicator.

Domain 3: Education — reach achieved, outcomes lagging

- Thalliki Vandanam — ₹15,000 a year per child, paid to the mother or guardian, reaching 67.27 lakh students in 2025-26 — keeps girls in school and channels resources through women.
- 9,958 Anganwadi Centres upgraded, with 192 new centres in PVTG areas under PM JANMAN.

Verdict: enrolment support works, but female literacy stood at 59.96% against male 74.77% (Census 2011), and AP’s overall literacy of 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States. Spending has not produced learning.

Domain 4: Safety and representation — mixed

- 33% reservation for women in government jobs and educational institutions.
- Shakti App with a seven-minute response target and 164 Shakti teams; One Stop (Sakhi) Centres.
- Stree Shakti free bus travel expands mobility — a genuine enabler of work and education.

Verdict: institutional mechanisms exist; the constraint is enforcement capacity and conviction rates, and women’s representation in higher decision-making remains limited.

Cross-cutting: Gender Responsive Budgeting

Adopted from FY 2021-22, with a five-year State Action Plan on GRB (2021-25) and departmental Gender Budget Cells; outlay expanded to about ₹55,015 crore in 2022-23, split into Part A (100% women-directed) and Part B (30-99%).

Verdict: the framework tracks allocations, not outcomes — there is no systematic gender impact audit, and no formalised Child Budget Statement at all.

## Conclusion

Evaluated against outcomes rather than outlays, Andhra Pradesh’s record is differentiated, not uniform: outstanding in

maternal and child health, genuinely transformative in community financial institutions, adequate in transfers and safety infrastructure, and weak in converting all of this into female workforce participation, literacy and leadership. The State has built the institutions; the unfinished task is to make them produce incomes and outcomes rather than access and coverage — through childcare, skilling linked to industry, enforcement against child marriage, and outcome auditing of the gender budget.

## Value addition
- AP Budget 2026-27: Women, Children, Differently Abled and Senior Citizens Welfare ₹4,582 crore; School Education ₹32,308 crore; Health ₹19,306 crore.
- AP health achievements: MMR 30 (lowest in India with Kerala, SRS 2021-23); U5MR 24; against India’s MMR of 88 (2021-23) and IMR of 25 (2023).

## Introduction

Exam technique: the question names five stages. Structure the answer under those five headings in that order — an examiner scanning for them should find each one immediately.

AePDS is the end-to-end digitisation of the food supply chain, linking Aadhaar-based biometric authentication at the point of sale with computerised records of procurement, movement and stock. Its purpose is to make every kilogram of subsidised grain traceable from the procurement centre to the beneficiary’s hand, thereby attacking diversion at every stage rather than only at the shop counter.

Stage 1: Purchase (Procurement)

- Paddy is procured at Rythu Bharosa Kendras and paddy procurement centres, with farmer registration linked to land records (Webland) and Aadhaar.
- Online registration and e-payment ensure payment goes directly into the farmer’s bank account, eliminating intermediaries.
- Procurement data is captured digitally at the point of purchase — quantity, moisture content, grade — creating the first record in the chain.
- APSCSCL lifts rice and wheat from FCI and levy sugar from factories against digital allotment orders.

Stage 2: Transportation

- Movement from procurement centres and FCI depots to State godowns, and from godowns to fair price shops, is tracked through the Depot Online System and vehicle-tracking mechanisms.
- GPS-enabled vehicles and digital gate-passes record dispatch and arrival, so diversion in transit becomes detectable.
- Transport contracts and route plans are managed electronically, reducing discretionary allocation of hauls.

Stage 3: Storage

- Stocks are held in FCI and State Civil Supplies Corporation godowns, with online stock accounting showing opening balance, receipts, issues and closing balance in real time.
- Digital records allow reconciliation between physical stock and book stock, which is the principal check on godown-level pilferage.
- Fortified rice is blended and stored under the universalised fortification programme to address micronutrient deficiency.

Stage 4: Allotment

- Monthly allotment is generated automatically from the beneficiary database — entitlements under NFSA (5 kg per person; 35 kg per AAY household) plus State-scheme quantities.
- Allotment orders flow electronically from the State to districts to mandals to individual fair price shops, with each shop’s indent calculated from its active cardholder base.
- Aadhaar seeding of ration cards enables de-duplication; the system will not generate an allotment for an unseeded or deleted card.

Stage 5: Delivery

- Distribution takes place through 29,796 fair price shops, each equipped with an electronic Point of Sale (ePoS) device.
- The beneficiary authenticates through Aadhaar biometric verification — fingerprint or iris — and the transaction is recorded in real time on the server.
- An SMS acknowledgement is generated, and the transaction appears on the public portal.
- Portability: under the revamped system a cardholder may collect from any fair price shop in the State, and under One Nation One Ration Card from any FPS in India.
- Doorstep delivery is retained for the differently abled and citizens above 65, after the State discontinued Mobile Dispensing Units in June 2025.
- Smart Ration Cards with QR codes have been issued across all districts from August 2026. What AePDS has achieved
- **De-duplication** — Aadhaar seeding removed duplicate and ghost cards from the database
- **Real-time traceability** — Every transaction is time-stamped and publicly visible on the portal
- **Portability** — Intra-State and inter-State, freeing beneficiaries from a single assigned shop — decisive for migrant workers
- **Direct farmer payment** — e-procurement eliminates intermediaries at the purchase stage
- **Transparency** — Public dashboards, the Mera Ration app and the epdsap.ap.gov.in portal allow citizen verification

Where it still fails

- Authentication failures affect the elderly, manual workers with worn fingerprints, and areas with weak connectivity

— technology can exclude as well as include.

- Diversion has shifted upstream: with the shop counter now monitored, leakage occurs in procurement, transport and storage — the PDS rice scam of May 2025 demonstrated this.
- Quality is not digitised: the system verifies that grain was delivered, not what quality it was.
- Connectivity gaps in tribal and remote areas disrupt real-time authentication.

## Conclusion

AePDS has converted Andhra Pradesh’s food distribution from a paper-based, discretionary system into a traceable digital chain, with genuine gains in de-duplication, portability and transparency. Its limitation is inherent to what technology can do: it can verify identity, quantity and transaction, but not quality, or intent upstream. Completing the reform therefore requires pairing digitisation with scientific storage, realistic dealer margins, physical quality audits and social audit by Gram Sabhas — technology as the backbone, not the whole system.

## Value addition
- Technology stack: ePoS devices; Aadhaar biometric and iris authentication; Depot Online System; Annavitran portal for inter-State portability tracking; Mera Ration app; IM-PDS (Integrated Management of PDS) for national de-duplication.

## Introduction

Absolute poverty measures deprivation against a fixed subsistence standard — a poverty line. Relative poverty measures deprivation against the prevailing living standard of society: a person is relatively poor if her income or consumption falls significantly below the societal norm, typically below 50-60% of median income. Relative poverty is therefore a measure of inequality and social exclusion, and it does not disappear as an economy grows richer.

Absolute versus relative poverty

- **Standard** — Fixed subsistence basket or income line · A proportion of the societal median
- **Changes with growth** — Falls as incomes rise · Persists unless the distribution changes
- **Indian measure** — Tendulkar/Rangarajan lines; National MPI · Gini coefficient; consumption distribution from HCES
- **Policy implication** — Raise incomes above the line · Redistribute and expand opportunity

Reasons for relative poverty in India

- Labour market dualism: a small formal sector with security and a vast informal sector without it — 42% of formal manufacturing workers are contractual and the unincorporated sector employs 12.9 crore persons.
- The agriculture-employment gap: roughly 45% of workers produce about 15% of output, so farm incomes structurally trail the rest of the economy.
- Skill and education premiums: returns to higher education and technical skills have risen sharply, widening the gap between the educated and the rest. AP’s literacy at 72.6% illustrates how far the base still lags.
- Regional divergence: per capita income varies several-fold between States, and within States between coastal and interior districts.
- Rural-urban divide: urban consumption remains well above rural, even though the gap has narrowed.
- Social stratification: caste, tribe, gender and religion continue to shape access to assets, credit, networks and jobs.
- Wealth concentration: consumption inequality is moderate in India, but wealth and asset inequality are far higher, since land and financial assets are concentrated.
- Unequal access to public services: differential quality of schooling and healthcare reproduces inequality across generations.

The Lorenz curve

A graphical device developed by Max Otto Lorenz (1905): - The horizontal axis plots the cumulative percentage of population, ranked from poorest to richest. - The vertical axis plots the cumulative percentage of income or consumption they receive. - The 45-degree diagonal is the line of perfect equality — where the bottom 20% receive 20% of income.

- The actual distribution always lies below this line, bowing outward. - The further the curve sags from the diagonal, the greater the inequality. Two societies’ Lorenz curves can be compared visually, and if one lies entirely inside another, it is unambiguously more equal.

The Gini coefficient

Derived by Corrado Gini (1912) directly from the Lorenz curve:

Gini = Area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve ÷ Total area under the line of equality (conventionally written as A / (A + B))

- **0** — Perfect equality — everyone has identical income
- **1 (or 100)** — Perfect inequality — one person has everything
- **Below 0.30** — Relatively equal distribution
- **Above 0.40** — High inequality

India’s position: the World Bank’s 2025 assessment places India’s Gini at about 25.5 on consumption — among the lower readings globally, and lower than the United States or China. The Household Consumption Expenditure Survey 2023-24 showed inequality declining further, with the rural Gini at about 0.237 and urban at 0.284.

A necessary caution: these are consumption Ginis, which are systematically lower than income Ginis, and lower still than wealth Ginis. India’s consumption inequality is moderate; its wealth inequality is not. Stating which variable is being measured is essential to a correct answer.

Limitations of the Gini - A single number cannot show where in the distribution inequality lies — two very different distributions can yield the same Gini. - It is more sensitive to changes in the middle of the distribution than at the extremes. - It ignores non-income dimensions of deprivation — which is why the MPI complements it.

## Conclusion

Relative poverty measures how far a society’s least advantaged fall behind its norm, and it persists in India through labour-market dualism, the agricultural productivity gap and unequal access to quality education and health. The Lorenz curve shows inequality visually and the Gini coefficient summarises it in a single number — both indispensable, both incomplete. Reducing relative poverty requires not transfers alone but equalising opportunity: quality schooling, formal jobs, and assets and credit for those who have neither.

## Value addition
- Other inequality measures: the Kuznets ratio (share of the top 20% to the bottom 20%), the Palma ratio (top 10% to bottom 40%), the Theil index, and the Inequality-adjusted HDI, which discounts HDI for the inequality in each dimension.
- Kuznets hypothesis: inequality rises in early development and falls later, producing an inverted-U — contested in the Indian context.
- Poverty line lineage: Dandekar and Rath (1971); Alagh (1979); Lakdawala (1993); Tendulkar (2009);

Rangarajan (2014). India has had no official poverty line since, with the National MPI and HCES filling the gap.

- Data source note: the HCES 2023-24 is the current basis for consumption distribution; PLFS supplies employment and earnings data.

## Introduction

Universal Basic Income is an unconditional, periodic cash payment made to every individual, regardless of income, employment status or any other criterion. The Economic Survey 2016-17, in a dedicated chapter, argued that UBI could serve as a “conceptually appealing” alternative to India’s fragmented welfare architecture — invoking Mahatma Gandhi’s talisman of judging every policy by its effect on the poorest.

The three defining features (Economic Survey 2016-17)

- **Universality** — Paid to everyone, not to a targeted group — which eliminates exclusion errors and the stigma of being identified as poor
- **Unconditionality** — No behavioural conditions, work requirements or eligibility tests
- **Agency** — Cash respects the recipient as an adult capable of deciding her own priorities — treating the poor as agents, not wards of the State

The Survey’s proposal

- Coverage of about 75% of the population — a “quasi-UBI” rather than full universality, achieved by excluding the demonstrably well-off.
- An estimated fiscal cost of roughly 4-5% of GDP, financed by rationalising existing subsidies and schemes.
- JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) identified as the infrastructure that finally made direct payment at scale feasible.

How UBI is expected to “wipe every tear”

- Eliminates exclusion errors: India’s welfare targeting rests on beneficiary lists still largely derived from the 2011 Census; universality removes the problem of the genuinely poor being left out.
- Provides insurance against shocks: a guaranteed floor protects against illness, crop failure, job loss and price volatility.
- Reduces leakage and administrative cost: one transfer replaces dozens of schemes, each with its own bureaucracy and rent-seeking opportunities.
- Enhances agency and choice: recipients allocate spending to their own priorities rather than to what the State supplies.
- Improves labour mobility and bargaining power: a floor income allows workers to refuse exploitative wages and to search longer for better work.
- Supports the informal sector, which lies outside every contributory social security system.

Objections — also set out in the Survey

- **Fiscal cost** — 4-5% of GDP is close to India’s entire fiscal deficit; it cannot be additional, so existing programmes must be dismantled
- **Political economy** — Rolling back MGNREGA, PDS or fertiliser subsidies to fund UBI is politically extremely difficult; the likely outcome is UBI plus existing schemes, which is unaffordable
- **Conspicuous consumption** — Cash may be spent on alcohol, tobacco or gambling rather than nutrition or schooling
- **Weakening the work incentive** — Contested empirically, but a persistent concern
- **Gender** — Payments to household heads may not reach women; payment to women directly is a design fix
- **Cash cannot buy what does not exist** — Where a functioning school or primary health centre is absent, cash cannot substitute for public provision — the strongest argument against replacing services with transfers

The live Indian debate

India never adopted UBI, but it has moved a long way toward quasi-basic-income instruments: PM-KISAN (₹6,000 a year, unconditional, DBT-based), and a rapid proliferation of State-level unconditional cash transfers, which reached

about ₹1.7 lakh crore in FY26 — with the number of States running such schemes rising more than fivefold between FY23 and FY26, nearly half of them already in revenue deficit. The Economic Survey 2025-26 and the 16th Finance Commission have both cautioned that these create expenditure rigidity and crowd out capital and human-capital spending, and have urged a shift to conditional, time-bound transfers with clear exclusion criteria, citing Mexico’s Progresa/Oportunidades model where payments were linked to school attendance and health check-ups.

## Conclusion

UBI’s appeal lies in its moral clarity — universality, unconditionality and respect for agency — and India’s DBT infrastructure has made it administratively feasible in a way it was not a decade ago. Its constraint remains fiscal and political: it can be financed only by replacing existing programmes, which no government has been willing to do. The Indian experience so far suggests the realistic path is not a full UBI but a well-designed floor — targeted, conditional where behaviour matters, and complementary to, not a substitute for, public provision of health and education. Cash empowers people to buy services; it cannot create the school or the clinic.

## Value addition
- Intellectual lineage: Thomas Paine’s Agrarian Justice (1797); Milton Friedman’s negative income tax; supported in India by Pranab Bardhan, Vijay Joshi and Guy Standing; the Economic Survey 2016-17 chapter was authored under Chief Economic Adviser Arvind Subramanian.
- Evidence base: the Madhya Pradesh UBI pilots (2011-13), supported by SEWA and UNICEF, found improvements in nutrition, school attendance and economic activity, with no rise in alcohol consumption.
- International experience: Finland’s 2017-18 trial improved wellbeing but not employment; Kenya’s GiveDirectly long-term trial and Alaska’s Permanent Fund Dividend are the other standard reference points.
- Constitutional anchor: Art. 38(2) (minimise inequalities in income), Art. 39(a) (adequate means of livelihood), Art. 41 (right to public assistance).
- The enabler: JAM, PFMS and Aadhaar-enabled payments; cumulative DBT savings exceed ₹3.5 lakh crore.

## Introduction

Andhra Pradesh occupies a singular place in Indian microfinance: it was both the cradle of the SHG movement and the epicentre of the 2010 crisis that nearly destroyed commercial microfinance in India. The State’s present position is best understood as the outcome of that collision between two competing models — community-owned SHG credit and profit-driven MFI lending.

The 2010 crisis — what happened and why

- **Over-lending and multiple lending** — Several MFIs lent to the same household; total indebtedness far exceeded repayment capacity
- **Commercial pressure** — Rapid growth targets and an IPO-driven valuation race pushed disbursement over due diligence
- **Coercive recovery** — Aggressive collection practices, publicly linked to a series of borrower suicides
- **Regulatory vacuum** — MFIs operated as NBFCs outside effective conduct regulation; no cap on interest, indebtedness or number of lenders
- **Institutional conflict** — Commercial MFIs competed directly with the State-backed SHG network, whose members they targeted

The State’s response: the Andhra Pradesh Microfinance Institutions (Regulation of Money Lending) Ordinance, 2010 required registration of MFIs, prohibited coercive recovery, and mandated monthly rather than weekly collection at panchayat offices. Repayments collapsed, and commercial MFI operations in the State effectively ceased.

The regulatory response it produced nationally

The crisis reshaped Indian microfinance regulation: - The Malegam Committee (2011) was constituted, and the RBI created a distinct NBFC-MFI category. - Conduct norms followed — caps on interest margins, limits on the number of lenders per borrower and on total indebtedness, prohibition of coercive recovery, and mandatory disclosure. - The RBI’s

2022 Regulatory Framework for Microfinance Loans replaced rigid caps with a household income-based repayment capacity test — a debt-service ratio limit rather than a lending cap. - Self-regulatory organisations were empowered to enforce credit-bureau checks.

In short: India’s microfinance regulation was born from Andhra Pradesh’s crisis. The present state

- The SHG model survived and became dominant in the State - SERP’s network of about 11 lakh SHGs covering over one crore women, with repayment consistently above 97%, continued lending when commercial MFIs withdrew. - Stree Nidhi, the credit cooperative federation governed by a Managing Committee of 20 directors — 13 elected from mandal samakhyas — provides rapid small-ticket credit, making women the directors of a financial institution rather than its clients. - The SHG network became the delivery platform for pensions, health insurance and DBT.
- Commercial microfinance returned nationally, under regulation - FY25 profile: 627 lakh active borrowers; gross loan portfolio ₹2.38 lakh crore; 95% women and 80% rural; operations across 685 districts and 37,380 branches. - Market share: NBFC-MFIs 39%, banks 32%, Small Finance Banks 16%, other NBFCs 12% — a diversified structure that reduces the concentration risk of 2010.
- But stress recurred in FY25 — the crisis’s lesson is not fully learned - MFI loans outstanding fell about 14% as over-lending resurfaced in several States. - The RBI responded on 6 June 2025 by reducing the minimum qualifying assets for NBFC-MFIs from 75% to 60%, allowing lenders to diversify their portfolios and reduce concentration in microfinance. - Self-regulatory organisations tightened borrower-indebtedness caps. - Stress began easing from Q2 FY26.
- The structural gap that remains Credit continues to finance consumption, health emergencies and debt-swapping more than enterprise. Loans that do not raise income cannot be repaid from income — the same mechanism that produced 2010.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s microfinance today is safer, better regulated and more diversified than in 2010, and the SHG model it pioneered has proved the more durable of the two competing approaches. But the FY25 stress shows that the underlying vulnerability — credit growth outpacing income growth — has not been eliminated. The next stage must shift microfinance from credit-led to enterprise-led: producer organisations with genuine market linkage, term credit for assets, and income monitoring rather than disbursement targets. Andhra Pradesh’s contribution to Indian finance was a hard lesson; consolidating it requires ensuring the lesson is not relearned.

## Value addition
- Malegam Committee (2011) recommendations: creation of the NBFC-MFI category; caps on margin and interest; a limit on lending to a borrower already indebted to two other MFIs; a ceiling on total indebtedness; prohibition of coercive recovery and of collection at the borrower’s residence.
- RBI framework (2025): minimum qualifying assets for NBFC-MFIs reduced from 75% to 60% with effect from 6 June 2025.
- Definition: a microfinance loan is a collateral-free loan to a household with annual income up to a specified threshold, with repayment obligations capped at 50% of monthly household income.
- Contrast worth drawing: the SHG-Bank Linkage model (NABARD, 1992) is savings-led and community-governed; the MFI model is credit-led and externally governed — the 2010 crisis was, at root, a clash between the two.

## Introduction

The Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty (SERP) is an autonomous body of the Government of Andhra Pradesh under the Department of Rural Development, established to reduce rural poverty through women-led community institutions rather than through departmental delivery. Its central insight — that the poor must be organised before they can be served — has made it one of India’s most studied poverty-reduction models.

The institutional architecture

- **Household** — Self-Help Group of 10-15 poor women
- **Village** — Village Organisation (federation of SHGs)
- **Mandal** — Mandal Samakhya
- **District** — Zilla Samakhya
- **Finance** — Stree Nidhi — a credit cooperative federation governed by a Managing Committee of 20 directors, 13 elected from mandal samakhyas

The network covers about 11 lakh SHGs with over one crore women members, with repayment rates consistently above 97%.

Functions and interventions

- Financial inclusion: SHG bank linkage, interest subvention (Pavala Vaddi and successors), and Stree Nidhi for rapid, small-ticket lending — a decisive alternative to moneylenders and to commercial microfinance.
- Livelihoods: Farmer Producer Organisations, collective procurement and marketing, dairy and non-farm enterprise, the Rural Retail Chain with mandal-level nodal stores.
- Community-Managed Sustainable Agriculture (CMSA): promotion of non-pesticide management and low-cost farming — a nationally recognised AP innovation.
- Human development: community-based nutrition, health and sanitation behaviour change, and monitoring of ICDS and health services.
- Social protection: One Stop Shops at mandal level to secure MGNREGA wages, pensions and insurance entitlements; SHGs act as the delivery and grievance channel.
- Social inclusion: dedicated strategies for SC, ST and PVTG households, persons with disabilities and the elderly.

Project lineage — three generations of World Bank support

- **Project** — Period · Scale
- **APDPIP (Velugu)** — 2000-06 · US$111 million IDA credit; six poorest districts
- **APRPRP (Indira Kranthi Patham)** — 2003-12 · US$150 million credit plus US$65 million (2007) and US$100 million (2009) additional financing
- **APRIGP** — 2015-20 · 150 backward mandals, about 5,000 villages; targets of 250,000 producers with 50% higher incomes and 500,000 households with better access to entitlements

Demonstrated impact

- Credit at scale on trust alone: repayment above 97% without collateral proved that the poor are bankable — the finding that reshaped Indian microfinance policy.
- Institutional resilience: when the 2010 microfinance crisis originated in Andhra Pradesh and commercial MFIs collapsed, the SHG network kept rural credit flowing. That crisis produced the Malegam Committee (2011) and the NBFC-MFI category — India’s microfinance regulation was born from AP’s experience.
- A national template: SERP’s federated model became the design basis for the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (2011), now DAY-NRLM.
- A delivery platform: the SHG network later carried Aarogyasri enrolment, pensions, DBT and financial inclusion — infrastructure whose value exceeded any single programme.
- Women’s agency: collective bargaining raised wages, reduced dependence on moneylenders and improved women’s decision-making within households.

Limitations

- Credit deepening outpaced livelihood creation: loans often financed consumption and debt-swapping rather than enterprise.
- Elite capture and unequal participation within some federations; the poorest and PVTG households are hardest to include.
- Over-indebtedness risk: multiple borrowing from SHGs, MFIs and banks contributed to the 2010 crisis and to the FY25 microfinance stress nationally.
- Dependence on external funding and political continuity, which affects programme stability.
- Federations’ sustainability beyond project cycles requires professional management and market linkages that outlast donor support.

## Conclusion

SERP’s contribution has been institutional rather than merely financial — it built a permanent, women-led delivery architecture that has outlasted individual schemes, governments and funding cycles. That architecture is now the vehicle for the State’s Zero Poverty goal under the P4 model in Swarna Andhra @2047. Its next task is to shift from credit-led to enterprise-led work: FPOs with genuine market linkage, higher-value livelihoods and skilling, so that group membership translates into rising incomes rather than only accessible loans.

## Value addition
- Full form and status: SERP is registered under the Societies Registration Act and functions under the Department of Rural Development, Government of Andhra Pradesh.
- National influence: the SHG-federation model informed NRLM (2011), now DAY-NRLM, which operates nationally; AP and Telangana together remain the most mature SHG ecosystems in India.
- Microfinance today (FY25): active borrowers 627 lakh; gross loan portfolio ₹2.38 lakh crore; 95% women, 80% rural; the RBI cut NBFC-MFI qualifying assets from 75% to 60% (June 2025) to let lenders diversify after FY25 stress.
- Related institution: MEPMA performs the analogous role for the urban poor in Andhra Pradesh.

## Introduction

Arogya Raksha, launched by the Government of Andhra Pradesh in 2017, was designed to close a specific gap in health protection: families above the poverty line were excluded from Aarogyasri-type cover yet could still be pushed into poverty by a single hospitalisation. It was among India’s early attempts at a contributory, voluntary insurance scheme for the “missing middle.”

Details of Arogya Raksha

- **Objective** — Extend cashless hospitalisation cover to APL families not eligible for Aarogyasri, preventing catastrophic health expenditure
- **Eligibility** — Voluntary enrolment by families above the poverty line; not means-tested out
- **Premium** — A modest annual contribution of about ₹1,200 per person per year — deliberately kept low to encourage enrolment
- **Coverage** — Up to about ₹2 lakh per family per year
- **Procedures** — Roughly 1,000+ listed procedures, broadly mirroring the Aarogyasri package
- **Delivery** — Cashless treatment at empanelled network hospitals on the PPP model, administered through the Aarogyasri/NTR Vaidya Seva Trust machinery
- **Design principle** — Contributory, unlike the fully State-funded schemes — the beneficiary shares the cost

Comparison with other health schemes of Andhra Pradesh

- **Feature** — Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva · Arogya Raksha · Employees Health Scheme (EHS) · Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY
- **Target group** — BPL / low-income families (income below ₹5 lakh) · APL families · Serving government employees and pensioners · Bottom 40% by SECC criteria; plus all citizens aged 70+ since 2024
- **Funding** — Fully State-funded · Contributory — annual premium · Employee contribution plus State support · Centre-State shared (60:40)
- **Coverage** — Base ₹5 lakh, extended to ₹25 lakh per family per year for high-end tertiary care · About ₹2 lakh · Cashless with post-hospitalisation benefits · ₹5 lakh per family per year
- **Enrolment** — Automatic on eligibility (white ration card) · Voluntary · Automatic for employees · Automatic on eligibility
- **Scale** — About 1.43 crore households covered · Limited uptake · Employees and pensioners · Converged with the State scheme

Assessment of Arogya Raksha

Strengths - Addressed a genuine and widely acknowledged gap — the near-poor who are excluded from subsidised cover but cannot afford commercial insurance. - Low premium relative to coverage; used existing empanelment and claims infrastructure, so administrative cost was minimal.

Weaknesses - Voluntary contributory schemes suffer adverse selection — the healthy do not enrol, the sick do, so the risk pool deteriorates and the scheme becomes actuarially unsustainable. This is the standard reason such schemes fail worldwide. - Uptake remained limited relative to the eligible population. - Awareness and last-mile enrolment were weak in rural areas.

The present architecture

Andhra Pradesh’s health protection now rests principally on Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva — renamed from Rajiv Aarogyasri in December 2014 and progressively expanded, now offering up to ₹25 lakh per family per year across 949+ procedures on a PPP model, converged with Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. It is supplemented by EHS for government employees, Nirmayya for persons with autism, cerebral palsy and multiple disabilities, and Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi, which provides up to ₹15 lakh for costs beyond ₹25 lakh at government super-specialty hospitals. The State has also shifted emphasis toward prevention through Project Sanjeevani.

A live challenge: in April 2026 empanelled private hospitals temporarily suspended services over pending reimbursements — a reminder that the viability of PPP-based insurance depends on timely settlement of claims, not merely on generous coverage limits.

## Conclusion

Arogya Raksha was a sound diagnosis — the near-poor are the most under-protected group in Indian healthcare — but a contributory, voluntary design proved the wrong instrument, because adverse selection undermines any insurance pool that people may opt out of. The durable answer has been universalisation on the tax-funded side: Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva’s expansion to ₹25 lakh, convergence with PM-JAY, and a decisive shift toward preventive care, which reduces the need for hospitalisation in the first place.

## Value addition
- Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva lineage: launched as Rajiv Aarogyasri (2007); renamed by G.O.Ms. No. 157 of 17 December 2014; Trust registered 23 September 2015; coverage raised from ₹2 lakh to ₹2.5 lakh, then to ₹5 lakh, and now up to

₹25 lakh for specified tertiary procedures. Telangana retained the Rajiv Aarogyasri name with ₹10 lakh cover.

- Why out-of-pocket expenditure matters: India’s OOP share of health spending has historically been among the world’s highest; government health expenditure rose from 1.13% of GDP (2014-15) to 1.84% (2021-22), still short of the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5%.
- AP health allocation: ₹19,306 crore for Health, Medical & Family Welfare in Budget 2026-27; legacy health-sector liabilities of about ₹6,486 crore have been largely cleared.
- National context: medical colleges rose from 387 (2013-14) to 819 (2025-26); AIIMS from 7 to 20.

## Introduction

The Andhra Pradesh State Mineral Policy (2015), reinforced by the Minor Mineral Policy, 2025, seeks to convert the State’s geological endowment — barytes, limestone, bauxite, granite and beach sands — into industrial output, revenue and employment, while remaining within ecological and social limits. It operates within the MMDR Act, 1957 as amended, and the National Mineral Policy, 2019.

## Objectives of the policy
- Translate mineral potential into production through systematic exploration and scientific mining.
- Attract investment into value addition — cement, ceramics, aluminium, beneficiation — rather than raw mineral export.
- Maximise revenue through transparent e-auction of leases.
- Protect tribal interests and the environment in mineral-bearing Scheduled Areas.

## Strategies for sustainable mining
- **Transparent allocation** — Mandatory e-auction of mineral concessions since the MMDR Amendment, 2015 — ending discretionary allotment
- **Environmental safeguards** — Environmental Impact Assessment, mine closure and reclamation plans, restrictions in the Eastern Ghats bauxite belt
- **Community benefit-sharing** — District Mineral Foundation (DMF) in every mining district, funding drinking water, health, education and livelihoods under PMKKKY
- **Exploration capacity** — State Mineral Exploration and Research Bureau; GSI and MECL partnerships
- **Enforcement** — GIS/drone-based surveillance, vehicle tracking and check-posts to curb illegal mining, especially of sand and red sanders
- **Value addition** — Mineral-based industrial parks and cement clusters in Kadapa and Kurnool

## Evaluating the “eco-friendly and sustainable” claim

Where it has worked:

- Revenue and transparency improved — e-auctions raised realisation and reduced discretion; DMF funds have financed local development in mining districts.
- Downstream linkage is genuine — AP’s cement belt and barytes processing add value domestically.
- Institutional monitoring has strengthened with digital surveillance.

Where it falls short:

- Illegal mining persists, especially in sand and minor minerals, where enforcement capacity is thinnest and rents are highest.
- Mine closure compliance is weak — abandoned pits and unreclaimed land remain across the barytes and limestone belts.
- Scheduled Area conflict is unresolved — bauxite mining in the Eastern Ghats remains effectively frozen by tribal opposition and the Samatha precedent, meaning “potential” has not become “reality” in the State’s largest mineral asset.
- DMF utilisation has been uneven, with funds accumulating faster than they are spent on affected communities.

## The changed national context that AP must now align with
- MMDR Amendment Act, 2023: empowered the Centre to auction 24 of 30 critical minerals and opened six previously reserved minerals to private exploration; introduced the Exploration Licence for 29 deep-seated and critical minerals.
- National Critical Mineral Mission (2025): securing domestic and overseas supply chains for energy-transition minerals.
- MMDR Amendment Act, 2025: replaced NMET with the National Mineral Exploration and Development Trust (NMEDT) (lessee contribution raised from 2% to 3% of royalty; ₹8,700 crore over five years earmarked under NCMM); allowed inclusion of additional minerals in an existing lease from 1 September 2025; permitted one-time area extension for deep-seated minerals; and provided for Mineral Exchanges.

## Conclusion

The AP State Mineral Policy has succeeded in making mineral allocation more transparent and revenue more buoyant, but “eco-friendly and sustainable” remains an aspiration more than an achievement — untested in the Eastern Ghats and unenforced in minor minerals. The next phase must link leasing to demonstrated reclamation performance, spend DMF funds where the damage occurs, and position AP within the National Critical Mineral Mission, whose beach sands, graphite and rare-earth-bearing formations offer the State a genuinely new opportunity.

## Value addition
- National Mineral Policy, 2019: private participation with safeguards, right of first refusal for exploration, Mining Tenement System, District Mineral Foundation, “zero-waste mining” as a goal, and inter-generational equity as a guiding principle.
- India’s mineral position: self-sufficient in iron ore (100%), chromite (95%), limestone (93%) and bauxite (85%); 100% import-dependent for lithium, cobalt, nickel, niobium and gallium. Mining contributes about 2% of India’s GDP against Australia’s 12% and Canada’s 6%.
- Critical minerals: 30 identified by the Ministry of Mines; import duty removed on 25 of them (Budget 2024-25);

Critical Mineral Recycling Incentive Scheme (₹1,500 crore) targeting 270 kt of recycling capacity and 70,000 jobs; KABIL (NALCO-HCL-MECL JV) acquiring lithium and cobalt assets abroad.

- Offshore mining: the Offshore Areas Mineral (D&R) Act amended in 2023 to introduce auctions; the first tranche of

13 offshore blocks launched in 2024 — directly relevant to AP’s long coastline.
