## Introduction

Rayalaseema — Kurnool, Nandyal, Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, Kadapa, Annamayya, Chittoor and Tirupati — receives 500-700 mm of rainfall against a potential evapotranspiration far higher, making it one of India’s most drought-prone tracts. The Handri Neeva Sujala Sravanthi (HNSS) lift irrigation scheme was conceived to break this dependence by importing Krishna flood water across the watershed divide.

## Important features
- **Source and allocation** — 40 TMC of flood water drawn from the foreshore of the Srisailam reservoir during roughly 120 flood days (August-November)
- **Conveyance** — Main canal of about 565 km — among the longest lift canals in the country
- **Lift system** — Water raised through 12-13 stages (8 in Phase-I, 4-5 in Phase-II) to a cumulative head of over 369 metres — an exceptional engineering undertaking
- **Storage** — Eight balancing reservoirs — Krishnagiri, Jeedipalle, Gollapalli, Marala and others — to regulate supply beyond the flood window
- **Tunnels** — Five tunnels totalling over 13 km through hill terrain
- **River interlinking** — Connects the Handri, Penna, Chitravathi, Papagni and Neeva systems — an intra-State river link
- **Supplementary scheme** — Mutchumarri Lift Irrigation Scheme draws from Srisailam backwaters when the main pump house cannot reach its minimum draw-down level

## Role in meeting Rayalaseema’s water needs
- Irrigation: designed to serve about 6.02 lakh acres — Phase-I in Kurnool and Anantapur; Phase-II extending to Kadapa and Chittoor through the Madakasira and Punganur branch canals.
- Drinking water: safe supply for nearly 33 lakh people across 81 drought-prone mandals — arguably the project’s most valuable output, since drinking-water security is what ends distress migration.
- Groundwater recharge: the canal fills hundreds of minor irrigation tanks and reservoirs (such as Bhairavanitippa), raising water tables in a region where borewell depletion is acute — an indirect benefit often larger than the direct command area.
- Drought mitigation and cropping shift: assured water enables a shift from rainfed groundnut monoculture towards horticulture, oil palm and high-value crops.

## Critical assessment
- Dependence on surplus flows: HNSS draws only flood water within a narrow 120-day window; in deficit monsoons — increasingly frequent under climate change — allocations may not materialise.
- Energy cost: lifting water 369 metres makes the scheme power-intensive, adding a recurring subsidy burden on discoms.
- Execution and utilisation gap: delays in branch canals, distributaries and lining mean the created potential exceeds the utilised potential.
- Inter-State dimension: Krishna water allocation between AP and Telangana remains unsettled before the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II (Brijesh Kumar Tribunal), with the Krishna River Management Board regulating operations.

## Where HNSS sits in AP’s wider water strategy

It is one node of a larger intra-State grid: Polavaram (targeted for completion by 2027) as the anchor Godavari project; Galeru-Nagari and Veligonda (Poola Subbaiah) for Rayalaseema and Prakasam; and the proposed Polavaram–Banakacherla link (about ₹80,000 crore, to divert 200 TMC of Godavari flood water, interlinking Godavari-Krishna-Penna and serving around 80 lakh people), which Telangana has opposed before the Centre citing the 1980 Godavari Tribunal Award and the AP Reorganisation Act.

## Conclusion

HNSS is a strategically vital lifeline that has converted Rayalaseema’s water question from one of pure scarcity into one of conveyance, storage and management. Realising its full promise requires completing distributaries and lining, reducing lift energy costs through solar pumping, integrating tank and command management, and — decisively — resolving the inter-State allocation framework so that assured supply replaces contested surplus.

- Poola Subbaiah Veligonda Project: draws 43.50 TMC of flood water from Kollam Vagu upstream of Srisailam through twin tunnels by gravity into Nallamala Sagar, formed by closing three gaps (Sunkesula, Gottipadia, Kakarla); three canals — Teegaleru, Gottipadia and Eastern Main Canal.
- Gundlakamma Reservoir: on the Gundlakamma river at Mallavaram, storage 12.845 TMC, ~₹592 crore, serving about 62,368 acres in kharif and 80,060 acres in rabi, plus drinking water to Ongole.

- Polavaram–Banakacherla link: ~₹80,112 crore; SPV “Jala Harathi Corporation”; 200 TMC diversion; 3 lakh ha of new irrigation plus supplementation to 9.14 lakh ha and 20 TMC for industry; contested by Telangana.
- Institutional framework: Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards (created under the APRA, 2014), Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II, and the Inter-State River Water Disputes framework.

## Introduction

Occupational structure is the distribution of the workforce across primary, secondary and tertiary activities. Andhra Pradesh’s is best described as agrarian in employment but diversified in output — a mismatch that is the single most important fact about the State’s labour market.

The structure and the mismatch

- **Primary (agriculture, allied)** — Roughly half the workforce — cultivators, agricultural labourers, aquaculture and livestock workers · 37%
- **Secondary (industry)** — Modest — construction is the largest employer within it · 23%
- **Tertiary (services)** — Rising but urban-concentrated · 40%

The critical evaluation — six findings

- The productivity gap is the defining feature. Agriculture supports about half the workforce while producing 37% of value added — and even that share is unusually high because AP’s aquaculture, horticulture and food processing are productive. In manufacturing, net value added per person engaged reached ₹10.7 lakh (ASI FY24) — a multiple of what a farm worker earns.
- Agricultural labourers outnumber cultivators. The shift from owner-cultivation to wage labour reflects fragmentation of holdings and rising tenancy — and tenants without recorded title remain excluded from institutional credit, which is why the State’s Annadata Sukhibhava explicitly covers them.
- Casualisation and informality dominate. The unincorporated sector nationally employs 12.9 crore persons, and 42% of formal manufacturing workers are contractual (ASI 2023-24). AP mirrors this: most non-farm work is informal, without contracts or social security.
- Seasonality and disguised unemployment. Farm work is concentrated in sowing and harvest, leaving substantial idle capacity between seasons. More people work on the land than the land requires — the classic Lewis surplus that structural transformation is supposed to absorb.
- Bifurcation removed the State’s largest services labour market. Losing Hyderabad in 2014 left AP only about 29.5% urbanised, so the urban service economy that would normally pull labour out of agriculture is smaller and more dispersed than in comparable States.
- Regional and gender dimensions. The Krishna-Godavari delta supports intensive agriculture and aquaculture; Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra show higher casual labour and out-migration. Female workers are concentrated in agriculture, construction and unpaid family work; AP’s female LFPR of about 35.8% trails the national 41.7% (UPSS, 2023-24).

What is changing

- Employment elasticity nationally improved to 1.11% job growth per 1% value added (2017-23) from near zero in the 2000s.
- ASI FY24 recorded over 10 lakh new factory jobs nationally, 57 lakh added over FY15-FY24.
- AP’s investment pipeline — the Global Partnership Summit 2025 commitments of ₹13.25 lakh crore with 16.13 lakh jobs potential, and Google’s US$15 billion AI data centre at Visakhapatnam — could shift the structure if it converts into payrolls.
- 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency, are the dispersal mechanism.

The binding constraint

AP’s literacy at 72.6% (PLFS 2023-24) is the lowest among Indian States. A workforce cannot move into modern manufacturing or services faster than its education allows — which is why occupational change in AP is a human-capital problem before it is an industrial-policy problem.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s occupational structure shows incomplete structural transformation — output has diversified far faster than employment. Genuine change requires three things simultaneously: raising agricultural productivity so that exit is voluntary rather than distress-driven; creating labour-intensive non-farm jobs through MSMEs, food processing and logistics; and closing the literacy and skills gap that currently caps how far any worker can

move. Without the third, the first two will produce growth without employment.

## Value addition
- Concepts: Work Participation Rate — workers as a share of total population; main workers — employed 183 days or more in a year; marginal workers — less than 183 days, a proxy for underemployment.
- National employment position: 56.2 crore persons employed in Q2 FY26; unemployment 3.1% (PLFS 2025); LFPR 59.3% (male 79.1%, female 40.0%); rural 62.8% against urban 52.2%.
- Formalisation instruments: the four Labour Codes (effective 21 November 2025) — universal minimum wage, statutory appointment letters, and social security extended to gig and platform workers; the ELI Scheme (₹99,446 crore) targeting over 3.5 crore jobs including 1.92 crore first-timers.
- Theory to cite: Lewis’s dual-sector model and the “Lewis turning point”; the Kuznets-Clark sequence, from which India — and AP — diverged by skipping the manufacturing stage.

## Introduction

On 8 November 2016, ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes — about 86% of currency by value — ceased to be legal tender. Announced under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934, it remains India’s most debated monetary intervention. Its verdict is best written in two parts: modest success on its stated goals, substantial success on an unstated one — digitalisation.

## Stated objectives
- Curb black money held in high-denomination notes.
- Eliminate counterfeit currency and choke terror financing.
- Widen the tax base and improve compliance.
- Push the economy towards formal, digital transactions.
- Provide legal finality — the Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017.

## Impact across sectors
- **Informal / MSME** — Worst hit — acute liquidity crunch; daily-wage workers, small traders and cash-based supply chains disrupted
- **Agriculture** — Cash shortage struck during the rabi sowing season and at mandis
- **Banking** — Deposit surge, huge operational load; but 99.3% of demonetised notes returned (RBI Annual Report 2018), undercutting the black-money rationale
- **Real estate & jewellery** — Sharp, prolonged correction in cash-intensive segments
- **Digital payments** — Structural acceleration — the durable legacy
- **Tax administration** — Rise in returns filed and detection of shell entities; base effects contested

## Impact across social categories
- Poor, rural and elderly: greatest hardship — queue costs, wage losses, limited banking access.
- Middle class: temporary disruption, rapid migration to digital channels.
- Women and SHG members: cash savings held outside banks were exposed, though Jan Dhan account use rose.
- Informal workers: the most enduring damage, since livelihoods depend on cash liquidity.

## Scope for a cashless economy — a measured analysis
- The transformation is real. In FY 2025-26 UPI processed about 241.6 billion transactions worth ₹314 lakh crore, up 30% in volume; May 2026 set a record of 23.2 billion transactions worth ₹29.9 lakh crore — nearly 738 million a day. India now accounts for roughly 49% of global real-time payment volume, over three times Brazil’s Pix.
- But “cashless” is the wrong frame. The Economic Survey 2025-26 records that over 90% of UPI users continue to use cash regularly — the ecosystem is hybrid, not cash-free. Currency in circulation is well above its 2016 level in absolute terms, even as its ratio to GDP trends down.
- The causal link is partial. Demonetisation coincided with UPI’s launch (April 2016), the JAM trinity and smartphone/data cost collapse; digital growth would likely have occurred anyway, though the shock accelerated adoption.
- Remaining challenges: the digital divide, cyber fraud (about 10.64 lakh UPI fraud cases worth ₹805 crore in FY26 up to November), zero-MDR sustainability, and merchant onboarding in small towns.

## Conclusion

Demonetisation fell short on black money and counterfeiting, and imposed real, regressive short-term costs. Its lasting contribution was behavioural — it pulled forward India’s shift to digital payments by several years, laying the ground for a digital public infrastructure that now underpins credit, welfare delivery and formalisation. The lesson is that structural reform works best when incremental and infrastructure-led, as GST and UPI have been, rather than through shock.

## Value addition
- Judgment: Vivek Narayan Sharma v. Union of India (2023) — a five-judge Constitution Bench upheld the 2016 notification by 4:1, holding that the decision-making process was not flawed and that Section 26(2) permits demonetisation of “all series” of notes; Justice B.V. Nagarathna dissented, holding that such action required legislation rather than an executive notification.
- ₹2,000 note withdrawal (19 May 2023): a calibrated, non-disruptive withdrawal under the Clean Note Policy, with legal tender status retained; over 98% of the notes have returned.
- UPI today: ~85% of India’s retail digital payments; cross-border acceptance in 8 countries; the India-Nepal P2P corridor launched 6 June 2026.
- Economic Survey 2025-26 finding: UPI’s transaction trail expanded formal credit — especially to new-to-credit borrowers — without a rise in default rates, showing digital public infrastructure deepens finance rather than merely digitising it.
- RBI Digital Payments Index: 493.22 (March 2025) against 153.47 (March 2019).

## Introduction

The Eleventh Plan (2007-12) introduced a decisive innovation: 27 monitorable socio-economic targets, disaggregated to the State level, so that “inclusive growth” could be measured rather than merely asserted. For Andhra Pradesh these were grouped into six categories — Income and Poverty, Education, Health, Women and Children, Infrastructure, and Environment.

## Monitorable targets for Andhra Pradesh (2007-12)
- **Income and Poverty** — GSDP growth of about 9.5%; agricultural growth of 4% per annum; reduce the head-count poverty ratio by 10 percentage points; create new work opportunities and reduce educated unemployment
- **Education** — Raise the net enrolment ratio at primary level and reduce dropout rates (Classes I-V) to 20%; raise literacy to 85% and reduce the gender gap in literacy to 10 percentage points
- **Health** — Reduce Infant Mortality Rate to 28 per 1,000 live births; Maternal Mortality Ratio to 1 per 1,000 live births; Total Fertility Rate to 2.1; reduce malnutrition among 0-3 year-olds and anaemia among women and girls by half
- **Women and Children** — Raise the child sex ratio (0-6 years) to 935; ensure that at least 33% of beneficiaries of all government schemes are women and girl children
- **Infrastructure** — Electricity connection to all villages and BPL households; all-weather road connectivity to habitations above 1,000 population; telephone and broadband connectivity to all villages; clean drinking water for all by 2009
- **Environment** — Increase forest and tree cover by 5 percentage points; treat all urban waste water; raise energy efficiency by 20%

## Pattern of resource allocation: Tenth versus Eleventh Plan
- **Theme** — Growth with poverty reduction · Faster and More Inclusive Growth
- **Plan size** — Modest; consolidation after the 1990s reforms · Substantially larger outlays across the board
- **Sectoral priority** — Agricultural revival, primary education, basic infrastructure · Marked shift to social sectors (health, education, nutrition) and physical infrastructure
- **AP-specific emphasis** — Fiscal correction under the AP FRBM Act, 2005; VAT introduction; power sector unbundling · Jalayagnam irrigation, APDRP power distribution reform, industrial corridors
- **Funding mix** — Largely State budgetary resources with central plan assistance · Rising share of centrally sponsored flagship schemes (NRHM, SSA, MGNREGA) and market/institutional borrowing (RIDF, NABARD)
- **Welfare orientation** — Selective · Expansive — Aarogyasri, fee reimbursement, Indiramma housing

## The key structural change

The Eleventh Plan altered not just the size but the channel of resources. As centrally sponsored schemes grew, State budgets were increasingly committed to matching shares and implementation costs, which raised social-sector spending but reduced the State’s discretionary space. Simultaneously, since the Twelfth Finance Commission (2005) ended Central on-lending, AP moved to direct market borrowings, which financed most of its plan capital outlay by 2011-12.

## Conclusion

The transition from the Tenth to the Eleventh Plan in Andhra Pradesh reflected a broader national shift — from growth-first to growth-with-inclusion, financed by larger outlays, more centrally sponsored schemes and greater market borrowing. Monitorable targets were the era’s most useful legacy: the idea that development must be measured against stated benchmarks survives today in NITI Aayog’s SDG India Index and Fiscal Health Index, even though the Plans themselves are gone.

## Value addition
- Swarna Andhra @2047 targets (the modern successor to monitorable targets): per capita income of about

₹5.42 lakh by 2029; State economy of US$2.4 trillion by 2047; sustained growth above 15% per annum; guided by the ten “Padhi Sutralu” — Zero Poverty, Skilling, Water Security, Farmer-Agritech, Global Best Logistics, Energy Cost Optimisation, Product Perfection, Swachh Andhra, and Deep Tech.

- Current AP social targets: IMR to 25 per 1,000; MMR to 1 per 1,000; child sex ratio to 950; TFR to 2.1; literacy above 75%; 37% green cover by 2030 and 50% by 2047.
- AP Budget 2026-27 sectoral allocations: School Education ₹32,308 crore; Panchayati Raj & Rural Development

₹22,942 crore; Higher Education ₹2,567 crore; Skill Development ₹1,232 crore.

## Introduction

The bifurcation of 2 June 2014 left Andhra Pradesh with a structural revenue deficit: Telangana retained Hyderabad and the bulk of the tax base, while the residuary State kept most of the population and welfare obligations. CAG recorded a revenue deficit of ₹24,194 crore in 2014-15, and the debt-GSDP ratio climbed from 22.3% (2014-15) to about 32.4% (2019-20).

## Nature of central assistance — four distinct categories
- **Statutory (Reorganisation Act)** — Section 46(2) resource-gap assistance; Section 94(3) capital city support; Section 90 Polavaram; Section 93 institutions · Legally grounded, but quantum left to executive discretion
- **Constitutional (Finance Commission)** — Tax devolution under Art. 270; grants-in-aid under Art. 275 · Formula-based, untied, predictable — the most reliable channel
- **Discretionary/administrative** — Special Development Package for backward districts; higher central share in centrally sponsored schemes; externally aided project support · Negotiated, conditional, variable
- **Institutional** — AIIMS Mangalagiri, IIT Tirupati, IIM Visakhapatnam, NIT Tadepalligudem, IIIT Kurnool, Central University Anantapur, IISER, Petroleum University · One-time capital, long-term human capital returns

## Extent — commitment against delivery
- **Commitment** — Assessed · Actually released
- **Revenue deficit / resource gap (Sec. 46(2))** — About ₹22,113 crore (14th FC assessment) · Roughly ₹3,980 crore up to 2019-20 (CAG) — under a fifth
- **Capital city (Amaravati)** — Requirement far larger · About ₹2,787 crore approved for capital-region infrastructure, including ₹1,500 crore initially
- **Special Development Package** — ₹50 crore per district per year for seven backward districts · Largely released
- **Polavaram (Sec. 90)** — 100% central funding of the irrigation component · About ₹8,614 crore released up to 2020; disputes over revised cost and pace continue
- **Tax devolution (14th FC)** — AP share 4.31% · About ₹1.70 lakh crore over 2015-20 — delivered in full
- **Aggregate central releases (2014-15 to 2020- 21)** — — · Approximately ₹83,000 crore

## The analytical finding

Assistance divided sharply by nature. Formula-based constitutional transfers were delivered reliably and in full; discretionary and negotiated assistance was delivered partially and late. Enhanced devolution under the 14th FC — untied and automatic — therefore did more for AP’s finances than the special assistance explicitly designed for it. The Special Category Status demand, which rested on a Rajya Sabha assurance rather than a statutory provision, was

superseded when the 14th FC abolished the SCS distinction for devolution purposes; the Centre offered instead a five-year special assistance package, largely routed through externally aided projects and a higher central share in centrally sponsored schemes — help that was temporary where SCS would have been structural.

## Conclusion

Central assistance cushioned Andhra Pradesh’s post-bifurcation shock but did not close its structural gap. The decisive lesson is institutional rather than financial: in Indian federalism, entitlements that flow from a formula are honoured, while those that depend on negotiation are discounted. That lesson is now sharper still, since the 16th Finance Commission has raised AP’s share to 4.22% (₹64,362 crore in 2026-27) while discontinuing revenue-deficit and state-specific grants — making the State’s own revenue effort more decisive than any assistance it can negotiate.

## Value addition
- Legal distinction to state precisely: Special Category Status was an assurance given in the Rajya Sabha (February 2014), not a provision of the AP Reorganisation Act — a distinction that determines its enforceability.
- Current external and central support: World Bank US$800 million and ADB US$788.8 million for Amaravati Phase-I (approved December 2024), of which about US$340 million had been released by early 2026; ₹6,544 crore under SASCI in 2025-26; ₹4,000 crore additional under UIDF over two years; AIIB-assisted AMRUT 2.0 projects.
- Unresolved issues: apportionment of assets and liabilities under Schedules IX and X, power dues, and division of institutions between the two States.

## Introduction

The Sixth Economic Census (2013-14) was the last complete enumeration of all non-farm establishments in India. For Andhra Pradesh — where micro and household enterprise is the dominant livelihood outside agriculture — it remains the benchmark against which later, sample-based surveys are read.

## Growth revealed by the Sixth Economic Census
- Nationally, establishments rose from 41.25 million (2005) to 58.5 million (2013) — growth of 41.79%.
- Own-account establishments (no hired workers) grew 56.02%, far faster than units with hired workers — growth was in the tiniest segment.
- Andhra Pradesh accounted for about 7.25% of all establishments in India and about 7.54% of handloom/handicraft units.

## Structure of the sector
- **Ownership form** — 71.74% own-account; 28.26% with hired workers
- **Employment size** — 95.50% employed 1–5 workers; only 1.37% employed 10 or more
- **Sector mix** — Retail trade 35.41%, manufacturing 22.77%
- **Ownership type** — 96.4% privately owned; 36.19% home-based
- **Average size** — 2.24 persons per establishment

For Andhra Pradesh this means an enterprise base that is overwhelmingly household-run, single-person or family-operated, low-capital and trade-dominated — high on livelihood value, low on productivity and scale.

## The picture today — the successor data source

The Economic Census has been superseded for policy purposes by the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), now released quarterly, with district-level estimates targeted from 2026. Its findings confirm both the scale and the persistence of the structure:

- The unincorporated non-farm sector comprises about 7.9 crore establishments employing 12.9 crore persons.
- Working owners rose from 58.9% (2023-24) to 60% of workers (Q2 FY26) — self-employment is deepening, not receding.
- Women form 28.7% of the sector’s workforce; the rural workforce is about 6 crore.
- Credit access is improving: average outstanding loan per establishment rose from ₹50,138 (2022-23) to ₹53,710 (2023-24), and the share of unincorporated manufacturing units using formal credit rose from 48% (2021-22) to 51% (2023-24), with commercial bank borrowing up 6 percentage points and reliance on moneylenders and suppliers falling.

## Implications for Andhra Pradesh
- Employment, not output, is the sector’s contribution — average productivity is a fraction of the organised sector, where net value added per person engaged reached ₹10.7 lakh (ASI FY24).
- The binding constraints are credit, market access and formalisation, not entrepreneurship.
- Policy must therefore push Udyam registration, cash-flow-based lending, cluster infrastructure and digital market linkage rather than merely subsidising entry.

## Conclusion

The Sixth Economic Census established that Andhra Pradesh’s non-farm economy rests on tiny, home-based, own-account units — and a decade of ASUSE data confirms the structure has not fundamentally changed, though formal credit penetration has improved. The task ahead is to convert survival enterprises into growth enterprises through credit, skills and scale — the precise objective of AP’s MSME & Entrepreneur Development Policy 4.0 and its plan for 175 MSME parks, one in every assembly constituency.

## Introduction

Gross Value Added measures output net of intermediate consumption, sector by sector — the cleanest lens on economic structure. For Andhra Pradesh, the period 2014-15 to 2016-17 captures the immediate post-bifurcation years, when the residuary State had lost Hyderabad’s services base and had to rebuild its growth engines.

## Concept
- At current prices: includes inflation; shows the nominal size and share of each sector.
- At constant (2011-12) prices: strips out price change; shows real growth.
- Reading both together separates genuine expansion from price effects.

## Sectoral composition, 2014-15 to 2016-17 (current prices)
- **Sector** — 2014-15 · 2016-17 · Character
- **Primary (agriculture and allied)** — ~35% · ~33% · Unusually high for a major State; livestock, fisheries and horticulture drove real growth; crop output monsoon-dependent
- **Secondary (industry)** — ~20-22% · ~20-22% · Construction, electricity and manufacturing; boosted by post-bifurcation corridor and capital-city investment
- **Tertiary (services)** — ~43% · ~45% · Largest and fastest-growing — trade, transport, banking, real estate, IT

At constant prices, overall GVA grew at an average of about 10.6% a year in this period, making AP one of India’s fastest-growing States. The primary sector fluctuated with rainfall, the secondary sector was steady, and services consistently outperformed.

## The structural verdict — and its limitation

The declining share of agriculture in GVA alongside a rising services share is the classic Fisher-Clark structural transformation. But AP’s transition is incomplete in a specific way: agriculture’s share of output has fallen much faster than its share of employment. Value added has moved to services; labour has not. This is the productivity gap that defines the State’s development challenge.

## Where the structure stands today
- By 2023-24, the sectoral split (current prices) was roughly agriculture 37%, manufacturing 23%, services 40% — agriculture retains an unusually large share, sustained by aquaculture, horticulture and food processing rather than by traditional cropping.
- Per capita GSDP stood at ₹2,70,295 (2023-24) against India’s ₹2,15,935 — AP is above the national average.
- GSDP is projected at about ₹19.8 lakh crore in 2026-27, following ₹18.3 lakh crore in 2025-26.
- Critical methodological update: MoSPI rebased the national accounts to 2022-23, released on 27 February 2026, superseding the 2011-12 series. Any current comparison must use the new base, which improves informal-sector coverage through regular ASUSE data.

## Conclusion

Between 2014-15 and 2016-17, Andhra Pradesh’s GVA structure showed services leading, industry stabilising and agriculture retaining exceptional social and economic weight. The State is best described as being in a transitional phase — diversified in output but still agrarian in employment. Completing the transformation requires raising farm productivity, expanding agro-processing to capture value at source, and converting the current industrial investment pipeline into job-rich manufacturing.

## Introduction

The period 2011-12 to 2016-17 straddles the single most disruptive event in Andhra Pradesh’s fiscal history. It divides cleanly into three years of undivided-State normality (2011-14), a year of rupture (2014-15), and two years of transfer-led recovery (2015-17).

## Sources of revenue — the constant framework
- Own tax revenue: VAT/sales tax, state excise, stamps and registration, motor vehicle tax — the dominant own source throughout.
- Own non-tax revenue: fees, user charges, royalties, interest and dividends — small and stable.
- Central transfers: share in central taxes plus grants-in-aid — the component whose relative weight changed decisively.
- Capital receipts and borrowings: used to finance deficits and one-time transitional liabilities, including unapportioned debt.

## Trends, phase by phase

Phase 1: 2011-12 to 2013-14 (pre-reorganisation)

- Revenue receipts of the undivided State grew steadily on a broad base spanning Hyderabad’s services economy and the coastal agricultural belt.
- The own-tax-to-GSDP ratio was relatively high, and central transfers formed a smaller residual — the profile of a fiscally self-reliant large State.
- However, the underlying trend was already weakening: the post-2008 slowdown, welfare expansion and the political uncertainty of the Telangana agitation had begun eroding buoyancy.

## Phase 2: 2014-15 (the rupture)
- Bifurcation on 2 June 2014 removed Hyderabad’s tax base mid-year, producing an immediate collapse in own revenue for the residuary State.
- Apportionment problems — unapportioned balances, division of institutions, disputed power dues — delayed reconciliation of accounts.
- Result: a revenue deficit of ₹24,194 crore in 2014-15 (CAG), against new expenditure commitments for an entire administrative apparatus.

## Phase 3: 2015-16 to 2016-17 (transfer-led recovery)
- The 14th Finance Commission raised the States’ share in the divisible pool from 32% to 42% with effect from 2015-16 — a windfall that arrived precisely when AP needed it. AP received ₹1,69,969 crore in devolution over 2015-20.
- Special assistance and revenue-deficit grants under the Reorganisation Act supplemented this.
- Own taxes recovered modestly as economic activity stabilised; by 2016-17 the fiscal deficit was budgeted at 3% of GSDP (₹20,497 crore) with a revenue deficit of ₹4,868 crore (0.7%) — although actual outturns reported by CAG were weaker than budgeted.

## The structural verdict

Recovery was transfer-led, not effort-led. The residuary State emerged more dependent on the Centre and on borrowings than the undivided State had ever been — a dependence that persists, with central transfers still funding about 41% of revenue receipts in 2026-27.

## Conclusion

Between 2011-12 and 2016-17, Andhra Pradesh’s revenue trajectory was interrupted rather than merely slowed. The shrinking of the tax base in 2014-15 was cushioned by the 14th Finance Commission’s enhanced devolution and special assistance, but the episode exposed a lasting structural vulnerability. Strengthening own-tax buoyancy and rationalising committed expenditure remained — and remain — the essential conditions for fiscal consolidation.

## Value addition
- AP Budget 2016-17 markers: GSDP ₹6,83,233 crore (+13.2%); total expenditure ₹1,35,689 crore; revenue deficit

₹4,868 crore (0.7% of GSDP); fiscal deficit ₹20,497 crore (3% of GSDP); primary deficit ₹8,239 crore.

- Devolution arc for AP: 14th FC share 4.31% → 15th FC 4.05% → 16th FC 4.22%.
- Long-run comparison: revenue receipts have grown from ₹1,10,578 crore (2016-17, receipts excluding borrowings) to ₹2,34,140 crore of revenue receipts in BE 2026-27 — a more than two-fold expansion in a decade.
- Analytical framing: a State’s fiscal resilience depends on the buoyancy of its own base, not on the size of transfers

— transfers stabilise, but only own revenue compounds.

## Introduction

The 1991 balance of payments crisis — foreign exchange reserves down to roughly three weeks of imports, an IMF loan of about US$2.2 billion, and gold pledged abroad — made debt management central to Indian macro-policy. Over the following three decades, India’s debt story has been one of repeated shocks, structural weaknesses, and gradually strengthening institutions.

## Causes of rising public debt (1991 → 2026)
- Structural: a persistently low tax-GDP ratio (11–12%), narrow direct-tax base, and large committed expenditure (interest, salaries, pensions, subsidies).
- Cyclical shocks: the 2008 global financial crisis stimulus; the COVID-19 pandemic, which pushed the Centre’s deficit to 9.2% of GDP in FY21.
- Institutional: the FRBM Act’s 3% target was met only once since 2003; escape clauses were used liberally; off-budget borrowings and guarantees kept true liabilities hidden.
- Sub-national: UDAY bonds (2015–17) transferred discom losses to State books; unconditional cash transfers now total about ₹1.7 lakh crore across States (FY26); State guarantees reached 3.9% of GDP.

## Consequences — a critical two-sided ledger
- **Financed infrastructure, MGNREGA, PMAY, Jal Jeevan Mission and pandemic relief** — Interest payments absorb ~20% of the Centre’s expenditure (₹14.04 lakh crore, FY27 BE)
- **Enabled counter-cyclical response without an external crisis** — Crowding-out of private credit, especially for MSMEs
- **Internal, rupee-denominated structure avoided an “original sin” trap** — Intergenerational transfer of repayment burden
- **Capex share of Centre’s spending rose from 12.5% (FY20) to 22.6% (FY25 PA)** — Sub-national fiscal stress in Punjab, Kerala and other high-debt States

## The critical assessment

The common charge of “fiscal profligacy” is only partly accurate. Two distinctions matter:

- Revenue vs. capital borrowing — debt that funds consumption is a burden; debt that funds assets is self-liquidating. In BE 2026-27, effective capex (₹17.15 lakh crore) exceeds the fiscal deficit, indicating the composition has improved.
- Growth vs. interest cost (g > r) — with nominal GDP growing about 10% and borrowing costs lower, the debt ratio can decline without repayment. India has reduced general government debt by ~7.1 percentage points since 2020, an unwinding rarer than in most peer economies.

The reform response: FRBM Act (2003) → N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee (2017, debt as the anchor) → GST and digital tax administration → subsidy rationalisation via DBT → and, from FY27, a debt-to-GDP anchor of 50±1% by March 2031. Three sovereign rating upgrades in FY26 validated the path.

## Conclusion

Since 1991, public debt has been both an enabler of development and a source of vulnerability. The decisive lesson is that the quality of borrowing matters more than its quantity. Sustained tax buoyancy, transparent accounting of off-budget liabilities, and protection of capital spending will determine whether debt continues to finance India’s growth or begins to constrain it.

## Value addition
- Milestones: 1991 IMF programme → FRBM Act 2003 → Fourteenth FC (42% devolution, 2015) → COVID spike (2020-21) → debt-anchored framework (Budget 2025-26) → 16th FC roadmap (2026-31).
- Active debt management: bond switching to lengthen maturity; weighted average maturity 10.4 years (FY19) → ~13 years (FY25).
- Subsidy rationalisation: over 4 crore duplicate LPG connections deactivated under PAHAL; DBT and Just-in-Time fund releases.
- Institutional gap: an independent Public Debt Management Agency and a Fiscal Council remain unimplemented recommendations (14th FC, N.K. Singh Committee).

## Introduction

Since Independence, India's national income has been fundamentally re-ordered — from an agrarian base to a services-dominated structure. As per the First Advance Estimates (Economic Survey 2025–26), agriculture contributes 15.2%, industry 24.3% and services 51.1% of GDP in FY26. The nature of this shift, however, reveals not a textbook transition but a truncated, services-led transformation.

## Trends in sectoral contribution since Independence
- **Sector** — Share 1950–51 · Share FY26 (FAE) · Workforce FY26 (PLFS, CWS) · Growth FY26
- **Agriculture & allied** — ~54% · 15.2% · 42.4% · 3.1%
- **Industry** — ~16% · 24.3% (Mfg 12.8%) · 24.2% · 6.2% (Mfg 7.0%)
- **Services** — ~30% · 51.1% (53.6% in H1) · 33.5% · 9.1%

## Nature of the contribution
- Agriculture — livelihood-heavy, income-light: It sustains ~42% of workers but generates ~15% of income, an adverse income–employment ratio of roughly 1:3. Crop growth remains volatile (3.1% in FY26, below the FY16–25 average of 4.5%), though livestock (+195% GVA, FY15–FY24) and fisheries provide stability.
- Industry — arrested at the middle: Industry rose to ~27% by the 1980s but has plateaued near 24–25%. Manufacturing has hovered at 12–17% for three decades — what Dani Rodrik terms "premature de-industrialisation."
- Services — high productivity, thin absorption: Services grew 9.1% in FY26. Computer & information services doubled their GVA share from 6.0% to 12.2% (2011–12 to 2023–24). Yet services employ only 33.5% of workers, and over 60% of urban but under 20% of rural workers.

## Examining the Kuznets–Clark hypothesis
- The hypothesis predicts a sequential shift: primary → secondary → tertiary, with industry as the employment-absorbing intermediate stage.
- Match (direction): Agriculture's share fell steadily; non-agriculture expanded — consistent with the theory.
- Divergence (path): India leapfrogged the manufacturing stage. Industry never became the dominant absorber of surplus labour, producing "premature tertiarisation" — a services-led income structure atop an agrarian employment structure.
- Consequence: Widening inter-sectoral productivity gaps, jobless growth, and persistent informality (over 80% of the workforce).

## Conclusion

India's sectoral trajectory reflects an "imbalanced transformation" — agriculture employment-heavy, services income-dominant, industry stagnant. India therefore follows Kuznets–Clark in direction but not in sequence. With medium-term growth potential now assessed at 7% (Economic Survey 2025–26), completing the transition demands labour-intensive manufacturing, rural non-farm diversification and skilling — the essence of Viksit Bharat @2047.

Q131:
## Introduction

Keyword discipline: this question is specifically about extension — the transfer of knowledge and technology to farmers — not about schemes generally. Keep the focus on how advice reaches the farmer.

Agricultural extension is the transfer of knowledge, technology and advisory services from research institutions to farmers. India’s traditional extension system was widely acknowledged to have failed: the extension worker to farmer ratio was poor, staff were burdened with non-extension duties, and — most damagingly — most farmers came to rely on input dealers for technical advice, a clear conflict of interest since the adviser profits from the sale. Andhra Pradesh’s response has been to rebuild extension around the village rather than the department.

Strategy 1: Rythu Bharosa Kendras — decentralising extension to the village

The State’s flagship strategy, and its most significant institutional innovation. RBKs are established at village-secretariat level — broadly one per Gram Panchayat, about five per mandal — as one-stop shops for all farmer needs:

- **Knowledge Centre** — A Farmer Knowledge Centre attached to each RBK, with digital kiosks, video advisories and reading material
- **Technical advisory team** — A resident Village Agriculture Assistant with agriculture, horticulture, animal husbandry and fisheries advisory support
- **Certified input supply** — Government-certified seed, fertiliser and pesticide, with delivery within 24-48 hours of ordering through kiosks — removing dependence on the dealer for both product and advice
- **e-crop booking** — Digital registration of the crop sown, which becomes the basis for crop insurance, input subsidy, procurement and compensation — a single administrative act that resolves the disputes which previously defeated claims
- **Custom hiring of machinery** — Farm Machinery Banks operated at or through the RBK, so mechanisation is available as a service rather than an asset
- **Procurement** — MSP procurement at the village with direct e-payment into the farmer’s account
- **CCRC issuance** — Crop Cultivator Rights Cards for tenant cultivators
- **Allied services** — Veterinary, fisheries and horticulture advisory delivered from the same point

The strategic insight: by bundling advice with inputs, insurance, machinery and procurement at one location, the RBK makes extension something the farmer visits for a transaction rather than something the department must persuade her to attend. That is why it works where standalone extension campaigns did not.

Strategy 2: Farmer field schools and demonstration

- Polambadi (Farmer Field Schools) — season-long, field-based learning in which farmers observe and experiment on a demonstration plot rather than attend a lecture.
- Polam Pilustondi-type field visit campaigns bringing officials to the field at critical crop stages.
- Demonstration plots at RBK level for new varieties and practices.

Strategy 3: Farmer-to-farmer extension — the APCNF model

The most successful extension strategy the State has deployed. Andhra Pradesh Community Managed Natural Farming, implemented by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha, uses practising farmers as extension agents: - Grown 25-fold from 40,000 farmers in 2016 to over 17.7 lakh farmers across 8,168 gram panchayats and 0.92 million hectares. - Women-led, anchored in the SHG network, which supplies both credibility and reach. - Whole-village saturation rather than scattered individual adoption, so peer effects reinforce learning. - Verified outcomes: income gains of 38-66%, water savings up to 50%, emission reductions up to 46% per acre — recognised by the Gulbenkian Prize (2024) and the Food Planet Prize (2026).

Why it works: a farmer trusts a neighbour who has done it more than an official who has read about it. This is the single most transferable lesson in Indian extension.

Strategy 4: Digital and ICT-based extension

- e-crop booking and digital crop registration as the data backbone.
- Integrated Agriculture Laboratories for soil, seed, fertiliser and pesticide testing, with results linked to advisory.
- Soil Health Cards translating test results into crop-specific recommendations.
- Weather-based crop advisories — APIIATP includes an integrated weather forecasting system delivering advisories scaled down to individual irrigation cluster areas.
- Kisan Call Centre, mobile advisories and video-based content in Telugu.
- Agristack and Farmer IDs for targeted advisory.

Strategy 5: Institutional convergence

- ATMA (Agricultural Technology Management Agency) at district level, integrating agriculture, horticulture, animal husbandry, fisheries and sericulture extension under one framework.
- Acharya N.G. Ranga Agricultural University, Krishi Vigyan Kendras and ICAR research stations providing the technical content.
- Sri Venkateswara Veterinary University and the fisheries university for allied advisory.

Strategy 6: Producer organisations as extension vehicles

Farmer Producer Organisations — part of the 10,000 FPO programme, with about 56.32 lakh farmers registered nationally, roughly 39% women — aggregate not only produce but also knowledge, and serve as the channel for market intelligence and quality standards.

Strategy 7: Skill development

Government ITIs with MoUs with 167 industry partners, 9,188 trainees completing in-plant industrial training and 98% securing placement or apprenticeship — the vocational counterpart to farm extension.

Assessment

Working: - RBKs solved the access problem — extension is now within walking distance and bundled with services the farmer already needs. - e-crop booking solved the verification problem — insurance and compensation now rest on a digital record rather than a disputed inspection. - APCNF solved the credibility problem — farmer-to-farmer transmission at scale.

Limitations: - Staff capacity — a single Village Agriculture Assistant covering all sub-sectors is stretched. - Uneven quality across RBKs, depending on the individual posted. - Advisory reach is thinner in Rayalaseema and the tribal agency areas. - Tenant cultivators, being unrecorded, are often missed by advisory targeting as well as by credit. - Digital divide — elderly and illiterate farmers cannot use kiosk-based content, which matters in a State with 72.6% literacy, the lowest in India.

## Conclusion

Andhra Pradesh’s extension strategy rests on three sound ideas: decentralise delivery to the village (RBKs), bundle advice with the services farmers already need (inputs, insurance, machinery, procurement), and use farmers themselves as extension agents (APCNF). Together these address the three classic failures of Indian extension — distance, irrelevance and lack of credibility. Consolidating the gains requires strengthening staff capacity, extending reach into Rayalaseema and the agency areas, and including tenant cultivators in advisory targeting as deliberately as in credit.

## Value addition
- The traditional model’s failure: India’s extension worker to farmer ratio has long been inadequate, and successive Economic Surveys have noted farmers’ reliance on input dealers for technical advice — the problem RBKs were designed to solve.
- Institutional framework: ATMA at district level under the National Mission on Agricultural Extension and Technology (NMAET); Krishi Vigyan Kendras under ICAR; ANGRAU for research.
- APCNF’s extension architecture: farmer-to-farmer transmission, women-led through SHGs, whole-village saturation, nine universal principles including 365-day green cover; funded by GoI, State resources and KfW’s €90 million agroecology grant.
- The measurable payoff: APCNF’s income gains of 38-66% achieved primarily by eliminating purchased inputs

— the clearest demonstration that extension delivering knowledge can substitute for extension delivering subsidy.
Q132:
## Introduction

In Andhra Pradesh, irrigation is destiny. Rainfall is unevenly distributed — the deltas receive assured canal water while Rayalaseema receives 500-700 mm against far higher evapotranspiration — so access to irrigation, more than soil or enterprise, determines which region prospers. The statement is therefore substantially correct: irrigation imbalance is the principal cause of the State’s regional inequality.

The nature of the imbalance

- **Coastal Andhra (Krishna-Godavari delta)** — Assured canal irrigation from the Godavari and Krishna anicuts, built from the mid-nineteenth century; highest irrigation intensity in the State · Double and triple cropping; India’s most productive rice tract; aquaculture, horticulture and oil palm; the “Rice Bowl”
- **Rayalaseema** — Semi-arid, groundwater-dependent; lowest canal coverage; borewell depletion acute · Rainfed groundnut and millets; frequent drought; low and volatile incomes; out-migration
- **North Coastal Andhra (Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram Manyam, Alluri Sitharama Raju)** — Limited canal irrigation; hilly, tribal agency terrain · Rainfed and shifting cultivation; lowest per capita incomes in the State

Historical causes of the imbalance

- Colonial investment followed the deltas The Godavari anicut at Dowleswaram (Sir Arthur Cotton, 1852) and the Krishna anicut at Vijayawada created assured irrigation in the deltas more than 170 years ago. That single historical decision compounds to this day.
- Geography The deltas are flat, alluvial and command-able by gravity flow. Rayalaseema is an elevated, undulating Deccan fringe, where water must be lifted — which is why HNSS requires raising water over 369 metres through 12-13 stages, at heavy energy cost.
- The Green Revolution reinforced it The HYV package required assured irrigation. It therefore delivered its gains to the deltas and bypassed the rain-fed regions, widening the pre-existing gap rather than narrowing it.
- Inter-State water disputes Krishna water allocation between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana remains unsettled before the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II (Brijesh Kumar Tribunal), with the Krishna River Management Board regulating operations — creating uncertainty for Rayalaseema schemes dependent on Srisailam flood water.
- Project delays Rayalaseema’s lift schemes have long gestation, high cost and heavy energy requirements, so they were repeatedly delayed while delta systems already functioned.

Consequences — the regional inequality

- **Income and productivity gap** — The delta districts generate far higher agricultural value per hectare than Rayalaseema
- **Poverty concentration** — Multidimensional deprivation is highest in Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra, lowest in the delta
- **Cropping pattern divergence** — Irrigated paddy, aquaculture and horticulture in the delta; rainfed groundnut and millets in Rayalaseema
- **Indebtedness and distress** — Crop failure in rainfed tracts drives informal borrowing, asset loss and, historically, farmer suicides
- **Out-migration** — Distress migration from Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra to Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai and the delta districts
- **Human development** — Lower literacy and health indicators in the lagging regions; AP’s overall literacy of 72.6% is the lowest among Indian States, with the deficit concentrated in these areas
- **Political consequence** — Persistent demands for special packages and, historically, for separate statehood for Rayalaseema

Corrective measures

- **Handri Neeva Sujala Sravanthi** — 40 TMC of Srisailam flood water through a 565-km canal, lifted over 369 metres in 12-13 stages, with eight balancing reservoirs; serves about 6.02 lakh acres and drinking water for nearly 33 lakh people in 81 drought-prone mandals
- **Galeru-Nagari Sujala Sravanthi** — Krishna flood water to Kadapa, Annamayya and Chittoor
- **Poola Subbaiah Veligonda** — 43.50 TMC from Kollam Vagu upstream of Srisailam by gravity through twin tunnels into Nallamala Sagar
- **Polavaram** — The anchor Godavari project, a national project under Section 90 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014; targeted completion by 2027
- **Proposed Polavaram-Banakacherla link** — About ₹80,112 crore to divert 200 TMC of Godavari flood water, interlinking Godavari-Krishna-Penna, serving around 80 lakh people — contested by Telangana
- **Micro-irrigation** — PMKSY “Per Drop More Crop”; AP is among India’s leaders in drip and sprinkler coverage
- **Watershed and rainfed development** — Rayalaseema Drought Mitigation Project; watershed programmes; APCNF natural farming, which achieves water savings of up to 50% — particularly valuable in water-scarce tracts
- **Non-farm dispersal** — Industrial nodes at Orvakal and Kopparthy in Rayalaseema; Drone City at Orvakal; 175 MSME parks, one per assembly constituency

A necessary qualification

Irrigation imbalance is the principal cause of regional inequality but not the only one. Urbanisation, industrial location, connectivity, education and the loss of Hyderabad in 2014 all contribute. Moreover, irrigation alone does not guarantee prosperity — the delta’s aquaculture boom has brought salinisation of adjoining paddy land, showing that water without regulation creates its own problems.

## Conclusion

The statement is substantially correct: colonial-era canal investment in the deltas, reinforced by a Green Revolution package that required assured water, created a durable divide that later lift schemes have narrowed but not closed. Correcting it requires completing HNSS, Galeru-Nagari and Veligonda, resolving the Krishna allocation, and reducing the energy cost of lift irrigation through solar pumping — but also accepting that water alone will not equalise the regions. Rayalaseema and North Coastal Andhra need dispersed industry, skills and connectivity as much

as they need canals — which is the logic of the MSME parks and industrial nodes now being located there.

## Value addition
- Historical anchor: Sir Arthur Cotton’s Dowleswaram anicut on the Godavari (1852) and the Krishna anicut at Vijayawada created the delta’s assured irrigation — the single most consequential investment in the State’s agricultural history.
- Institutional framework: Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards (created under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014); Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal-II (Brijesh Kumar Tribunal); the Inter-State River Water Disputes framework.
- The energy dimension: lifting water 369 metres makes HNSS power-intensive, adding a recurring subsidy burden on discoms — AP budgets about ₹11,000 crore in agricultural power subsidy.
- The counter-example within the State: APCNF’s water savings of up to 50% across 0.92 million hectares show that demand-side management can complement supply-side irrigation investment.

Q133:
## Introduction

On the eve of Independence, the Telangana region formed part of the princely State of Hyderabad under the Nizam, and its land system was therefore not shaped by British land settlements but by an older, more overtly feudal structure. Roughly 40% of the State’s land was held outside normal revenue administration as jagirs and the Nizam’s personal estates, and cultivators were subject to obligations that had no parallel in the ryotwari areas of the Andhra region.

The categories of land tenure

- **Sarf-e-khas** — The Nizam’s personal estates, whose revenue went directly to him; administered separately from the State
- **Jagir lands** — Granted to nobles, military commanders and officials in return for service; the jagirdar collected revenue and exercised quasi-governmental powers — police, judicial and administrative — within his grant. About 6,500 jagirs existed
- **Inam lands** — Rent-free or concessional grants to temples, mosques, religious functionaries and village officers
- **Diwani or Khalsa lands** — Directly administered by the State on a ryotwari-type basis, covering roughly 60% of the area, where the pattadar held from the government
- **Banjar and assigned lands** — Waste and government land, often informally occupied

The intermediary class

- Deshmukhs and deshpandes — originally revenue officials, they had converted their offices into hereditary landed power, some holding estates running to tens of thousands of acres.
- Doras — the local term for the dominant landlord, whose authority in the village was social and coercive as much as economic.
- Patels and patwaris — village officers responsible for revenue collection and land records, whose control over records enabled manipulation of tenancy and title.

The condition of cultivators

- Tenancy-at-will Most cultivators held without security of tenure, liable to eviction at the landlord’s discretion. There was no recorded lease and no statutory rent ceiling.
- Rack-renting Rents commonly absorbed a very large share of the produce, leaving the cultivator at subsistence and unable to invest in the land.
- Vetti — the defining feature Unpaid, hereditary, bonded labour owed by the cultivator and his family to the dora

— agricultural work, domestic service, construction, transport of the landlord’s goods, and personal attendance. Whole families and specific caste groups were bound to particular households across generations. Vetti made the Telangana system a question of personal freedom, not merely of property.

- Debt bondage Advances from the landlord-cum-moneylender, at compounding interest, bound the cultivator permanently.
- Illegal exactions Beyond rent, cultivators paid customary levies for festivals, weddings and the landlord’s expenses.
- Caste and land coincided Landlessness and vetti fell overwhelmingly on Dalit and backward-caste households, so economic exploitation and social hierarchy reinforced each other.
- No security in records Since patwaris controlled land records and were themselves part of the landed structure, tenants had no documentary basis on which to assert any claim.

The consequence — the Telangana Armed Struggle (1946-51)

The system’s severity produced the largest peasant movement in modern Indian history: - Led by the Andhra Mahasabha and subsequently the Communist Party, spreading across some 3,000 villages. - Its demands were direct: abolition of vetti, security of tenure, and land to the tiller. - Peasant committees seized and redistributed an estimated one million acres and, in many villages, functioned as parallel administrations. - The movement was suppressed after Operation Polo (September 1948), when Hyderabad acceded to India, and was formally withdrawn in 1951. - Its lasting effect was to make land reform politically unavoidable in the region.

The reforms that followed

- **Hyderabad Abolition of Jagirs Regulation, 1949 and the Jagirs Commutation Regulation** — Abolished jagirdari, bringing about 6,500 jagirs under State administration
- **Hyderabad (later AP Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950** — Conferred protected-tenant status, regulated rent, and gave the right to purchase — substantially more radical than the Andhra area’s 1956 Act
- **Bhoodan** — Vinoba Bhave began the movement at Pochampally, Nalgonda, on 18 April 1951 — India’s first Bhoodan village — prompted directly by the Telangana struggle
- **Abolition of bonded labour** — Vetti legally ended; reinforced nationally by the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976
- **Ceiling legislation** — Culminating in the AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973

The historical assessment

The reforms succeeded in abolishing the institutions — jagirdari, vetti, intermediary tenures — which was the region’s most urgent need, since these concerned personal freedom. They failed to redistribute the asset, because benami transfers and exemptions defeated ceiling laws. As the earlier Barucha Committee (1937), constituted by the Nizam himself, had recognised in recommending occupancy rights for those cultivating uninterruptedly for twelve or more years, the problem had been visible long before it was addressed.

## Conclusion

On the eve of Independence, Telangana’s land system was among the most feudal in the subcontinent — jagirdari tenure, absolute landlord power through the doras and deshmukhs, tenancy-at-will, rack-renting and, above all, vetti bonded labour. It produced India’s largest peasant uprising and made land reform a matter of political survival rather than policy preference. The reforms that followed ended feudal servitude but not landlessness — a distinction that continues to shape land politics in the region.

## Value addition
- Terms to use precisely: sarf-e-khas (the Nizam’s personal estates), jagir, inam, diwani/khalsa (directly administered),

dora (landlord), deshmukh and deshpande (hereditary revenue officers), vetti (bonded labour).

- Scale: about 40% of Hyderabad State’s land was held as jagirs and sarf-e-khas; roughly 6,500 jagirs were abolished in 1949.
- The armed struggle: 1946-51, some 3,000 villages, about one million acres redistributed before suppression; ended after Operation Polo (September 1948).
- Bhoodan: Pochampally, Nalgonda, 18 April 1951 — Vinoba Bhave’s first bhoodan, when a landlord donated 100 acres to Harijan families who had asked for land.
- The contrast to state: the Andhra region was under the ryotwari system of the Madras Presidency, with a direct State-cultivator relationship — which is why the two regions required different tenancy statutes and why Andhra Pradesh has never had a single tenancy law.

Q134:
## Introduction

The goal of doubling farmers’ income (DFI) by 2022 was announced in February 2016. The Ashok Dalwai Committee, constituted in April 2016, gave it analytical form in a fourteen-volume report: doubling real farm household income over the 2015-16 base, which required a compound annual growth rate of about 10.4% — against a historical trend of roughly 3-4%. The scale of that requirement is the key to any honest assessment.

The Dalwai Committee’s seven sources of growth

- Improvement in crop productivity
- Improvement in livestock productivity
- Resource-use efficiency and savings in cost of production
- Increase in cropping intensity
- Diversification toward high-value crops
- Improved real prices received by farmers
- Shift from farm to non-farm occupations

Progress on each — what actually happened

- **Crop productivity** — Record output — foodgrain at 3,577.3 lakh MT in 2024-25, up 254.3 LMT over the previous year — but yield growth remained modest; crop GVA grew only 3.5% a decade
- **Livestock** — Strongest performer. Livestock GVA rose about 195% between FY15 and FY24 (CAGR 12.77% at current prices); the sub-sector grew 7.1% over the decade
- **Fisheries** — Fish production rose over 140% during 2014-2025; the sub-sector grew 8.8% a decade — the fastest in agriculture
- **Cost savings** — Soil Health Cards, neem-coated urea, micro-irrigation under PMKSY — real but incremental
- **Cropping intensity** — Limited progress; irrigation expansion slower than planned
- **Diversification** — Horticulture output (362.08 MT) exceeded foodgrain output and now contributes about 33% of agricultural GVA — genuine structural diversification
- **Better prices** — MSP raised to at least 1.5 times the A2+FL cost of production (from 2018-19); e-NAM now covers 1,656 mandis with cumulative trade of ₹4.84 lakh crore; but price realisation remains the weakest link
- **Non-farm shift** — Slowest of all — roughly 46.1% of the population still depends on agriculture

The income evidence

- The NSS Situation Assessment Survey 2018-19 recorded average monthly income of an agricultural household at

₹10,218, against ₹6,426 in 2012-13 — a rise of about 59% in nominal terms over six years.

- Adjusted for inflation, real income growth was far below the doubling trajectory.
- Crucially, wages and income from animal husbandry, rather than crop cultivation, accounted for a growing share
- confirming that where income did rise, it came from allied activities and non-farm wages, exactly as the Committee’s sources 2, 7 predicted.
- No official government assessment of whether the target was met has been published, and the 2022 deadline passed without a formal evaluation.

The verdict

The target was not achieved in real terms. It was arithmetically demanding — requiring more than triple the historical growth rate — and was set back by drought years, the COVID-19 disruption and volatile output prices.

But the framing succeeded even where the number did not. Three lasting shifts followed: 1. Policy attention moved from production to income — the single most important conceptual change in Indian agricultural policy in decades. 2. Allied sectors were mainstreamed. Livestock and fisheries are now recognised as the growth engines they are, driving the highest decadal agricultural growth in fifty years — 4.45% (FY16-FY25). 3. Income-support instruments were created — PM-KISAN, KCC expansion to allied activities, PMFBY, and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund.

## Conclusion

India did not double farmers’ real income by 2022, and the target was probably never achievable at the growth rates available. Its value lay elsewhere: it redefined the objective of agricultural policy from tonnes produced to rupees earned, and it directed attention to livestock, fisheries and horticulture — which have since delivered the fastest agricultural growth in five decades. The unfinished agenda is the one the Committee identified as hardest: better price realisation and a genuine shift of labour out of farming, neither of which can be achieved by agricultural policy alone.

## Value addition
- Committee detail: the Ashok Dalwai Committee on Doubling Farmers’ Income (April 2016) submitted a

fourteen-volume report; base year 2015-16; target real income doubling by 2022-23, requiring 10.4% CAGR.

- MSP framework: since 2018-19, MSP fixed at a minimum of 1.5 times the A2+FL cost; the Swaminathan Commission (National Commission on Farmers, 2004-06) had recommended C2+50%, a difference that remains politically live.
- Income data source: the NSS Situation Assessment Survey of Agricultural Households — 2012-13 and 2018-19 rounds; the next round is awaited.
- Current growth architecture: Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (₹11,440 crore); PM Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana; National Mission on Edible Oils; PM Matsya Sampada Yojana; the 10,000 FPO programme with 56.32 lakh farmers registered.

## Introduction

Land reform in Telangana carries a distinctive history. Unlike the ryotwari areas of Coastal Andhra, the Telangana region under the Nizam of Hyderabad had a deeply feudal structure — jagirdari, and the notorious vetti (bonded labour) system under the doras and deshmukhs. The Telangana Armed Struggle (1946-51) — in which peasants seized and redistributed land in thousands of villages — made land reform not merely a policy choice but a political necessity.

The pre-reform structure

- About 40% of Hyderabad State’s land was held as jagirs and sarf-e-khas (the Nizam’s personal estates), outside normal revenue administration.
- Deshmukhs and doras held vast estates, some running to tens of thousands of acres, with cultivators as tenants-at-will.
- Vetti — unpaid, hereditary bonded labour — bound entire families to landlords.
- The Telangana Armed Struggle redistributed an estimated one million acres before it was suppressed, establishing land redistribution as the region’s central political demand.

The measures adopted

- **Hyderabad Abolition of Jagirs Regulation, 1949 and the Jagirs Commutation Regulation, 1359F** — Abolished jagirdari, bringing about 6,500 jagirs under State administration
- **Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950** — Conferred protected-tenant status, regulated rent and gave tenants the right to purchase
- **Ceiling legislation — culminating in the AP Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973** — Imposed family-based ceilings, with surplus land to be redistributed to the landless
- **Bhoodan and Gramdan** — Vinoba Bhave began the Bhoodan movement at Pochampally, Nalgonda, on 18 April 1951 — the first Bhoodan village in India, prompted directly by the Telangana struggle
- **Assignment of government land** — Laoni rules for assigning waste and government land to landless SC/ST families
- **Abolition of bonded labour** — Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976
- **Tribal protection** — The Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation, 1959 (Regulation 1 of 70) barring transfer of tribal land to non-tribals in Scheduled Areas

Achievements — the case for

- Jagirdari and intermediary tenures were genuinely abolished, ending the Nizam-era system of revenue farming
- the clearest and most complete success.
- Vetti was legally ended, and the social power of the dora class was broken — an achievement of dignity as much as economics.
- Protected tenancy conferred security on a substantial number of cultivators.
- Pattas were distributed to landless SC and ST households from ceiling-surplus and government land, creating a class of small owner-cultivators where none had existed.
- The Bhoodan movement, though limited in acreage, established the moral case for redistribution and originated in Telangana.
- Later, the Dharani integrated land records portal (2020) digitised records and reduced the discretion that had enabled manipulation — though its own implementation has been contested.

Failures — the critical evaluation

- **Benami transfers** — Landlords partitioned holdings among relatives, servants and fictitious persons before the ceiling laws took effect — the single greatest cause of failure. The long gap between announcement and enactment gave ample warning
- **Ceiling exemptions** — Plantations, orchards, religious and charitable trusts and specified categories were exempted, allowing large holdings to survive legally
- **Low surplus declared** — Land actually declared surplus and redistributed was a small fraction of the holdings above ceiling
- **Poor quality of redistributed land** — Assignees frequently received unirrigated, rocky or inaccessible land, so pattas conferred title without livelihood
- **Litigation** — Ceiling cases ran for decades; the placing of land reform laws in the Ninth Schedule protected them from challenge but did not speed implementation
- **Tenancy went underground** — Rather than conferring ownership, tenancy legislation drove tenancy into oral, unrecorded arrangements — leaving tenants without credit, insurance or compensation, a problem that persists today
- **Weak land records** — Outdated and inaccurate records made both identification of surplus and enforcement of rights difficult
- **Bhoodan’s limits** — Much donated land was infertile or already under dispute; a significant share was never actually transferred
- **Political economy** — Implementation depended on a revenue bureaucracy socially and often familially connected to the landed class

The differentiated verdict

Telangana’s land reforms succeeded where the target was an institution — jagirdari, vetti, intermediary tenures — and failed where the target was an asset. Abolishing a legal category is administratively achievable; taking land from those who hold power in the village is not. The result was a transformation of agrarian social relations without a corresponding transformation of the land distribution itself.

That distinction matters for the question’s premise: the reforms were aimed at redistribution from large farmers to labourers and the landless. In intent, unquestionably so. In outcome, they delivered dignity and freedom from bondage far more successfully than land.

## Conclusion

Land reform in Telangana ended feudalism but did not create equality. It abolished the jagirdar and the vetti system, conferred tenancy security and distributed some pattas — genuine and irreversible gains. But benami transfers, exemptions and weak records ensured that ceiling-surplus redistribution remained marginal, and tenancy simply became informal. The contemporary agenda follows directly: recognising and recording tenancy so that tenants can access credit and insurance, completing land records digitisation, and improving the productivity of already-assigned land — since for most of the landless, redistribution is no longer the realistic route out of poverty.

## Value addition
- Historical anchor: the Telangana Armed Struggle (1946-51) covered some 3,000 villages and redistributed around a million acres before suppression — the largest peasant movement in modern Indian history.
- Bhoodan: initiated by Vinoba Bhave at Pochampally (Nalgonda) on 18 April 1951, when Harijan families asked for land and a landlord donated 100 acres — India’s first Bhoodan village.
- Constitutional protection: land reform laws were placed in the Ninth Schedule (Art. 31B) to immunise them from judicial review; land is a State subject (Entry 18, List II).
- Contemporary relevance: the Model Agricultural Land Leasing Act, 2016 (NITI Aayog) proposed legalising tenancy to give tenants access to credit and insurance while protecting owners’ rights — the unfinished business of land reform, and directly relevant to Andhra Pradesh’s Crop Cultivator Rights Cards and the inclusion of tenant farmers in Annadata Sukhibhava.

## Introduction

Poverty is not merely a shortage of income but a deprivation of the ability to live a life one has reason to value. Two influential responses to this insight — the Human Poverty Index, developed by UNDP, and Amartya Sen’s capability approach — differ in kind: the first is a statistical measure, the second a philosophical framework from which measures are derived.

- The Human Poverty Index (HPI)

Introduced in the Human Development Report 1997, the HPI measured deprivation rather than achievement — the mirror image of the HDI.

- **HPI-1** — Developing countries · Probability of not surviving to age 40; adult illiteracy rate; deprivation in economic provisioning — lack of access to safe water and the percentage of underweight children
- **HPI-2** — Developed countries · Probability of not surviving to age 60; functional illiteracy; population below the income poverty line; long-term unemployment

Significance: it shifted attention from average achievement to the condition of the deprived, and made cross-country comparison of deprivation possible.

Limitations: - Used aggregate national averages, so it could not identify who was poor or whether the same people suffered multiple deprivations. - Ignored overlapping deprivation — a household deprived in health and education and living standards was counted no differently from three households each deprived once. - Indicators were not always comparable across countries. - Consequently, UNDP replaced the HPI with the Multidimensional Poverty Index in the Human Development Report 2010.

- The capability approach (Amartya Sen)

Sen argued that development should be assessed by the expansion of substantive freedoms, not by income, utility or resources.

- **Functionings** — What a person actually is and does — being nourished, literate, healthy, able to participate in community life
- **Capabilities** — The real freedom to achieve alternative combinations of functionings — the genuine opportunity set
- **Conversion factors** — Personal, social and environmental factors that determine how well a person converts resources into functionings — a disabled person needs more income for the same mobility
- **Agency** — People as active agents of change, not passive recipients of benefits

Key insight: two people with identical incomes may have very different capabilities. Poverty is therefore best understood as capability deprivation, not income shortfall. Sen’s collaborator Martha Nussbaum extended this into a list of ten central human capabilities.

Comparing the two

- **Nature** — A composite statistical index · A normative and conceptual framework
- **Focus** — Observed deprivation outcomes · Freedom and opportunity to achieve
- **Unit** — National aggregates · The individual
- **Strength** — Simple, comparable, policy-usable · Philosophically complete; explains why deprivation matters
- **Weakness** — Cannot identify the poor or overlapping deprivation · Difficult to operationalise and measure directly
- **Relationship** — The capability approach provides the theory; HPI and MPI are attempts to measure it

Convergence: the Multidimensional Poverty Index

Developed by Sabina Alkire and James Foster (OPHI, University of Oxford) with UNDP, the MPI (2010) resolved the HPI’s central flaw by measuring deprivation at the household level across 10 indicators in three dimensions — health, education and standard of living — so that overlapping deprivations are visible. It reports both the incidence of poverty (headcount) and its intensity (average deprivations suffered).

Influence on Indian policy

- NITI Aayog’s National MPI uses 12 indicators across the same three dimensions, adding maternal health and bank accounts to reflect Indian priorities. It reports that about 24.8 crore people exited multidimensional poverty in nine years.
- Programme design reflects capability thinking: Ayushman Bharat (health capability), NEP 2020 and NIPUN Bharat (education), Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat (living standards), PMJDY (financial agency).
- The SDG India Index applies the same multidimensional logic at State level, with a composite score of 71 in 2023-24.

## Conclusion

The Human Poverty Index and the capability approach are complementary rather than competing: the capability approach supplies the philosophy — that poverty is the denial of real freedom — while the HPI, and now the MPI, supply the measurement. India’s policy architecture has absorbed both, moving from a single income line to a multidimensional understanding of deprivation. As Sen put it, income is a means; the expansion of substantive freedoms is the end — and it is against that standard that poverty reduction must ultimately be judged.

## Value addition
- National MPI dimensions and indicators: Health — nutrition, child and adolescent mortality, maternal health; Education — years of schooling, school attendance; Standard of living — cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account.
- MPI reports two measures: headcount ratio (H) — the proportion who are multidimensionally poor; and intensity

(A) — the average share of deprivations they experience. MPI = H × A.

- Thinkers to name: Amartya Sen (Development as Freedom, 1999; Nobel 1998), Mahbub ul Haq (architect of the HDI), Martha Nussbaum (central capabilities), Sabina Alkire and James Foster (MPI methodology).
- Related indices: HDI, Inequality-adjusted HDI, Gender Inequality Index, Gender Development Index, Planetary pressures-adjusted HDI. India ranked 130 of 193 with an HDI of 0.685 in HDR 2025.
- One-line revision point: The HPI told us how much deprivation existed; the capability approach told us why it mattered; the MPI told us who was suffering it.

- **XVI** — 115 – 120 · Uneven poverty reduction across States in the post-reform period · rural–urban poverty trends in Andhra Pradesh · the role of SERP in reducing rural poverty · Universal Basic Income and the Economic Survey 2016-17 · relative poverty, the Gini coefficient and the Lorenz curve · limitations of India’s poverty alleviation strategy
